A stronger local parameter

For a canonical Boolean relation system over a proof field F, let \(R_a\) be its allowed rows on scopes \(X_a\), of maximum width w. Call \(S\subseteq[v]\) locally filtered if, for every row and \(U=S\cap X_a\), the monomial \(x_U\) has no representative of degree at most \(|U|-1\) on \(R_a\). Degrees and representatives are in that row's Boolean algebra. Equivalently, the exact retraction theorem says that the row admits an \(F[x_U]\)-linear unital degree-nonincreasing map to the retained coordinate algebra, annihilating its full row ideal. Let \(\rho_F\) be the maximum size of such S, with \(\rho_F=-1\) when an empty row makes even the empty set fail.

The parameter depends only on the stated finite row tables, incidence geometry and proof field, not on an unknown global proof space. Every locally filtered set is locally shattered: if a shared assignment is missing, its indicator has leading term a nonzero multiple of \(x_U\), with all other terms of smaller degree. Rescale that vanishing polynomial to obtain the prohibited lower-degree representative. Thus \(\rho_F\le\sigma\), where sigma is the earlier projection parameter.

Theorem (filtered shattering ceiling). For an unsatisfiable canonical Boolean relation system, \[d_F\le\max\{w,2,\rho_F+2\}.\tag{1}\] Consequently a barrier through \(D\ge\max\{w,2\}\) requires \(\rho_F\ge D-1\).

Proof. Assume the ordinary degree-D PC closure is proper. Its multilinear part is a proper cutoff kernel containing the inputs and closed under legal Boolean multiplication, by the paid Boolean reduction argument in the kernel-dimension proof. That proof gives more than linear injectivity: for a degree-compatible monomial order, there is a standard monomial \(x_S\) of degree exactly \(D-1\). In particular \(x_S\) is not congruent modulo that kernel to any polynomial of smaller total degree, even one using coordinates outside S.

Suppose some row violates the new condition, with \(U=S\cap X_a\). Write \(x_U-q\in I(R_a)\), with \(\deg q\le|U|-1\). In the canonical encoding the literal full-row indicator expansion derives this multilinear relation through original degree at most \(|X_a|\le w\le D\). Multiply its derived final line by \(x_{S\setminus X_a}\). The supports are disjoint and the final degree is \(D-1\), so the full derivation stays through \(\max\{w,D-1\}\le D\). It yields \[x_S-qx_{S\setminus X_a}\in C_D,\qquad \deg(qx_{S\setminus X_a})\le D-2,\] contradicting standardness. Hence S is locally filtered and \(\rho_F\ge D-1\). Taking \(D=\max\{w,2,\rho_F+2\}\) proves (1). The empty-row case is included by the canonical indicator derivation. \(\square\)

Using only the kernel theorem's ungraded coordinate injection would not justify this argument: a low-degree representative can involve outside variables. The degree-compatible standard-monomial part of its full proof is the relevant premise. Equation (1) refines the previous shattering ceiling without changing the width floor or its original-degree convention.

Non-vacuity and the termwise failure

Proposition (filtered guarded witness). The existing guarded width-five family has \(\rho_F=v-1\) over every field. It retains linear size, block minimality, essential scopes, at least two occurrences, branching fraction at least \(2/5\), full binary affine row hulls, no common Horn polarity and a positive-linear ordinary PC degree lower bound. Its rowwise filtered retractions need not respect joint polynomial identities when chosen term by term.

Construction and ledger. Use the already proved minimal branching family \(F_N\), with N variables, \(M=O(N)\) clauses of widths three or four, branching count \(h\ge2N/5\) and degree at least \(cN\). On disjoint copies x,y and one new guard t, take \[\{t\vee C(x):C\in F_N\}\cup\{\neg t\vee C(y):C\in F_N\}.\tag{2}\] There are exactly \(v=2N+1\) variables and \(2M\) clauses, of width at most five. Either guard value activates an unsatisfiable copy. Deleting one guarded clause allows its copy's deletion witness and disables the other copy, proving minimality. Every proper clause is essential; old occurrences are unchanged and t has \(2M\) occurrences. The branching fraction is \((2h+1)/(2N+1)\ge2/5\). Each row is the complement of one Boolean point and has full affine hull. If a common polarity made all clauses Horn, the copy with positive guard would have all remaining literals negative, making that old unsatisfiable copy satisfiable by zeros. Finally restricting one guard value and the unused copy in a PC refutation leaves a refutation of \(F_N\), so the new degree is at least \(cN=c(v-1)/2\). These are the original guarded witness's proved properties, with no changed encoding.

The stronger local condition. Select all non-guard coordinates S. In a row of the first copy, substitution \(t=1\) fixes all selected coordinates and annihilates its row ideal; in a row of the second, use \(t=0\). Both are unital module maps preserving degree. The exact row criterion gives local filtration on S, hence \(\rho_F\ge v-1\). The full set cannot qualify for a non-universal row: with no discarded coordinates the only linear module retraction fixing its whole coordinate algebra is the identity. Therefore \(\rho_F=v-1\). This proves unbounded non-vacuity of the stronger specification; it does not establish near-half degree.

The exact termwise consistency test. Let nonzero old clause polynomials be f(x) and g(y). The two guarded inputs are \((1-t)f\) and \(tg\), and their ordinary polynomial multiples satisfy \[(1-t)fg+tfg=fg.\tag{3}\] Every term has degree at most \(\deg f+\deg g+1\le9\). Extend each row retraction by the identity on all spectator coordinates. The first row's retraction sends its displayed multiple to zero, and the second row's retraction sends its multiple to zero. But both retractions fix the nonzero polynomial fg in the selected-coordinate algebra. Thus applying the row-specific map separately to each summand and fixing selected-coordinate polynomials is not a well-defined linear operation on the polynomial represented by that sum. No common linear map on these lines can both kill the two multiples and fix fg.

This reuses the old guarded product as a control for the newly proposed maps. A correct global kernel is allowed to contain fg while retaining one; (3) does not itself refute the family. It rejects the stronger termwise rule that keeps the entire selected algebra fixed. Consequently local filtration is an admissibility screen, not a substitute for global compatibility, and the positive-linear witness remains consistent with the obstruction.

The strengthening is strict already locally

Proposition (projection filtration gap). For the binary relation \[R=\{(x,u,v):x_1\cdots x_s=\sum_{j=1}^r u_jv_j\},\qquad s,r\ge3,\quad k=s+2r,\tag{4}\] the maximum locally shattered coordinate set has size \(\sigma=k-2\), but \(\rho_{\mathbb F_2}\le k-3\). This is a satisfiable single-row control, not a new unsatisfiable-family claim.

Classify the maximal projections. Omitting both coordinates of one private pair leaves a full projection: its product can be selected as either zero or one to satisfy (4). No projection omitting only one coordinate is full. If the omitted coordinate is shared, set another retained shared bit to zero and the private sum to one. If it is private, set its retained partner to zero, another complete pair's product to one and the shared product to zero.

Among projections omitting exactly two coordinates, the same-pair omissions are the only full ones. If both omitted coordinates are shared, at least one retained shared coordinate remains and can be set to zero while the private sum is one. If one is shared and one private, set another shared coordinate and the omitted private coordinate's partner to zero and a different pair's product to one. If two private coordinates from different pairs are omitted, set both retained partners to zero and a third pair's product to one, again with shared product zero. These assignments have no extension. Thus \(\sigma=k-2\), and every set achieving that size omits a full private pair.

For such a set S, omitting pair j, multiply (4) by the product H of all other private coordinates. On R this gives \[x_S=(r-1)H+H u_jv_j.\tag{5}\] The scalar is taken in the binary field. The right side has degree at most \(2r<s+2r-2=|S|\). Every maximally shattered set therefore fails the filtered criterion. Since filtration implies shattering, \(\rho_{\mathbb F_2}\le k-3\). \(\square\)

The exact control takes the smallest \(s=r=3\). Among 512 assignments it finds 280 allowed points; all 36 seven-coordinate projections and all nine eight-coordinate projections are checked. Precisely the three complete-private-pair omissions give full seven-coordinate projections, and none of the eight-coordinate projections is full. All 840 pointwise instances of (5) pass. This verifies the strict \(\sigma=7,\rho\le6\) control, not a near-half lower bound.

The guarded witness preserves every prior proved property, the same \(2N+1\) variables and width-five/linear-size budget. The new condition implies the former projection condition and is strictly stronger as a local invariant. No conjectural hardness conclusion is inserted into admissibility.

The earlier central-source proof establishes only local shattering, and its later raw conditional moment sections do not establish the new filtered condition. That source application is now explicitly open rather than silently promoted. Likewise no near-half value of rho is established here for the random-half source. Both remain possible sources with separate growing-width transfer obligations.

The new degree ceiling gives a useful structural refinement, but neither necessary open statement has advanced.

9 October 2026 — Large independent sets rule out the actual Kneser cores

Working characteristic-two degree ceiling; the queued compact Kneser-core family is excluded. Produced by Codex (gpt-6-astra, medium reasoning).

Question. On near-half-family, develop the Kneser/core head. The missing implication is a near-half PC barrier on an actual unbounded source. The previous full-graph topological bound did not address edge-minimal cores. Test whether independent sets inherited by every such core, combined with paid star projection, give an upper bound in the core's own Boolean variable count.

New mathematics. Compact four-colouring on a non-four-colourable N-vertex graph with independent set I has binary PC degree at most \(\lfloor3(N-|I|)/2\rfloor+2\). After eliminating I, fixing the first boundary bits turns each star determinant into a product of linear forms on disjoint second-bit groups. Conditioning the smaller group leaves inconsistent binary affine equations. Every actual core of the recorded Kneser source therefore has degree at most \(3v/8+o(v)\), on its own \(v=2N\) bits. The argument also covers non-four-colourable graphs mapping homomorphically to that source.

Goal progress. Unchanged for the general near-half-family obligation: this is a decisive exclusion of the queued candidate, not a construction of the missing family. It resolves the previously open scope issue for those cores by a different argument, without transferring a full-graph proof backwards. Complete Frege transfer remains open.

General statement. lem:bipartite-product-ceiling gives the paid affine-product branch certificate. thm:independent-colour-degree-ceiling is an all-graph upper bound in the stated encoding. cor:kneser-core-degree-ceiling applies to all actual cores and homomorphic replacements. cor:colour-independence-screen records the necessary graph condition; prop:compact-colour-filtration explains why the latest local specification does not itself exclude these graphs. ex:independent-colour-compiler-checks records complete bounded certificates.

Route comparison. A direct lower-bound construction on these cores is worth pursuing only if their inherited independent-set geometry survives the explicit projection test. The crude full-assignment bound after projection remains above half, so it would not settle anything. The second-bit product structure below supplies the missing gain. No universal half-variable bound for arbitrary Boolean polynomial systems is assumed, and no topological premise on the deleted-edge cores is used.

Two groups of affine products

Work over any characteristic-two proof field F, but let all coefficients of the following affine inputs lie in its binary prime subfield. Split Boolean variables into disjoint sets X,Y, of sizes a,b. Inputs may be arbitrary affine equations solely in X, arbitrary affine equations solely in Y, and products \(L_i(X)M_i(Y)\) of such binary affine forms, together with Booleanity.

Lemma (bipartite product ceiling). If this system has no Boolean solution, it has an ordinary Nullstellensatz refutation, hence a PC refutation, through degree at most \(\min(a,b)+2\).

Proof. Suppose \(a\le b\) and fix \(\alpha\in\{0,1\}^X\). A left affine input may become a nonzero constant; otherwise the residual equations in Y are the original right affine equations and those \(M_i\) with \(L_i(\alpha)=1\). They are inconsistent over the binary field: consistency would give a binary solution, hence a Boolean model of the full restricted system. Therefore a binary linear combination of these affine inputs equals one. This remains a valid identity in F.

Put \(\delta_\alpha=\prod_{j\in X}(x_j+1-\alpha_j)\), of degree a. For a binary affine L, \[\delta_\alpha(L-L(\alpha))=\sum_{j\in X}L_j(x_j^2-x_j)\prod_{h\in X\setminus\{j\}}(x_h+1-\alpha_h),\tag{1}\] where \(L_j\) is the coefficient of \(x_j\); signs coincide in characteristic two. Multiplying (1) by \(M_i(Y)\) costs at most \(a+2\). Thus every weighted residual affine equation is an ordinary combination of original inputs and Boolean-axiom multiples through \(a+2\). The residual linear certificate gives \(\delta_\alpha\), including the constant-input case. Sum all \(\delta_\alpha\) to one. This is a literal NS identity at that degree. Interchange X,Y for the stated minimum. \(\square\)

The binary-coefficient hypothesis is used when affine consistency is equated with a Boolean solution. No assertion for arbitrary extension-field affine coefficients is needed. This is a paid conditioning-and-linear-elimination mechanism, not a new general Gaussian-elimination principle.

Project an independent set, then split the palette

Let G be a finite simple graph with N nonisolated vertices, not four-colourable. Its original variables are two bits \((u_i,v_i)\) per vertex; each edge has the four canonical equal-colour forbidden clauses. Fix any independent set I, put \(B=V(G)\setminus I\) and \(b=|B|\). Necessarily \(b\ge4\), since otherwise distinct colours on B and one additional colour on I would suffice.

Theorem (independent colour ceiling). Over every characteristic-two proof field, \[d_F(G)\le b+\lfloor b/2\rfloor+2=\lfloor3b/2\rfloor+2.\tag{2}\] In particular choose I maximum, so \(b=N-\alpha(G)\). No polynomial proof-size bound or reverse projection simulation is asserted.

First use the already paid projection. On the \(2b\) boundary bits retain the edge quadratics \[q_{ij}=(1+u_i+u_j)(1+v_i+v_j),\qquad ij\in E(G[B]),\] and, for every centre \(c\in I\) and four-subset U of its neighbours, retain \[\Delta_U=\det[(1,u_i,v_i,u_iv_i)]_{i\in U}.\tag{3}\] The star-projection proof and its common-boundary composition were read in full. Independence of I makes the boundary system exactly the extendible-colouring relation, hence unsatisfiable. Each displayed input has an ordinary derivation through degree four from the original CNF. In detail, writing a star equation as the matrix row \(((1+u_i)(1+v_i),1+v_i,1+u_i,1)\) times \((1,u_c,v_c,u_cv_c)^T\), the first adjugate row gives \(\Delta_U\) as a sum of degree-two cofactors times star quadratics. This pays degree four; the quadratics themselves are derived through four from the canonical clauses. Final lines are reused.

Fix the first bits. For \(\eta\in\{0,1\}^B\), split B into \(B_0,B_1\) according to the first bit. A boundary edge becomes zero when its ends lie in different groups, and becomes \(1+v_i+v_j\) within one group. For a four-neighbour determinant, if its first bits are not split two and two, its restricted polynomial is identically zero. If \(U=\{i,j\}\sqcup\{h,l\}\) with \(i,j\in B_0\) and \(h,l\in B_1\), then literally \[\Delta_U|_\eta=(v_i+v_j)(v_h+v_l).\tag{4}\] This follows by grouping the two types of matrix rows in (3) and subtracting one row from the other in each pair. It is also a multilinear polynomial identity, not only equality after Boolean reduction. Thus the restricted system is exactly of the preceding lemma's type, on the two disjoint second-bit groups. Its degree ceiling is \(\min(|B_0|,|B_1|)+2\le\lfloor b/2\rfloor+2\).

Pay both stages without flattening the first. Write \(\delta_\eta\) for the first-bit point indicator, of degree b. For every boundary input g of degree at most four, derive \(\delta_\eta g|_\eta\) through degree at most \(b+4\). To see the Boolean cost explicitly, replace the first-bit variables one at a time in g. Multilinearity gives \[g-g|_\eta=\sum_i(u_i-\eta_i)h_i,\qquad \deg h_i\le\deg g-1.\] Multiplication by \(\delta_\eta\) replaces each \(u_i-\eta_i\) factor by its Boolean polynomial times the indicator on the other first bits, exactly as in (1). Every correction has degree at most \(b+\deg g\le b+4\). The final weighted residual inputs have degree at most \(b+2\).

Now use the lemma's proof on the smaller second-bit group, with all its lines multiplied by \(\delta_\eta\). Its starting weighted inputs are the just-derived final lines. Multiplying them by the smaller group's indicator and using the same Boolean corrections costs at most \(b+\min(|B_0|,|B_1|)+2\). The affine certificate then gives \(\delta_\eta\). Weighted Boolean inputs are obtained directly from the original Boolean axioms within this budget. Since \(b\ge4\), both the initial ceiling \(b+4\) and every branch ceiling fit \(b+\lfloor b/2\rfloor+2\). Sum \(\delta_\eta\) over all first-bit assignments to obtain one. This proves (2).

The reuse is essential to the stated ledger: multiplying the entire first-stage proof by every second-bit indicator would give an unnecessarily larger bound. The theorem is an ordinary PC ceiling. It does not claim that flattening both stages into one original-input NS identity preserves (2).

Inventory. The original CNF has \(2N\) actual bits and \(4|E(G)|\) width-four clauses. The boundary has at most \(\binom b2+\sum_{c\in I}\binom{\deg(c)}4=O(N^5)\) polynomial inputs, of degree at most four and support at most eight bits, with no new variables. Unused boundary bits may be removed, but counting all \(2b\) only weakens the bound. No free canonical-CNF conversion of the boundary polynomials is used. The proof is replayed on the original system after its degree-four input derivations.

The core exclusion and what it teaches

Corollary (Kneser core ceiling). Let G be any non-four-colourable graph on N nonisolated vertices admitting a graph homomorphism to \(KG(n,k)\), with \(k\ge1\) and \(n\ge2k\). Then its compact four-colour CNF satisfies \[d_F(G)\le\left\lfloor\frac32\left(N-\left\lceil\frac{kN}{n}\right\rceil\right)\right\rfloor+2\tag{5}\] over every characteristic-two proof field. In particular every recorded edge-minimal core of \(KG(2k+4,k)\), with its isolated vertices removed and \(v=2N\), satisfies \[d_F(G)\le\frac{3v}{8}+\frac{3v}{4(k+2)}+2 =\frac{3v}{8}+o(v)\qquad(k\to\infty).\tag{6}\] It cannot meet the near-half target.

Proof. For each ground element j, the vertices whose image k-set contains j form an independent set: adjacent image sets are disjoint. Each vertex occurs in exactly k of these n sets, even when the homomorphism is not injective. One such independent set therefore has size at least \(\lceil kN/n\rceil\). Apply (2). At \(n=2k+4\), its continuous bound is \(3N/4+3N/(2(k+2))+2\), giving (6). The recorded cores have \(N\ge2\lceil k/4\rceil+1\to\infty\), so the constant term is negligible. This is a bound on each core itself, not a reverse transfer from the full graph. \(\square\)

More generally, any unbounded homomorphic family with \(n/k\le3-\varepsilon\), for a fixed positive epsilon, has a fixed gap below half its \(2N\) bits by (5). Thus replacing the original core by a high-girth graph that still maps to the same near-two-ratio Kneser graph does not evade the reason for the bound. Long odd girth, minimality and strong local row properties do not cancel its inherited independent-set cover.

Corollary (colour independence screen). If a compact four-colour family has no refutation through \(D=\lfloor N-s\rfloor\), with \(s\ge0\), then \[\alpha(G)<\frac N3+\frac{2s}{3}+\frac43.\tag{7}\] Hence a near-half family must have \(\limsup\alpha(G)/N\le1/3\). A fractional colouring of total weight \(t<3\) bounded away from three also rules it out asymptotically.

Proof. Integer degree greater than \(\lfloor N-s\rfloor\) is greater than \(N-s\). Compare this with \(\frac32(N-\alpha)+2\) and rearrange. If nonnegative weights on independent sets cover each vertex by total weight at least one and have total t, then \(N\le\sum_I\lambda_I|I|\le t\alpha\); thus \(\alpha\ge N/t\), giving the last claim. \(\square\)

Specification disposition. This is a new necessary condition for the compact four-colour sub-specification. Its conjunction with all existing graph screens does not yet have a proved unbounded witness here, so it is provisional rather than an adopted non-vacuity assertion. The earlier high-girth critical-graph construction did not control its independence ratio after selecting a minimal core. The general guarded formula specification is unaffected and retains its witness.

The structural reason also applies to other four-colouring candidates with an independent-set cover of total weight below three; it is not specific to the Kneser presentation. The earlier two-anchor graphs are already excluded more strongly by their degree-six proof. The modular and random-relation candidates do not have this graph encoding, so no transfer to them is asserted. Raising the Kneser ground-set ratio to at least three would evade this particular fixed-gap argument, but loses the old growing-odd-girth justification of unbounded cores and does not supply a replacement hardness proof. Adding a common palette anchor instead reduces to the already excluded three-colour setting. A stronger replacement must establish its own actual core-size, independence and degree budgets.

The local filtration screen alone does not see this obstruction

Proposition (compact colour filtration). For the canonical proper-colouring relation on \(2^b\) states, with an integer \(b\ge1\) bits per vertex and any proof field, every proper subset of an edge's \(2b\) bits admits a degree-preserving row retraction. The full set does not. Consequently for a graph on N declared vertices, \[\rho_F=\sigma=(b-1)N+\alpha(G).\tag{8}\] In particular compact four-colouring always has \(\rho_F\ge N\), so its local filtration condition alone cannot exclude a barrier just below N.

Proof. Choose a missing bit at one endpoint. If the corresponding bit at the other endpoint is retained, set the missing one to its complement. If that other bit is also missing, set the two to opposite constants. Set any remaining discarded bits to constants. This affine substitution fixes every retained bit and always produces unequal endpoint colours; it is a unital degree-preserving algebra retraction annihilating the row ideal. The full coordinate set cannot retract through a non-universal relation. Its projection likewise is not full, whereas every proper projection extends by the same construction.

Thus a selected set of bits qualifies exactly when the vertices with all b bits selected form an independent set. At every other vertex at most \(b-1\) bits are selected, giving the upper bound in (8); choose a maximum independent set in full and \(b-1\) bits at every other vertex to attain it. For actual-variable applications discard isolated graph vertices first. \(\square\)

This is another reason to retain actual upper-bound screens across equivalent paid representations: the newly strengthened local admissibility test still allows the Kneser cores that (6) rules out globally.

It then removes the four independent clone vertices from the Mycielski graph of the complete four-vertex graph. The five-vertex boundary has six edge quadratics and four star determinants.

All 32 first-bit assignments and all 102 smaller-side second-bit branches yield native binary affine certificates. The checker verifies 320 first-stage and 1,020 second-stage literal identities, reusing the weighted restricted inputs, and their complete sum is the ordinary polynomial one. The maximum degree of the actual staged derivation is nine, matching (2) at b=5. Omitting the four star determinants leaves 24 consistent branches, a falsifying control. The full branch certificates are retained in the output. Two initial script errors—a reserved identifier and polynomial constants not converted to native matrix entries—are retained separately. Only the corrected run reached the final success marker. These checks validate the compiler, not an asymptotic lower bound or an enumeration of growing cores.

9 October 2026 — Deep-hole circuit bounds give separators beyond graphical charts

Working code and PC bounds from an audited matroid theorem; larger radius deficits remain open. Produced by Codex (gpt-6-astra, medium reasoning).

Question. On near-half-family, return to the code head's highest-risk metric compatibility gap. The immediate test is the quintic zero-deficit regime, whose adapted columns may have three or four nonzero leader positions. Does the full code geometry still force a small puncture separator without assuming a graphical chart?

New mathematics. The deep-hole comparison works in every parity-check basis, not only one extending a minimum-weight leader. Consequently every circuit has size at most \(q(t+1)\), where t is the redundancy-radius deficit. An audited contraction-depth theorem and a direct contraction-tree count turn this into a coordinate puncture separator. Fixed-field canonical modular systems with \(t=o(\sqrt v)\) have a fixed degree gap below half, including the exact quintic endpoint. Near-half candidates therefore require at least square-root-scale deficit, with the explicit constant below.

Goal progress. Unchanged for the general near-half family. This excludes a genuine nongraphical regime and narrows the provisional code conditions, but constructs no near-half-hard source. It does not handle every positive sublinear deficit or prove the necessary code conditions jointly non-vacuous. The growing-modulus source and the complete Frege transfer are not covered by the fixed-field asymptotic conclusion.

General statement. thm:deep-hole-circuit-bound is an all-finite-field statement. imp:contraction-depth-circumference records the external upper bound at its audited scope. lem:contraction-tree-separator counts actual contracted elements, and thm:circuit-puncture-separation translates them into actual code-coordinate punctures. cor:subroot-radius-degree-ceiling and cor:near-half-radius-gap give the original-degree and structural consequences.

Route comparison. A direct construction with both large radius and large separator is still a competing route. Before seeking one at exact quintic redundancy, the all-basis comparison provides a concrete test independent of column arity. Circuit size is intrinsic, whereas a sparse chosen basis alone was insufficient. The matroid depth theorem supplies the missing bridge to separators; no classification of all maximally distant codes or assumption of bounded component rank is needed.

The comparison holds in every basis

Let \(\mathcal C\subseteq\mathbb F_q^v\) be a linear code, where q is any finite prime power and \(v\ge1\). Write \(k=v-\dim\mathcal C\), let \(\rho\) be its covering radius, and put \(t=k-\rho\ge0\). Let H be a rank-k parity-check matrix with \(\ker H=\mathcal C\). Its column matroid has circuits equal to supports of support-inclusion-minimal nonzero codewords of \(\mathcal C\). This means minimal support, not minimum Hamming weight. Let c be its largest circuit size, with \(c=1\) if there is no circuit.

Theorem (deep hole circuits). Every circuit has size at most \(q(t+1)\). More precisely, choose a syndrome at distance rho and any parity-check column basis B. Write H in that basis as \([I_B\mid P]\), let y be the syndrome's coordinate vector, and let \(z_B\) be the number of zero coordinates of y. Then \(z_B\le t\). If a nonbasis column h has z nonzero coordinates at the zero positions of y, its support on the nonzero positions of y is at most \[(q-1)(t-z_B+z+1),\tag{1}\] and its total support is at most \(q(t+1)-1\).

Proof. Representing the syndrome on B gives a word of weight \(k-z_B\), at least its minimum weight \(\rho=k-t\); hence \(z_B\le t\). For \(\lambda\in\mathbb F_q^\times\), put \(\lambda\) on h and \(y-\lambda h\) on B. If \(M_\lambda\) counts positions with nonzero y where \(\lambda h_i=y_i\), this representative has weight \[1+k-z_B-M_\lambda+z\ge k-t.\] Thus \(M_\lambda\le t-z_B+z+1\). Each nonzero h entry at a nonzero y position contributes to exactly one of the \(q-1\) match counts. Summation gives (1), and \[|\operatorname{supp}h|\le(q-1)(t-z_B+z+1)+z \le(q-1)(t+1)+z_B\le q(t+1)-1.\tag{2}\] For a circuit Q and \(e\in Q\), extend the independent set \(Q\setminus\{e\}\) to a basis B. The fundamental circuit of e in \(B\cup\{e\}\) is Q, so its column has exactly \(|Q|-1\) nonzero basis entries. Apply (2). A loop gives a singleton circuit and also obeys the bound; the circuit-free convention is harmless. \(\square\)

The basis representative y need not itself be a coset leader. Comparing it with the same global minimum rho is exactly what permits arbitrary B. In a leader-adapted basis \(z_B=t\), (1) recovers the older one-column bound. The new circuit conclusion uses the freedom to choose a basis around each circuit. It is a refinement of that mechanism, not a claim of a new general covering-radius method. At t=0 it gives \(c\le q\), covering wider quintic columns directly. The old length-q one-dimensional sharpness control has \(\rho=q-1\) and circuit size q; it is not a hard-family witness.

The imported contraction-depth theorem

Use ordinary matroid contraction depth: the empty matroid has depth zero, a disconnected matroid takes the maximum over components, and a connected nonempty matroid has depth one plus the minimum depth after contracting one actual ground-set element. This yields a rooted forest whose nodes are the actual elements and whose child subtrees are the components after the chosen contraction. It is not contraction-star depth allowing arbitrary new vectors.

Imported theorem (contraction depth bound). If every circuit of a finite matroid has size at most c, with \(c=1\) in the circuit-free case, its contraction depth is at most \(c(c+1)/2\). This is the upper half of DeVos–Kwon–Oum, Theorem 5.7. Its proof and recursive definition were read in full. The induction contracts a largest circuit in each connected component and uses Seymour's circuit-shrinking theorem. That dependency's statement and complete proof were read as Ding–Oporowski–Oxley, Theorem 3.4, printed pages 35–37. This is an imported theorem, not new notebook mathematics.

The source proof uses actual contractions, which is the direction needed below. We do not use the false general inference that contraction depth decreases under every arbitrary minor; the source itself distinguishes these notions. Only the displayed upper bound, definition and its circuit-contraction dependency are imported.

Turn depth into a small actual puncture

Lemma (contraction tree separator). If a matroid on v elements has an actual-element contraction forest of height at most d, then for every integer \(b\ge1\) some set Z of at most \(d\lfloor v/(b+1)\rfloor\) elements has the property that every component of \(M/Z\) has at most b elements.

Proof. In the chosen forest, select exactly the nodes whose rooted subtrees have more than b nodes. This set Z is ancestor-closed. At each depth the selected subtrees are disjoint and each has at least \(b+1\) nodes, so there are at most \(\lfloor v/(b+1)\rfloor\) selected nodes. There are at most d depths. Contracting the selected ancestors exposes the child-component subtrees in the recursive construction. The remaining components are contained in the first unselected subtrees, each of size at most b. Contractions in distinct components do not interfere. Thus Z has the claimed size and effect. \(\square\)

Theorem (circuit puncture separation). For any linear code on v coordinates over any field, let c be the maximum circuit size of its parity-check column matroid, with the preceding convention. Put \(d_c=c(c+1)/2\). Its coordinate puncture parameter satisfies \[\kappa(\mathcal C)\le\min\left\{v,\ b+d_c\left\lfloor\frac{v}{b+1}\right\rfloor\right\}\quad(b\ge1),\tag{3}\] so in particular \[\kappa(\mathcal C)\le\min\{v,\sqrt{2c(c+1)v}+1\}.\tag{4}\] For a finite-field code with redundancy-radius deficit t, one may replace c in this bound by \(q(t+1)\).

Why contraction means puncturing here. The matroid is represented by a parity-check matrix H of the row code \(\mathcal C\), not by the original modular constraint matrix's columns. After puncturing coordinates Z, a vector \(x_U\), \(U=[v]\setminus Z\), extends to a member of \(\mathcal C\) exactly when \[H_Ux_U\in\operatorname{span}\{H_j:j\in Z\}. \] Thus the punctured code is the kernel of the remaining column map after quotienting its target by that span. This represents the actual matroid contraction \(M/Z\); it is not shortening the code.

Every kernel vector of the quotient column map decomposes into vectors on its matroid circuits: choose a circuit in its support, subtract a scalar circuit relation to cancel one nonzero coordinate, and repeat. Circuits lie within single matroid components, so the punctured code is a coordinate direct sum over those components, including singleton loops or coloops as full or zero one-coordinate codes. Apply the imported depth bound and the lemma. Actual puncture count plus largest remaining block is bounded by (3). The trivial one-block decomposition gives v. Taking \(b=\lceil\sqrt{d_cv}\rceil\) gives \(b+d_cv/(b+1)\le2\sqrt{d_cv}+1\), proving (4), with the trivial bound covering any oversized choice of b. The finite-field substitution follows from the all-basis circuit theorem. \(\square\)

This argument counts ground-set coordinates, rather than a separator rank or unrepresented auxiliary directions. No row generator is replaced for free in a proof-system application.

Pay the PC consequence

Return to a field-consistent Boolean-empty affine system \(Ax=b_0\) over a fixed odd prime field \(\mathbb F_q\), on v actual Boolean variables. Let \(\mathcal C\) be its row code, \(r=\operatorname{rank}A\ge1\), and let the original row width be at most w. The proof field has characteristic different from q. Keep the canonical row clauses and original Booleanity. Define \[a=q(t+1),\qquad s_0=\min\{v,\lceil\sqrt{2a(a+1)v}\rceil+1\},\] \[M_{s_0}=\min\{v,\lceil(1-1/q)v+s_0/q+w\sqrt{2r\log(4r+2)}\rceil\},\qquad B_{s_0}=\max\{\lceil M_{s_0}/2\rceil+w+1,s_0+2\}.\tag{5}\]

Corollary (subroot radius ceiling). The original canonical system has ordinary PC degree at most \(B_{s_0}\). At fixed q,w, if \(t=o(\sqrt v)\), then \[d_F\le\left(\frac12-\frac1{2q}\right)v+o(v).\tag{6}\] In particular exact redundancy-radius equality, and every sub-square-root deficit, is excluded from the near-half goal without a graphical-chart hypothesis.

Proof. Equation (4) gives an actual coordinate puncture with puncture count plus largest block at most \(s_0\). Apply the proved puncture-separator ceiling, whose complete proof was reread. Its local-consequence transport already charges the pin indicators in the same support budget, so no extra conditioning cost is added. It uses the original width w, not a newly chosen code basis. At fixed q and \(t=o(\sqrt v)\), \(s_0=o(v)\); also \(r\le v\) and \(w\sqrt{r\log(r+1)}=o(v)\) for fixed w. Substitution into (5) gives (6). \(\square\)

For the queued quintic exact endpoint, this gives \(d_F\le2v/5+o(v)\), including all three- and four-support adapted columns. The older ternary theorem remains stronger on its graphical positive-deficit subclass, where it handles \(t=o(v)\). The new theorem instead removes graphicality in the smaller \(t=o(\sqrt v)\) range and works over every fixed odd prime modulus. Neither conclusion is silently extended to growing q or to all positive sublinear deficits.

The inexpensive necessary gap

Corollary (near half radius gap). In the same fixed-q, fixed-w modular regime, a family with a PC barrier through \(D=\lfloor v/2-s_v\rfloor\), \(s_v=o(v)\), eventually satisfies \[(D-2)^2\le2c(c+1)v\le2q(t+1)(q(t+1)+1)v.\tag{7}\] Consequently \[c\ge\left(\frac1{2\sqrt2}-o(1)\right)\sqrt v,\qquad t\ge\left(\frac1{2\sqrt2\,q}-o(1)\right)\sqrt v.\tag{8}\] Its parity-check matroid's contraction depth is at least \((D-2)^2/(4v)\), hence at least \((1/16-o(1))v\).

Proof. The existing separator necessity gives \(\kappa(\mathcal C)\ge D-1\) eventually. Combine it with (4) and square the positive inequality \(D-2\le\sqrt{2c(c+1)v}\). The all-basis bound gives the second part of (7). Since \(D/v\to1/2\), solving these quadratic inequalities gives (8). Applying the tree separator lemma with the actual depth d, rather than its upper bound \(d_c\), gives \(\kappa\le2\sqrt{dv}+1\), hence the depth assertion. \(\square\)

Specification disposition. Retain (7)–(8) as necessary code-specific restrictions. The existing rank/radius/Boolean-projection/separator conjunction still lacks an unbounded witness meeting the full formula conditions, so this refinement remains provisional. The general filtered formula specification and its guarded witness are unchanged. These are bounds on the original modulus-field row code; proof-field extension is not a change of that code's covering-radius domain.

The lesson applies beyond one quintic support pattern: every near-redundancy code has short support-minimal words in every basis, and the resulting matroid depth supplies a small puncture. A different sparse presentation cannot remove that intrinsic obstruction. The larger regime \(\Omega(\sqrt v)\le t=o(v)\) remains material; neither an impossibility theorem there nor a suitable family has been obtained.

9 October 2026 — Radius deficit pays for removing long circuits

Working radius–separator tradeoff and rank-half exclusion; the general family remains open. Produced by Codex (gpt-6-astra, medium reasoning).

Question. On near-half-family, can the code route retain both near-redundancy covering radius and a large actual puncture separator when the deficit exceeds square-root scale? The previous circuit-size argument stopped at that scale because its depth bound is quadratic. The necessary implication is compatibility of the radius and separator screens, not merely a better chosen basis.

Route comparison. A positive large-separator construction competes with a stronger structural restriction. The initial attempt to improve the general circumference-to-depth bound encounters a published quadratic sharpness example. That does not rule out a size-sensitive separator. More decisively, the covering radius carries information discarded by circuit size: its redundancy deficit decreases under a paid circuit contraction. We use this budget instead of improving the general matroid theorem.

New mathematics. Radius is subadditive across a represented restriction and contraction, so redundancy deficit is superadditive. A circuit of length \(L\) contributes exactly \(\lfloor(L-1)/q\rfloor\) deficit. Repeatedly contracting a basis of each circuit longer than \(q\) therefore removes at most \((2q-1)t\) actual coordinates in total and leaves circumference at most \(q\). Consequently \(\kappa(C)\le(2q-1)t+O_q(\sqrt v)\). All sublinear deficits are excluded at fixed modulus and original width, including the entire rank-half regime. A surviving fixed-modulus candidate must have a fixed linear rank gap below half.

Goal progress. Unchanged for the general near-half family. The rank-half code subroute is excluded, and the formerly open radius–separator compatibility question is answered negatively at sublinear deficit. Lower-rank fixed-modulus sources, growing-modulus sources and non-code formulas are not excluded. No near-half lower bound or complete Frege transfer is obtained; the stronger code specification still lacks a joint unbounded witness.

General statement. lem:radius-contraction-budget and thm:deficit-circuit-removal hold for every finite-field represented code. cor:deficit-puncture-separation converts the removal to actual coordinate separation. thm:sublinear-deficit-degree-ceiling applies the paid PC compiler; cor:near-half-rank-gap extracts the inexpensive necessary deficit and rank restrictions.

Keep the representation and its syndrome metric

Let \(H=(h_e)_{e\in E}\) be a finite list spanning a vector space \(V\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), where \(q\) is any prime power. Zero columns and parallel columns are permitted. Set \(v=|E|\), \(k=\dim V\), and \(C=\ker H\subseteq\mathbb F_q^E\). For \(y\in V\), let \(\mu_H(y)\) be the minimum support size of coefficients representing \(y\) using these columns. Define \[\rho(H)=\max_{y\in V}\mu_H(y)=\rho(C),\qquad t(H)=k-\rho(H)\ge0.\] The equality is the usual syndrome description: a received word and its code coset have exactly the representations of its syndrome. A column basis proves \(\rho(H)\le k\). Empty and rank-zero representations have radius and deficit zero. The metric depends on the represented columns, not merely the abstract matroid; no representation-invariance of covering radius is assumed.

For \(Z\subseteq E\), let \(V_Z=\operatorname{span}\{h_z:z\in Z\}\). The restriction \(H|Z\) has target \(V_Z\). The contraction \(H/Z\) is the list of remaining columns in \(V/V_Z\). Both radii are taken in those spanned targets.

Lemma (radius contraction budget). For every such \(Z\), \[\rho(H)\le\rho(H|Z)+\rho(H/Z),\qquad t(H)\ge t(H|Z)+t(H/Z).\tag{1}\] If \(Q\) is a circuit of length \(L\), then \[\rho(H|Q)=L-\lceil L/q\rceil,\qquad t(H|Q)=\lceil L/q\rceil-1=\lfloor(L-1)/q\rfloor.\tag{2}\]

Proof. Given \(y\in V\), first represent its quotient class using at most \(\rho(H/Z)\) columns outside \(Z\). The residual lies in \(V_Z\), so represent it using at most \(\rho(H|Z)\) columns in \(Z\). The supports are disjoint. Taking the maximum over \(y\) gives the radius inequality. Since \(\dim V=\dim V_Z+\dim(V/V_Z)\), subtracting it from this rank identity gives the deficit inequality.

For a circuit, \(\ker(H|Q)\) is one-dimensional, generated by a vector \(a\) with all \(L\) entries nonzero; this includes a singleton loop. For a received word \(x\in\mathbb F_q^Q\), its distance to \(\langle a\rangle\) is \(L\) minus the largest multiplicity among the \(q\) ratios \(x_i/a_i\). That multiplicity is at least \(\lceil L/q\rceil\), and a word distributing the ratios as evenly as possible attains this lower bound. The restriction has rank \(L-1\), giving (2). \(\square\)

This elementary composition inequality is proved here in the exact convention needed. It is not a claim that contraction preserves radius, nor that the covering radius is an abstract matroid invariant. The contracted representation can develop new circuits; the budget below is recalculated on that actual representation at every step.

Remove every expensive circuit with one global budget

Theorem (deficit circuit removal). There exists an actual coordinate set \(Z\subseteq E\), with \[|Z|\le(2q-1)t(H),\tag{3}\] such that every circuit of \(H/Z\) has size at most \(q\).

Proof. At any stage with a circuit \(Q\) of length \(L>q\), choose \(e\in Q\) and contract \(I=Q\setminus\{e\}\). This is an independent set of \(L-1\) actual remaining columns and spans the same space as \(Q\). After contracting \(I\), the column \(e\) is a zero column. Deleting a zero column changes neither the target rank nor syndrome radius. Thus \[t(H/I)=t(H/Q).\] Apply (1) to the full circuit \(Q\), not merely its independent subset \(I\), and use (2): \[t(H)-t(H/I)\ge\delta_L:=\lfloor(L-1)/q\rfloor\ge1.\tag{4}\] Write \(L-1=q\delta_L+r_L\), with \(0\le r_L\le q-1\). Since \(\delta_L\ge1\), \[|I|=L-1\le(2q-1)\delta_L.\tag{5}\] Repeat on the remaining quotient representation until no circuit longer than \(q\) remains. Each step removes at least one coordinate and reduces the nonnegative integer deficit by at least \(\delta_L\). Therefore the sum of all \(\delta_L\)'s is at most the initial \(t(H)\). The contracted coordinate sets are disjoint subsets of the original coordinates, and sequential quotienting is contraction of their union. Summing (5) proves (3). No largest-circuit choice, disjointness of the successive circuit supports before quotienting, or circuit-size monotonicity is required. \(\square\)

The distinction between \(Q\) and \(I\) is essential: the independent restriction \(H|I\) has zero deficit and gives no decrease by itself. The circuit restriction supplies the decrease, while leaving its last element as a harmless loop saves one actual puncture. No auxiliary direction is contracted.

Coordinate separator and ordinary PC costs

Corollary (deficit puncture separation). For every finite-field linear code on \(v\ge1\) coordinates, with redundancy-radius deficit \(t\), \[\kappa(C)\le\min\{v,(2q-1)t+\sqrt{2q(q+1)v}+1\}.\tag{6}\] More precisely, if the construction contracts \(h\) coordinates and leaves \(n=v-h\), then for each integer \(b\ge1\), \[\kappa(C)\le\min\{v,h+b+\tfrac12q(q+1)\lfloor n/(b+1)\rfloor\}.\tag{7}\]

Proof. Puncturing \(C=\ker H\) on the set \(Z\) in (3) corresponds to contraction of its parity-check column representation, as proved in the circuit separator record. The remaining matroid has circumference at most \(q\), so its actual-element contraction depth is at most \(q(q+1)/2\), by the audited imported theorem. Apply the contraction-tree separator lemma to the remaining \(n\) actual columns. Puncturing its additional selected coordinates splits the code into coordinate blocks of size at most \(b\), proving (7). Taking \(b=\lceil\sqrt{q(q+1)n/2}\rceil\), and using the trivial bound \(v\) for any empty remainder, gives \(\kappa\le h+\sqrt{2q(q+1)n}+1\). Now use \(h\le(2q-1)t\) and \(n\le v\). \(\square\)

Return to a nonempty Boolean-empty affine system \(Ax=b_0\) over an odd prime field \(\mathbb F_q\), with \(r=\operatorname{rank}A\ge1\), original row width at most \(w\), and row code \(C\). Here \(H\) is a parity-check matrix of that row code, not the original matrix \(A\). The proof field \(F\) has characteristic different from \(q\), and all canonical row clauses and original Booleanity remain the inputs. Put \[s_* =\min\{v,(2q-1)t+\lceil\sqrt{2q(q+1)v}\rceil+1\},\] \[M_{s_*}=\min\{v,\lceil(1-1/q)v+s_*/q+w\sqrt{2r\log(4r+2)}\rceil\},\quad B_{s_*}=\max\{\lceil M_{s_*}/2\rceil+w+1,s_*+2\}.\tag{8}\]

Theorem (sublinear deficit ceiling). The original canonical system has ordinary PC degree at most \(B_{s_*}\). At fixed \(q,w\), if \(t=o(v)\), then \[d_F\le(1/2-1/(2q))v+o(v).\tag{9}\]

Proof. The actual puncture and block budget (6) is at most the integer \(s_*\). Apply the puncture-separator PC theorem, whose indicator supports already pay both the pinned coordinates and the bad remaining block. Its bound is monotone in that total support. No sparse code basis is substituted for the original rows and no old derivation is multiplied for free. When \(q,w\) are fixed and \(t=o(v)\), \(s_*=o(v)\) and \(w\sqrt{r\log(r+1)}=o(v)\), giving (9). \(\square\)

This resolves the positive-sublinear-deficit scope left by the earlier ternary graphical and all-field subroot arguments. It covers nongraphical parity-check representations, including all quintic columns and all their quotient circuits. Growing modulus is governed only by the exact (8); it is not covered by the fixed-gap asymptotic statement.

The rank-half route is excluded

Corollary (near half rank gap). In the same fixed-\(q,w\) regime, a family having a PC barrier through \(D=\lfloor v/2-s_v\rfloor\), \(s_v=o(v)\), must eventually obey \[t\ge\frac{D-2-\sqrt{2q(q+1)v}}{2q-1},\tag{10}\] and hence \[t\ge\frac{v}{2(2q-1)}-o(v),\qquad r\le\frac{q-1}{2q-1}v+o(v).\tag{11}\] In particular no fixed-modulus bounded-row-width family with \(r=v/2+o(v)\) has the required near-half PC barrier.

Proof. The earlier separator necessity gives \(\kappa(C)\ge D-1\) eventually. Combining it with (6) gives (10). Since \(D/v\to1/2\), the first part of (11) follows. The radius necessity independently gives \(\rho\ge v/2-o(v)\). Substituting both lower bounds into \(r=v-\rho-t\) proves the second part. Its coefficient is strictly below one half for fixed \(q\), proving the final exclusion. \(\square\)

Specification disposition. The conjunction of rank-half, near-half radius and near-half puncture separation is now proved impossible at fixed modulus and width; it must not continue as an unproved existence task. A replacement fixed-modulus code specification may retain \(\rho\ge v/2-o(v)\), \(\beta\ge D-1\), \(\kappa\ge D-1\), and the accepted formula requirements, but must instead have the lower-rank bound (11) and linear deficit. This replacement is provisional: no joint unbounded witness is proved. The accepted general filtered specification and its guarded witness survive unchanged. The growing-modulus central source is not excluded, because its modulus and width violate the fixed-parameter hypotheses.

The old coupled width-ten witness is consistent with the theorem: its deficit is at most its sublinear hub count and its separator is already sublinear. Paired maximal-radius witnesses are likewise excluded rather than rehabilitated by row mixing. The point is intrinsic: a different bounded-width presentation of the same row code does not avoid (6). Lowering rank is a substantive structural change; it trades away the rank-half ansatz without asserting that the remaining formula conditions can still be jointly met.

All new checks are analytic. Formula (2) handles every length and finite field, including loops; when \(L\le q\) its contribution is zero, exactly explaining the stopping threshold. For \(L=q+1\), it pays one deficit and \(q\) contractions; at \(L=2q\), the paid ratio is \(2q-1\), showing why (5) needs that factor. Rank-zero remainders cause no loss. The old wide ternary and quintic examples are within the new all-representation argument, with no unsupported extension of their old graphical gain rule. No finite experiment, new encoding or new PC inference rule is introduced.

For each fixed relevant depth \(\ell\ge2\), one polynomial-size Boolean CNF family on actual \(v\to\infty\), independent of the proposed proof-size exponent, must have \(1\notin C_D\) over \(\mathbb F_2\), \(D=\lfloor v/2-s\rfloor\), \(s=o(v/(\log v)^{\ell-2})\). This choice does not make upper bounds the default objective: proving the relevant local monomial survival would validate a source prerequisite; proving enough interpolation improvement would force a structural change.

Decisive test. Use the original nine-partition source \(v=l2^l,k=16l,m=9v/k,q\in(v^2,2v^2)\), and its actual central rows \(R_a\). For each zero slice \(Q_a\) on \(k-1\) bits, determine the binary evaluation space at degree \(k/2-2\), starting analytically from its exact uniform affine modular-row law. The negative endpoint is a uniformly positive probability, at least some fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), that one nonempty slice interpolates completely there, along a chosen deterministic admissible prime sequence \(q=q_l\). Independent row coefficients then make at least \(\varepsilon m/2\) rows improved with probability \(1-o(1)\): their count has mean at least \(\varepsilon m\), variance at most \(m/4\), and Chebyshev bounds failure by \(O(1/(\varepsilon^2m))\). Intersect with the already proved source good event. For those rows the split gives \(\tau(R_a)\le k/2-1\) on those rows. Their fractional weights \(1/9\) then give an original PC improvement \(\Omega(v/k)\), excluding this original source for depth at least three. An improvement by a fixed positive fraction of k on a positive fraction of rows would also settle depth two. If instead the top filtered classes survive, identify whether their monomial supports admit a common selected set of size \(D-1\); a surviving local dimension alone does not prove that. The endpoints are an all-parameter degree exclusion or a proved necessary filtration property for an unbounded source, not a fit to small ranks.

The full fractional-cover argument depends only on the available local interpolation degrees: an E-set meeting every row in at most \(\tau(R_a)\) would satisfy \(E\le\sum_a\lambda_a\tau(R_a)\). The existing paid interpolation ceiling therefore gives degree at most \(\max\{k,2,\lfloor\sum_a\lambda_a\tau(R_a)\rfloor+1\}+1\). This is the already proved argument with improved local degrees, not a new proof rule. The row-law calculation must precede any minimal-core selection; original-instance upper bounds do not automatically reverse to selected cores.

A free bit splits the entire local filtration

For a nonempty Boolean relation \(R\subseteq\{0,1\}^k\), let \(h_R(d)\) be the dimension, over a fixed characteristic-two field \(F\), of evaluations of polynomials of total degree at most \(d\) on \(R\). Put \(h_R(-1)=0\), and let \(\tau(R)\) be the least degree whose evaluations give every function on \(R\).

Lemma (complement filtration split). Suppose \(k\ge1\), \(R\ne\varnothing\), and simultaneous complementation preserves \(R\). Define \(Q=\{y\in\{0,1\}^{k-1}:(y,0)\in R\}\). Then \[h_R(d)=h_Q(d)+h_Q(d-1)\quad(d\ge0),\qquad \tau(R)=\tau(Q)+1.\tag{1}\]

Proof. Set \(z=x_k\) and \(y_i=x_i+x_k\) over \(F\) for \(i

In the new coordinates, a degree-at-most-d Boolean polynomial has the form \(f(y)+zg(y)\), with \(\deg f\le d\) and \(\deg g\le d-1\). Its function is zero on both z-fibres exactly when both \(f\) and \(g\) vanish on \(Q\), by first setting z to zero and then to one. The two evaluation spaces are therefore a direct sum, proving the Hilbert formula. It equals all \(2|Q|\) functions exactly when both summands have dimension \(|Q|\), first at \(d=\tau(Q)+1\). This includes \(k=1\), when \(Q\) is a singleton in zero variables. \(\square\)

For a central row \(\sum_{i=1}^k a_i x_i=\frac12\sum_i a_i\) over an odd finite field, \(Q\) is the ordinary modular row \(\sum_{i

The substitution is used to analyze one row's function space, not to re-encode the overlapping global formula. Distinct rows generally choose different anchor coordinates, so their local changes are not one common global variable change. No new auxiliary variables, PC inference rule or uncharged proof substitution is introduced.

The central table is not an independent erasure sample

Proposition (central table correlations). Let \(a\) be uniform in \(\mathbb F_q^k\), \(q\) odd, \(k\ge1\), and put \(R_a=\{x\in\{0,1\}^k:a\cdot(2x-\mathbf1)=0\}\). Then \(x\) and its complement have identical membership indicators. Indicators on distinct complement pairs are pairwise independent, and \[\mathbb E|R_a|=2^k/q,\qquad \operatorname{Var}|R_a|=\frac{2^{k+1}}q(1-1/q).\tag{2}\] For \(k\ge3\), the indicators on complement pairs are not jointly independent: there are four distinct pairs whose simultaneous membership probability is \(q^{-3}\), rather than \(q^{-4}\).

Proof. The sign vectors \(2x-\mathbf1\) and its negative define the same zero event. Two sign vectors are proportional over an odd field only when their scalar ratio is \(1\) or \(-1\), so distinct complement pairs give independent linear equations in uniform \(a\). Each event has probability \(1/q\). Summing over the \(2^{k-1}\) pairs and multiplying their count by two gives (2). For the higher correlation, fix all but the first two bits to zero and take the four choices on those bits. Their sign vectors satisfy the rectangle relation \(d_{00}+d_{11}=d_{01}+d_{10}\). They have rank three: the first vector has a nonzero third coordinate, and the two differences give independent first and second coordinate directions since two is invertible. The four complement pairs are distinct, and their joint zero event therefore has probability \(q^{-3}\). \(\square\)

This rejects a direct independent-erasure transfer, even after folding complement pairs. It does not imply poor interpolation, and (2) is not a rank theorem. The exact slice law still gives a concrete coefficient model for the test in Decisive test.

Three bounded translation controls

Proposition (central unimodular feasibility). If an integer matrix \(A\) is totally unimodular and every row sum is even, then \(Ax=A\mathbf1/2\) has a Boolean solution over the integers. Its reduction in an odd prime field therefore cannot be a Boolean-empty central source; odd characteristic is the application scope, not needed for the integer proof.

Proof. The polytope \(P=\{x\in[0,1]^v:Ax=A\mathbf1/2\}\) is nonempty, since it contains \(\mathbf1/2\), and bounded. Choose a vertex. Its active equations have a full-rank square subsystem drawn from the rows of \(A\) and coordinate unit rows; otherwise a nonzero direction preserving all active equations could be perturbed slightly in both directions inside P, contradicting extremality. Every nonsingular such square matrix has determinant \(\pm1\): expand along the unit rows and use total unimodularity. Its right side is integral by the even-row-sum hypothesis. Cramer's rule makes the vertex integral, hence Boolean. \(\square\)

This is the elementary Hoffman–Kruskal integrality mechanism, with its proof supplied here. It rules out a central totally-unimodular replacement as a Boolean-empty source. It says nothing about generic finite-field coefficient matrices without this integral lift, and no real positivity statement is reduced modulo two.

Lemma (fixed weight clause cost). For \(1\le k\le n-1\), a CNF on exactly \(n\) variables, with no auxiliaries, whose satisfying assignments are precisely the points of weight k needs at least \[\binom n{k-1}+\binom n{k+1}\tag{3}\] clauses. This bound is attained.

Proof. Remove tautological clauses and repeated literals. Every clause must hold on every weight-k assignment. Write its positive-variable set as P and its negative-variable set as N. Falsifying it fixes P to zero and N to one. Such a subcube avoids weight k exactly when either \(|N|>k\) or \(|P|>n-k\). A clause falsified by a weight-\(k-1\) assignment cannot have \(|N|>k\), so it must use all \(n-k+1\) zeros of that assignment as positive variables. It can therefore exclude only that one weight-\(k-1\) assignment. Dually, a clause falsified at weight \(k+1\) must use all its ones negatively and can exclude only that one weight-\(k+1\) assignment. No clause can serve both roles, since that would need disjoint sets P,N of total size at least \(n+2\). Summing proves (3). All positive clauses of size \(n-k+1\) and all negative clauses of size \(k+1\) attain the bound. \(\square\)

In particular at \(n=2^m-1\), \(k=2^{m-1}\), the two neighboring binomial coefficients are \(2^{n-O(\log n)}\). The elementary central-binomial estimate follows because the maximum coefficient is at least \(2^n/(n+1)\) and these neighboring coefficients differ from it by bounded rational factors. Thus a direct microcanonical slice relation is not a polynomial CNF on its original variables. Auxiliary encodings change the denominator and require a separate ledger.

Proposition (diagonal state obstruction). Over any field, let \(V\) have basis \(e_x\) indexed by all Boolean assignments. For each canonical input falsity polynomial \(p_a\), let \(D_a e_x=p_a(x)e_x\). Then \(\bigcap_a\ker D_a\) is exactly the span of the satisfying assignments. For an unsatisfiable input it is zero, regardless of any tensor-network representation of a vector.

Proof. Write \(\psi=\sum_x c_xe_x\). If an assignment violates input a, then \(p_a(x)=1\), so \(D_a\psi=0\) forces \(c_x=0\). Conversely every satisfying basis vector is killed by every \(D_a\). This proves both inclusions. \(\square\)

The common-kernel requirement is essential: the kernel of \(\sum_aD_a\) is not a substitute in characteristic two, where an even number of violations can cancel. A truncated functional annihilating only paid multiples is a different object from a full physical state killed by each local projector.

A weighted middle matrix

Let \(K\) be a field of characteristic two, let \(s\ge1\), \(n=2s+1\), and choose nonzero weights \(w_1,\ldots,w_n\in K\). Index rows and columns by the s-subsets of \([n]\). Put \(w_S=\prod_{i\in S}w_i\), and let \(A_{S,T}=1\) if \(S\cap T=\varnothing\), and zero otherwise. Thus A is the adjacency matrix of the odd Kneser graph, and has zero diagonal. Define \(M=A+\alpha\operatorname{diag}(w_S)\).

Lemma (weighted middle inverse). If \[\alpha\ne0,\qquad \alpha^2\prod_iw_i\ne\sum_iw_i,\tag{1}\] then M is invertible.

Proof. We may pass to an algebraic extension containing square roots \(c_i\) of all \(w_i\); invertibility descends because the determinant is in K. Let \(c_* =\prod_i c_i\), \(\sigma=\sum_i c_i^2\), and \(G=\operatorname{diag}(\prod_{i\in S}c_i)\). When S and T are disjoint, their union misses one coordinate j, so \((G^{-1}AG^{-1})_{S,T}=c_j/c_*\). Thus \[G^{-1}MG^{-1}=c_*^{-1}(T+\beta I),\qquad\beta=\alpha c_*,\tag{2}\] where \(T_{S,T}=c_j\) for disjoint S,T with complement \(\{j\}\), and zero otherwise.

Work in the square-zero algebra \(E=K[y_1,\ldots,y_n]/(y_i^2)\). Let m be multiplication by \(\sum_i c_i y_i\), let \(d=\sum_i c_i\partial_i\), and let \(*y_S=y_{[n]\setminus S}\). Characteristic two makes \(m^2=d^2=0\), \(dm+md=\sigma I\), and \(*m*=d\). These identities follow on each squarefree basis monomial: distinct-coordinate terms occur twice, and the matching-coordinate terms give \(\sum_i c_i^2\). On \(E_s\), the operator \(*m\) is exactly T. Hence \[T^2=dm,\qquad T^4=(dm)^2=\sigma dm=\sigma T^2.\tag{3}\] Writing \(P=T^2\), we obtain \[(P+\beta^2I)(P+(\beta^2+\sigma)I)=\beta^2(\beta^2+\sigma)I.\tag{4}\] The scalar is nonzero by (1). Since \((T+\beta I)^2=P+\beta^2I\), this proves invertibility; an inverse is \[\frac{(T+\beta I)(T^2+(\beta^2+\sigma)I)}{\beta^2(\beta^2+\sigma)}.\] Now use (2). \(\square\)

No converse to (1) is asserted. The square-zero algebra is a device for this finite matrix calculation, not an old Boolean proof quotient or a claimed proper PC invariant.

Inverse characters expose the middle layer

Let \(q\) be an odd prime, let \(F\) have characteristic two, and consider the Boolean row \[R=\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:\textstyle\sum_i a_ix_i=b\text{ in }\mathbb F_q\},\qquad n=2s+1\ge3,\quad a_i\ne0.\] Choose a primitive q-th root \(\zeta\) in a finite extension of F, put \(z_i=\zeta^{a_i}\), \(A_0=\sum_i a_i\), \(c=2b-A_0\), and \(w_i=z_i+z_i^{-1}\ne0\).

Lemma (odd character drop). If \[c\ne0,\qquad \zeta^c+\zeta^{-c}\ne\sum_i(\zeta^{a_i}+\zeta^{-a_i}),\tag{5}\] then every function on R has a polynomial representative of degree at most \(s-1\) over F. Every resulting local vanishing relation is derivable from the original canonical row clauses through degree n.

Proof. Put \(\eta_i=z_i-1\), \(P_U=\prod_{i\in U}\eta_i\), and \(P_*=P_{[n]}\). For a set T of size \(s+1\) and its complement S of size s, the two balanced character relations \[G_T^+=\prod_{i\in T}(1+\eta_i x_i)-\zeta^b\prod_{i\in S}(1+(z_i^{-1}-1)x_i),\] \[G_T^-=\prod_{i\in T}(1+(z_i^{-1}-1)x_i)-\zeta^{-b}\prod_{i\in S}(1+\eta_i x_i) \] vanish on R. Normalize each by its coefficient of \(x_T\) and add. The degree-\(s+1\) terms cancel. The coefficient on \(x_{T\setminus\{i\}}\) is \[\frac1{z_i-1}+\frac1{z_i^{-1}-1}=1\] in characteristic two. The coefficient on \(x_S\) is \[\left(\zeta^{b-A_S}+\zeta^{A_T-b}\right)\frac{P_S}{P_T} =\alpha\prod_{i\in S}w_i,\qquad \alpha=\frac{\zeta^b+\zeta^{A_0-b}}{P_*}.\tag{6}\] Here \((z_i-1)^2z_i^{-1}=z_i+z_i^{-1}=w_i\). These are all degree-s terms. Thus the top coefficient matrix of these relations, with row index S, is exactly the weighted middle matrix.

Noncentrality gives \(\alpha\ne0\), and \[\alpha^2\prod_iw_i=\zeta^{2b-A_0}+\zeta^{A_0-2b}=\zeta^c+\zeta^{-c}.\tag{7}\] The matrix lemma makes every degree-s monomial a combination of lower-degree functions on R. The earlier balanced-character reduction already lowers every degree greater than s, so evaluation through \(s-1\) is onto. After matrix inversion, apply an F-linear coefficient component fixing one to each solved monic relation \(x_U-p_U\). This descends the normalized relations from the finite extension without increasing degree. Finally, a multilinear polynomial vanishing on R is literally the sum of its values on forbidden assignments times their full row indicators. That is an ordinary PC derivation through n from the canonical clauses; no low-degree final relation is treated as a free original axiom. \(\square\)

All characters give an exact pairing classification

A multiset of nonzero elements of \(\mathbb F_q\) is sign-pairable if its indices can be partitioned into pairs whose coefficients are equal or opposite. Equivalently every class \(\{a,-a\}\) occurs an even number of times. Let \(\tau(R)\) denote interpolation degree over F for nonempty R.

Theorem (modular pairing criterion). Let every row coefficient be nonzero and let q be an odd prime.

  • For an even central row on \(k=2h\ge4\) variables, \(2b=\sum_i a_i\), sign-pairability implies \(R\ne\varnothing\) and \(\tau(R)=h\). If the coefficients are not sign-pairable, evaluation through degree \(h-1\) is onto R, including when R is empty. Thus for nonempty central rows, attaining the half-width interpolation bound is equivalent to sign-pairability.
  • For an odd noncentral row on \(n=2s+1\ge3\) variables, put \(c=2b-\sum_i a_i\ne0\). If the augmented multiset \((a_1,\ldots,a_n,c)\) is sign-pairable, then \(R\ne\varnothing\) and \(\tau(R)=s\). Otherwise evaluation through \(s-1\) is onto.

Central upper bound. Form the polynomial, with exponents reduced modulo q, \[P(X)=\sum_{i=1}^{2h}(X^{a_i}+X^{-a_i})\in\mathbb F_2[X]/(X^q-1),\qquad\deg P<q.\tag{8}\] It is zero exactly when the coefficients are sign-pairable. If it is nonzero, it cannot vanish at all q distinct q-th roots in characteristic two. Since \(P(1)=0\), some nontrivial root \(\zeta\) has \(P(\zeta)\ne0\); because q is prime, this root is primitive.

Take the zero slice of one coordinate, say the last. It is an odd row with coefficient list \(a_1,\ldots,a_{2h-1}\), target b, and \(c=2b-\sum_{i<2h}a_i=a_{2h}\ne0\). Its condition (5) is exactly \(P(\zeta)\ne0\). The odd-character lemma gives slice interpolation through \(h-2\), and the exact complement split gives full-row interpolation through \(h-1\). If the slice is empty, complement symmetry makes the full row empty as well, and surjectivity is trivial.

Paired sharpness. Choose a pairing. For equal coefficients in a pair \(u,v\), the preferred Boolean assignments have \(x_u+x_v=1\); for opposite coefficients they have \(x_u=x_v\). Every preferred assignment solves the central modular row. Its indicator over F is respectively \(x_u+x_v\) or \(1+x_u+x_v\). Their product f over all h disjoint pairs is a nonzero degree-h polynomial supported on R. For any polynomial g of degree at most \(h-1\), \(fg\) has degree below \(2h\), so its sum over the full Boolean cube is zero: each multilinear monomial misses a coordinate. If such g represented the indicator of one preferred point on R, the same sum would be one. Therefore degree \(h-1\) does not interpolate R. The existing central-row bound gives \(\tau(R)\le h\), proving equality.

Odd rows. Add one variable of coefficient c and keep target b. The augmented row is central, with nonzero coefficients, and its zero slice is the original row. The just-proved central classification and exact complement split give the two odd assertions. In the paired case, the preferred assignment space has a point in the zero slice of the added variable, so that slice is nonempty. \(\square\)

Primality is used in passing from a nonzero polynomial (8) to a primitive character for which every \(z_i-1\ne0\). No extension to arbitrary composite moduli or vector-valued field equations is asserted. Using only one primitive root can miss an unpaired row; all characters are essential to the exact criterion. The initial pair-free hypothesis now follows for every odd noncentral row of width at least three: adding one coefficient cannot make all its distinct sign classes occur evenly.

The original central random sources lose one degree per row

Corollary (random central ceiling). Prescribe m scopes of a common even width \(k\ge4\) on v variables, each variable occurring in exactly \(r\ge1\) scopes, so \(m=rv/k\). Choose all supported coefficients independently uniformly in \(\mathbb F_q\), q an odd prime, and centralize each row target. Except with probability at most \[\min\{1,mk/q+2m/q\},\tag{9}\] every row has nonzero coefficients and interpolates through \(k/2-1\) over every characteristic-two field. On this event, if the original formula is unsatisfiable, its canonical ordinary PC degree is at most \[\max\{k,2,\lfloor v/2-v/k\rfloor+1\}+1.\tag{10}\]

Proof. Fix one primitive q-th root in a finite binary extension. Conditional on all but the last coefficient in one row, the equation \[\sum_i(\zeta^{a_i}+\zeta^{-a_i})=0\] asks \(z+z^{-1}\) to take one prescribed value, with \(z=\zeta^{a_k}\). Multiplying by z gives a nonzero quadratic polynomial in z, which has at most two roots. Since \(a_k\) is uniform, the probability is at most \(2/q\). A union bound over rows, and over the mk possible zero coefficients, proves (9). On the complementary good event the central upper-bound proof applies in every row; the Boolean evaluation ranks do not change upon extending a characteristic-two proof field.

Give each row fractional-cover weight \(1/r\). The total interpolation budget is \[\sum_a\frac1r(k/2-1)=v/2-v/k.\] Apply the existing fractional-cover proof with these actual interpolation degrees, retaining the original width k floor. This proves (10). An empty local row is already refutable through k and causes no problem. \(\square\)

For both recorded central sources, \(v=l2^l\), \(q\in(v^2,2v^2)\), and \((k,r)=(8l,5)\) or \((16l,9)\). The failure probability in (9) is o(1), and the already proved source good event includes unsatisfiability. Thus both original formulas have, with probability \(1-o(1)\), \[d_2\le v/2-v/k+2.\tag{11}\] This excludes every barrier deficit \(s=o(v/\log v)\), hence every \(\ell\ge3\) target and the proposed near-square-root deficit. It does not exclude every permitted depth-two deficit \(o(v)\). Original-variable and polynomial canonical-length counts are unchanged. The bound does not transfer backwards to arbitrary selected cores after they lose the exact cover.

Proof. Paired rows interpolate through \(k_a/2\), and unpaired rows through \(k_a/2-1\). Exact cover gives total budget \(T=v/2-\Delta\). The same E-subset counting and paid local-interpolation proof gives (12). Comparing with D gives \(\lfloor T\rfloor+2>D\), hence \(T\ge D-1\), so \(\Delta\le v/2-D+1<s+2\). \(\square\)

New mathematics. Preferred paired affine cubes give degree-preserving local retractions that survive every coordinate projection.
