9 October 2026 — The alternative endpoints need a barrier at half the shattered dimension, and no frame alone guarantees less than the cube

Working proofs of a necessary condition common to the alternative endpoints; it closes the search for a better frame. Research cycle on the general form behind the product-tree frame. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort low).

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement: the product-tree frame has the engine's cutoff at four fifths of its ceiling, the cube at one half of its trivial ceiling. Can any frame make the ratio smaller, and what do the thin-kernel and extension-count hypotheses require in general? If no frame beats one half, the alternative endpoints do not relax the barrier relative to what the closure can shatter, and the search returns to the cube in the free dimension with that fact stated.

New mathematics. Call a set \(Q\) of variables shattered through degree \(K\) if every multilinear monomial of degree at most \(K\) on \(Q\) is standard for \(C_D\). The thin-kernel hypothesis forces \(|Q|\le X\) and the extension-count hypothesis forces \(|Q|\le(2+1/\Delta)(K-\Delta)+1+1/\Delta\) for every such \(Q\); an unsatisfiable system with a proper closure has such a \(Q\) of size \(D-1\). With the thin-kernel theorem's \(X=2(K-\Delta)+1+(K-\Delta+1)/\Delta\), both endpoints share one necessary condition: the closure is proper at \(D\) and shatters nothing larger than about \(2D\). For a frame whose top standard degree is \(\tau\), the cutoff at which the extension-count hypothesis can be verified on the frame alone is at least about \(\tau/(2+1/\Delta)\), while its ceiling is \(\tau+w\); the cube attains this ratio.

Goal progress. Unchanged. The result is a necessary condition for two sufficient hypotheses. It removes the hope that a frame alone changes the ratio of cutoff to ceiling and gives the reformulations since the review a common necessary condition; it supplies no family.

General statement. prop:shattered-dimension-bound holds for every Boolean system over \(\mathbb F_2\), cutoff and window. cor:frame-ratio-half holds for every satisfiable frame whose closure is its truncated vanishing ideal.

Shattered sets

Notation as in the extension-count entry: \(\mathfrak M_0\) the standard monomials of \(C_D(\Gamma)\) of degree at most \(K\) for a degree-compatible order, \(e(S)\) the number of variables \(x\notin S\) with \(x\,x_S\in\mathfrak M_0\), \(m_j(\mathfrak M_0)\) the number of standard monomials of degree \(j\). A set \(Q\) of variables is shattered through degree \(K\) if \(x_T\in\mathfrak M_0\) for every \(T\subseteq Q\) with \(|T|\le K\).

Proposition (shattered dimension bound). Let \(Q\) be shattered through degree \(K\) and \(1\le\Delta<K\).

  1. If \(m_j(\mathfrak M_0)\le\binom Xj\) for some \(j\le K\) and real \(X\ge j\), then \(|Q|\le X\).
  2. If \(e(S)\le(1+1/\Delta)(|S|+1)\) for every standard \(x_S\) with \(|S|=K-\Delta\), then \(|Q|\le(2+1/\Delta)(K-\Delta)+1+1/\Delta\).
  3. If \(\Gamma\) is unsatisfiable with axioms of degree at most \(D\), \(D\ge2\), and \(1\notin C_D(\Gamma)\), some set of \(D-1\) variables is shattered through every degree up to \(D-1\).

Proof. 1. If \(|Q|<j\) there is nothing to prove. Otherwise level \(j\) contains the \(\binom{|Q|}{j}\) monomials on \(Q\), and \(\binom{\cdot}{j}\) is increasing on \([j-1,\infty)\). 2. If \(|Q|\le K-\Delta\) there is nothing to prove. Otherwise take \(S\subseteq Q\) with \(|S|=K-\Delta\). Each \(x\in Q\setminus S\) gives \(x\,x_S\) of degree \(K-\Delta+1\le K\) on \(Q\), hence standard; so \(|Q|-(K-\Delta)\le e(S)\le(1+1/\Delta)(K-\Delta+1)\). 3. The kernel dimension theorem shows that the quotient is not exhausted in degree \(D-2\), so for any degree-compatible order there is a standard monomial of degree at least \(D-1\). It is multilinear, and standard monomials are closed under divisors, so any \(D-1\) of its variables form a set all of whose subsets are standard. \(\square\)

The thin-kernel theorem takes \(X=2(K-\Delta)+1+(K-\Delta+1)/\Delta\), the same quantity as the bound in 2. So under either hypothesis every shattered set has size at most about \(2K\), and by 3, when \(K\le D-1\), the largest has size at least \(D-1\ge K\). With \(q_K\) the largest size of a set shattered through degree \(K\), both alternative endpoints require

\[D-1\ \le\ q_K\ \le\ (2+1/\Delta)K+O(1),\]

a barrier at half the shattered dimension, up to the window. In the cube and after affine elimination \(q_K\) is the number of variables, respectively the free dimension. Nothing here says that \(q_K\le2K\) suffices: on the product-tree frame, for \(K\ge2\), a shattered set is a sibling-free antichain, so \(q_K=n/2\), from one leaf of each pair, while the proved cutoff for the extension counts is \(2n/5\) and the near-sharp example there shows that counts of about \(2(n-2s)\) do occur.

Not claimed. That the bound on \(q_K\) is necessary for the source theorem itself. It is necessary for the two sufficient hypotheses. For the engine's rate the natural reading is that a cube on \(q\) variables inside the standard monomials has ratio \(N_q(K-\delta)/N_q(K)\), exponentially small in \(\delta\) when \(K\) is a constant fraction below \(q/2\); but the engine's families \(\mathfrak M_P\) need not include that cube, so this is a limit of the proof method's estimate, not of the method.

Frames

A frame is a satisfiable Boolean system \(\Pi\) with zero set \(W\) and \(C_D(\Pi)\cap V_j=I(W)\cap V_j\) for \(j\le D\), for every \(D\ge2\), as the cube, a cube with affine definitions, and the product-tree cube are. Let \(\tau\) be the largest degree of a standard monomial of \(I(W)\).

Corollary (frame ratio one half). Let \(\Pi\) be a frame with top standard degree \(\tau\).

  1. Every system \(\Gamma\supseteq\Pi\) in the variables of the frame with further axioms of degree at most \(w\) and no common zero on \(W\) has \(1\in C_{\tau+w}(\Gamma)\).
  2. If the extension-count condition \(e_\Pi(S)\le(1+1/\Delta)(|S|+1)\) holds for all standard \(x_S\) of the frame with \(|S|=K-\Delta\), where \(1\le\Delta<K\le\tau\), then \(K-\Delta\ge(\tau-1-1/\Delta)/(2+1/\Delta)\). For the thin condition \(m_j\le\binom Xj\) on the frame at a level \(j\le\tau\) with \(X\ge j\), one gets \(X\ge\tau\), since level \(j\) contains the \(\binom\tau j\) divisors of a top standard monomial; with the theorem's \(X\) this is the same lower bound on the cutoff.

Proof. 1. As for the product tree: write the multipliers of an identity \(\sum g_af_a=1\) on \(W\) in standard monomials, of degree at most \(\tau\); the products lie in \(C_{\tau+w}(\Gamma)\), and their sum differs from \(1\) by an element of \(I(W)\cap V_{\tau+w}\subseteq C_{\tau+w}(\Pi)\). 2. The variables of a standard monomial of degree \(\tau\) form a set shattered through every degree, since standard monomials are closed under divisors. Apply the proposition to the frame with \(|Q|=\tau\). \(\square\)

So a condition verified on the frame, hence uniformly for all systems containing it, places the cutoff at no less than about half the frame's ceiling. The cube attains one half, with \(\tau=n\) and cutoff \(n/2\); for the product tree the proved cutoff is four fifths of the ceiling. A system containing a frame may have a smaller standard family than the frame, so this does not bound what a particular contradiction needs; it bounds what the frame alone can guarantee.

Consequence for the route. The forms since the review share one necessary condition, not shown sufficient: a closure proper at \(D\) that shatters no set larger than about \(2D\), where the shattered dimension may be counted after affine elimination. A condition verified on the frame alone cannot place the cutoff below half of the frame's own ceiling. What could still help is a contradiction that itself destroys shattering, so that \(q_K\) of the system is far below that of its frame while the closure stays proper; equivalently a system whose kernel is proper and whose standard monomials near the cutoff are few for reasons the contradiction supplies. The recorded sources all have \(q_K\) equal to the number of variables up to their local deficits.

Specification decision. No change is adopted. Considered: adding the necessary upper bound "no set larger than \((2+1/\Delta)K\) is filtered through degree \(K\) on joins of \(g\) rows" as a screen for candidates aimed at the alternative endpoints. The clause is not implied by those endpoints; it implies their necessary bound on \(q_K\): by the joint filtration argument a monomial that is standard in the closure is filtered on every join, so a small filtered dimension bounds \(q_K\) from above, while a large one does not show that \(q_K\) is large. The clause would therefore be sufficient for a necessary condition and not itself necessary; it is not adopted. The accepted specification with the free-dimension count stands, and the old witness serves.

Verification gate. One fresh-context medium reviewer passed the algebra and required corrections that are applied: part 3 now derives the shattered set from a standard monomial of degree at least \(D-1\) and closure under divisors, not from the theorem's injection alone; the thin endpoint's bound on the cutoff cites the theorem's \(X\); the frame property is assumed for every cutoff; the product-tree remark states its range and speaks of the proved cutoff; the route paragraph says the forms share a necessary condition and no longer calls them one requirement; the specification paragraph's direction of implication is corrected; the title is restricted. Unused hypotheses removed: \(|Q|\ge K\), the window in part 1, \(K\le D-1\) in part 3. Dependencies reread in full: the extension-count entry, the kernel dimension entry, the product-tree entry, the thin-kernel review's theorem. Record: review.txt.

Follow-up. No queue item is developed; the entry carries out the first part of the step named by the preceding entry.

On random \(k\)-CNF it gives the following first-moment calibration, for a fixed set and not for the closure: the scope-free ceiling, the thinness threshold and the size from which a typical set has fewer scope-free extensions than elements. For the frames, the dense-parity class and the modular sources no reduction of shattering by the contradiction is available at all.

Goal progress. Unchanged. No candidate with a missing implication at a reachable fraction of a ceiling is obtained. The best calibration, random 3-CNF at threshold density, would need a degree lower bound at about half of its scope-free ceiling, above what the recorded lower-bound method can give even by its optimistic estimate.

General statement. No new all-parameter claim. The entry applies cor:scope-free-thinness and prop:shattered-dimension-bound, which hold for all CNF families and all Boolean systems, to the mechanisms below; the numbers are evaluations of closed formulas and make no statement about any closure.

Clause scopes

If a clause's falsifying indicator lies in \(C_D\), the monomial on its variables is a leading monomial, so a set shattered through degree \(K\) contains no such scope of size at most \(K\). The input clauses qualify, and so do clauses derived by resolution within the cutoff width (derived-clause transversal). So the shattered dimension is at most the largest set avoiding these scopes, and it shrinks as the derivable clauses multiply. The contradiction destroys shattering exactly as fast as it derives narrow clauses, which is also how it approaches a refutation. A proper closure with small shattered dimension therefore needs many narrow consequences whose scopes cover every set of size about \(2D\), and no refutation: a formula whose width-\(D\) consequences are dense yet consistent.

For \(m=\Delta v\) uniformly random \(k\)-clauses, three first-moment quantities for the input clauses alone (evaluation, script): \(\alpha\), the least \(c\) with no scope-free \(cv\)-sets expected; \(c^*\), the thinness threshold of the review; and \(c_{\mathrm{ext}}\), the least \(c\) at which a fixed \(cv\)-set has in expectation at most \(cv\) variables outside it not completing a scope, \((1-c)e^{-\Delta kc^{k-1}}\le c\).

Reading, with its limits. \(c_{\mathrm{ext}}\) is for a fixed set; the extension-count hypothesis quantifies over every standard monomial, and a scope-free set chosen to complete few scopes can have many more extensions, so \(c_{\mathrm{ext}}v\) is an optimistic value and not a cutoff at which the hypothesis is known. \(\alpha v\) bounds the degree from above only through the input scopes; the true ceiling is lower. With those caveats the most favourable row is the first: an optimistic cutoff at \(0.51\) of the scope-free ceiling, and the proved thin cutoff at \(0.63\) of it. The expansion method's optimistic limit recorded in the review, about \(0.184v\), is below \(0.2755v\). For larger \(k\) at threshold density \(\alpha\) tends to one half and both cutoffs rise toward it, so the alternative endpoints approach the old one. Higher density lowers all three numbers together, and by the reviewer's unchecked pointer lowers the true degree faster.

The other mechanisms

Frames. By the frame ratio corollary a frame alone guarantees nothing below half its own ceiling, and a frame's axioms reduce shattering only by lowering that ceiling in proportion.

Dense parity rows. By the dense-parity proposition every set of free variables of size below about \(n/2\) is filtered on joins of up to almost linearly many rows. Any reduction of shattering must come from combinations of at least that many rows, and nothing is known about them; the heuristic count suggests refutation long before.

Modular rows. The paired source shatters half of its variables through its own cutoff by construction, and its local deficits, of order \(v/k\), are what the shared-pin ceiling measures. Its shattered dimension is the number of variables up to those deficits, which is the old endpoint.

Outcome. No mechanism gives a proper closure with shattered dimension near \(2D\) and far below the free dimension. The alternative endpoints remain formally available and have no candidate. The route's working endpoint is near half of the free dimension, and its open difficulty is unchanged: no lower-bound method reaches a constant fraction near one of any ceiling.

Considered: a clause for CNF candidates requiring the scope-free ceiling to be at most twice the cutoff. It is necessary for the alternative endpoints only, the accepted specification aims at the free-dimension endpoint, and no witness with a proper closure is known; not adopted.

The expansion figure \(0.184v\) is the review's estimate, not a computation.

9 October 2026 — The family only has to be hard on some subspace; the barrier at half remains and no method reaches it

Goal-level review with one working reduction; the endpoint is weakened to a hidden subspace, the barrier itself is not. Review of the near-half line after six research entries. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort low).

Question. Six research entries since the last review report unchanged goal progress. They produced one weakening, the free-dimension count, two alternative endpoints with a common necessary condition and no candidate, a class in which local screens are empty, and a negative search for a mechanism. Is a barrier at half of some dimension forced by the engine, what is the weakest object the goal needs, and is there any method that could reach it?

New mathematics. One reduction, which is immediate and had not been stated: the source theorem's hypothesis may be verified for the family together with arbitrary additional polynomial axioms that are not part of the formula. So a polynomial-size family suffices if on some affine subspace of dimension \(n\), with \(v\le n^C\), it has no refutation through degree \(\lfloor n/2-s\rfloor\). The subspace need not be encoded, bounded-width or explicit. The review also records why the barrier at half does not go away: for inputs of degree \(d\) the engine's contraction is, heuristically and under a semi-regularity assumption not proved here, tight on the cube up to constants.

Goal progress. Unchanged. The hidden-subspace form is a weaker sufficient target for the first open statement, like the free-dimension count it extends; no family is supplied, and the available lower-bound theorem, by its recorded form, would reach at most an eighth of the free dimension in the most favourable class, if it applies there at all. The complete Frege transfer is untouched.

General statement. lem:auxiliary-axiom-endpoint holds for every Boolean system over \(\mathbb F_2\), every set of additional axioms and all parameters of the moving-cutoff theorem.

Across the goal

  • Boolean PC family. Open. All six entries took it as primary: the free-dimension normalization, dense parity rows, the extension-count form, the product-tree frame, the shattered-dimension bound and the search for a shatter-breaking mechanism. Result: the statement now reads near half of the free dimension; the thin-kernel and extension-count alternatives need a closure that shatters no more than about twice its cutoff and have no candidate; no entry produced a proper closure at any stated cutoff. Six cycles; the open-item count is two, as twelve research entries back.
  • Complete Frege transfer. Open. Zero cycles. The reductions of this block move the family further from a bounded-width CNF in the variables the theorem counts, which the transfer statement must eventually pay for.

Obstacle

The line is stuck on a lower bound, not on a construction. Every form of the endpoint asks for a closure that is proper at about half of a dimension it cannot exceed: half the free dimension, or half the shattered dimension. Constructions in which nothing local prevents this now exist, the dense-parity class. What is missing is any argument that a polynomial-size system is not refuted below such a cutoff. The recorded methods give at most a quarter of the variables on the families examined, and a count of row multiples suggests that unstructured instances are refuted well below a third.

Architecture review

Necessary target. The weakest endpoint identified, sufficient and not shown necessary: for each fixed \(\ell\ge2\), a polynomial-size family \(\Gamma_v\) and, for each \(v\), some set \(L_v\) of polynomials of any size such that \(1\notin C_D(\Gamma_v\cup L_v)\) at a cutoff \(D\) for which the engine's rate holds on \(\Gamma_v\cup L_v\). The form with non-affine \(L_v\) is parked: it is the thin-kernel or extension-count condition for a larger closed space, and has no candidate. With affine \(L_v\), the working form, this is \(D=\lfloor n/2-s\rfloor\), \(s=o(n/(\log n)^{\ell-2})\), on an affine subspace of dimension \(n\ge v^{1/C}\).

Extra requirements. The route had demanded more in two places. It asked that the affine equations be rows of the formula, with a bounded-width encoding; they may be auxiliary. And it treated the closure of the family as the object to be thin; any proper closed space containing the family will do, which is the same remark, already noted in Working context for kernels and not used for the endpoint. A requirement not known to be droppable inside this engine: a cutoff at half of what the closed space shatters, proved necessary only for the two alternative hypotheses.

Independent alternative. Given only the goal, the engine and the block's results with their scopes, the review's medium reviewer answered that it found no clean escape from near half: for down-closed standard sets the required rate is essentially equivalent to the thin condition, and a weighted potential gives the same loss. It proposed three changes: design the closed space instead of the family (any proper closed \(W\supseteq\Gamma\)); prove the rate only for the prefactors that occur; shrink the input degree by applying the engine level by level. The first is adopted for affine additional axioms only, in the lemma below; its general form, a closed space that is thin, is parked with the alternative endpoints, and its proposed falsifier, an exhaustive enumeration of maximal closed spaces on a small system, was not run. The second is expected by the reviewer and by the heuristic below to fail on the cube. The third in its level-by-level form is, in my reading and not checked by the reviewer, the main notebook's route, to which this notebook is the alternative; in its other form it gains one logarithm. Record: independent-review.txt.

Rank normalization. Losses and survivors are counted in one quotient, and the last review asked whether relative contraction could replace absolute smallness. The block answers, for the two proved sufficient conditions: the rate they give is limited by the largest cube inside the standard monomials of the closed space and holds only from half that cube's dimension. Normalizing by the quotient instead of by the variables changes which cube is meant and nothing else.

Decision. Keep the engine and the first open statement, in the hidden-subspace form. Park the thin-kernel and extension-count endpoints, also for larger closed spaces; they stay as recorded sufficient conditions with a necessary condition and no candidate. Since the obstacle is a lower-bound method, the next test is of a method, not of another endpoint.

Decisive test. Next cycle: read Alekhnovich–Razborov's immunity theorem in full and decide whether it applies to rows that are relations on linear forms when the forms of any \(r\) rows are independent, and with which constant. By the recorded form of its Theorem 3.8, degree above \(r(l/4-(s-c))\), ideal expansion \(s=c\) and maximal immunity \(l=k/2\) on \(r\le n/k\) rows give at most \(n/8\). If the theorem applies with that constant, the dense-parity class has a proved linear barrier at an eighth of the free dimension and the missing implication becomes a factor of four in a named theorem; then examine whether its proof loses that factor necessarily. If it does not apply to forms, state where the proof uses variables. In the same cycle attempt to make the dimension count rigorous for parity-row systems of bounded \(k\): a proved ceiling of the heuristic size, a constant fraction below half for every such system, would end the dense-parity class and with it the hidden-subspace form for bounded-width formulas, and the route would then have to change the engine.

Auxiliary axioms are free

Lemma (auxiliary axiom endpoint). Let \(\Gamma\subseteq\mathbb F_2[x_1,\ldots,x_v]\) contain the Boolean axioms and let \(L\) be any set of polynomials in the same variables. If the system obtained from \(\Gamma\cup L\) by adding a family of ENS blocks has no PC refutation through degree \(B\), then neither has the system obtained from \(\Gamma\) by adding the same blocks. In particular, if \(L\) consists of affine polynomials of rank \(\varrho\) with \(1\notin\operatorname{span}L\), \(n=v-\varrho\), and \(1\notin C_D(\Gamma\cup L)\) for \(D=\lfloor n/2-s\rfloor\), \(s=o(n/(\log n)^{\ell-2})\), \(D\ge2\) and at least the degrees of \(\Gamma\), then the product-only ENS source over \(\Gamma\) with at most \(n^A\) blocks of accuracy \(\lfloor n^\epsilon\rfloor\), \(0<\epsilon<1/(3\ell)\), has no PC refutation through degree \(\lfloor n^{1/3}\rfloor\), for large \(n\).

Proof. A refutation from fewer axioms is a refutation from more. The second statement is the affine free dimension lemma and its consequence applied to \(\Gamma\cup L\), followed by the first statement. \(\square\)

Polynomial size enters only through the block count: a bound of \(v^{A'}\) blocks is covered when \(v\le n^C\). The reviewer's excerpts did not contain item 1 of the free-dimension lemma or the product-only grammar; both are as recorded in that entry and in the moving-cutoff theorem.

The formula whose Frege proofs are bounded is \(\Gamma\); \(L\) is used only in the analysis and may depend on \(v\) arbitrarily. Restricted to the zero set of \(L\), a clause of \(\Gamma\) on \(k\) variables becomes a relation on \(k\) linear forms in the free variables. So every bounded-width CNF carries, for each subspace, a parity-row system of the kind studied in the dense-parity entry, and the family is good if one of them is hard at half its dimension. For a random subspace of a random \(k\)-CNF these are the random instances for which the heuristic count is discouraging; the freedom lies in choosing formula and subspace together.

Specification. By the rule in Where we stand the weakened target is matched in the specification: the free-dimension count may use affine equations that are auxiliary and not rows of the formula, with the pairwise filtration condition read on the formula's rows together with them. This is a relaxation of the specification adopted in the free-dimension entry, so its witness, the guarded family with no affine equations, serves.

Why half stays

On the plain cube with only the Boolean axioms and cutoff \(K=\alpha v\), \(\alpha<1/2\), let the inputs be polynomials of degree \(d\) and \(q\) a combination of them. The engine's step multiplies the prefactor by \(1+q\), and the functions of degree at most \(K\) killed by it include the products \(qg\) of degree at most \(K\), which bounds the rank drop from below. Assume, as the semi-regularity hypothesis, that the kernel of \(1+q\) on \(V_K\) is exactly \(q\,V_{K-d}\) and that these products have dimension about \(N_v(K-d)-N_v(K-2d)+\cdots\), so one step lowers the rank by a factor about \(1/(1+\rho^d)\), \(\rho=\alpha/(1-\alpha)\), which is the engine's bound up to constants. With \(d\) polylogarithmic at the upper levels this is too little contraction unless \(\rho^d\) is at least an inverse polylogarithm, that is \(\alpha=1/2-O(\log\log v/d)\). This is a heuristic computation, not a proof that no choice of \(q\) does better; it agrees with the reviewer's expectation for its second proposal and with the main notebook's two-layer budget.

Falsification attempt on this line

The line's general claim after this block: some polynomial-size family is hard at half the dimension of some subspace. Three attacks. A general ceiling below half for all parity-row systems of bounded \(k\) would refute it; none is known, and the dense-parity proposition shows that no local argument gives one. The dimension count would refute it for random instances if made rigorous; it says nothing about structured ones. A general ceiling of about half for every unsatisfiable system would show the window is at most \(O(1)\) wide; it is neither proved nor refuted, as recorded. The claim survives because nothing is known in either direction, which is the weakest kind of survival.

Outside leads

  • Affine restrictions in proof complexity (Itsykson–Sokolov, Resolution over linear equations modulo two, where lower bounds are obtained by restricting to affine subspaces). Target: the Boolean PC family, by letting the subspace be chosen in the analysis. It would break if the source theorem needed the affine equations inside the formula. Answers. It turns the obstacle from "find a formula hard at half of its variables" into "find a formula hard at half of some subspace", a strictly larger search space. Test. Passed: the auxiliary axiom lemma above is proved; the source theorem does not need the equations in the formula.
  • Alekhnovich–Razborov immunity bound (Lower bounds for polynomial calculus: non-binomial case, Theorem 3.8, as recorded under cor:ar-criterion-dense-families: degree above \(r(l/4-(s-c))\) for \(l\)-immune constraints on an \((r,s,c)\)-expander). Target: a lower bound in the dense-parity class, where any \(r\le n/k\) rows have independent forms. It would break if the proof needs variables and not forms. Answers. It is a method, which is what the obstacle lacks, and the class offers it ideal expansion. Test. Falsified as a way to reach half, by the recorded form and not by a reading of the paper: with \(s=c\), \(l\le k/2\) and \(r\le n/k\) the bound is at most \(n/8\). Whether it applies to forms at all is the next cycle's test.
  • Clements–Lindström and Macaulay bounds (Clements and Lindström, A generalization of a combinatorial theorem of Macaulay). Target: a better rate for the engine than the Kruskal–Katona one. It would break if the bound is tight for down-closed families. Answers. A better rate would lower the cutoff below half of the shattered dimension. Test. Falsified: these theorems are the statement that the Kruskal–Katona families are extremal, so the rate is tight over down-closed families; the reviewer's independent remark on weighted potentials gives the same loss.
  • Sum-of-squares exactness on the cube (Sakaue, Takeda, Kim and Ito, exactness of the Lasserre hierarchy at level \(\lceil(n+d-1)/2\rceil\) for binary polynomial problems). Target: the undecided half ceiling for polynomial calculus over \(\mathbb F_2\). It would break because the proof uses positivity. Answers. A ceiling at half would fix the window's upper end and tell whether cutoffs above half can exist. Test. Not run: no analogue of the positivity step over \(\mathbb F_2\) was found or excluded in this cycle.

Absurd bridges

  • Coset leaders of cut codes. Translation: for binomial systems such as Tseitin in multiplicative variables, standard monomials are minimum-weight representatives of cosets of the cut space, so thin counts become counts of coset leaders of a given weight, and a covering-radius theorem would bound the shattered dimension. For a cubic graph on \(N\) vertices there are \(2^{N/2+1}\) cosets, thin from weight about \(N/4\), a sixth of the variables. Smallest test: whether the translation exists in characteristic two. Answers. It would give a family whose quotient is small for a structural reason. Test. Falsified for the parity formulation over the goal's field: its multiplicative variables need characteristic different from two, and over \(\mathbb F_2\) Tseitin parity systems are refuted in constant degree. Binomial systems modulo an odd prime over an extension of \(\mathbb F_2\) containing the roots of unity were not tried.
  • Whitney numbers of matroids. Translation: with affine axioms kept in the original variables, a monomial on a dependent set is reducible and monomials on bases of one flat agree modulo lower degree, so standard monomials of degree \(j\) would be counted by flats of rank \(j\), and unimodality theorems for Whitney numbers would describe the levels. Smallest test: compare with the count in free coordinates. Answers. It would let the choice of subspace thin the quotient. Test. Falsified: an affine substitution preserves the degree filtration, so the Hilbert function is that of the cube on the free variables in any coordinates; the flats count the same \(\binom nj\) classes and nothing is gained.

Checks, scope and verification

Scope. The lemma is a remark about supersets of axioms plus the previous entry's lemma. The paragraph on why half stays is heuristic. No lower bound is claimed for any family. The preceding entry, which had no reviewer, is covered by this review's second stage.

Corrections to the preceding entry. The shatter-breaking entry had no reviewer; this review's second stage found three points. Its \(\alpha\) column uses the bound \((1-c^k)^m\le e^{-mc^k}\), so it is an upper bound on the first-moment value and not that value: with the exact exponent \(-\Delta\ln(1-c^k)\) the reviewer's hand arithmetic gives about \(0.531\) at \((3,4.27)\) and \(0.402\) at \((3,10)\), and the ratios become about \(0.52\) and \(0.64\); the thinness threshold \(c^*\) shares the approximation, on the conservative side. "Destroys shattering exactly as fast as it derives narrow clauses" should read "at least as fast"; only that direction is shown. "Proved thin cutoff" should read "first-moment thin cutoff". The entry's conclusion is unaffected.

Follow-ups whose status changed. The thin-kernel and extension-count endpoints are parked. The sub-ideas asking for frames with a better ratio are answered by the frame ratio corollary.

Verification gate. The review's single medium reviewer worked in two stages. Stage one is described under Independent alternative. Stage two passed the lemma and required corrections that are applied: \(D\ge2\) is stated and the unused bound \(v\le n^C\) moved to a remark; the adoption of the reviewer's first proposal is limited to affine axioms and the non-affine form is parked, not dropped; every statement resting on the semi-regularity heuristic is marked as heuristic, its assumption is stated, and its conclusion corrected to \(\alpha=1/2-O(\log\log v/d)\); the immunity lead's outcome is attributed to the recorded form; the decisive test gains an outcome that would end the dense-parity class; the coset-leader outcome is narrowed; three corrections to the preceding entry are recorded. Not checked by the reviewer: item 1 of the free-dimension lemma, the product-only grammar, and the identification of the level-by-level proposal with the main notebook's route. Dependencies reread in full: the free-dimension entry, the moving-cutoff entry, the six entries of the block. Records: review.txt, stage-one brief.

Sub-ideas

  • Carry out the decisive test: read Alekhnovich–Razborov's proof and decide whether Theorem 3.8 holds for rows on linear forms with locally independent forms, and with which constant.
  • For the hidden-subspace endpoint, choose formula and subspace together: describe which parity-row systems arise as restrictions of polynomial-size bounded-width CNFs, and whether structured ones with many syzygies among row multiples are among them.
  • Test binomial systems modulo an odd prime over an extension field of \(\mathbb F_2\) for the coset-leader translation, and whether the source theorem admits that field.
  • Make the semi-regularity heuristic for one engine step on the cube rigorous for some explicit \(q\) of degree two, or find a \(q\) that contracts faster.

Process assessment. Twelve research entries and two reviews in this session have changed the statement of the first open obligation three times, each time to something weaker, and have not changed its status. The block's errors were of one kind, overstating a sufficient condition as a weakening or as general, and the reviewer caught each. The honest position is that the route has a clean target and no method; the decisive test is therefore aimed at the one classical method the dense-parity class might admit.

Decision. Core: the first open statement, the Boolean PC family in its hidden-subspace form, is worked next, by the decisive test above. No publication, stopping or Lean work follows from this review.

9 October 2026 — Whether expansion bounds reach half on parity rows depends on the notion of expansion for linear forms

No result: budgets under two readings of expansion and a count, none proved; applicability to linear forms is the open point. Architecture test after the subspace-endpoint review. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort low).

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement, the review named the obstacle as a lower-bound method and asked whether Alekhnovich–Razborov's theorems apply to rows on linear forms and with which constant, and whether the dimension count can be made a ceiling. Before reading the proof for forms: if the theorems did apply with ideal expansion, how close to half could they come? If the best case is far from half, the method is not the missing one whatever its applicability.

Architecture test. Outcome of the decisive test named in the subspace-endpoint review: undecided, and sharpened. The source was not read beyond the statement recorded in the earlier entry. Evaluated in a random model under the assumption that the theorems extend to forms: if a set of rows expands only when all its forms are independent, Theorem 3.13 stays below \(n/4\) and Theorem 3.8 below about \(0.16n\); but if expansion is measured by rank, the reviewer's estimate is that sets of \(n/k\) rows have rank deficiency only of order \(\sqrt n\), and an extension of Theorem 3.13 would then give about \(n/2\) for rows forbidding a single tuple. So for Theorem 3.13 the applicability to forms, and with which notion of expansion, is the whole question, not a side issue. Theorem 3.8 is below a quarter under either reading. The dimension count was evaluated and is not a ceiling: the same count on random 3-CNF gives degree about \(n^{2/3}\), where the true degree is linear.

New mathematics. None is proved. Two first-moment evaluations for \(m\) rows on \(k\) random forms each, forbidding a fraction \(2^{-\beta k}\) of value tuples. First, the largest number \(r\) of rows such that all sets of \(r\) rows are expected to have independent forms, and the resulting best case of the two theorems and of two hypothetical stronger ones. Second, the degree at which the multiples of balanced generic rows of width \(k=c\log_2n\) number as many as the monomials: \(\alpha(c)n\) with \(\alpha(c)=\tfrac12-\tfrac12\sqrt{1-4^{-1/c}}\).

Goal progress. Unchanged. The entry supplies neither a family nor a bound. It shows that Theorem 3.8 is not the missing method in the random model under either reading, and that Theorem 3.13 could be only under a rank notion of expansion whose validity is untested.

General statement. No new all-parameter claim. The entry concerns the class of prop:dense-parity-local-filtration and the endpoint of lem:auxiliary-axiom-endpoint; its numbers are evaluations of closed formulas under stated assumptions.

Best case of expansion and immunity

The recorded statements: for constraints on the rows of an \((r,s,c)\)-expander, Theorem 3.8 gives degree above \(r(\ell/4-(s-c))\) when every constraint is \(\ell\)-immune, and Theorem 3.13 gives degree above \(rc/2\) for constraints forbidding a single tuple. Suppose both held for rows on linear forms, with a set of rows counted as fully expanding when all its forms are independent, so \(c=s=k\). This extension is an assumption, and so is this strict notion of expansion; the rank notion is treated after the table. The model is random forms and generic predicates; structured systems, which need only \(2^{\beta k}\) rows, are not covered.

The budget is then limited by how many rows can be independent in every set while the system is unsatisfiable. With forbidden fraction \(2^{-\beta k}\) the first moment needs \(m=n\ln2\cdot2^{\beta k}\) rows, and sets of \(r=\rho n\) rows with dependent forms are expected once \(\log_2\binom mr+kr>n\). A generic predicate with that forbidden fraction has immunity \(\lambda k\) with \(H_2(\lambda)=1-\beta\), \(\lambda\ge\tfrac12\). Evaluation (output, script), as fractions of \(n\); the grid makes the last digit unreliable at \(k\ge20\) (at \(k=40\), \(\beta=1\) the true \(rk\) is about \(0.458\)):

\(k\)\(\beta\)\(rk\)Thm 3.13, \(rk/2\)Thm 3.8, \(r\ell/4\)hypothetical \(r\ell/2\)hypothetical \(r\ell\)
310.2910.1460.0730.1460.291
1010.3900.1950.0980.1950.390
4010.4400.2200.1100.2200.440
100.250.570–0.1120.2240.448
200.250.640–0.1260.2510.503
400.250.700–0.1370.2750.550

Under strict independence, for single forbidden tuples the independent rows carry less than half of the dimension, because unsatisfiability needs \(2^kn\) rows and sets of rows spanning half the space then become dependent; Theorem 3.13 stays below \(n/4\). Predicates with larger forbidden sets allow more independent rows but have lower immunity; as \(k\) grows \(rk\) tends to \(1/(1+\beta)\), so Theorem 3.8 tends to \(\lambda/(4(1+\beta))\), below about \(0.16n\), and a bound \(r\ell/2\) to about \(0.32n\).

Rank expansion. The strict notion is not the only reading. If a set \(I\) of rows is credited with the rank of its forms, a deficiency \(t\) has probability about \(2^{-t(n-k|I|+t)}\), and by the reviewer's estimate \(t\) of order \(\sqrt{2n}\) already beats the union bound at \(|I|=n/k\). Then \(rc\) is \(n(1-o(1))\) and a version of Theorem 3.13 for forms with this notion would give about \(n/2\) for single forbidden tuples, with a deficit of order \(k\sqrt n\), inside what the goal allows. Neither the estimate nor such a version is proved. A consistency test is available at \(k=2\): the rows are then products of two affine forms, a quadratic system with about \(2.8n\) equations, and refutation degrees of generic quadratic systems of that density are believed to be a small fraction of \(n\); if that holds for these products, a rank-expansion version of Theorem 3.13 is false at \(k=2\). So either the extension fails, or products of affine forms are far harder than generic quadratics. Both outcomes are informative and neither is established here.

The dimension count, and why it is not a ceiling

For a generic balanced predicate on \(k\) forms the leading monomials of its row ideal are, up to lower order, the monomials of degree above \(k/2\) in the forms. The degree-\(\alpha n\) multiples of one row then fill about a fraction \(2^{-kD(1/2\,\|\,\alpha)}\) of the monomials of that degree, \(D\) the binary relative entropy. With about \(n\) rows, the multiples are as many as the monomials when \(D(\tfrac12\|\alpha)=\log_2n/k=1/c\), which is \(\alpha(c)=\tfrac12-\tfrac12\sqrt{1-4^{-1/c}}\): \(0.229\) at \(c=4\), \(0.356\) at \(c=16\), \(0.441\) at \(c=100\), \(0.481\) at \(c=1000\). If the multiples were as independent as their number allows and filled the space, the system would be refuted near \(\alpha(c)n\). Canonical tables of width \(c\log_2n\) have size \(n^c\), so for every polynomial size the deficit is a constant fraction of \(n\), of order \(n/\sqrt c\), while the goal allows \(o(n)\) at depth two and less above. Only rows wider than logarithmic, hence with succinct non-canonical descriptions, would bring the count to half, and such descriptions use non-affine auxiliary variables, which the free-dimension count does not ignore.

This count is not a ceiling. Leading monomials covering most monomials does not derive \(1\), and the same count applied to random 3-CNF with about \(5n\) clauses gives degree about \(n^{2/3}\), while the true degree there is linear. So it underestimates the degree on the one family where the truth is known, and it is recorded only as the point below which nothing forces a refutation by counting. The series used for semi-regular systems, which accounts for the obvious syzygies, would be the better estimate and was not evaluated.

Outcome

In the random model Theorem 3.8 is below a quarter of the free dimension under either reading of expansion. Theorem 3.13 is below a quarter under strict independence and could reach about half under rank expansion, for rows forbidding a single tuple on \(k\) random forms, that is for the restriction of a random \(k\)-CNF to a random subspace. Whether its proof admits forms with that notion is now the route's sharpest question, with a consistency test at \(k=2\). The counting argument gives no ceiling.

Specification decision. No change. Nothing here weakens the target. Considered: restricting the specification to rows wider than logarithmic, since the count disfavours logarithmic width. The count is not a ceiling and the restriction would exclude the only class with a proved local property; not adopted.

Verification gate. One fresh-context medium reviewer checked two output rows, the table, the immunity value, the closed form and its quoted values by hand, and required corrections that are applied: the negative conclusion for Theorem 3.13 held only for strict independence, and under rank expansion its hypothetical extension gives about \(n/2\); the model is random, not the whole class; the limits \(0.16n\) and \(0.32n\) replace table maxima; the grid's precision is stated; the dimension count is not a ceiling, by the random 3-CNF calibration; a sentence comparing it with the hypothetical bound \(r\ell\) is deleted. Not verified by anyone in this cycle: the recorded statements of Theorems 3.8 and 3.13 against the source, the rank-deficiency estimate, and the belief about generic quadratic systems. Record: review.txt.

Follow-up. No queue item is developed; the entry performs the review's architecture test, which the turn guidance requires first.

  • Read Alekhnovich–Razborov's proof of Theorem 3.13 and decide whether it holds for rows on linear forms with expansion measured by rank; prove the rank-deficiency estimate for random forms.

  • Look for an \(\mathbb F_2\) system with one or few wide rows and knapsack-like syzygies whose rows have succinct descriptions by affine auxiliaries only; the symmetric functions of block parities are the first case to examine.

9 October 2026 — The expansion proof's elimination step has a semantic analogue for linear forms but no operator built on it

Working proof of the semantic step and a refutation of its term-order analogue; no degree bound for forms is obtained. Research cycle reading the Alekhnovich–Razborov proof for rows on linear forms. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort low).

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement, the immunity budget left one sharp question: does the proof of Alekhnovich–Razborov's Theorem 3.13 work for rows forbidding one tuple of values of \(k\) linear forms, with expansion measured by rank? A yes would give a barrier near half of the free dimension for a random \(k\)-CNF restricted to a random subspace; a no should name the step that needs variables.

New mathematics. The proof was read in the source (Sections 2.3 and 3 through Lemma 3.17). Its one algebraic step, Lemma 3.14, removes a row \(Q\) divisible by \(z-\epsilon\) for a variable \(z\) occurring neither in the other rows \(P\) nor in the term \(t\), by the restriction \(z=\epsilon\). For forms there is a correct semantic analogue: if a form \(\ell\) of the row lies outside the span of the other rows' forms and of the variables of a polynomial \(g\), the projection onto the hyperplane \(\ell=\epsilon\) along a direction on which all of those vanish kills \(Q\), fixes \(P\) and \(g\), and does not raise degree. But the lemma's conclusion concerns leading terms, and the projection does not preserve them: with \(Q=x_1+x_2+\epsilon\), no other rows and \(t=x_1\), the hypothesis holds and the conclusion fails. The same holds with \(t=x_2\) when \(x_2\) is on top, so the stated analogue of Lemma 3.14 fails for every admissible order. Moreover no linear operator on the monomial basis can be invariant under adding rows with a private direction in this rank sense: on the same example invariance forces the operator to fix \(1,x_1,x_2\) and hence not to vanish on the axiom. This does not exclude a different proof of the step, or an operator on another basis.

Goal progress. Unchanged. No lower bound for rows on forms is obtained. The rank reading of expansion that made half look reachable in the preceding entry has no operator of the Alekhnovich–Razborov kind behind it; what is left is an operator on a non-monomial basis or with a support rule that is not symmetric in ranks, for which there is no proposal.

General statement. lem:private-direction-projection holds over \(\mathbb F_2\) for every polynomial system, form and polynomial satisfying its hypothesis. ex:private-direction-leading-term refutes the leading-term analogue for every admissible order, and the rank-invariant operator on the monomial basis.

The proof, as read

Source: Alekhnovich and Razborov, Lower bounds for polynomial calculus: non-binomial case, author manuscript, pages 9–17 (not redistributed). The lower bound comes from a linear operator \(R\) on polynomials of degree at most \(d\) with \(R(f_i)=0\) for the axioms and \(R(x_jt)=R(x_jR(t))\) for terms of degree below \(d\) (Lemma 2.10); \(R\ne0\) then excludes a refutation of degree \(d\). It is defined by \(R(t)=R_{\mathrm{Span}(\mathrm{Sup}(t))}(t)\), the classical reduction of the term \(t\), for a fixed admissible order, modulo the ideal of a small set of rows. For Theorem 3.13 a set \(I_1\) of at most \(r/2\) rows is inferred from \(I\) when every boundary variable of \(I_1\) lies in the rows of \(I\) or in \(t\) (Definition 3.15); \(\mathrm{Sup}(t)\) is what can be inferred from the empty set. Lemma 3.16: for \(\deg t\le cr/2\), \(|\mathrm{Sup}(t)|\le r/2\), because the boundary of the inferred rows lies inside the variables of \(t\). Lemma 3.17: for \(I\supseteq\mathrm{Sup}(t)\), \(|I|\le r/2\), \(R_{\mathrm{Span}(I)}(t)=R_{\mathrm{Span}(\mathrm{Sup}(t))}(t)\); a row of \(I\setminus\mathrm{Sup}(t)\) has a boundary variable \(z\) outside \(t\), and is removed by Lemma 3.14: if \(Q\) is divisible by \(z-\epsilon\), \(z\) occurs neither in \(P\) nor in \(t\), and \(t\) is the leading term of some \(f\) with \(P,Q\models f\), then \(t\) is the leading term of \(f|_{z=\epsilon}\) and \(P\models f|_{z=\epsilon}\).

For rows on forms the combinatorial steps have rank analogues: the variables of \(t\) span a space \(U_t\) of dimension \(\deg t\); a row has a private direction relative to \(I\) and \(t\) when one of its forms lies outside \(W=\operatorname{span}(\text{forms of }I\setminus\{i\})+U_t\); and a count of private directions against \(\dim U_t\) plays the role of Lemma 3.16. These analogues are not written out here, because the step they feed fails.

The semantic step holds

Lemma (private direction projection). Work over \(\mathbb F_2\) on \(\{0,1\}^n=\mathbb F_2^n\). Let \(W\) be a space of linear forms, \(\ell\notin W\) a linear form, \(\epsilon\in\mathbb F_2\). Choose \(u\in\mathbb F_2^n\) with \(\lambda(u)=0\) for all \(\lambda\in W\) and \(\ell(u)=1\), and put \(\pi(x)=x+(\ell(x)+\epsilon)u\), \(g^\pi=g\circ\pi\). Then:

  1. \(\pi\) maps \(\mathbb F_2^n\) onto the hyperplane \(\ell=\epsilon\) and fixes it pointwise; \(g^\pi\) has degree at most \(\deg g\) as a multilinear polynomial;
  2. \(g^\pi=g\) for every polynomial \(g\) in forms of \(W\), in particular for every polynomial in variables whose coordinate forms lie in \(W\);
  3. if \(Q\) is divisible, as a function, by \(\ell+\epsilon\), then \(Q^\pi=0\);
  4. if \(P\) is a set of polynomials in forms of \(W\), \(Q\) is as in 3, and \(P\cup\{Q\}\models f\), then \(P\models f^\pi\).

Proof. Such \(u\) exists because \(\ell\notin W\). 1. \(\ell(\pi(x))=\ell(x)+(\ell(x)+\epsilon)=\epsilon\), and \(\pi(x)=x\) when \(\ell(x)=\epsilon\). Each coordinate of \(\pi(x)\) is an affine polynomial in \(x\) over \(\mathbb F_2\), so composition does not raise degree, and multilinear reduction does not either. 2. \(\lambda(\pi(x))=\lambda(x)\) for \(\lambda\in W\). 3. \(Q\) vanishes on the hyperplane. 4. If \(P(x)=0\), then \(P(\pi(x))=0\) by 2 and \(Q(\pi(x))=0\) by 3, so \(f(\pi(x))=0\). \(\square\)

So a row with a private direction can be eliminated from any semantic consequence whose statement lives in \(W\): if \(P\) and \(g\) are polynomials in forms of \(W\), \(Q\) is as in 3 and \(P,Q\models g\), then \(P\models g\). The degree statement in 1 is not used below. This is the content of Lemma 3.14 for forms, without the leading term.

The leading-term step fails

Example (private direction, leading term). Let \(n=2\), \(P=\emptyset\), \(Q=x_1+x_2+\epsilon\), \(t=x_1\), and take any admissible order with \(x_1\succ x_2\). Here \(Q=\ell+\epsilon\) with \(\ell=x_1+x_2\), which lies outside \(U_t=\operatorname{span}(x_1)\), so the row has a private direction relative to \(t\). The term \(t\) is the leading term of \(Q\), hence reducible modulo \(\mathrm{Span}(P,Q)\). It is not reducible modulo \(\mathrm{Span}(P)\), which contains only the Boolean axioms. So the analogue of Lemma 3.14 with "\(\ell\notin\operatorname{span}(P)+U_t\)" in place of "\(z\) occurs neither in \(P\) nor in \(t\)" is false; if \(x_2\succ x_1\), take \(t=x_2\). The example has one row and \(k=1\); it refutes the stated analogue, not every possible proof of the step it serves.

No rank-invariant operator on monomials. In the same example \(\ell\) lies outside \(U_g\) for each of \(g=1,x_1,x_2\), so the row has a private direction relative to each. An operator \(R\) whose value on a term is its reduction modulo the rows without a private direction relative to that term must then reduce each of them modulo the Boolean axioms alone, which is the identity. By linearity \(R(Q)=Q\ne0\), contradicting \(R(f_i)=0\). The same happens at \(k=2\) for \(Q=(x_1+x_2+\epsilon)(x_3+x_4+\delta)\), since no term of \(Q\) has either form in its \(U_t\). The cause is that the lemma gives invariance of ideal membership inside the polynomials in forms of \(W\), and \(W\) changes with the term, so the invariances do not assemble into one linear operator on the term basis. This objection was found by the reviewer.

The projection shows why: here \(u=(0,1)\), \(\pi(x)=(x_1,x_1+\epsilon)\), and \(Q^\pi=0\) as the lemma says, but the polynomial witnessing reducibility is \(Q\) itself and its image is zero; the leading term is not preserved under \(\pi\), because \(\pi\) replaces variables outside \(t\) by forms involving variables of any rank in the order. In the variable case the restriction \(z=\epsilon\) touches no other variable. Requiring instead that the top variable of \(\ell\) in the order be outside \(t\) and outside \(P\) restores the proof but is the variable hypothesis again: with dense forms the top variables of the forms of different rows are few and lie in every other row.

What is left. An operator as in Lemma 2.10 on a basis other than monomials in the given variables, or with a support rule that is not symmetric in ranks, for instance one tied to a distinguished coordinate system per row. No such construction is proposed. A reason for doubt about the conclusion itself, recorded in the preceding entry and still untested: at \(k=2\) it would give degree near \(n/2\) for about \(2.8n\) products of two random affine forms, against the belief that such quadratic systems are refuted at a small fraction of \(n\).

Considered: requiring candidates in the hidden-subspace form to have, for some term order, top variables of their rows' forms spread as in a variable expander, so that the original proof applies. That is the variable case, where expansion is limited as the budget entry computed; not adopted.

9 October 2026 — A small test of random parity 2-clauses matches the series within one and does not separate it from a barrier near half

Finite check with a conjecture stated as an untested hypothesis; the test is too small to decide the question it was run for. Research cycle running the consistency test. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort low).

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement, the last two entries left a test: is the refutation degree of random products of two affine forms near \(n/2\), as a rank-expansion bound would give, or a small fraction of \(n\), as the series for semi-regular systems would give? The preceding entries cited the second as a general belief. A belief is not evidence (user, 9 October 2026: "Our research is evidence based"); this entry runs the test and says what it does and does not show.

New mathematics. A finite check. For \(m=3n\) products of two random affine forms, the static refutation degree found is \(3\) at \(n=12\) and \(n=16\) and \(4\) at \(n=20\), three instances each; the series index is \(3\) at all three sizes. The test does not separate the two hypotheses: the rank-expansion reading predicts a degree above about \(n/2-\sqrt{2n}\) at \(k=2\), which is between one and four at these sizes. The conjecture that the series governs the degree is registered as a hypothesis to test, with this check as its only support.

Goal progress. Unchanged. No conclusion about a barrier near half follows from this check, in either direction. The statements of the two preceding entries that rested on the belief are corrected below.

General statement. conj:parity-clause-semiregular-degree is the all-parameter hypothesis under test; ex:parity-two-clause-static-degree is the check at \(k=2\), density three, \(n\le20\).

The test

Stated before the run: for \(k=2\), \(m=3n\), the series \((1+t)^n/(1+t^2)^m\) has its first non-positive coefficient at degree \(3\) for \(n=12,16,20\). The script computes the least \(D\le4\) for which \(1\) lies in the \(\mathbb F_2\)-span of the multilinear products \(x_Tf_i\) with \(|T|\le D-2\). Products with \(|T|=D-1\) whose degree drops are not used, so the reported value can exceed the true static degree and never falls below it; the static degree in turn bounds the polynomial-calculus degree from above. Forms are uniform, conditioned to be nonzero and distinct within a row. Arithmetic is exact over \(\mathbb F_2\); at most \(6196\) monomials and \(12660\) products; the nine instances took seven seconds.

Results: results.json, script. The script's stated prediction, equality with the index, failed at \(n=20\) by one. There the series coefficient at degree three is \(-60\) out of \(1140\); whether the excess is real or an effect of the multiplier convention is not determined. Three sizes with excess \(0,0,1\) cannot tell a constant excess from slow growth.

What the test can distinguish. It shows that these systems are unsatisfiable with certificates of degree at most \(3\) or \(4\), at most half of \(n/2\). The hypothesis it was meant to test against is not \(n/2\) itself but \(n/2\) minus a deficit of order \(k\sqrt n\); with the estimate of the immunity budget, \(n/2-\sqrt{2n}\) at \(k=2\), which is about \(1.1\), \(2.3\) and \(3.7\) at \(n=12,16,20\). Sizes at which they separate by at least three are \(n\) of about forty and more, where the static computation has millions of monomials and needs a compiled kernel.

The series at larger sizes. Evaluated, not tested (output, script): at density \(\ln2\cdot2^k\) the index divided by \(n\) is \(0.080,0.055,0.044\) for \(k=2\) at \(n=100,400,1600\); \(0.130,0.100,0.087\) for \(k=3\); \(0.170,0.135,0.119\) for \(k=4\); \(0.230,0.183,0.163\) for \(k=6\). The ratio is still decreasing in \(n\), and only these four widths were evaluated. These are values of a formula; whether the formula describes these systems is the conjecture.

The hypothesis and its status

Conjecture (parity clause semi-regular degree). For fixed \(k\ge2\) and \(m\ge\ln2\cdot2^kn\) independent rows, each forbidding one uniformly random tuple of values of \(k\) independent uniform linear forms on \(n\) Boolean variables, the polynomial-calculus refutation degree over \(\mathbb F_2\) is, with probability tending to one, at most the index of regularity of \((1+t)^n/(1+t^k)^m\) plus \(o(n)\). Separately, and only suggested by the evaluated values: that index is at most \(c_kn\) with \(c_k<1/2\).

Status: untested beyond the check above, which covers \(k=2\), density three, \(n\le20\), with forms conditioned as stated, and which agrees with the index within one. I have read no source on the semi-regularity of such systems in this cycle, and none is recorded in the registry. No decision of the route is based on this conjecture.

Corrections to the two preceding entries. The immunity budget and the private-direction entry each give, as a reason for doubt, "the belief that such quadratic systems are refuted at a small fraction of \(n\)". That reason is withdrawn as evidence; it is the conjecture above, untested at sizes that matter. What stands from those entries without it: the semantic lemma, the refutation of the leading-term analogue and of the rank-invariant operator on monomials, and the budgets under their stated assumptions.

What would decide it. A computation at sizes where the predictions differ by at least three, with the prediction of each hypothesis stated in advance from saved formulas; or a proof of an upper bound of the form \(cn\), \(c<1/2\), for the degree at \(k=2\); or a proof of a lower bound. The first is a build: a compiled kernel for the static span over \(\mathbb F_2\) on FLINT or fflas-ffpack, sized before it is run.

The rewritten text was not sent back to the reviewer; it only removes or weakens claims. Record: review.txt.

9 October 2026 — At up to twenty-eight variables parity 2-clauses are refuted in degree four, below the explicit forms of the near-half bound at the larger sizes

Refutation of two explicit numerical forms by exact computation; the asymptotic question stays open. Research cycle with a compiled kernel. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort low).

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement, the preceding check could not separate the semi-regular series from a barrier near half for random products of two affine forms. With a compiled kernel, at sizes where the predictions written down beforehand differ, which one do the measured degrees follow? The predictions were saved before the run: series index \(4\) at \(n=24,28,32\); \(n/2-\sqrt{2n}=5.07,6.52,8.0\); \(n/2-\sqrt{n/2}=8.54,10.26,12.0\).

New mathematics. A refutation by exact instances. For \(m=3n\) products of two random affine forms, three instances each, \(1\) lies in the span of the products \(x_Tf_i\), \(|T|\le D-2\), at \(D=4\) for \(n=24\) and \(n=28\). So the polynomial-calculus degree is at most \(4\) there, below \(n/2-\sqrt{2n}\) at both sizes, and the degrees found are below \(n/2-\sqrt{n/2}\) at every size from \(12\) to \(28\). At \(n=32\) no certificate exists through \(D=4\) under this multiplier convention, so the value computed there is at least five, above the series index of four.

Goal progress. Unchanged. Two explicit forms of a near-half bound for these systems are refuted at the sizes run. A bound \(n/2-c\sqrt n\) with a larger constant, about two or more, fits all the data, and so does a small linear rate; the sizes reachable do not separate them.

General statement. conj:parity-clause-semiregular-degree remains the all-parameter hypothesis under test; in its registered form, index plus \(o(n)\), it is compatible with the data, and the value computed under the multiplier convention exceeds the index at \(n=20\) and \(n=32\); the polynomial-calculus degree itself may still equal it. ex:parity-two-clause-bound-forms-refuted records the instances.

Kernel and validation

The kernel (span_kernel.cpp) reads an instance, builds each product \(x_Tf_i\) with \(|T|\le D-2\) as a bit vector over the multilinear monomials of degree at most \(D\), and eliminates incrementally with one stored pivot row per leading column; exact over \(\mathbb F_2\). Instances come from the generator of the preceding entry (gen_instances.py). On the nine instances solved by the Python check it returns the same degrees, \(3,3,3,3,3,3,4,4,4\), with full rank (validation.jsonl against the Python results.json). This agreement is one integer per instance; ranks at failing degrees were not compared. No second linear-algebra library was used. For \(n\ge24\) there is no cross-check and the kernel outputs no certificate, only the answer; the reviewer read the kernel and found no error. The \(n=32\) records lack the rank at degree four because the driver discards the kernel's progress output.

9 October 2026 — No bound proved for rows that are unions of two hyperplanes

No result: two proof attempts for random parity 2-clause systems fail; the asymptotic law stays open. Research cycle attempting a proof after the measurements. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort low).

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement, the measurements left the asymptotic refutation degree of \(3n\) random products of two affine forms open between a law \(n/2-c\sqrt n\) and a small linear rate. Can either an upper bound \(cn\) with \(c<1/2\) or a lower bound of order \(n\) be proved from the structure of the rows, each a union of two hyperplanes? A proved upper bound would close random parity 2-clauses as a source; a lower bound would be the first for rows on dense forms.

New mathematics. None. Two attempts at an upper bound are recorded with the step at which each fails, and no approach to a lower bound was found.

Goal progress. Unchanged. No bound in either direction is proved for random parity 2-clause systems, so the first open statement, a family hard at half the dimension of some subspace, has neither a candidate nor a method more than before; the Frege transfer is untouched.

General statement. No new all-parameter claim. The hypothesis under test remains conj:parity-clause-semiregular-degree, untested beyond the registered instances; nothing in this entry supports or weakens it.

Attempt 1: branch on literals, then linearize

A row \((\ell_1+b_1)(\ell_2+b_2)=0\) says \(\ell_1=b_1+1\) or \(\ell_2=b_2+1\). Branching on the value of a linear form costs one degree in polynomial calculus over \(\mathbb F_2\). After branching on \(t\) independent forms the system lives on an affine space of dimension \(n'=n-t\) and still has about \(3n\) quadratic rows. If \(3n\) exceeds the number \(\binom{n'}2+n'+1\) of multilinear monomials of degree at most two and the restricted rows span them, the branch is refuted in degree two. This needs \(n'\) about \(\sqrt{6n}\), so the total degree is \(n-\sqrt{6n}+2\), far above \(n/2\). The spanning statement was not proved either. Branching less and finishing in higher degree needs a bound on the degree at which the multiples of the restricted rows span, which is the original question at a higher density.

Attempt 2: count multiples

At degree \(D\) there are \(3n\binom{n}{\le D-2}\) multiples against \(\binom n{\le D}\) monomials, more multiples than monomials from \(D\) of order \(\sqrt n\) on. A refutation at such a degree follows if the multiples have nearly full rank, and that is what cannot be shown: the multiples satisfy the relations \(f_if_j=f_jf_i\) and \(f_i^2=f_i\), and the claim that there are essentially no others is the semi-regularity hypothesis itself. As far as I recall, and without a source read in this cycle, this hypothesis is unproved even for generic quadratic forms; the statement is therefore marked as recollection, and nothing here rests on it. For products of two affine forms there is the additional relation \((\ell_1+b_1+1)\cdot f=0\) for each factor, a linear syzygy generic quadrics do not have, so even the generic heuristic does not transfer without change. That extra relation may be the reason the computed value exceeds the series index at \(n=20\) and \(n=32\); this is a guess.

Lower bound

No approach. The expansion method needs private variables and has no operator for private directions (recorded). A reduction from a known hard system would have to produce dense forms from sparse ones without lowering the degree, and none is known to me.

Outcome. The asymptotic degree of random parity 2-clause systems is not determined by proof or by reachable computation. The line of the last five entries, which followed a possible barrier for random parity rows, ends here without a result in either direction: no method gives a barrier, the two explicit forms written down were refuted at small sizes, and no ceiling is proved. The route returns to its main question.

Specification decision. No change; nothing is weakened or shown unnecessary.

Verification gate. No new lemma, theorem, rule or encoding; no reviewer was used. The monomial counts are the binomial expressions stated. One statement is marked as unverified recollection and carries no weight.

Follow-up. No queue item is developed; the entry carries out the step named by the preceding entry.

Sub-ideas

  • Account for the linear syzygies \((\ell+b+1)f=0\) of products of affine forms in the Hilbert series and compare the corrected index with the computed values at \(n=20\) and \(n=32\).
  • Read a source on the status of the semi-regularity hypothesis for Boolean quadratic systems before any further use of it.

Five entries since the review went into one possibility, a barrier for random parity rows; they produced a lemma, two refutations and measurements, and no change in the goal's missing implication. The queue is two items short of backpressure, so the coming entries will develop queued leads; the next review must weigh whether the engine can be kept without a lower-bound method.

9 October 2026 — A truncated Buchberger criterion certifies a proper closure by the pairs the lcm lattice shows below the cutoff

Working proof of a known-type criterion adapted to degree-bounded closures; a certificate format, not a lower bound. Queue development of the LCM-lattice lead while draining. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort low).

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement, the queue's head is the LCM-lattice lead of the global architecture review: the lcm lattice of leading monomials locates cancellations, and "a costed lift of these relations, including subsequent new relations and their multiplier images, could organize the global defect calculation". The route lacks a way to certify that a closure is proper at a cutoff. Does the lattice, cut off at the degree of the closure, give one? A criterion would say exactly which cancellations have to be checked for a candidate; if every pair must be checked for the systems of interest, the lead organizes the calculation without shortening it.

New mathematics. A truncated Buchberger criterion. If, for a set \(G\) of polynomials, every S-polynomial of two elements whose leading monomials have an lcm of degree at most \(D\) has a standard representation, then the static span of the multiples of \(G\) within degree \(D\) is closed, equals the closure \(C_D\) of any axiom set generating it, has exactly the monomials outside the leading-monomial ideal as standard monomials, and contains \(1\) only if \(G\) contains a constant. Pairs whose lcm has degree above \(D\) need no check, and pairs with coprime leading monomials resolve automatically.

Goal progress. Unchanged. The criterion is a format for a lower-bound proof and for the standard monomials the engine needs; it supplies no family. For rows that are clauses on dense linear forms the pairs with overlapping leading monomials and the pairs with Boolean axioms remain real obligations, and no shortcut for them is found.

General statement. lem:truncated-buchberger-closure holds over every field, for every degree-compatible monomial order, every cutoff and every finite \(G\) satisfying its pair condition.

The criterion

Work in \(F[x_1,\ldots,x_v]\) with a degree-compatible monomial order, so that the leading monomial \(\mathrm{LM}(f)\) has degree \(\deg f\). For a finite set \(G\) of nonzero polynomials of degree at most \(D\) and \(j\le D\) put

\[S_j(G)=\operatorname{span}\{\,m\,g:\ g\in G,\ m\text{ a monomial},\ \deg m+\deg g\le j\,\}.\]

For \(g,h\in G\) let \(L=\operatorname{lcm}(\mathrm{LM}g,\mathrm{LM}h)\) and \(S(g,h)=(L/\mathrm{LT}g)\,g-(L/\mathrm{LT}h)\,h\) the S-polynomial, with \(\mathrm{LT}\) the leading term including its coefficient. Say the pair is resolved if \(S(g,h)=\sum_ic_im_ig_i\) with \(g_i\in G\) and \(\mathrm{LM}(m_ig_i)\prec L\) for all \(i\).

Lemma (truncated Buchberger closure). Suppose every pair \(g,h\in G\) with \(\deg L\le D\) is resolved. Then:

  1. for \(j\le D\), every nonzero \(f\in S_j(G)\) has \(\mathrm{LM}(f)\) divisible by \(\mathrm{LM}(g)\) for some \(g\in G\), and \(f=\sum c_im_ig_i\) with \(\mathrm{LM}(m_ig_i)\preceq\mathrm{LM}(f)\);
  2. if \(f\in S_D(G)\) and \(\deg f\le D-1\), then \(x_af\in S_D(G)\) for every variable;
  3. if \(\Gamma\) is a set of polynomials whose elements of degree at most \(D\) lie in \(S_D(G)\), and \(G\subseteq C_D(\Gamma)\), then \(C_D(\Gamma)=S_D(G)\), where \(C_D\) is the smallest space containing the elements of \(\Gamma\) of degree at most \(D\) and closed under multiplying elements of degree at most \(D-1\) by variables;
  4. in that case \(1\in C_D(\Gamma)\) if and only if \(G\) contains a nonzero constant, and the standard monomials of \(C_D(\Gamma)\) of degree at most \(D\) are the monomials of degree at most \(D\) divisible by no \(\mathrm{LM}(g)\).

Proof. 1. Write \(f=\sum c_im_ig_i\) with \(\deg(m_ig_i)\le j\), and among such representations choose one whose largest leading monomial \(M=\max\mathrm{LM}(m_ig_i)\) is least, and then with fewest terms attaining \(M\). Suppose \(M\succ\mathrm{LM}(f)\). Then at least two terms attain \(M\) and their leading coefficients cancel, so the sum of the top terms is a combination of differences \(m_ig_i/\mathrm{lc}(g_i)-m_{i'}g_{i'}/\mathrm{lc}(g_{i'})=(M/L)\,S(g_i,g_{i'})\) with \(L=\operatorname{lcm}(\mathrm{LM}g_i,\mathrm{LM}g_{i'})\) dividing \(M\). Here \(\deg L\le\deg M\le j\le D\), so the pair is resolved: \(S(g_i,g_{i'})=\sum cmg\) with \(\mathrm{LM}(mg)\prec L\), hence \(\deg(mg)\le\deg L\). Multiplying by \(M/L\) gives terms with leading monomial below \(M\) and degree at most \(\deg M\le j\). Substituting contradicts the choice. So \(M=\mathrm{LM}(f)\), which is then divisible by the leading monomial of the \(g_i\) attaining it. 2. By 1, \(f=\sum c_im_ig_i\) with \(\deg(m_ig_i)\le\deg f\le D-1\), and \(x_af=\sum c_i(x_am_i)g_i\) has all terms of degree at most \(D\). 3. \(S_D(G)\) contains the elements of \(\Gamma\) of degree at most \(D\) and is closed by 2, so it contains \(C_D(\Gamma)\). Conversely each \(mg\) with \(\deg(mg)\le D\) is reached from \(g\in C_D(\Gamma)\) by multiplying one variable at a time through degrees at most \(D-1\). 4. By 1 the leading monomials of elements of \(S_D(G)\) are multiples of the \(\mathrm{LM}(g)\); conversely \(m\,\mathrm{LM}(g)=\mathrm{LM}(mg)\) with \(mg\in S_D(G)\) when the degree is at most \(D\). And \(\mathrm{LM}(1)=1\) is such a multiple only for constant \(g\). \(\square\)

Finiteness of \(G\) and the bound \(\deg g\le D\) are not needed. Pairs with coprime leading monomials are resolved at any degree by the product criterion, since \(S(g,h)\) is then a combination of \(g\) and \(h\) with all terms below \(L\). For Boolean systems \(G\) contains the \(x_a^2-x_a\), and the pairs of an element with a Boolean axiom are among those to resolve. The criterion is the standard Buchberger argument with every step kept inside degree \(D\); it is recorded because the notebook's closures are degree-bounded and inhomogeneous, where a degree-truncated basis computed by a system is not by itself a certificate (COMPUTATION_RULES.md). Novelty is not claimed.

What the lattice at the cutoff says

Cost. The obligations are the pairs of the lcm lattice of \(\mathrm{LM}(G)\) in degrees at most \(D\), together with whatever new elements their resolution adds. This is the costed lift the lead asked for: nothing above the cutoff enters, and the engine's standard monomials are read off from \(\mathrm{LM}(G)\) by part 4.

Checks against the record. For the product-tree frame the three families of rewriting rules are such a \(G\): they are leading-monomial rewrites for any degree-compatible order, and their pairs resolve because, as proved there, the irreducible monomials are linearly independent modulo a space that contains the S-polynomials; part 4 gives the sibling-free antichains again. Rows of degree above \(D\) are ignored by \(C_D\) altogether, which is why a system whose only non-Boolean axioms have degree above the cutoff is trivially proper there.

For the route's systems. A row that is a clause on \(k\) linear forms contributes an element with a leading monomial of degree at most \(k\). In the regime \(2k\le D\) every pair of rows has an lcm within the cutoff. Pairs with coprime leading monomials resolve automatically; pairs with overlapping leading monomials, pairs with Boolean axioms, and the pairs created by resolving them are the obligations. With dense forms the leading variables of different rows overlap heavily, so most pairs are obligations. A certificate of properness is a set \(G\subseteq C_D(\Gamma)\) satisfying the pair condition without a constant; it need not be a Gröbner basis of the ideal through degree \(D\), since \(C_D\) can be smaller than the ideal's part of degree at most \(D\). Whether a system with mostly coprime leading monomials can be unsatisfiable and hard is not argued here.

Specification decision. No change. The criterion suggests a structural condition, generators whose leading monomials have large pairwise lcm, but it is tied to a term order and to a generating set, not to the formula, and it has no witness that is unsatisfiable; not adopted.

Verification gate. One fresh-context medium reviewer confirmed the lemma and its proof and required corrections that are applied: the S-polynomial convention and leading coefficients are explicit; part 3 assumes only that the elements of \(\Gamma\) of degree at most \(D\) lie in the span; the converse inclusion in part 4 is stated; unused hypotheses are dropped. In the prose: the product criterion is added, which shows that the draft's "nothing is saved" was false; the wide-rows remark is restated; \(2k\le D\) is a regime assumption; an unjustified final sentence is removed; "full Gröbner basis" is replaced by the correct object. Next attempt, named and not made here: use the criterion as the certificate format for one explicit small system in the hidden-subspace class, computing a basis through the cutoff with a computer algebra system and checking the pair condition independently, so that properness at a stated degree is certified and not inferred from a truncated run.
