9 October 2026 — A properness certificate with coprime leading monomials belongs to a satisfiable system

Working proofs of two structural facts about certificates; the review's test ends with neither a certificate nor a kill. Queue development of the LCM-lattice lead while draining. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort low).

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement, the review asked, on the LCM-lattice lead: for one structured unsatisfiable system exhibit a set \(G\) with mostly coprime leading monomials satisfying the pair condition of the truncated Buchberger criterion up to a stated cutoff, or prove that every such \(G\) forces a cutoff a constant fraction below half. Before choosing a system: how coprime can the leading monomials of a certificate for an unsatisfiable system be at all?

Architecture test. Outcome of the decisive test named in the method-gap review: neither branch. No certificate for a structured system is exhibited. The kill condition as stated is false without a width restriction, since axioms of degree above the cutoff give a trivial certificate at any cutoff, and for bounded-degree axioms no bound on the cutoff is obtained. What is obtained limits the form of any certificate: coprime leading monomials together with resolved Boolean pairs are impossible for unsatisfiable systems, and a certificate with elements of degree at most \(D\) must contain an element of degree \(D\) or two overlapping elements of total degree at least \(D+2\).

New mathematics. If the non-Boolean elements of \(G\) have pairwise coprime leading monomials and their pairs with the Boolean axioms are resolved, \(G\) is a Gröbner basis outright and, having no constant, its ideal has a Boolean zero. Hence a properness certificate at cutoff \(D\) for an unsatisfiable system with axioms and generators of degree at most \(D\) contains an unresolved pair above the cutoff: either a generator of degree exactly \(D\) with a Boolean axiom, or two generators with overlapping leading monomials whose lcm has degree above \(D\), one of them of degree at least \(D/2+1\). Also recorded: a certificate, in the general sense of the truncated entry, exists whenever the closure is proper.

Goal progress. Unchanged. The facts constrain what a lower-bound proof in this format looks like; they give no family, no bound on the cutoff and no certificate.

General statement. prop:coprime-certificate-satisfiable holds over \(\mathbb F_2\) for every set of multilinear polynomials and every degree-compatible order; cor:certificate-forced-overlap for every unsatisfiable Boolean system with axioms of degree at most the cutoff.

Statements and proofs

Work in \(\mathbb F_2[x_1,\ldots,x_v]\) with a degree-compatible order. Let \(B\) be the Boolean axioms \(x_a^2+x_a\) and \(H\) a set of nonzero multilinear polynomials; \(G=B\cup H\). Pairs are resolved in the sense of the truncated Buchberger entry.

Proposition (coprime certificate satisfiable). Suppose the leading monomials of the elements of \(H\) are pairwise coprime, \(H\) contains no constant, and for every \(h\in H\) and every variable \(x_a\) dividing \(\mathrm{LM}(h)\) the pair \((h,x_a^2+x_a)\) is resolved. Then \(G\) is a Gröbner basis of the ideal it generates, that ideal is proper, and the polynomials of \(H\) have a common zero in \(\{0,1\}^v\).

Proof. Every pair of \(G\) is resolved: two elements of \(H\), an element of \(H\) with a Boolean axiom in a variable not dividing its leading monomial, and two Boolean axioms all have coprime leading monomials, and a pair with coprime leading monomials is resolved by the product criterion; the remaining pairs are resolved by hypothesis. Buchberger's criterion, or the truncated lemma applied at every cutoff, shows that every element of the ideal has a leading monomial divisible by one of \(G\). No element of \(G\) is constant, so \(1\) is not in the ideal. The quotient is then a nonzero algebra spanned by multilinear monomials in which every element is idempotent, hence a nonzero finite product of copies of \(\mathbb F_2\), and a projection to a factor is a common zero in \(\{0,1\}^v\). \(\square\)

Corollary (certificate forced overlap). Let \(\Gamma\) be an unsatisfiable Boolean system over \(\mathbb F_2\) whose axioms have degree at most \(D\), and let \(G=B\cup H\) be a properness certificate at cutoff \(D\): \(H\) multilinear without constant and of degree at most \(D\), every pair with lcm of degree at most \(D\) resolved, and \(\Gamma\subseteq S_D(G)\). The degree bound is no restriction: discarding elements of higher degree changes neither \(S_D(G)\) nor the pair condition. Then some pair of \(G\) is not resolved, and every unresolved pair has lcm of degree above \(D\). Such a pair is either \((h,x_a^2+x_a)\) with \(x_a\mid\mathrm{LM}(h)\) and \(\deg h=D\), or \((h,h')\) with overlapping leading monomials and \(\deg h+\deg h'\ge D+2\), so that one of them has degree at least \(D/2+1\).

Proof. If every pair were resolved, \(G\) would be a Gröbner basis without a constant by the argument above, which needs only that all pairs are resolved, and its ideal, which contains \(\Gamma\), would be proper, against unsatisfiability. Unresolved pairs have lcm of degree above \(D\) by the definition of a certificate. A pair of an element of \(H\) with a Boolean axiom in a variable of its leading monomial has lcm of degree \(\deg h+1\). A pair of two elements of \(H\) with coprime leading monomials is resolved; with overlapping ones, \(\deg\operatorname{lcm}\le\deg h+\deg h'-1\). \(\square\)

Existence of certificates. In the general sense of the truncated entry, a set \(G\) with the pair condition, without the form \(B\cup H\): if \(1\notin C_D(\Gamma)\), then \(G=C_D(\Gamma)\setminus\{0\}\) is one. For \(g,h\) in it with lcm \(L\) of degree at most \(D\), the S-polynomial is a combination of monomial multiples of \(g\) and \(h\) of degree at most \(\deg L\le D\), so it lies in \(C_D(\Gamma)\); if it is zero the empty sum represents it, and otherwise it is its own standard representation, its leading monomial being below \(L\). Conversely, by the lemma, a set \(G\) with the pair condition, without a constant and with the elements of \(\Gamma\) of degree at most \(D\) in \(S_D(G)\) gives \(1\notin C_D(\Gamma)\), since \(S_D(G)\) is then closed and contains the closure; \(G\subseteq C_D(\Gamma)\) is not needed for this direction. So \(1\notin C_D(\Gamma)\) if and only if such a set exists. A certificate of the form \(B\cup H\) with \(H\) multilinear is obtained, for \(D\ge2\), from the multilinear elements of the closure; this variant is not written out. The point was made by the reviewer of the preceding review: the format loses nothing, and the content of any lower bound is the description of the leading monomials.

What it says about the search

For axioms of bounded degree \(w\), a certificate at cutoff \(D\gg w\) of the form in the corollary must contain at least one element of degree above \(D/2\) that is not an axiom, overlapping another, or an element of degree exactly \(D\). The axioms alone never suffice, and coprimality can describe only part of the set. The corollary forces one or two such elements, not a family; that a lower-bound proof for a structured system will have to describe many of them is my expectation and is not shown. Nothing here says how large the cutoff can be.

The kill condition of the review is not established and is false in the unrestricted form: if every non-Boolean axiom has degree above \(D\), then \(H=\emptyset\) is a certificate, as for wide rows. With axioms of degree at most \(w\) fixed, whether certificates can reach half of the free dimension is the open statement itself.

Specification decision. No change. The corollary is a property of certificates, not of formulas, and weakens nothing.

Verification gate. One fresh-context medium reviewer confirmed the proposition and the core of the corollary, including every coprimality claim, the step to a common zero and the degree arithmetic, and required corrections that are applied: the certificate in the corollary has generators of degree at most \(D\), without loss; the existence statement is for the general certificate notion, covers a zero S-polynomial, and names the hypotheses each direction uses; "full coprimality is impossible" is restated; the product-tree sentence and the word "family" are removed or marked as expectation. Unused: multilinearity and the field \(\mathbb F_2\) in the proposition. Dependency reread: the truncated Buchberger entry. Record: review.txt.

Follow-up. Continuing. Second entry on this lead. Next attempt, concrete: take the smallest structured unsatisfiable family for which the derived elements of degree above \(D/2\) can be written in closed form, two contradictory parity-defined rows on disjoint blocks joined by one shared form, and write its certificate; this is a calculation, not a search.

9 October 2026 — Two contradictory rows are refuted by a sum of their axioms, whatever they share

Working proof that two-row systems have refutation degree at most their width; the calculation named for the lead is trivial. Queue development of the LCM-lattice lead while draining. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort low).

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement, the preceding entry named a calculation for the LCM-lattice lead: write the certificate or the refutation for two contradictory rows sharing one form, as a function of their immunity, and read off the cutoff. The hope was a smallest structured system whose certificate has elements of degree above half the cutoff in closed form. If the cutoff of every two-row system is bounded by the row width, the smallest interesting structure needs at least three rows arranged in a cycle.

New mathematics. For any two relations in canonical encoding that are jointly unsatisfiable, \(1\) is a linear combination of their axioms with constant coefficients. The refutation degree is at most the larger width, independently of immunity and of how many variables or forms the rows share. So no certificate above the width exists for two rows.

Goal progress. Unchanged. The result removes two-row systems of small width as test structures and says nothing about a family.

General statement. prop:two-row-axiom-identity holds over every field for every pair of jointly unsatisfiable relations on arbitrary variable sets.

The identity

For a set \(X\) of Boolean variables and \(\tau\in\{0,1\}^X\) let \(\chi_\tau=\prod_{i\in X}(x_i\text{ if }\tau_i=1,\ 1-x_i\text{ if }\tau_i=0)\), the indicator of \(\tau\), of degree \(|X|\). A row is a relation \(R\subseteq\{0,1\}^X\); its canonical axioms are the \(\chi_\tau\) for \(\tau\notin R\).

Proposition (two row axiom identity). Let \(R_A\subseteq\{0,1\}^{X_A}\) and \(R_B\subseteq\{0,1\}^{X_B}\) have no common extension to \(X_A\cup X_B\). Then there are sets \(N_A\subseteq\{0,1\}^{X_A}\setminus R_A\) and \(N_B\subseteq\{0,1\}^{X_B}\setminus R_B\) with

\[\sum_{\tau\in N_A}\chi_\tau+\sum_{\tau'\in N_B}\chi_{\tau'}=1\]

as polynomials. In particular the system has a Nullstellensatz refutation of degree at most \(\max\{|X_A|,|X_B|\}\) with constant multipliers, without use of the Boolean axioms, and \(1\in C_D\) for that \(D\).

Proof. Put \(T=X_A\cap X_B\) and let \(P_A,P_B\subseteq\{0,1\}^T\) be the projections of the two relations. They are disjoint: a common point extends to a tuple of \(R_A\) and to a tuple of \(R_B\), which agree on \(T\) and so glue. For any \(X\supseteq T\) and \(t\in\{0,1\}^T\), \(\sum_{\tau\in\{0,1\}^X,\ \tau|_T=t}\chi_\tau=\chi_t\), since \(\sum_{u\in\{0,1\}}(x_i\text{ or }1-x_i)=1\) for each variable outside \(T\). Let \(N_A\) be the tuples on \(X_A\) whose restriction to \(T\) lies in \(P_B\), and \(N_B\) the tuples on \(X_B\) whose restriction lies outside \(P_B\). A tuple of \(N_A\) is not in \(R_A\), as its restriction is not in \(P_A\); a tuple of \(N_B\) is not in \(R_B\). Then \(\sum_{N_A}\chi_\tau=\sum_{t\in P_B}\chi_t\) and \(\sum_{N_B}\chi_{\tau'}=\sum_{t\notin P_B}\chi_t\), and the two sums add to \(\sum_{t\in\{0,1\}^T}\chi_t=1\). If \(T=\emptyset\) the same reads with a one-point space, and one of the relations is empty. \(\square\)

For rows on linear forms over \(\mathbb F_2\), with coefficient field of characteristic two, the same holds with width counting forms when the distinct forms of both rows are linearly independent, after a linear change of coordinates, which preserves degree. That condition is sufficient and not necessary.

Consequence for certificates. For two jointly unsatisfiable rows no closure is proper at the larger width, so no properness certificate exists there. Immunity does not enter: the identity uses the axioms as given and no multiplication. More generally a system with a proper closure above its width has no two rows that are jointly contradictory. The identity does not extend to one row against the rest of a larger system: the projections onto the shared variables are disjoint there too, but the indicators on the rest's side are not axioms and may be costly to derive. Which three-row structures are the smallest not covered is not determined here.

Specification decision. No change; nothing is weakened. The proposition is not a new condition: under the specification's requirement that every variable lies in at least two blocks, a two-row system has both rows on all variables, and the bound is then the number of variables and says nothing.

Verification gate. One fresh-context medium reviewer confirmed the proposition and its proof over any field and required corrections to the prose, all applied: "at most" in the degree; the linear-forms remark needs characteristic two and independence of the distinct forms; the sentence on tree-like overlaps and cycles was an overclaim and is replaced; the specification sentence did not make sense and is rewritten; the scope is two-row systems of small width. Record: review.txt.

Follow-up. Continuing. The lead asked for a costed lift of the lcm relations to organize the calculation of when a closure stays proper. It has given the truncated criterion, the equivalence of certificates with properness, the forced overlap, and this bound for its named test structure. Its queued sub-ideas are still open, so it is not developed: the next attempt is the first of them, the pair-condition checker, to be built against the three-row structure below so that a claimed certificate there can be verified exactly. This is the third entry of the lead's spell of four.

Finite check with a new tested tool; exact degrees at small sizes, the three-row structure not reached. Queue development of the LCM-lattice lead while draining. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort low).

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement, the last entry of the LCM-lattice lead's spell was to build the pair-condition checker of the truncated Buchberger criterion and use it on a three-row structure. The measured parity 2-clause instances had only upper bounds on their refutation degree. Does a completion that adds S-polynomial remainders within the cutoff give the exact degree in practice, and does it agree with the static values?

New mathematics. A finite check. The tool tools/truncated_buchberger.py completes a generating set under the pair condition within degree \(D\) and reports whether a constant appears; a produced constant lies in the closure, and without one the criterion gives non-membership, so this decides \(1\in C_D\) exactly. For \(3n\) products of two random affine forms it gives refutation degree exactly \(3\) at \(n=8,10,12,16\), three instances each: no refutation in degree \(2\), one in degree \(3\). At \(n=12\) and \(16\) this equals the static value, so the static test did not overestimate there. The run at \(n=20\) did not finish within its time limit.

Goal progress. Unchanged. The check certifies lower bounds of three on small instances, the first lower bounds measured on this route, and gives no information on the asymptotic law or on any family.

General statement. The tool's correctness rests on lem:truncated-buchberger-closure, which holds for every system and cutoff. ex:parity-two-clause-exact-degree records the instances; the hypothesis they bear on is conj:parity-clause-semiregular-degree, still untested beyond small sizes.

The tool

Polynomials over \(\mathbb F_2\) are sets of exponent tuples; the order is degree, then the exponent tuple; the Boolean axioms are ordinary generators. complete(G, D) keeps one polynomial per leading monomial, and for each pair with non-coprime leading monomials and lcm of degree at most \(D\) top-reduces the S-polynomial and adds a nonzero remainder. Axioms of degree above \(D\) are dropped, as the closure requires. Each input is first top-reduced against the earlier ones, so it equals its stored remainder plus multiples of degree at most its own and still lies in the span of the stored set. Every added element lies in the degree-\(D\) closure: the S-polynomial is a combination of monomial multiples of degree at most \(\deg\operatorname{lcm}\le D\) of elements of the closure, and each reduction step subtracts such a multiple of degree at most the current leading degree. When no pair remains, the pair condition holds, so by the lemma the closure is the span of the multiples and contains \(1\) only if a constant was produced. pc_degree returns the least cutoff with a constant. check_pairs lists unresolved pairs of a given set. Nine tests are in tools/tests/test_truncated_buchberger.py, among them a comparison with an independent linear-algebra computation of the closure on forty random three-variable systems at cutoffs one to three, covering both outcomes; the framework suite passes with them (557 tests, 7.7 s).

Limits: pure Python, top reduction only, no selection strategy; meant as checker and reference for a few hundred leading monomials. Coprime pairs are skipped by the product criterion.

Exact degrees

Prediction stated in the script before the first run, for \(n=8,10,12\): the exact degree equals the static value with multipliers \(|T|\le D-2\), which was \(3\) at \(n=12\); a smaller exact degree would have shown the static value too high. The size \(n=16\), static value \(3\), was added in a second run with the same expectation.

The second invocation, for \(n=16\) and \(20\), was stopped by its 110-second limit during the first instance at \(n=20\), after about 49 seconds on \(n=16\); that is a time limit, not a mathematical outcome, and no time for \(n=20\) is recorded. After the reviewer's fixes to the tool, which do not touch the completion, the twelve finished instances were rerun with identical results (rerun). Whether the degree at \(n=20\) is \(3\) or \(4\), that is whether the static value there carries an excess from its multiplier convention, is therefore still open.

Scope. Twelve instances, one density, \(k=2\). The lower bound "no refutation in degree two" on these instances comes from this tool alone, whose completion is cross-checked only on three-variable systems; the upper bound agrees with two independent static implementations at \(n=12,16\). The three-row structure named in the preceding entry was not examined.

Specification decision. No change; nothing is weakened by a measurement on random instances.

Verification gate. One fresh-context medium reviewer read the tool, its tests, the script and the data and found no bug affecting the reported degrees. It found two defects, both fixed: check_pairs dropped elements sharing a leading monomial, and pc_degree started at cutoff one. It asked for an independent test of the lower-bound direction; the brute-force comparison was added, and its first version failed because my reference closure was wrong, not the tool: it multiplied only generators and missed elements whose degree drops by cancellation. The corrected reference agrees on all cases. Corrections to the draft applied: twelve instances, not fifteen; no converse is used; the treatment of inputs; what was predicted before which run; the unrecorded time at \(n=20\). Record: review.txt.

Follow-up. Continuing. Fourth entry of the lead's spell, with no proof, refutation or reduction in the spell that advances the open statement, so no extension is claimed and the lead rotates to the tail. Its sub-idea for the checker is carried out here, at tools/truncated_buchberger.py. When the lead returns: the three-row structure, and a compiled completion for \(n\ge20\).

9 October 2026 — With every variable in two rows the expansion theorems give at most a quarter of the variables

Working proof of a ceiling on what two named theorems can give; a limit of a method, not of the degree. Queue development of the sparse affine sources lead while draining. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort low).

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement, the queue's head is the sparse affine sources lead of the invariant architecture review: the growing-modulus modular source exists with all its structural properties, and what it lacks is "minimal-core control and a uniform degree theorem". Core control was supplied by later entries; the degree theorem was not. The only general degree theorems for rows on variables read in this session are Alekhnovich–Razborov's Theorems 3.8 and 3.13. Can either give a bound near half for this source, or for any source meeting the specification's requirement that every variable lies in at least two rows?

New mathematics. A ceiling for the method, by averaging over sets of rows. If every variable lies in at least two rows, then for any expansion parameters \((r,s,c)\) the matrix satisfies, the bound \(rc/2\) of Theorem 3.13 is at most \(v/4+s/2\) and the bound \(r(\ell/4-(s-c))\) of Theorem 3.8 is at most \(0.0335v+s/4\), with \(s\) the row width. So for rows on variables of width \(o(v)\) these theorems stop at a quarter and at about a thirtieth of the variables, whatever the rows are.

Goal progress. Unchanged. The proposition shows that the recorded degree theorems cannot be the uniform degree theorem the lead asks for. It bounds a method and says nothing about the true degree of any source.

General statement. prop:two-occurrence-expansion-ceiling holds for every 0/1 matrix with at least two ones in each column and every \((r,s,c)\) for which it is an expander in the sense of Alekhnovich–Razborov; it concerns rows on variables, not rows on linear forms.

Setting

As read in the source in the private-direction entry: \(A\) is an \(m\times v\) 0/1 matrix, row \(i\) carrying a constraint \(f_i\) on the variables \(X_i\) of its ones. The boundary \(\partial I\) of a set \(I\) of rows is the set of columns with exactly one \(1\) in the rows of \(I\). \(A\) is an \((r,s,c)\)-expander if every row has at most \(s\) ones and \(|\partial I|\ge c|I|\) for every \(I\) with \(|I|\le r\). Theorem 3.8: for \(\ell\)-immune \(f_i\) with \(s\le r(\ell/4-(s-c))\), every refutation has degree above \(r(\ell/4-(s-c))\). Theorem 3.13: for constraints forbidding a single tuple, degree above \(rc/2\). An \(\ell\)-immune nonconstant \(f_i\) has \(\ell\le\deg f_i\le s\), since \(f_i\) implies itself.

Proposition (two occurrence expansion ceiling). Let \(A\) be an \((r,s,c)\)-expander with \(1\le r\le m\), in which every column has at least two ones. Then

\[\frac{rc}{2}\le\frac v4+\frac s2,\qquad r\Bigl(\frac{\ell}{4}-(s-c)\Bigr)\le0.0335\,v+\frac s4\quad\text{for every }\ell\le s.\]

Proof. Let \(I\) be a uniformly random set of exactly \(r\) rows. A column \(x\) with \(d\) ones lies in \(\partial I\) with probability \(P_d=d\,\frac rm\prod_{j=1}^{d-1}\frac{m-r-j+1}{m-j}\). If \(d-1>m-r\) a factor is zero and \(P_d=0\). Otherwise all factors are nonnegative and each is at most \(\beta=(m-r)/(m-1)\), because \((m-r-j+1)(m-1)\le(m-r)(m-j)\) is \((j-1)(m-1)\ge(j-1)(m-r)\). With \(\rho=r/m=1-\beta\frac{m-1}m\le1-\beta+\frac1m\), \(P_d\le d(1-\beta)\beta^{d-1}+\frac dm\). For \(d\ge2\), \(\max_{\beta\in[0,1]}d(1-\beta)\beta^{d-1}=(1-\tfrac1d)^{d-1}\le\tfrac12\). The matrix has at most \(ms\) ones, so \(\sum_xd_x/m\le s\) and \(\mathbb E|\partial I|\le v/2+s\); some \(I\) of size \(r\) has boundary at most that, and expansion gives \(rc\le v/2+s\). This is the first inequality.

For the second, \(\ell\le s\) gives \(r(\ell/4-(s-c))\le rc-\tfrac34rs\). The expected number of ones in the rows of \(I\) is \(\rho\sum_xd_x\), and it is at most \(rs\). Hence, with the same \(I\) in expectation, \(rc-\tfrac34rs\le\mathbb E|\partial I|-\tfrac34\rho\sum_xd_x\le\sum_x\bigl(P_{d_x}-\tfrac34\rho d_x\bigr)\); here \(rc\le|\partial I|\) holds for every \(I\) of size \(r\), so it holds for the expectation. For one column, \(P_d-\tfrac34\rho d\le d\rho(\beta^{d-1}-\tfrac34)\), which is positive only if \(u=\beta^{d-1}>\tfrac34\); then \(\rho\le1-\beta+\tfrac1m\) and \(1-\beta=1-u^{1/(d-1)}\le\ln(1/u)/(d-1)\), so with \(d/(d-1)\le2\) the term is at most \(2\ln(1/u)(u-\tfrac34)+\tfrac d{4m}\). The function \(2\ln(1/u)(u-\tfrac34)\) on \((\tfrac34,1]\) has maximum below \(0.0335\), attained near \(u=0.87\). Summing over columns, with \(\sum_xd_x/(4m)\le s/4\), gives the second inequality. \(\square\)

The constants are not optimized; at \(d=2\) the maximum of \(2\rho(\tfrac14-\rho)\) is \(1/32\), up to the \(1/m\) term. The term in \(s\) cannot be dropped: three rows on all variables with \(r=1\) have \(rc=v\), the trivial case of axioms as wide as the variable set. Not used: the immunity hypothesis beyond \(\ell\le s\), and the side condition of Theorem 3.8.

What it says for the lead

The growing-modulus source of the lead and the balanced paired source have rows on variables of logarithmic width with every variable in at least two rows. For them Theorem 3.8 gives at most about \(0.0335v\) under any expansion and immunity they may have; Theorem 3.13 does not apply directly to modular rows, and for a clause encoding with single-tuple rows it gives at most about a quarter. The same holds for every source of the specification whose rows are on variables with width \(o(v)\); rows on linear forms and auxiliary affine equations are admitted by the specification and are not covered. So the "uniform degree theorem" of the lead cannot be either of these theorems as stated. Whether the source satisfies the hypotheses of Theorem 3.8 at all is not examined. The statements of the two theorems are as read in the private-direction entry; the reviewer had no excerpt of the source.

Where the ceiling comes from: for each \(r\) some set of \(r\) rows has at most \(v/2+s\) boundary variables once every variable occurs twice, so \(rc\) is capped near \(v/2\). The quarter comes from the factor \(\tfrac12\) in Theorem 3.13. A theorem charging boundary variables without that factor is not excluded by this argument.

Specification decision. No change. Considered: dropping the two-occurrence requirement so that expansion bounds could be larger. It is a normalization of the specification with its own degree-preserving proof, and without it private variables can be projected away; the ceiling is a property of the method, and the requirement stays.

Verification gate. One fresh-context medium reviewer checked the proof by hand, including the hypergeometric formula, the factor bound, both inequalities and the maximum \(0.03342\) near \(u=0.8706\), and found the proposition correct. Corrections applied: the case of a vanishing factor; the error term is now \(s\), from the count of ones, so no bound on occurrences is needed; "a thirtieth" was false as an upper bound since \(0.0335>1/30\); the scope excludes rows on linear forms; the last paragraph claimed more than the averaging shows. Not checked by the reviewer: the statements of Theorems 3.8 and 3.13, taken from this session's reading of the source. Record: review.txt.

Follow-up. Continuing. First entry on this lead. The uniform degree theorem it asks for is not available from the recorded theorems; next attempt, on its first queued sub-idea: for a small normalized modular core, use tools/truncated_buchberger.py to compute the exact degree and the leading monomials of the closure just below it, and compare with the filtered half the source is proved to keep.

Sub-ideas

  • Decide whether the paired source satisfies the hypotheses of Theorem 3.8 with some immunity and expansion, which would give it a proved positive linear degree, at most about \(0.0335\) of its variables.

Process assessment. The budget entry had estimated these limits in a random model; the averaging argument here needs no model and no assumption on the rows, and could have been tried first. The lead is old and its question was half answered by entries that did not close it; this entry answers the other half negatively for the methods at hand.

9 October 2026 — Single-tuple rows on linear forms with fully independent row sets are satisfiable

Working proof that the rank form of expansion cannot be perfect for an unsatisfiable system; how much slack is needed is open. Queue development of the sparse affine sources lead while draining. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort low).

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement, the preceding entry capped the expansion theorems for rows on variables and left rows on linear forms uncovered. The immunity budget noted that a single-tuple expansion bound would read about \(n/2\) if it extended to linear forms with expansion measured by rank; that extension is unproved. Independently of whether it can be proved: do unsatisfiable systems exist whose rows have the rank expansion that reading needs? The planned computation on a small modular core was not done; this question came first because its answer decides whether the lead's affine sources can use the rank reading at all.

New mathematics. Measure a set of rows by the dimension its forms span. If each row forbids one tuple of \(k\ge2\) linear forms, \(n=kr\), and any at most \(r\ge3\) rows have jointly independent forms, the system is satisfiable. So the rank reading with full expansion \(c=k\) never attains \(rk/2=n/2\) on an unsatisfiable system; with expansion \(c<k\) the proposition says nothing, and with slack \(g=n-kr\ge1\) the argument gives no obstruction, and how small \(g\) can be is a question about additive codes that is left open.

Goal progress. Unchanged. The proposition removes one exact extremal case, full expansion with no slack, of a reading whose degree theorem is itself unproved. It gives no family and no bound.

General statement. prop:independent-rows-satisfiable holds for all \(k\ge2\), \(r\ge3\), every number of rows and every choice of forbidden tuples.

Statement and proof

Let \(V=\mathbb F_2^n\). A row \(i\) is a \(k\)-dimensional space \(W_i\) of linear forms on \(V\) with one forbidden tuple of values: the forbidden set \(A_i\subseteq V\) is an affine subspace of codimension \(k\). Rows are independent if the sum of their spaces is direct. The system is satisfiable if \(\bigcup_iA_i\ne V\).

Proposition (independent rows satisfiable). Let \(k\ge2\), \(r\ge3\) and \(n=kr\). If any at most \(r\) of the rows are independent, then \(\bigcup_iA_i\ne V\).

Proof. Put \(q=2^k\ge4\). If there are at most \(r\) rows, all are independent and each can be given an allowed value separately. Otherwise fix \(r-3\) rows, let \(U\) be the sum of their spaces, of dimension \(k(r-3)\), and choose for each of them a tuple of values other than its forbidden one. The points with these values form an affine subspace \(F\) of dimension \(n-k(r-3)=3k\), disjoint from the forbidden sets of the fixed rows. Linear forms modulo \(U\) are the affine functions on \(F\) modulo constants, a space \(Q\) of dimension \(3k\).

Let \(i\) run over the \(m'\) remaining rows and let \(\overline W_i\) be the image of \(W_i\) in \(Q\). Any one, two or three remaining rows together with the fixed ones are at most \(r\) rows, hence independent, so \(\overline W_i,\overline W_j,\overline W_l\) have dimension \(k\) each and their sum is direct, equal to \(Q\). For a uniform point \(x\) of \(F\), the event \(E_i=\{x\in A_i\}\) fixes the values of \(k\) independent affine functions, so it has probability \(q^{-1}\), and any two or three of the events are independent.

Count: fix one remaining row \(i_0\). In \(Q/\overline W_{i_0}\), of dimension \(2k\), the images of the other \(\overline W_i\) have dimension \(k\) and pairwise intersect in zero, by independence of triples. Their sets of nonzero vectors are disjoint, so \((m'-1)(q-1)\le q^2-1\) and \(m'\le q+2\).

By the Bonferroni inequality at the third level, \(\Pr[\bigcup E_i]\le S_1-S_2+S_3\) with \(S_j=\binom{m'}j q^{-j}\), exact for \(j\le3\) by the independence above. Put \(g(m)=1-\frac mq+\binom m2q^{-2}-\binom m3q^{-3}\). Then \(g(m+1)-g(m)=-\frac1q\bigl(1-\frac mq+\frac{m(m-1)}{2q^2}\bigr)\), and with \(t=m/q\) the bracket is \(1-t+\frac{t^2}2-\frac t{2q}\ge1-\frac98t+\frac{t^2}2>0\), its discriminant \(\frac{81}{64}-2\) being negative. So \(g\) decreases and \(\Pr[\text{no }E_i]\ge g(m')\ge g(q+2)\). Finally

\[g(q+2)=-\frac2q+\frac{(q+2)(q+1)}{2q^2}-\frac{(q+2)(q+1)}{6q^2}=\frac{(q+2)(q+1)-6q}{3q^2}=\frac{(q-1)(q-2)}{3q^2}>0.\]

Some point of \(F\) lies in no forbidden set. \(\square\)

Remarks. For \(k=1\) the statement is false: the four rows \(x=1\), \(y=1\), \(z=1\), \(x+y+z=0\) forbidden on \(\mathbb F_2^3\) have any three independent and cover everything; there \(g(q+2)=0\). Rows that forbid more than one tuple are not covered: the events then have larger probability. An example meeting the hypotheses: evaluation at up to \(q\) points of \(\mathbb F_q\) of polynomials of degree below \(r\), each row forbidding one value at its point. The hypothesis must include sets of fewer than \(r\) rows: four rows on one space \(W\) forbidding all four tuples, with \(k=2\), \(r=5\), satisfy it vacuously for sets of exactly \(r\) and are unsatisfiable.

What it says about the rank reading

Suppose a theorem gave degree above \(rc/2\) for single-tuple rows on forms whenever every set of at most \(r\) rows spans dimension at least \(c\) times its size; no such theorem is proved, and the leading-term form of its elimination step is false. Here \(c\le k\) and \(rc\le n\). With full expansion \(c=k\) the value is \(rk/2\le n/2\), with equality exactly when \(n=kr\), and by the proposition no unsatisfiable system has that. Equality \(rc=n\) with \(c<k\) is not excluded: the four 2-clauses on two variables have \(k=2\), \(c=1\), \(r=n=2\) and are unsatisfiable. With \(c=k\) and slack \(g=n-kr\ge1\) the proof does not apply: on the fibre, of dimension \(3k+g\), the count becomes \((m'-1)(q-1)\le2^{2k+g}-1\) and allows more rows than the Bonferroni bound excludes.

What unsatisfiability needs under \(c=k\), by the same inequality: \(g(m')\le0\), hence at least \(q+3\) remaining rows. In coding terms, the relations \(\sum_i\lambda_i=0\) with \(\lambda_i\in W_i\) form an additive code of length \(m\) over an alphabet of size \(q\) with no nonzero word supported on at most \(r\) coordinates, and \(n\) is its redundancy in bits; the Singleton bound is \(n\ge kr\). How the least redundancy grows with the length the system needs is not determined here; I have not read the coding bounds that would decide it, and make no claim either way.

Specification decision. No change. The proposition would justify a necessary condition only for a reading that is not a theorem; nothing is added or weakened.

Verification gate. One fresh-context medium reviewer checked the fibre, the events, the count, the Bonferroni step, the monotonicity and the closed form by hand and found the core proof correct. It found the hypothesis wrong as first stated, vacuous for fewer than \(r\) rows, with a counterexample now recorded; the hypothesis is "any at most \(r\) rows". It found the claim about the rank reading wrong: equality \(rc=n\) does not need \(c=k\), so the conclusion is restricted to full expansion, with its counterexample recorded. The coding reformulation is restated as the relation code, and "length well above \(q\)" is replaced by what the proof gives. Unused hypotheses: none. Record: review.txt.

Follow-up. Continuing. Second entry on this lead. Next attempt: decide the slack question from the coding literature and a direct count, since it tells whether rows on forms can have near-perfect rank expansion in an unsatisfiable system; the small modular core computation remains queued under the lead.

Sub-ideas

  • For additive codes over an alphabet of size \(2^k\) with no nonzero word on \(r\) coordinates, find the least redundancy at lengths of order \(r2^k\) from the recorded bounds, read in the source, and compare with \(kr\).

Process assessment. The cycle's planned computation was replaced by a question that had to be answered first and could be answered by proof. The result is small and exact; the entry states that the quantitative question it opens is not answered.

9 October 2026 — Unsatisfiable single-tuple systems with independent row sets need many rows and extra dimension

Working proofs: such systems need more than \(r2^k/4\) rows and, for \(k\ge4\), dimension at least \((2k+0.156)\lfloor r/2\rfloor\) up to a logarithmic term. Queue development of the sparse affine sources lead while draining. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort low).

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement, the preceding entry showed that single-tuple rows on \(k\) linear forms with any at most \(r\) rows independent are satisfiable when \(n=kr\), and left open how much slack \(g=n-kr\) an unsatisfiable system needs. A slack linear in \(n\) would close the rank reading of the expansion bound at full expansion; a sublinear one would leave it open as a reading without a theorem.

New mathematics. Two counts and their combination. An unsatisfiable system of this kind has more than \(r2^k/4\) rows, by inclusion–exclusion to level \(r\). Independence of at most \(r\) rows forces \(\binom m{\lfloor r/2\rfloor}(2^k-1)^{\lfloor r/2\rfloor}\le2^n\), since sums over half-size sets are distinct. Together, for \(k\ge4\): \(n\ge2k\lfloor r/2\rfloor+0.156\lfloor r/2\rfloor-\log_2(e\sqrt{r})\). This is a lower bound on the slack, of order \(r\) for even \(r\); for odd \(r\) it exceeds the trivial \(n\ge kr\) only when \(k<0.078r\). For \(k=2,3\) it says nothing.

Goal progress. Unchanged. The bounds concern a reading of the expansion bound that is not a theorem, at full expansion only. They show that this reading, even if proved, would for \(k\ge4\) fall short of \(n/2\) by at least about \(0.0195\,n/k-k/2\).

General statement. lem:independent-rows-count holds for all \(k\ge2\), \(r\ge1\); lem:independent-sums-packing for all \(k\ge1\), \(r\ge2\); prop:independent-rows-slack for all \(k\ge4\), \(r\ge2\).

Statements and proofs

Setting as in the preceding entry: \(V=\mathbb F_2^n\); row \(i\) is a \(k\)-dimensional space \(W_i\) of linear forms with a forbidden affine subspace \(A_i\) of codimension \(k\); \(q=2^k\), \(m\) rows; the standing hypothesis is that any at most \(r\) rows have a direct sum. No relation between \(n\) and \(kr\) is assumed.

Lemma (independent rows count). Let \(k\ge2\), \(r\ge1\). If \(\bigcup_iA_i=V\), then \(m>rq/4\).

Proof. For uniform \(x\in V\) the events \(E_i=\{x\in A_i\}\) have probability \(p=1/q\le\frac14\), and any at most \(r\) of them are independent. Let \(t\) be the largest odd integer with \(t\le r\), so \(t+1\ge r\), and suppose \(\mu=mp\le(t+1)/4\). If \(m\le t\) all events are independent and \(\Pr[\text{none}]=(1-p)^m>0\). Otherwise, by the Bonferroni inequality at the odd level \(t\), \(1-\Pr[\bigcup E_i]\ge\sum_{j=0}^t(-1)^ja_j\) with \(a_j=\binom mjp^j\), exact terms because \(t\le r\). Since \(\sum_{j=0}^m(-1)^ja_j=(1-p)^m\), the right side is \((1-p)^m-\sum_{j=t+1}^m(-1)^ja_j\). For \(j\ge t+1>\mu\) the ratio \(a_{j+1}/a_j=(m-j)p/(j+1)\) is below one, so that tail is an alternating sum of decreasing terms starting with \(+a_{t+1}\), and lies in \([0,a_{t+1}]\). Now \(a_{t+1}\le\mu^{t+1}/(t+1)!\le(e\mu/(t+1))^{t+1}\le(e/4)^{t+1}\), and \(\ln(1-p)\ge-p-p^2\ge-\tfrac54p\) for \(p\le\frac14\) gives \((1-p)^m\ge e^{-5\mu/4}\ge e^{-5(t+1)/16}\). As \(e^{-5/16}>0.73>0.68>e/4\), \(\Pr[\text{none}]>0\). So covering forces \(\mu>(t+1)/4\ge r/4\). \(\square\)

Lemma (independent sums packing). Let \(r\ge2\) and \(s=\lfloor r/2\rfloor\). Then \(\binom ms(q-1)^s\le2^n\).

Proof. For a set \(J\) of \(s\) rows and nonzero \(w_i\in W_i\), \(i\in J\), consider the form \(\sum_{i\in J}w_i\). If two different choices \((J,w)\), \((J',w')\) gave the same form, their sum would be a relation \(\sum_{i\in J\cup J'}u_i=0\) with \(u_i\in W_i\), where \(u_i=w_i\) or \(w'_i\) for \(i\) in exactly one of the sets and \(u_i=w_i+w'_i\) for \(i\) in both. Some \(u_i\) is nonzero: if \(J\ne J'\) take \(i\) in the symmetric difference, otherwise some \(w_i\ne w'_i\). This contradicts the independence of the at most \(2s\le r\) rows of \(J\cup J'\). So the \(\binom ms(q-1)^s\) forms are distinct elements of a space of \(2^n\) forms. \(\square\)

Proposition (independent rows slack). Let \(k\ge4\), \(r\ge2\), \(s=\lfloor r/2\rfloor\). If \(\bigcup_iA_i=V\), then

\[n\ \ge\ 2ks+s\log_2\!\Bigl(\tfrac e2\bigl(1-\tfrac2q\bigr)\bigl(1-\tfrac1q\bigr)\Bigr)-\log_2(e\sqrt s)\ \ge\ 2ks+0.156\,s-\log_2(e\sqrt s).\]

Proof. By the first lemma \(m>rq/4\), so \(s\le r/2<2m/q\) and \(m-s\ge m(1-\tfrac2q)\), and \(m/s>q/2\). With \(s!\le e\sqrt s\,(s/e)^s\), \(\binom ms\ge(m-s)^s/s!\ge\bigl(e(1-\tfrac2q)\tfrac ms\bigr)^s/(e\sqrt s)\ge\bigl(\tfrac e2(1-\tfrac2q)q\bigr)^s/(e\sqrt s)\). The second lemma gives \(2^n\ge q^{2s}\bigl(\tfrac e2(1-\tfrac2q)(1-\tfrac1q)\bigr)^s/(e\sqrt s)\). For \(q\ge16\) the base is at least \(1.1149\), with binary logarithm above \(0.156\). \(\square\)

Remarks. For \(q=4,8\) the base is below one and the proposition is weaker than the trivial \(n\ge kr\); its first inequality holds for all \(k\ge2\), and \(k\ge4\) is used only for the number \(0.156\); the constants \(\tfrac14\) and \(0.156\) are not optimized. The first lemma uses only the independence of the events; the second only the independence of the rows; neither uses that a row forbids exactly one tuple beyond the probability \(1/q\).

Consequence for the rank reading

For the hypothetical bound "degree above \(rc/2\)" at full expansion \(c=k\ge4\): its value is \(rk/2\le(2s+1)k/2\). If \(s<n/(4k)\) this is below \(n/4+k/2\). Otherwise the proposition gives \(2sk\le n-0.156s+\log_2(e\sqrt s)\), so \(rk/2\le n/2-0.078s+\tfrac k2+\tfrac12\log_2(e\sqrt s)\le n/2-0.0195\,n/k+\tfrac k2+\tfrac12\log_2(e\sqrt s)\). Either way the value is at most \(n/2-0.0195\,n/k+k/2\) plus a logarithmic term. At constant \(k\ge4\) the deficit is linear in \(n\). The first lemma bounds the width: a polynomial number of rows needs \(q<4m/r\), so \(k=O(\log n)\), and the deficit is then at least of order \(n/\log n\). The open statement asks for deficit \(o(n/(\log n)^{\ell-2})\), as recorded in this notebook's open statements, which the reviewer could not check; against it, this reading at full expansion could serve depth \(\ell=2\) only, and only with \(k\to\infty\). The shared-pin ceiling gave the modular source the same limit by a different count. Not addressed: \(k=2,3\), partial expansion \(c<k\), rows forbidding several tuples, and the truth of the reading itself.

Specification decision. No change. A necessary condition could be read off, at least \(r2^k/4\) rows when any \(r\) are independent, but it concerns a structural property the specification does not ask for; nothing is added or weakened.

Verification gate. One fresh-context medium reviewer checked both lemmas and the proposition step by step by hand, including the independence of the events, the direction of the Bonferroni inequality, the tail bound, the numerical comparisons and the constants, and found no gap. Its corrections concern the summaries and are applied: the bound in the form \(kr+0.078r\) fails for odd \(r\); the slack statement is a lower bound; the deficit \(0.039\,n/k\) was obtained by inserting the largest \(s\) and is replaced by a two-case argument with constant \(0.0195\); the deficit claims need \(k\ge4\), and depth two needs \(k\to\infty\). Unused: the single-tuple structure beyond the probability \(1/q\); covering in the packing lemma. Record: review.txt.

9 October 2026 — The ceiling attempt fails at the lifting step; even the half term has no proof

No ceiling proved; working proof of a weak bound by simultaneously violated rows. Queue development of the sparse affine sources lead while draining. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort low).

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement, the review asked for an attempt to prove that an unsatisfiable system of relations on at most \(k\) affine forms over an \(n\)-dimensional space is refuted in degree \(\max\{k,n/2-cn/k\}+O(1)\), by splitting on one row and inducting on the dimension.

Architecture test. Outcome of the decisive test named in the ceiling-question review: no proof, with the obstruction named. Splitting on the values of one row's forms lowers the dimension by \(k\) and costs \(k\) in degree when the fibre refutations are lifted, so the induction gives only the trivial bound \(n\). The attempt also showed that the test was posed above an unproved base: the record has no proof that such systems are refuted in degree \(n/2+O(k)\), without the term \(-cn/k\), and I found none. No small counterexample was sought, since with \(c\) and the additive constant unspecified no instance of reachable size can contradict the statement.

New mathematics. One elementary bound, by expanding a product: the refutation degree is at most the largest rank of the forms of a set of rows that some assignment violates simultaneously. It is weak; typical systems have assignments violating many rows.

Goal progress. Unchanged. The ceiling is neither proved nor refuted, and the required implication is as before.

General statement. lem:violated-rows-ceiling holds over \(\mathbb F_2\) for every unsatisfiable system of relations on linear forms; the ceiling of the review remains a question and is not registered as a claim.

The induction and where it stops

Let row \(1\) be a relation \(R\subseteq\mathbb F_2^k\) on independent forms \(l_1,\ldots,l_k\). For \(b\in\mathbb F_2^k\) let \(\chi_b=\prod_j(l_j+b_j+1)\), the indicator of \(l=b\), of degree \(k\); \(\sum_b\chi_b=1\). For \(b\notin R\), \(\chi_b\) is an axiom. For \(b\in R\), the system restricted to the subspace \(l=b\), of dimension \(n-k\), is unsatisfiable and consists of relations on at most \(k\) forms; if it is refuted in degree \(d\), then \(\chi_b\) is derived from the original system in degree \(d+k\), by multiplying the restricted refutation by \(\chi_b\) and using \(l_j\chi_b=b_j\chi_b\). Summing over \(b\) gives a refutation of degree \(d(n-k)+k\). The recurrence \(d(n)\le d(n-k)+k\) gives \(d(n)\le n\).

For a bound near \(n/2\) each step would have to cost about \(k/2\) for \(k\) dimensions. The cost \(k\) is the degree of the indicator of a point of \(\mathbb F_2^k\), and no polynomial of lower degree is supported on one point. Replacing points by larger pieces of \(\mathbb F_2^k\) with indicators of degree \(k/2\) lowers the cost and also the gain: on such a piece the forms of the row are not fixed, and the restricted system keeps more than \(n-k\) dimensions. I did not find a choice of pieces for which cost and gain stay in the ratio one half. This is the named obstruction: for a relation on \(k\) forms I found no partition of its allowed set into pieces of indicator degree about \(k/2\) on each of which the restricted system loses about \(k\) dimensions. Whether such partitions exist for some row types is not decided.

The base is open too. The statement needs, before any \(-cn/k\), that every such system is refuted in degree \(n/2+O(k)\). The record has ceilings of this shape only for particular sources and encodings, and no general one; the engine's own half comes from annihilators of functions on the cube, which bound the degree of consequences and not of refutations. Whether a bounded-width system can need degree well above \(n/2\) is unknown to me; no example is recorded, and none is claimed impossible.

A bound by violated rows

Lemma (violated rows ceiling). Over \(\mathbb F_2\), let \(\Gamma\) be an unsatisfiable system of rows on Boolean variables, row \(i\) a relation on independent linear forms spanning \(W_i\), in canonical encoding. Let \(\nu\) be the largest dimension of \(\sum_{i\in J}W_i\) over sets \(J\) of rows that some assignment violates simultaneously. Then \(1\in C_\nu(\Gamma)\).

Proof. Let \(g_i\) be the sum of the canonical axioms of row \(i\), the indicators of its forbidden tuples; as a function it is the indicator that row \(i\) is violated, of degree at most \(\dim W_i\) in the forms of \(W_i\). A row that no assignment violates has \(g_i=0\) and plays no part. Since every assignment violates some row, \(\prod_i(1-g_i)=0\) as a function, so \(1=\sum_{J\ne\emptyset}\prod_{i\in J}g_i\) as functions, the signs being immaterial. If no assignment violates all rows of \(J\), the product is the zero function and is dropped. For a remaining \(J\) fix \(i_0\in J\), a basis of \(W_{i_0}\) and an extension \(e_1,\ldots,e_t\) to a basis of \(\sum_JW_i\), of dimension at most \(\nu\); in particular \(\dim W_{i_0}\le\nu\). As a function of these basis forms, \(\prod_Jg_i\) is a sum of terms \(\chi_b\,e_T\), with \(\chi_b\) an indicator of a forbidden tuple of row \(i_0\) and \(e_T\) a product of distinct \(e_j\): expand the other factors in the basis and replace each form of \(W_{i_0}\) by its value on \(\chi_b\); this is an identity of functions used only to choose the polynomial \(h_J=\sum\chi_be_T\). Each term is derived from the axiom \(\chi_b\) by multiplying by the forms \(e_j\), \(j\in T\), one at a time, with degrees at most \(\dim W_{i_0}+t\le\nu\). So \(h_J\in C_\nu\). Finally \(1-\sum_Jh_J\) is a polynomial of degree at most \(\nu\) that vanishes as a function, hence lies in the Boolean ideal within degree \(\nu\). \(\square\)

Outside characteristic two the indicators are not products of \(k\) affine factors and the lemma is not claimed.

For a system hard at \(D\) the lemma says that some assignment violates rows whose forms span more than \(D\) dimensions. A count of violated rows is not a rank, so I do not derive this from row counts; I know of no recorded candidate it excludes, and have not checked the recorded sources against it one by one. It is a necessary condition of the same kind as the kernel-dimension bound, not a ceiling near half.

Specification decision. No change. The necessary condition, an assignment violating rows of joint rank above \(D\), is not added to the specification: it is not known to exclude any candidate, and a condition is adopted only with a witness and a use. Nothing is weakened.

Verification gate. One fresh-context medium reviewer found the induction, its recurrence and the one-point degree claim correct, and the statement that the half term has no elementary proof fair: it knows neither a proof of \(n/2+O(k)\) nor a bounded-width example needing well above \(n/2\), with moderate confidence from memory. In the lemma it found the scope "any field" false, since the indicators are products of affine factors only in characteristic two, and the lemma is restricted to \(\mathbb F_2\); the degree is \(\nu\) alone; the reduction step is restated so that every polynomial in the derivation stays within \(\nu\). The obstruction no longer asserts that no partition exists, and the remark on row counts is withdrawn. Record: review.txt.

Follow-up. Continuing. Fourth entry of the lead's spell. The spell proved limits on expansion methods and on full rank expansion and no change of the open statement, so no extension is claimed and the lead rotates to the tail. When it returns: the small modular core computation queued under it, and the base question below.

Question. On frege-consequence and the open statement complete Frege transfer: which parts of the passage from an \(\mathrm{AC}^0[2]\)-Frege proof to the hypothesis of a source theorem are established, by Pang's paper or by the record, and what does the transfer require of the family?

New mathematics. None; this entry reads Pang's paper for its statements and the registry for the recorded compiler, and lists what each establishes.

Goal progress. Unchanged. The transfer statement is as open as before; what changes is that its unverified parts are now named, and that one constraint on the family, the clause-width budget, is read off the recorded statements.

General statement. The statements relied on are thm:moving-cutoff-source-exclusion and cor:binary-unbalanced-CNF-source, as registered; nothing is added to them.

What Pang's paper states

Source: arXiv:2610.00837v1, first read in this cycle through a tool that returns a summary, then checked against the page's text: the reviewer retrieved the HTML and searched it, and I read Section 8 in full in that text. The abstract lists "an implication of super-polynomial \(\mathrm{AC}^0[p]\)-Frege bounds from very strong PC degree lower bounds" among the applications. No numbered statement of the paper has an \(\mathrm{AC}^0[p]\)-Frege bound as its conclusion; the word Frege occurs in the abstract, in one remark of Section 7 and in Section 8: Theorem 1.1 is the degree–size relation for \(\mathrm{Res}(\mathrm{PC}_r/\mathbb F_p)\), and the Frege implication appears in Section 8, the conclusions, as a discussion. That section says that "the rank count is subadditive, and inference preservation extends to syntactic \(AC^0[p]\)-Frege rules given the error relations (34) for each gate"; it carries out a depth-two dimension count, with approximators of degrees \(\Delta_1=(p-1)rt_1\) and \(\Delta_2=(p-1)\Delta_1t_2\), closing when \(M_1(1-\eta_K(r))^{t_1}+M_2(1-\eta_K(\Delta_1))^{t_2}<1\), and requiring \(1\notin C_D\) for \(D=K+O(w(F))+O(\Delta_2)\); it identifies the regime \(K=n/2-s\), \(s=O(\sqrt n)\), where the rate is constant and approximator degrees \(O((\log M)^\ell)\) suffice at depth \(\ell\); and it states: "The difficulty lies in proving a PC degree lower bound near or above \(n/2\). This is unknown for \(o(n)\)-width polynomial-size CNFs." The abstract says the approach works "without introducing extension variables".

So the answer to the user's question: the implication is Pang's, as a sketch with its quantitative condition worked out at depth two and described for depth \(\ell\); it is not a theorem that can be cited, and "very strong" is not made precise beyond Section 8's regime. The transfer is therefore not immediate in the sense of a citation. It may well be short to write out; that has not been done in this notebook.

What the record has

The main notebook did not write out Pang's sketch directly. Its source theorem, under the hypothesis \(1\notin C_D(\Gamma)\) at \(D=\lfloor v/2-s\rfloor\), excludes PC refutations of degree \(\lfloor v^{1/3}\rfloor\) of the base system with polynomially many complete approximation blocks adjoined, in a product-only grammar, and says in its own text that it "does not assert that every presentation of Frege automatically has this grammar or coherent boundary". The passage from a proof to such a system is the binary unbalanced CNF source corollary: for an unsatisfiable CNF with non-tautological literal clauses of width at most \(w\), a binary proof DAG interpreted by complete costed profiles with structural values bounded by \(L\), at accuracy \(h\ge\max(1,w)\), gives a PC refutation of the clauses with the blocks through degree \(\max(M_{\rm fr},10)L\). Its hypotheses, coherent costed profiles and a flat literal presentation, are assumptions on the presentation of the proof. I read the corollary's statement and proof paragraph in this cycle and not the compiler it applies.

Not established anywhere I have read: that every \(\mathrm{AC}^0[2]\)-Frege proof of depth \(d\) and polynomial size has such a presentation with \(L\) small enough that \(\max(M_{\rm fr},10)L\le\lfloor v^{1/3}\rfloor\); which approximation depth \(\ell\) a Frege depth \(d\) uses; that the blocks produced have the product-only dependencies of the source theorem; and that the replacement of \(v\) by the free dimension and the auxiliary affine equations of this notebook pass through the compiler, whose boundary is stated for literal clauses in the variables.

What it requires of the family

  • The formula is a literal CNF of polynomial size in the actual variables. Rows on dense linear forms are not clauses; they need auxiliary variables defined through a chain of affine equations on three variables each, since a parity of width \(t\) costs \(2^{t-1}\) clauses. Those definitions have full rank, so the free dimension is unchanged, but they must be part of the refuted formula unless the remaining clauses are unsatisfiable alone.
  • Clause width is paid: additively as \(O(w(F))\) in Pang's count, and as \(h\ge w\) in the recorded corollary, where the source theorem takes \(h=\lfloor v^\epsilon\rfloor\) with \(\epsilon<1/(3\ell)\). So clauses of width up to \(v^{\epsilon}\) are admitted by the corollary alone. Its composition with the source theorem is unchecked: the theorem takes block inputs to be old polynomials of fixed degree at most \(r\), while the corollary's substitution puts clause values of degree \(w\) into later inputs, and the composition also needs \(\max(M_{\rm fr},10)L\le\lfloor v^{1/3}\rfloor\). Working proof conditional on Pang's Theorem 4.3 (arXiv v1); the proof system is a one-sided sequent system whose equivalence with standard definitions is not checked. User-picked, out of queue order. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort low).

Question. On frege-consequence and the open statement complete Frege transfer: Section 8 of Pang's paper says that inference preservation "extends to syntactic \(AC^0[p]\)-Frege rules given the error relations (34) for each gate" and gives a depth-two count. Can this be stated and proved for a definite bounded-depth proof system with parity gates over \(\mathbb F_2\), for every depth, with the affine equations and free dimension of this notebook?

New mathematics. Yes, for the system defined below. Every formula gets a value polynomial, built level by level with one approximator per disjunction and per proof line; Pang's Theorem 4.3, applied level by level, gives one multiplier \(f\notin C_D\) annihilating all error polynomials modulo \(C_D\) when a count over gates is below one; and every rule of the system preserves the invariant \(fP_L\in C_D\) within degree \(K+4\Delta\). Hence a refutation with few gates forces \(1\in C_D\). The count uses the free dimension when the base contains affine equations.

Goal progress. Advanced on the transfer statement, in this sense: the implication from a degree barrier to the nonexistence of small refutations is now a theorem, thm:bounded-depth-degree-transfer, a conditional reduction with a complete proof for one explicit depth-\(\ell\) system with negation, unbounded disjunction and parity gates, in place of a sentence in a paper's conclusions. It is conditional on Theorem 4.3 of an arXiv first version, whose proof and the lemmas under it I read in this cycle without finding a gap, and which has had no reviewer here. Still required for the open statement: that this system is polynomially equivalent, with a stated change of depth, to the \(\mathrm{AC}^0[2]\)-Frege system the goal names; and the numerical choice of parameters, which is the recorded moving-cutoff budget and is not re-derived for this system here.

General statement. thm:bounded-depth-degree-transfer holds for every CNF, every set of affine equations, every depth and all parameters satisfying its displayed conditions; lem:leveled-common-multiplier for every finite leveled collection of families.

Imported statements

From Pang's paper, read in its text in this cycle (Sections 2, 4, 5). The paper fixes an arbitrary polynomial set \(\mathcal Q\) throughout its Sections 2–5 and states that its algebraic tool uses only that \(C_D\) contains the Boolean axioms and absorbs multiplication within degree \(D\); this is what allows adding affine equations to the base. \(\mathcal Q\) is a set of polynomials over \(\mathbb F_2\) containing the Boolean axioms, \(C_D\) its degree-\(D\) closure, \(V_k\) the polynomials of degree at most \(k\). Fact 2.1: if \(g\in C_D\) and \(\deg g+\deg u\le D\) then \(gu\in C_D\). Fact 2.2: the Boolean axioms derive \(g-\operatorname{ML}(g)\) within degree \(\deg g\), \(\operatorname{ML}\) the multilinear form; as a corollary, a polynomial of degree at most \(D\) vanishing on the cube lies in \(C_D\). For a family \(g_1,\ldots,g_s\) of degree at most \(d\) and \(P=\prod_{j\le t}(1+q_j)\), \(q_j\in\operatorname{span}\{g_i\}\), let \(c_P(K)\) be the rank of \(u\mapsto([Pg_iu])_i\) from \(V_K\) to \((V_D/C_D)^s\). Theorem 4.3, first part, at \(p=2\): if \(1\notin C_D\), \(d\le K\le n\) and \(dt+K+d\le D\), there is such a \(P\) with \(c_P(K)\le h_K(1-\eta_K(d))^t\), where \(h_K=\dim V_K/(C_D\cap V_K)\) and \(\eta_K(d)=\tfrac12N_n(K-d)/N_n(K)\). I read the proofs of Lemmas 4.1 and 4.2 and of the theorem, and of Section 3 under them (Lemmas 3.1 to 3.3 and Corollary 3.5: rank under specialization by a multiplicity count, descent of a Frobenius-stable kernel, and their application to multiplication maps), and found no gap; that is one reading, not a review. The theorem is imported as stated.

Free dimension. If \(\mathcal Q\) contains consistent affine equations of rank \(\varrho\) (consistency follows from \(1\notin C_D\)), Lemma 4.1 and hence the theorem hold with \(n=v-\varrho\) in \(N_n\), \(v\) the number of variables, for \(1\le d\le K\le n\). Order the variables so that the pivots of the reduced affine equations are largest; in a degree-respecting order each pivot is then the leading monomial of an element of \(C_D\cap V_1\), which lies in the kernel \(Z_P(K)\) because \(K\ge1\). Leading monomials of \(Z_P(K)\) are closed under multiplication within degree \(K\), so no quotient basis monomial of Lemma 4.1's proof contains a pivot; the basis monomials use only the \(n\) other variables, and the double count gives \((j+1)b_{j+1}\le(n-j)b_j\). Nothing else in Lemma 4.2 or Theorem 4.3 uses the number of variables.

Leveled multiplier

Lemma (leveled common multiplier). Let \(1\notin C_D\), with \(n\) the free dimension. Let \(\Delta_0\ge1\) and \(t_1,\ldots,t_\ell\ge1\) be integers, \(\Delta_i=\Delta_{i-1}t_i\), with \(\Delta_{i-1}\le K\le n\) and \(\Delta_i+K+\Delta_{i-1}\le D\) for all \(i\). Suppose finitely many families are arranged in levels \(1,\ldots,\ell\), with \(S_i\) families at level \(i\), where the members of a family at level \(i\) are polynomials of degree at most \(\Delta_{i-1}\) that may depend on the approximators chosen at lower levels. If \(\sum_iS_i(1-\eta_K(\Delta_{i-1}))^{t_i}<1\), then approximators \(P_\nu\) with \(t_i\) factors at level \(i\) and a multilinear \(f\in V_K\setminus C_D\) exist with \(f\,g\,P_\nu\in C_D\) for every family \(\nu\) and member \(g\).

Proof. Choose the approximators level by level by the first part of Theorem 4.3 with \(d=\Delta_{i-1}\), \(t=t_i\); that part is a statement about one family, so different \((d,t)\) may be used at different levels, and it does not involve \(f\); the choice for a family depends only on \(C_D\) and on its members, which are fixed once the lower levels are chosen. Each map \(u\mapsto([P_\nu gu])_g\) on \(V_K\) annihilates \(C_D\cap V_K\) by Fact 2.1, as \(\Delta_i+\Delta_{i-1}+K\le D\), and has rank at most \(h_K(1-\eta_K(\Delta_{i-1}))^{t_i}\). The sum of the ranks is below \(h_K\), which is positive, so some \(u\in V_K\) outside \(C_D\cap V_K\) lies in all kernels; its multilinear form \(f\) differs from it by an element of \(C_D\) and has the same properties. \(\square\)

The proof system

Formulas: variables; \(\neg A\); \(\bigvee S\) and \(\bigoplus S\) for finite sets \(S\) of formulas. A line is a finite set of formulas, read as their disjunction. A refutation of a CNF \(F\) is a sequence of lines ending with the empty line, each an initial line or obtained by a rule:

  • Clause: the set of literals of a clause of \(F\), a negative literal being \(\neg x\).
  • Identity: \(\{A,\neg A\}\).
  • Parity axioms: \(\{\neg\bigoplus\emptyset\}\); and for \(S=S'\sqcup\{A\}\) the four lines \(\{\neg\bigoplus S,\bigoplus S',A\}\), \(\{\neg\bigoplus S,\neg\bigoplus S',\neg A\}\), \(\{\bigoplus S,\neg\bigoplus S',A\}\), \(\{\bigoplus S,\bigoplus S',\neg A\}\).
  • Weakening: from \(\Gamma\) infer \(\Gamma\cup\{B\}\).
  • Double negation: from \(\Gamma\cup\{A\}\) infer \(\Gamma\cup\{\neg\neg A\}\), and conversely.
  • Disjunction: from \(\Gamma\cup\{A\}\) infer \(\Gamma\cup\{\bigvee S\}\) for \(A\in S\).
  • Negated disjunction: from the lines \(\Gamma\cup\{\neg A\}\), one for each \(A\in S\), infer \(\Gamma\cup\{\neg\bigvee S\}\).
  • Cut: from \(\Gamma\cup\{A\}\) and \(\Gamma\cup\{\neg A\}\) infer \(\Gamma\).

The level of a disjunction is one more than the largest level of a disjunction occurring properly inside it, and one if there is none; negation and parity do not raise the level. The level of a line is one more than the largest level of a disjunction occurring in its members, and one if there is none. The depth \(\ell\) of a refutation is the largest level of its lines. Let \(S_i\) be the number of distinct disjunctions of level \(i\) occurring in the refutation, as members or as subformulas of members, including weakening and cut formulas, plus the number of distinct lines of level \(i\). A refutation of depth \(\ell\) thus has disjunctions nested at most \(\ell-1\) deep, and nested disjunctions are counted without flattening; this matters when the system is compared with a standard one.

The theorem

Theorem (bounded depth degree transfer). Let \(F\) be a CNF of width \(w\) on \(v\) variables, \(\Lambda\) a set of affine equations of rank \(\varrho\) over \(\mathbb F_2\), \(n=v-\varrho\), and \(C_D\) the degree-\(D\) closure of the clause polynomials of \(F\), the Boolean axioms and \(\Lambda\). Suppose \(1\notin C_D\). Let \(t_1,\ldots,t_\ell\ge1\), \(\Delta_0=1\), \(\Delta_i=\Delta_{i-1}t_i\), \(\Delta=\Delta_\ell\), and \(K\) with \(\Delta\le K\le n\) and

\[K+\max\{4\Delta,\ \Delta+w\}\le D.\]

Then every refutation of \(F\) of depth at most \(\ell\) in the system above satisfies \(\sum_{i=1}^\ell S_i\bigl(1-\eta_K(\Delta_{i-1})\bigr)^{t_i}\ge1\), with \(\eta_K(d)=\tfrac12N_n(K-d)/N_n(K)\).

Proof. Suppose the sum is below one. Define value polynomials for all formulas occurring in the refutation, by level: \(V_x=x\); \(V_{\neg A}=1+V_A\); \(V_{\bigoplus S}=\sum_{A\in S}V_A\); and for a disjunction \(G=\bigvee S\) of level \(i\), \(V_G=1+P_G\) with \(P_G=\prod_{\nu\le t_i}(1+q_\nu)\), \(q_\nu\in\operatorname{span}\{V_A:A\in S\}\), to be chosen. For a line \(L\) of level \(i\), \(P_L=\prod_{\nu\le t_i}(1+Q_\nu)\), \(Q_\nu\in\operatorname{span}\{V_m:m\in L\}\). By induction the value of a formula all of whose disjunctions have level at most \(i\) has degree at most \(\Delta_i\), and the members of the family of a level-\(i\) gate or line have degree at most \(\Delta_{i-1}\). Over \(\mathbb F_2\) every polynomial is \(0/1\)-valued on the cube. Each formula has one value polynomial, used in every line and gate where it occurs. The lemma applies, since \(\Delta_i+K+\Delta_{i-1}\le K+2\Delta\le D\), with the free dimension by the remark above. It gives the approximators and a multilinear \(f\in V_K\setminus C_D\) with

\[\text{(E)}\quad fV_AP_G\in C_D\ (A\in S),\qquad fV_mP_L\in C_D\ (m\in L).\]

Expanding the products gives exact identities

\[\text{(X)}\quad 1+P_G=\sum_{A\in S}U_{G,A}V_A,\qquad 1+P_L=\sum_{m\in L}U_{L,m}V_m,\]

with \(\deg(U_{G,A}V_A)\le\Delta\) and \(\deg(U_{L,m}V_m)\le\Delta\): \(1+\prod_\nu(1+q_\nu)=\sum_\nu q_\nu\prod_{\mu<\nu}(1+q_\mu)\). All values and approximators have degree at most \(\Delta\).

Claim: \(fP_L\in C_D\) for every line \(L\) of the refutation. For the empty line \(P=1\), so the claim gives \(f\in C_D\), a contradiction. In each case below every displayed product has degree at most \(K+\max\{4\Delta,\Delta+w\}\le D\), so memberships pass to multiples by Fact 2.1, and a polynomial of degree at most \(D\) vanishing on the cube is in \(C_D\) by Fact 2.2. Write \(X\equiv Y\) for \(X+Y\in C_D\).

A tool. If \(L'\) is a line, \(R\) a polynomial with \(K+\deg R+2\Delta\le D\), and \(fRV_mP_L\in C_D\) for every \(m\in L'\), then \(fRP_L\equiv fRP_LP_{L'}\), by (X) for \(L'\). In particular this holds for the members of \(L'\) that are members of \(L\), by (E).

Clause. \(L\) is the set of literals \(l_1,\ldots,l_k\), with values \(V_{l_i}\), and the clause polynomial is \(Q=\prod_i(1+V_{l_i})\in C_D\). From \(1=Q+\sum_i\bigl(\prod_{j<i}(1+V_{l_j})\bigr)V_{l_i}\), \(fP_L=QfP_L+\sum_i(\cdots)fV_{l_i}P_L\), in \(C_D\) by the axiom and (E); degree at most \(K+\Delta+w\).

Identity. \(L=\{A,\neg A\}\): \(fP_L=fV_AP_L+f(1+V_A)P_L\), both in \(C_D\) by (E).

Parity axioms. For \(\{\neg\bigoplus\emptyset\}\) the member has value \(1\) and \(fP_L\) is an instance of (E). For the other four, the members \(m_1,m_2,m_3\) have values with \(\prod_i(1+V_{m_i})\) vanishing on the cube, because \(V_{\bigoplus S}=V_{\bigoplus S'}+V_A\) identically; this is the validity of each line under \(\bigoplus S=\bigoplus S'\oplus A\). If two members coincide as formulas the product is taken over the distinct members and still vanishes. Then \(fP_L=fP_L\prod_i(1+V_{m_i})+fP_L\bigl(1+\prod_i(1+V_{m_i})\bigr)\); the first term vanishes on the cube and has degree at most \(K+4\Delta\); the second is a combination of the \(fP_LV_{m_i}\), in \(C_D\) by (E).

Weakening. Premise \(\Gamma\), conclusion \(L\supseteq\Gamma\). By the tool with \(L'=\Gamma\), \(R=1\): \(fP_L\equiv fP_LP_\Gamma\), and \(fP_\Gamma\in C_D\) by induction.

Double negation. \(V_{\neg\neg A}=V_A\). With premise \(L'\) and conclusion \(L\), every member of \(L'\) has the value of a member of \(L\), so the tool gives \(fP_L\equiv fP_LP_{L'}\), in \(C_D\) by induction.

Disjunction. Premise \(L'=\Gamma\cup\{A\}\), conclusion \(L=\Gamma\cup\{G\}\), \(G=\bigvee S\), \(A\in S\). First \(fV_AP_L=fV_AP_LV_G+fV_AP_LP_G\), as \(V_G+P_G=1\); the first term is in \(C_D\) by (E) for the member \(G\) of \(L\), the second by (E) for the gate \(G\). So the tool applies to \(L'\): \(fP_L\equiv fP_LP_{L'}\in C_D\).

Negated disjunction. Premises \(L_A=\Gamma\cup\{\neg A\}\), \(A\in S\); conclusion \(L=\Gamma\cup\{\neg G\}\). Write \(fP_L=f(1+V_G)P_L+fV_GP_L\). The first term is (E) for the member \(\neg G\). By (X) for \(G\), the second is \(\sum_AU_{G,A}V_A\,fP_L\). For each \(A\), apply the tool with \(L'=L_A\) and \(R=U_{G,A}V_A\): for \(m\in\Gamma\) the hypothesis is (E); for \(m=\neg A\), \(fRV_mP_L=fU_{G,A}V_A(1+V_A)P_L\) vanishes on the cube. So \(fRP_L\equiv fRP_LP_{L_A}\in C_D\) by induction. Degrees: at most \(K+3\Delta\).

Cut. Premises \(L_1=\Gamma\cup\{A\}\), \(L_2=\Gamma\cup\{\neg A\}\); conclusion \(L=\Gamma\). If \(A\in\Gamma\) or \(\neg A\in\Gamma\) the conclusion equals a premise and there is nothing to prove; assume neither. By (X) for \(L_1\), \(fP_L=fP_LP_{L_1}+\sum_{m\in\Gamma}U_{L_1,m}V_mfP_L+U_{L_1,A}V_AfP_L\); the first term is in \(C_D\) by induction and the sum by (E). For the last, apply the tool with \(L'=L_2\), \(R=U_{L_1,A}V_A\): for \(m\in\Gamma\) by (E), for \(m=\neg A\) the product contains \(V_A(1+V_A)\) and vanishes on the cube. So it is \(\equiv fRP_LP_{L_2}\in C_D\). \(\square\)

Scope and what remains

The theorem is the implication of Pang's Section 8 for this system, with the depth-two count generalized to \(\ell\) levels and the cutoff condition \(D\ge K+\max\{4\Delta,\Delta+w\}\). It rests on Theorem 4.3 as imported. Not done: the comparison of this system with the \(\mathrm{AC}^0[2]\)-Frege system of the goal, which I expect, without having checked it against a source, to cost a constant change of depth and a polynomial change of size, the points to check being parity over sets, the one-element-at-a-time parity axioms and unflattened nested disjunctions; and the choice of \(K\), \(t_i\) from the moving-cutoff budget, whose recurrence has the same form but was stated for another construction. Conjunctions are \(\neg\bigvee\neg\); they add no level, and each is a counted gate. Only \(\Delta_{\ell-1}\le K\) is used of \(\Delta\le K\), and \(4\Delta\) is needed only for the parity axioms, \(3\Delta\) elsewhere. The clause width enters once, additively. The affine equations \(\Lambda\) need not be part of \(F\): they enlarge \(C_D\) and enter only through the hypothesis \(1\notin C_D\) and the free dimension.

Specification decision. One requirement is now grounded in a proved statement and adopted as a note to the specification, not as a new property: the refuted formula is a literal CNF whose width is paid additively against \(D\), and auxiliary affine equations may stay outside it. Nothing else changes; no property becomes unnecessary.

It judged "advanced" defensible as a proved conditional reduction, provided the dependence on Theorem 4.3 is stated, and asked that Section 3 be read; I read it. Record: review.txt.
