9 October 2026 — Four-cliques give affine equations: the circular cliques, the cycle joins and the gadget ring all fall in degree at most nine

Working proof of one upper bound that covers the three graphs which had passed an earlier screen; candidates for two-bit four-colouring must be free of the relations it uses. Queue development of a chosen check while draining. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort low).

Chosen. Third entry on the two-bit four-colour check, which bears on the family statement as the one encoding with a proved upper bound at half; it comes before the head because the goal-level review named the question of affine consequences there.

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement: the goal-level review found that the gadget ring is easy through affine equations its gadgets imply. Which graphs have such equations, and what do the screens look like once they are taken into account?

New mathematics. In a proper colouring by \(\mathbb F_2^2\) the four colours of a four-clique sum to zero. These two equations per clique are derivable in degree nine. If the equations of all four-cliques imply that the two ends of some edge have equal colours, the graph is refuted in degree nine. This holds for the circular cliques with \(q\ge2\), for the join of an odd cycle with an edge, and for the gadget ring: the three graphs that had defeated one or more of the earlier bounds.

Goal progress. Unchanged. A stronger exclusion of examples already excluded or expected to be, and a sharper statement of what a candidate graph must avoid; no family is obtained and the required implication is as before.

General statement. prop:clique-sum-ceiling holds for every graph.

The relations

Two-bit four-colouring as before: colour \(c_v=(x_v,y_v)\in\mathbb F_2^2\), one axiom \((x_u+x_v+1)(y_u+y_v+1)\) per edge, multilinear polynomial calculus over \(\mathbb F_2\) with closure \(C_D\). For a four-clique \(K\) of \(G\) put \(\sigma^x_K=\sum_{v\in K}x_v\) and \(\sigma^y_K=\sum_{v\in K}y_v\), and let \(\Lambda_4(G)\) be the span of all \(\sigma^x_K,\sigma^y_K\).

Proposition (clique sum ceiling). (a) For every four-clique \(K\), \(\sigma^x_K\) and \(\sigma^y_K\) lie in \(C_9\). (b) If for some edge \(uv\) both \(x_u+x_v\) and \(y_u+y_v\) lie in \(\Lambda_4(G)\), the system is refuted in degree nine.

Proof. (a) The six edge axioms of \(K\) involve eight bits, and their common zeros are the assignments of four distinct colours, on which the colours sum to \(0\) in \(\mathbb F_2^2\), the sum of all four elements. So \(\sigma^x_K\) and \(\sigma^y_K\) vanish on the zero set and lie in the ideal generated by those axioms and the Boolean axioms, which is radical. In multilinear polynomial calculus on eight variables every polynomial has degree at most eight, so with \(D=9\) every product of a variable with a derived polynomial is allowed, and the degree-nine closure of the six axioms is their whole ideal; it is contained in the closure of the full system. (The reviewer notes that eight suffices, multiplying each axiom first by factors in its own four bits; nine is what is claimed.) (b) Linear combinations stay in \(C_9\), so \(x_u+x_v\) and \(y_u+y_v\) are in \(C_9\). With \(Q=(x_u+x_v+1)(y_u+y_v+1)\) the edge axiom, \(1=Q+(x_u+x_v)(y_u+y_v+1)+(y_u+y_v)\), and the middle term is a multiple of a derived form by a form, of degree two. \(\square\)

The three graphs

  • Two four-cliques sharing a triangle, \(\{t,a,b,c\}\) and \(\{t',a,b,c\}\), give \(\sigma_K+\sigma_{K'}=c_t+c_{t'}\): the complete graph on five vertices minus the edge \(tt'\) forces equal colours at \(t,t'\).
  • Gadget ring: consecutive terminals are such pairs, so \(c_{t_0}+c_{t_k}\in\Lambda_4\), and \(t_0t_k\) is an edge. Degree nine, improving the twelve of the review.
  • Circular clique \(K_{(4q+1)/q}\), \(q\ge2\): the positions \(c-1,c\) with the triangle \(c+q,c+2q,c+3q\) are such a pair for every \(c\), by the distances checked in the exclusion entry. So all colours are equal modulo \(\Lambda_4\), and any edge gives (b). Degree nine for every \(q\ge2\), improving \(\lceil\log_2q\rceil+8\); for \(q=1\) the graph is \(K_5\), where the same two cliques exist and (b) applies as well.
  • Join of an odd cycle \(u_1,\ldots,u_{2k+1}\) with an edge \(ab\): each cycle edge with \(a,b\) is a four-clique, giving \(c_{u_i}+c_{u_{i+1}}+c_a+c_b\in\Lambda_4\). Summing over the \(2k+1\) cycle edges, each \(c_{u_i}\) occurs twice, leaving \((2k+1)(c_a+c_b)=c_a+c_b\). So (b) applies to the edge \(ab\). Degree nine, where the game bound gave \(N+2\).

What it teaches

The game of the game entry conditions on bits and cannot use an equation; the three graphs on which the adversary did well, or which needed a logarithmic search, are graphs dense in four-cliques, and their difficulty in that model was an artefact of the model. The count of free dimensions has the same defect: by the free-dimension lemma the system is equivalent, from degree nine on, to the one with \(\Lambda_4\) substituted away, on \(2N-\operatorname{rank}\Lambda_4\) free bits, and the screens of the earlier entries should be read in that system. The bridge to the lemma, which takes the affine forms as axioms: \(\Lambda_4\subseteq C_9\), so for \(D\ge9\) the closure is the same with \(\Lambda_4\) added to the axioms, and \(\Lambda_4\) is homogeneous, hence consistent.

A candidate graph for a barrier near \(N\) must therefore have \(\Lambda_4\) of small rank, at most the deficit allows; the clean case is no four-clique at all. More generally the same holds for any bounded subgraph whose proper colourings span less than the full affine space; a triangle's do span it: for each vertex, by symmetry, with the other two coloured \(a\ne b\) the two completions differ by \(a+b\), which runs over all nonzero vectors, so an affine function vanishing on all proper colourings has zero part at every vertex. Absence of four-cliques is necessary for this and not sufficient: as the reviewer points out, a five-critical graph without four-cliques, such as a Mycielski graph, with one edge \(uv\) removed forces \(c_u=c_v\) on boundedly many bits, and a ring of such gadgets has no four-clique and falls in constant degree. So the question of the previous two entries becomes: a graph in which no bounded subgraph has an affine consequence, not four-colourable, with every large induced subgraph four-colourable, independence number at most about \(N/3\), and game value near \(N\). Of the examples examined in this notebook, as far as I have checked, only the Kneser cores have no four-clique, and they fail on independence number.

Specification decision. For candidates of the two-bit four-colouring kind, a necessary condition is added: for no refutation at a degree \(D\ge9\), \(\Lambda_4(G)\) must not contain the colour difference of an edge, by (b). It is binding: all three graphs above fail it. A stronger form, that the rank of \(\Lambda_4\) must be small against the deficit, would need an upper bound for the substituted system in its own dimension, for instance the transversal rank ceiling applied there; I have not verified its hypotheses in that system and do not claim it.

Verification gate. One fresh-context medium reviewer checked the proposition and all four applications by hand, including the smallest cases, and found them correct. Corrections applied: the degree nine is valid and not tight, eight suffices; the passage to the free-dimension lemma needed the step that \(\Lambda_4\) may be added to the axioms; the triangle argument needed "for each vertex"; my reformulation in terms of graphs without four-cliques was necessary and not sufficient, by the reviewer's example of a ring of Mycielski-type gadgets; the sentence on the record's examples is hedged; the stronger form of the specification condition is no longer claimed. Unused: non-adjacency of the two vertices in the first bullet, so the restriction to \(q\ge2\) is not needed. Record: review.txt.

Follow-up. Continuing. Third entry on this check. Next attempt on it: graphs in which no bounded subgraph has an affine consequence. Decide the game value and the independence number for a concrete family of that kind that is not four-colourable, or show that the conditions cannot hold together; absence of four-cliques alone is not the condition.

Process assessment. The logarithmic theorem of two entries ago was true and beside the point: the same configuration it used gives a constant bound once it is read as an equation and not as a constraint on an adversary. The reviewer of the goal-level review saw that for the ring; I had not seen it for the family I had just studied.

New mathematics. No. Among all 245 vertex-critical non-four-colourable graphs on at most nine vertices, 61 have game value at least \(N-1\), and 34 of those have no edge forced by \(\Lambda_4\); two of them, on nine vertices with independence number two, have game value \(N\). General statement. The hypothesis tested concerned prop:first-bit-game-ceiling and prop:clique-sum-ceiling for all graphs; it is refuted by ex:small-critical-graph-census. No all-parameter statement replaces it.

Test design, before the run

Hypothesis: for every graph that is not four-colourable, whose vertex-deleted subgraphs all are, and with \(\tau\ge N-1\), some edge \(uv\) has \(c_u+c_v\in\Lambda_4\). A graph that is not four-colourable while every vertex-deleted subgraph is must be connected, since otherwise a component would already fail, and has minimum degree at least four, since a four-colouring of the graph minus a vertex of degree at most three extends to it. So the graphs produced by nauty-geng -c -d4 on \(N\) vertices include all of them; the program checks non-four-colourability and vertex-criticality for each and discards the rest. Non-vacuity: the complete graph on five vertices has \(\tau=N\) and a forced edge; the hypothesis predicts that the count of graphs with \(\tau\ge N-1\) and no forced edge is zero, and one such graph refutes it. Sizes: five to nine vertices, the smallest that give more than a handful of critical graphs; no graph without a four-clique exists at these sizes, so the test concerns \(\Lambda_4\) only and not the general notion of bounded affine consequences.

9 October 2026 — Expansion by rank with one private form per row does not give degree; with all forms independent it fails at width one and is open above

Working proof of a counterexample: it excludes lower bounds from one private direction per row at every width, and from full independence at width one; the case of full independence at width two or more stays open. Queue development of a chosen check while draining. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort low).

Chosen. The check on a pseudo-reduction for rows on linear forms bears on the family statement through the one thing the line lacks, a lower-bound method reaching beyond a quarter; it comes before the head because the goal-level review turned the route away from the colouring frame.

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement: the private-direction entry showed that the expansion proof does not transfer to rows on linear forms with expansion measured by rank, on the monomial basis, and left open an operator on another basis. Can any such operator exist; that is, is the conclusion itself true?

New mathematics. Partly false. For every \(k\ge1\) there are unsatisfiable systems of single-tuple rows on \(k\) linearly independent forms in which every row of every set of at most \(r\) rows has a private direction, with \(r=n\) for \(k=1\) and \(r\) about \(n'/(k+\log n')\) in general, and which are refuted in degree \(k\) by a combination of the axioms with constant coefficients. So a hypothesis of one private direction per row, expansion by rank with constant one, gives no degree bound growing with \(r\), on any basis; the example contradicts a bound of order \(r\) once \(r\) exceeds about \(2k\). At \(k=1\) this is full independence of the forms of small sets of rows. For \(k\ge2\) the rows of the example share \(k-1\) forms, so it says nothing about systems in which all forms of every small set of rows are independent, the case of random forms; that case is undecided.

Goal progress. Unchanged. A route to a lower-bound method is closed in one form and at width one; no method is obtained, no family, and the required implication is as before.

General statement. prop:rank-expansion-without-hardness holds for every \(k\ge1\) and all \(n\) satisfying its displayed condition.

Definitions

A row on forms forbids one tuple of values of \(k\) linear forms on \(\mathbb F_2^n\); its polynomial is the product of the corresponding affine forms. In a set \(I\) of rows, a row has a private direction when one of its forms lies outside the span of the forms of the other rows of \(I\). Call the system \(r\)-private when in every set of at most \(r\) rows every row has a private direction. This is expansion by rank with constant one, every row on the boundary. It is weaker than full independence, in which the forms of every set of at most \(r\) rows have rank \(k\) times the number of rows; the two coincide at \(k=1\). The notion of the earlier entry also took a term \(t\) into account, asking for a form outside the span of the other rows' forms and of the variables of \(t\); at \(k=1\) the example survives that, since modulo \(d\) coordinates the \(n+1\) forms still have every \(n-d\) of the remaining ones independent, and for \(k\ge2\) I have not checked it.

The counterexample

Proposition (rank expansion without hardness). Let \(k\ge1\), \(n'\ge1\), \(n=k-1+n'\), \(N=2^{k-1}(n'+1)\), and let \(r\ge1\) satisfy \(\sum_{j=0}^{r-1}\binom{N-1}{j}<2^{n'}\); for \(k=1\) take \(r=n\). Then there is an unsatisfiable system of \(N\) single-tuple rows on \(\mathbb F_2^n\), each on \(k\) linearly independent forms, that is \(r\)-private and in which \(1\) is a combination with constant coefficients of the row polynomials, of degree \(k\). The condition holds for \(r=\lfloor n'/(k-1+\log_2(n'+1))\rfloor\) when this is at least \(1\).

Proof. Write \(x=(u,y)\) with \(u\in\mathbb F_2^{k-1}\), \(y\in\mathbb F_2^{n'}\). Choose linear forms \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_N\) on \(y\) of which every \(r\) are linearly independent: by the Gilbert–Varshamov argument they exist under the displayed condition, choosing the forms one at a time outside all sums of at most \(r-1\) earlier ones; for \(k=1\) take the \(n\) coordinate forms and their sum, of which every \(n\) are independent. Index them as \(\lambda_{a,i}\), \(a\in\mathbb F_2^{k-1}\), \(0\le i\le n'\). For each \(a\) the \(n'+1\) forms \(\lambda_{a,i}\) are dependent: there is a nonempty \(J_a\) with \(\sum_{i\in J_a}\lambda_{a,i}=0\). Choose \(b_{a,i}\in\mathbb F_2\) with \(\sum_{i\in J_a}b_{a,i}=1\).

The row \((a,i)\) forbids \(u=a\) together with \(\lambda_{a,i}(y)=b_{a,i}+1\); its forms are \(u_1,\ldots,u_{k-1},\lambda_{a,i}\), independent, and its polynomial is \(Q_{a,i}=\chi_a(u)\,(\lambda_{a,i}+b_{a,i})\) with \(\chi_a=\prod_{j<k}(u_j+a_j+1)\), of degree \(k\).

Refutation: \(\sum_{i\in J_a}Q_{a,i}=\chi_a\sum_{i\in J_a}(\lambda_{a,i}+b_{a,i})=\chi_a\), and \(\sum_a\chi_a=1\). So \(1=\sum_a\sum_{i\in J_a}Q_{a,i}\); in particular the system is unsatisfiable.

Privacy: let \(I\) be a set of at most \(r\) rows and \((a,i)\in I\). The forms of the other rows lie in the span of \(u_1,\ldots,u_{k-1}\) and of their own \(\lambda\)'s, at most \(r-1\) of the \(\lambda\)'s, all different from \(\lambda_{a,i}\) when \(r\ge2\); for \(r=1\) privacy says only that each row has a nonzero form. A form in \(y\) lies in that span only if it lies in the span of those \(\lambda\)'s, and \(\lambda_{a,i}\) does not, every \(r\) of the \(\lambda\)'s being independent. So \(\lambda_{a,i}\) is a private direction.

The last sentence of the statement: \(\sum_{j\le r-1}\binom{N-1}{j}\le N^{r-1}\) for \(N\ge2\), and \(N^{r-1}<N^r=2^{r(k-1+\log_2(n'+1))}\le2^{n'}\). \(\square\)

What it teaches

For \(k=1\) the example is the familiar one: \(n+1\) affine equations, any \(n\) of them independent, jointly inconsistent, refuted in degree one. Every local set of rows is as free as rows can be, and the contradiction is a single linear dependency among all the private forms. With variables in place of forms this cannot happen: private variables of different rows are different coordinates and satisfy no relation. That is the property the expansion proofs use and the rank count loses. A notion of expansion for forms that is to give degree must exclude global linear dependencies among directions that are locally private, on every fibre of the shared forms. Whether full independence of small sets of rows does so at width two or more is the open case.

This agrees with the pattern of the last entries: affine structure is free in polynomial calculus over \(\mathbb F_2\), and each bound or counterexample found since the transfer has used it. The immunity budget entry hypothesised, without claiming it, that the single-tuple bound might extend to rows on forms with expansion measured by rank and then reach about \(n/2\) for random rows. In the general form with constant one that extension is false; its instance for random rows of width at least two, where all forms are locally independent, is undecided.

Specification decision. No change to the specification. The remark in the remaining-route text that the single-tuple bound could reach about half for forms with expansion by rank is marked as unsupported: false with constant one, undecided under full independence at width two or more.

Verification gate. One fresh-context medium reviewer found the proposition and proof correct: the greedy count, the choice at \(k=1\), the dependency, the row polynomial, the refutation identity, the degree and the privacy argument. It required the claims drawn from it to be narrowed, applied: for \(k\ge2\) the rows share \(k-1\) forms, so only expansion with constant one is refuted there and full independence only at \(k=1\); the earlier notion's term is addressed at \(k=1\) and marked unchecked above; the floor may be zero; distinctness needs \(r\ge2\); my sentence about the immunity budget entry was unfair to it; the item is Continuing and its dependent check is not closed. Unused: independence of each row's forms; distinctness of the forms in the refutation. Record: review.txt.

Follow-up. Continuing. First entry on this check. Excluded: an operator whose locality is one private direction per row, at every width, and under full independence at width one. Open: full independence at width two or more. Next attempt on it: a system of width two in which the forms of every small set of rows are independent and which is refuted in low degree, or a reason there is none, starting from the recorded fact that such systems need many rows and slack.

Process assessment. The counterexample at \(k=1\) is one line and was available when the question was first asked three reviews ago; I looked for an operator and for consistency tests instead of asking whether the conclusion could be true in the simplest case. I then drafted this entry as a refutation for every width and a closure; the reviewer pointed out that for width two or more my rows share forms and so miss the case that mattered.

9 October 2026 — Width two with the forms of every small set of rows independent is also easy: three symplectic bases give an odd cover refuted in degree two

Working proof of a counterexample at width two under full independence by rank through \(n/10\) rows; width three and more is not addressed. Queue development of a chosen check while draining. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort low).

Chosen. Second entry on the check on rows on linear forms, which bears on the family statement through the missing lower-bound method; it comes before the head because the preceding entry left exactly this case open.

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement: the preceding entry refuted degree bounds from one private form per row and left open full independence at width two or more, where the forms of every small set of rows are linearly independent. Does full independence at width two give degree?

New mathematics. No. For \(n\) divisible by four there are \(3n/2\) single-tuple rows of width two on \(\mathbb F_2^n\) whose polynomials sum to \(1\), so the system is refuted in degree two with constant coefficients, while the forms of every \(r\) rows are linearly independent for \(r=\lfloor n/10\rfloor\). The rows come from symplectic bases of three alternating forms with \(\Omega_1+\Omega_2+\Omega_3=0\). The forbidden values are special; the independence hypothesis does not see them, and an expansion theorem would hold for all of them.

Goal progress. Unchanged. The hoped-for lower-bound method is excluded at width two as well; no method is obtained, no family, and the required implication is as before.

General statement. prop:three-family-odd-cover holds for every \(n\) divisible by four and every \(r\) satisfying its displayed condition.

The construction

Linear forms on \(V=\mathbb F_2^n\). For a pair of forms put \(l\wedge m\) for the alternating bilinear form \((x,y)\mapsto l(x)m(y)+m(x)l(y)\). A symplectic basis of a nondegenerate alternating form \(\Omega\) on \(V\) is a basis \(l_1,m_1,\ldots,l_{n/2},m_{n/2}\) of the forms with \(\Omega=\sum_i l_i\wedge m_i\). The row of a pair \((l,m)\) with constants \((a,b)\) forbids \(l=a+1,m=b+1\); its polynomial is \((l+a)(m+b)\).

Proposition (three-family odd cover). Let \(n=4s\). There are nondegenerate alternating forms \(\Omega_1,\Omega_2\) on \(\mathbb F_2^n\) with \(\Omega_3=\Omega_1+\Omega_2\) nondegenerate. For any symplectic bases \(B_j\) of \(\Omega_j\), \(j=1,2,3\), there are points \(p_1,p_2,p_3\) with \[\sum_{j=1}^{3}\ \sum_{(l,m)\in B_j}(l+l(p_j))(m+m(p_j))=1\] as functions, hence as multilinear polynomials: the \(3n/2\) rows are refuted in degree two by a combination with constant coefficients, and every point lies in an odd number of the forbidden planes. If \(r\ge1\) satisfies \(2\binom{3n/2}{r}4^r<2^n-1\), the bases can be chosen so that the \(2r\) forms of every set of \(r\) rows are linearly independent. This holds for \(r=\lfloor n/10\rfloor\) when \(n\ge12\).

Proof. Existence of the forms: on \(\mathbb F_2^4\) take \(\Omega_1=e_1\wedge e_2+e_3\wedge e_4\) and \(\Omega_2=e_1\wedge e_2+e_1\wedge e_3+e_2\wedge e_4\), so \(\Omega_3=e_1\wedge e_3+e_2\wedge e_4+e_3\wedge e_4\); the Pfaffian \(a_{12}a_{34}+a_{13}a_{24}+a_{14}a_{23}\) is \(1\) for each. Take \(s\) orthogonal copies.

The identity. Put \(q_j(z)=\sum_{(l,m)\in B_j}l(z)m(z)\). Then \(q_j(x+y)=q_j(x)+q_j(y)+\Omega_j(x,y)\). Let \(g(z)=\sum_jq_j(z+p_j)\), which is the left side. For each \(j\), \(q_j(x+y+p)+q_j(x+p)+q_j(y+p)+q_j(p)=\Omega_j(x,y)\), so \(g(x+y)+g(x)+g(y)+g(0)=\sum_j\Omega_j(x,y)=0\): \(g\) is affine. Its linear part is \(g(z)+g(0)=L(z)+\sum_j\Omega_j(z,p_j)\), where \(L=q_1+q_2+q_3\) is additive, hence a linear form. Given \(p_1,p_2\), nondegeneracy of \(\Omega_3\) gives a unique \(p_3\) with \(\Omega_3(\cdot,p_3)=L+\Omega_1(\cdot,p_1)+\Omega_2(\cdot,p_2)\); then \(g\) is the constant \(c(p_1,p_2)=\sum_jq_j(p_j)\). It remains to get \(c=1\). Fix \(p_2\). In matrix terms \(p_3=\Omega_3^{-1}\Omega_1p_1+\text{const}\), and the polarization of \(p_1\mapsto c\) is \(\Omega_1+\Omega_1\Omega_3^{-1}\Omega_3\Omega_3^{-1}\Omega_1=\Omega_1\Omega_3^{-1}(\Omega_3+\Omega_1)=\Omega_1\Omega_3^{-1}\Omega_2\), which is not zero. So \(c\) is not affine in \(p_1\), hence not constant, and takes the value \(1\).

Independence. Fix one symplectic basis \(B_j^0\) of each \(\Omega_j\) and let \(B_j=g_jB_j^0\) with \(g_1,g_2,g_3\) independent and uniform in the groups of linear maps of the dual space preserving the dual forms; each \(B_j\) is a symplectic basis of \(\Omega_j\), because a basis with matrix \(P\) satisfies \(\Omega=P^{\mathsf T}JP\) exactly when \(P\Omega^{-1}P^{\mathsf T}=J\), that is, when it is a symplectic basis of the dual space for the dual form \(\Omega^{-1}\), a property the group preserves. Each group is transitive on nonzero forms, so for a fixed set of \(a\) rows of \(B_j\), with span \(U\) of dimension \(2a\), and a fixed nonzero form \(x\), \(\Pr[x\in U]=(4^a-1)/(2^n-1)\). Take a set of rows, \(a,b,c\) from the three families, \(a+b+c=r\), with spans \(U_1,U_2,U_3\). Summing over the nonzero \(x\in U_1\): \(\Pr[U_1\cap U_2\ne0]\le 4^a4^b/(2^n-1)\). Given \(U_1,U_2\), summing over nonzero \(x\in U_1+U_2\): \(\Pr[U_3\cap(U_1+U_2)\ne0]\le4^r/(2^n-1)\). So the \(2r\) forms are dependent with probability at most \(2\cdot4^r/(2^n-1)\). There are \(\binom{3n/2}{r}\) sets of \(r\) rows, and independence of every \(r\) rows gives that of fewer. Under the displayed condition some choice works. For the last sentence, with \(N=3n/2\) and \(r\le N/15\), \(\binom Nr\le2^{NH(1/15)}\) with \(H(1/15)<0.354\), so \(2\binom Nr4^r\le2^{1+0.531n+0.2n}\), and \(1+0.731n<n-0.1\) for \(n\ge12\) (the count by binomials, in place of my \((3n/2)^r\), is the reviewer's; I checked the arithmetic). \(\square\)

What it teaches

Three quadratic forms whose polarizations cancel sum to an affine function; shifting each makes the sum the constant one. Each family is a full coordinate system, the forms of every \(n/10\) rows are independent (beyond \(n/2\) rows that is impossible), and the contradiction is one identity among all \(3n/2\) rows. So a threshold theorem of the form "independence through \(\epsilon n\) rows gives degree \(\delta n\)" fails for \(\epsilon\le1/10\). Full independence implies every expansion hypothesis by rank with constant at most two, so those fail with it. This is the width-two form of the lesson at width one: over \(\mathbb F_2\) the obstruction to transferring the expansion proof from variables to forms is not technical. The comparison with variables is not exact: rows on pairwise disjoint variables are satisfiable, so full independence has no variable analogue, and the variable theorems assume expansion with shared variables; like them, a rank version would hold for all forbidden values, and here some values fail.

Scope. The example has few rows, \(3n/2\), and chosen constants. It does not say that random systems of products of two forms are easy; the queued consistency question about them stays as it is, but at width two it can no longer be answered by a theorem whose hypothesis is independence of small sets of rows. The notion of the earlier entry also took a term into account; I have not checked the example against it. Width three and more is not addressed: the polarization argument is special to quadratic forms.

Sanity check. check_cover.py builds random symplectic bases at \(n=4\) and \(n=8\), five instances each, finds \(p_3\) by search for random \(p_1,p_2\) and verifies the identity at every point: it holds in all ten (check.jsonl). The independence count at these sizes is one or two rows and tests nothing; the independence statement rests on the proof.

Reviewer's suggestions, unverified

Asked whether the construction extends to width three and more, the reviewer proposed the following; I have not verified them.

  • Every width \(k\), by counting, with many rows: for \(N\) about \(2^k\ln2\) times the dimension of the polynomials of degree at most \(k\), random rows of width \(k\) span all of them, including \(1\), because a nonzero functional is nonzero on a random row polynomial with probability at least \(2^{-k}-2^{k-n}\); a fixed set of \(r\) rows is dependent with probability at most \(2^{kr-n}\), giving independence through about \(n/(k\log n)\) rows. If right, independence of small sets gives no degree bound at any width, and a transfer theorem must use the number of rows.
  • Why three families stop at width two: a trivector that is a sum of \(n/3\) decomposables on a basis has only that decomposition, so there is no group to randomize the families; a first-moment count suggests about \(n/6\) families would be needed.
  • Products and padding with new forms always share forms between rows; nothing found there.

Specification decision. No change to the specification. The living text's remark on expansion by rank is updated: false at width one and two, open at width three and more.

Verification gate. One fresh-context medium reviewer checked by hand the Pfaffians, the identity, the solution for \(p_3\), the polarization, the row polynomial as the exact indicator, the dual-form bookkeeping, transitivity, both union bounds and the formula for \(r\), and found the proposition correct. Corrections applied: counting sets of rows by binomials gives independence through \(n/10\) rows instead of \(n/\log n\), which is needed to exclude a threshold theorem with linear \(r\); two overstatements in the discussion and the comparison with variables are rewritten; the scope sentence is restricted to width two; the script's search is described as it is; the title is narrowed. Unused: divisibility by four beyond existence. First review under the rule that the reviewer also helps: its suggestions are listed above as unverified. Record: review.txt.

Follow-up. Continuing. Second entry on this check. Excluded now: degree bounds from independence of small sets of rows at width one and two. Open: width three and more, and the term-relative notion. Next attempt on it: verify the reviewer's counting argument for every width, which would settle the question with polynomially many rows, and then ask what remains for linearly many rows at width three.

Process assessment. The construction came from asking what the width-one dependency becomes for products, which is the step the preceding entry's reviewer forced by refusing the closure. A first version of the check script confused a form with its dual and failed its own assertion; the assertion was worth having.

Working proof of the reviewer's counting argument: independence through about \(n/(k\log n)\) rows gives no degree above the width, at any width; a linear threshold is refuted only at widths one and two. Chosen. Third entry on the check on rows on linear forms, which bears on the family statement through the missing lower-bound method; it comes before the head because the preceding entry's reviewer supplied an argument that would settle it.

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement: the preceding entry recorded, unverified, a counting argument for every width. Is it correct?

New mathematics. Yes. For every \(k\ge1\), with \(D=\sum_{i=0}^{k}\binom ni\) and \(N=2^k(D+1)\), there are \(N\) single-tuple rows of width \(k\) on \(\mathbb F_2^n\) whose polynomials span all multilinear polynomials of degree at most \(k\), in particular \(1\), while the \(kr\) forms of every \(r\) rows are linearly independent for \(r=\lfloor(n-2)/(k+\log_2N)\rfloor\), about \(n/(k\log_2n)\) for fixed \(k\). So a theorem of the form "independence of the forms of every \(r\) rows gives degree growing with \(r\)", uniform in \(r\), is false at every width. With a threshold linear in \(n\) it is refuted only at widths one and two; at width three and more that form is open, and this construction cannot reach it.

Goal progress. Unchanged. The hope of a lower-bound method from expansion by rank is closed in its form uniform in the number of rows, and at widths one and two outright; no method is obtained, no family, and the required implication is as before.

General statement. prop:random-row-span holds for every \(k\ge1\) and \(n\ge1\).

Statement and proof

A row of width \(k\) is given by linear forms \(l_1,\ldots,l_k\) on \(\mathbb F_2^n\) and constants \(a_1,\ldots,a_k\); its polynomial \(R=\prod_i(l_i+a_i)\), reduced multilinearly, lies in the space \(P_k\) of multilinear polynomials of degree at most \(k\), of dimension \(D\). When the forms are independent it is the indicator of one forbidden tuple of values.

Proposition (random row span). Let \(k,n\ge1\), \(N=2^k(D+1)\), and let \(r\ge1\) satisfy \(\binom Nr2^{kr-n}<1/2\). Then there are \(N\) rows of width \(k\) such that (i) their polynomials span \(P_k\), so \(1\) is a combination of them with constant coefficients, a refutation of degree \(k\); (ii) the \(kr\) forms of every set of \(r\) rows are linearly independent. The condition holds for \(r=\lfloor(n-2)/(k+\log_2N)\rfloor\) when this is at least one.

Proof. Choose the rows independently, each with all \(kn\) coefficients \(c_{i,v}\) of its forms and all \(k\) constants uniform and independent.

One row against one functional. The coefficient of \(x_T\) in \(R\), \(|T|\le k\), is \(\sum_{I\subseteq[k]}\prod_{i\notin I}a_i\sum_f\prod_{i\in I}c_{i,f(i)}\), the inner sum over maps \(f\) from \(I\) onto \(T\): each factor contributes its constant or one of its variables, and repeated variables merge by \(x^2=x\). As a polynomial in the parameters, each term is a product of exactly one parameter of each factor, so it is multilinear of degree \(k\); and the parameter monomial \(\prod_{i\notin I}a_i\prod_{i\in I}c_{i,f(i)}\) determines \(I\), \(f\) and \(T=f(I)\). Hence for a functional \(\varphi=(\varphi_T)\) on \(P_k\), \(\varphi(R)=\sum_T\varphi_T[x_T]R\) is a multilinear polynomial of degree at most \(k\) in the parameters in which the monomials coming from different \(T\) are different; if \(\varphi_T\ne0\) for some \(T\), a map from some \(I\) onto \(T\) exists because \(|T|\le k\), and its monomial has coefficient \(\varphi_T\). So \(\varphi(R)\) is a nonzero polynomial of degree at most \(k\) over \(\mathbb F_2\), and it is nonzero at a uniform point with probability at least \(2^{-k}\), the minimum distance of the Reed–Muller code.

(i) For a fixed nonzero \(\varphi\), all \(N\) rows are annihilated with probability at most \((1-2^{-k})^N\le e^{-(D+1)}\). There are fewer than \(2^D\) nonzero functionals, and \(2^De^{-(D+1)}<1/2\). So with probability above \(1/2\) no nonzero functional annihilates all row polynomials, that is, they span \(P_k\).

(ii) For a fixed set of \(r\) rows the \(kr\) forms are uniform and independent vectors; a fixed nonzero combination of them is zero with probability \(2^{-n}\), so they are dependent with probability at most \(2^{kr-n}\). Over the \(\binom Nr\) sets the failure probability is below \(1/2\) by hypothesis, and independence of every \(r\) rows gives that of fewer.

Both hold together with positive probability. For the last sentence, \(\binom Nr2^{kr}\le2^{r(k+\log_2N)}\le2^{n-2}\). \(\square\)

What it teaches

Independence of the forms of sets of \(n/(k\log n)\) rows survives a number of rows at which the row polynomials already span everything of their degree. With variables this cannot happen: \(N>\binom nk\) rows of width \(k\) include two on the same variables. At linear scale, however, rank does see the number of rows, as the reviewer points out: if the forms of every \(r\) rows are independent, all sets of at most \(r/2\) of the \(kN\) forms have distinct sums, so \(\sum_{j\le r/2}\binom{kN}{j}\le2^n\), and for \(r=\epsilon n\) the number of rows is at most linear in \(n\). So the proposition cannot be pushed to a linear threshold, and it sits near the limit this count allows for its own \(r\).

The outcome for the check so far: a pseudo-reduction whose hypothesis is independence through \(r\) rows, with a conclusion growing with \(r\) for all \(r\), has a false conclusion at every width; with \(r\) linear in \(n\) it is excluded at widths one and two by the examples with \(n+1\) and \(3n/2\) rows; at width three and more, independence through \(\epsilon n\) rows with linearly many rows is undecided.

The earlier estimate in the immunity budget entry concerned about \(2.8n\) random rows of width two. That instance stays undecided; what the width-two example excludes is a theorem by rank valid for all forbidden values, not an argument that uses random values.

Reviewer's suggestions, unverified

  • Degree over \(\mathbb F_2\) with Boolean axioms should be invariant under invertible affine changes of coordinates. Then rows whose forms extend to one basis are a CNF in that basis, and the expansion theorems apply in any basis; lifting by disjoint parities adds no degree for the same reason.
  • A global hypothesis that would work: a basis in which every form is sparse and the rows-against-coordinates support graph is a boundary expander; the expansion theorems for local constraints on expanding supports (Alekhnovich–Razborov; Mikša–Nordström) would then give linear degree for linearly many products of sparse random parities. The reviewer had not re-read their exact local condition.
  • For dense generic forms it knows no proved linear lower bound; the semi-regularity prediction for random quadrics is unproved and concerns generic quadrics, not products of two forms.

Specification decision. No change to the specification. The living text's remark on expansion by rank is updated: false at widths one and two, false uniformly in the number of rows at every width, open at width three and more with a linear threshold.

Verification gate. One fresh-context medium reviewer checked the coefficient formula including the empty set and merged variables, that distinct choices give distinct parameter monomials, the probability bound, both parts and the formula for \(r\), and found the proposition correct. Corrections applied: the sum defining \(D\) starts at zero; the conclusion holds for thresholds up to about \(n/(k\log n)\) and not for linear ones at width three and more; "rank is blind to the number of rows" was false at linear scale, by a distinct-sums count now stated; the closure was premature and is withdrawn, with the dependent check left open; the sentence on the immunity budget instance is restricted. Its suggestions are listed above as unverified. Record: review.txt.

Follow-up. Continuing. Third entry on this check. Open: width three and more with independence through \(\epsilon n\) rows and linearly many rows. Next attempt on it: the reviewer's first suggestion, affine invariance of the degree, which I expect to be an easy lemma, and what it says about this open case: whether sparse forms in a hidden basis are the only way the variable theorems transfer.

Process assessment. The argument is the reviewer's, from the first review in which it was asked to help; I verified it and made the functional step explicit. I again drafted a closure and a statement about every width; the reviewer showed by a counting bound that the linear-threshold case at width three is out of this construction's reach, and the item stays open.

Source read: Impagliazzo, Pudlák and Sgall

The user supplied the journal version (Computational Complexity 8, 1999); Sections 4 and 5 read by me, not redistributed. What it contains for the ceiling question:

  • Lemma 4.1: a derivation in which every monomial has at most \(b\) distinct variables can be carried out in degree \(\max(d,b+1)\), \(d\) the degree of the axioms and the conclusion.
  • Theorem 4.2: \(m-\sum_jy_j\), under the printed hypothesis that \(m>n\) and \(m\) is larger than the characteristic, is refuted in degree \(\lceil n/2\rceil+1\); the proof uses only that \(m\) lies outside \(\{0,\ldots,n\}\) in the field. In characteristic \(p\le n\) that set is the whole prime field, so the theorem is void over \(\mathbb F_2\). The proof derives from the Boolean axioms of each half of the variables a polynomial in that half's sum, of degree about \(n/2\), transfers the second to the first half through the linear axiom, and ends inside the first half by Lemma 4.1. It uses that there is one linear axiom relating the two halves, and that each half-sum takes few values.
  • Theorem 5.1: over the reals, \(m-\sum c_ix_i\) with nonzero \(c_i\) has no refutation of degree \(\lceil n/2\rceil\); the proof is that multiplication by the single axiom raises degree below the middle, by the full rank of the inclusion matrices, with an induction on multilinear representatives modulo the Boolean axioms.

Consequences. The upper bound is not a general ceiling and its mechanism, splitting along one linear axiom, has no counterpart in a covering system; the untested hypothesis conj:covering-half-ceiling gets no support from it and stays an untested hypothesis. The lower bound is for one linear equation over a field of characteristic zero; over \(\mathbb F_2\) a linear equation is affine and free. Neither result transfers. The same paper's pigeonhole lower bound, \(\lceil n/2\rceil+1\) over every field, is in the number of holes with about \(n^2\) variables.

  • The queued check waited on this paper. Follow-up. Unblocked: the user supplied the journal version on 9 October 2026 and its Sections 4 and 5 are read above.

Obstacle

No lower-bound method over \(\mathbb F_2\) is known that certifies degree beyond about a quarter of the free dimension for any polynomial-size family, while every structured candidate examined has fallen to a cheap upper bound using affine consequences. The block removed one method in the forms tested: independence or expansion by rank of small sets of rows, at widths one and two and uniformly in the number of rows. That suggests, and does not prove, that a method must use a hypothesis on the whole system; width three and more with a linear threshold is open.

Architecture review

Necessary target. For every fixed depth: polynomially many clauses of width \(w\), auxiliary affine equations, free dimension \(n\to\infty\), and \(1\notin C_{\lfloor n/2-s\rfloor}\) over \(\mathbb F_2\), with \(s+w\le n^{1-\epsilon}\). Existence of one family suffices; nothing need hold for arbitrary choices.

Extra requirements. The work of this block asked for more than the target in two places. The colouring frame fixes the encoding and then asks for a graph; the target does not need a graph. The rank route asked for a theorem valid for all systems with a local property and all forbidden values; the target needs one system. The second demand is now known to be unsatisfiable in the forms tested, and can be weakened to a hypothesis on one explicit, highly structured system.

Independent alternative. The reviewer, given only the goal and the available results (review.txt, stage one), found that none of the classical half bounds transfers: Razborov's pigeonhole bound is half the holes and about the square root of the dimension; the subset-sum bound is trivial over \(\mathbb F_2\); the Tseitin bounds need odd characteristic and give about a quarter for random systems. It proposed one different architecture: identify \(\mathbb F_2^n\) with \(\mathbb F_{2^k}^N\), in the extreme one coordinate in \(\mathbb F_{2^n}\), where degree is the binary weight of exponents, affine forms are traces, and rows are products of trace forms; take a family of rows invariant under Frobenius and a multiplicative subgroup, and use the theory of affine-invariant codes and the self-duality of Reed–Muller codes at half degree. Its expected break: an invariant family may collapse by a cyclic analogue of lem:symmetric-system-ceiling. It also suggested proving the static version first, where by its rough count dimension gives no obstruction once \(s\gg\sqrt{n\log n}\), and noted that the two-bit ceiling makes any family encoded over \(\mathbb F_4\) tight. These are the reviewer's statements, unverified by me.

Rank normalization. The question applies to the static version: the dual witness is a function of degree \(n\) whose restriction to each row's subspace has degree at most \(n-D-1\) there, and the count compares the span of these constraints with \(2^n\) in one space, the functions on the cube. The reviewer's rough count is of that kind; it is not verified, and a count gives no witness.

Decision. Test the alternative. Compared with the current practice, developing queue items in the colouring frame and on rows on forms, it differs in what supplies structure: a transitive symmetry of the whole system, a global hypothesis of the kind the block suggests is needed; the theory it comes with at half degree is self-duality of codes, not a result about polynomial calculus. The colouring frame is not continued in the next block except through its queued items.

Decisive test. Next cycle, as the fourth entry on the check on rows on linear forms. First the lemma that degree over \(\mathbb F_2\) with Boolean axioms is invariant under invertible affine changes of coordinates, so that the field description is legitimate. Then the smallest well-posed version of the invariant family, as the reviewer corrected my first wording: a cyclic subgroup of polynomial order need not exist, the group and Frobenius fix \(0\) so covering needs linear base subspaces, and covering needs the orbit to have at least \(2^w\) rows. Outcomes: if such orbits cannot cover, or every covering orbit system falls under a ceiling of degree \(O(w)\) or a small fraction of \(n\), the alternative is closed in this form and the route returns to the queue head; if a covering system without a visible ceiling exists, the next step is its degree at small \(n\) by exact computation. Working proofs of affine invariance of the degree and of the existence of invariant covers of codimension \(\log_2 n\); whether they are hard is not addressed. Queue development of a chosen check while draining. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort low).

Chosen. Fourth entry on the check on rows on linear forms, which bears on the family statement through a global hypothesis on the system of forms; it comes before the head because the goal-level review made this its decisive test.

Architecture test. The goal-level review asked for affine invariance of the degree and, for \(n+1\) prime with \(2\) a primitive root, whether orbits of polynomially many linear subspaces under the \((n+1)\)-th roots of unity and Frobenius can cover \(\mathbb F_{2^n}\), and whether a ceiling applies. Outcome: invariance holds; covers exist for codimension up to \(\log_2(n+1)\) with \(2n\) base subspaces, short of the \(2\log_2n\) the review named; I found no proved ceiling for them and no lower bound, and the reviewer's rank count predicts degree about \(n/8\). By the review's rule the alternative is not closed, and the next step is the exact degree at small \(n\).

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement: is the invariant family of the review well defined, non-empty, and visibly easy?

New mathematics. Degree over \(\mathbb F_2\) with Boolean axioms is invariant under invertible affine changes of coordinates. For \(p=n+1\) prime with \(2\) a primitive root, \(\mathbb F_{2^n}\) is the space of two-colourings of \(\mathbb Z_p\) modulo complementation, and the roots of unity with Frobenius act on it as the full affine group of \(\mathbb Z_p\) permuting the points, of order \(n(n+1)\) and sharply two-transitive. For \(w\le\log_2(n+1)\), \(n\ge3\), there are \(2n\) linear subspaces of codimension \(w\) whose orbits cover the space: an unsatisfiable invariant system of at most \(2n^2(n+1)\) rows of width \(w\) in free dimension \(n\). Covering needs \(2^w\le mn(n+1)\) for \(m\) base subspaces.

Goal progress. Unchanged. A family is defined and shown non-empty; nothing is proved about its degree, so the required implication is as before.

General statement. lem:affine-coordinate-invariance holds for every system and every invertible affine map; prop:cyclotomic-orbit-cover for every \(n\ge3\) with \(n+1\) prime and \(2\) a primitive root modulo \(n+1\).

Affine invariance

Lemma (affine coordinate invariance). Let \(A\) be an invertible affine map of \(\mathbb F_2^n\) and, for a multilinear polynomial \(f\), let \(f^A\) be the multilinear polynomial of the function \(f\circ A\). For a set \(\Gamma\) of multilinear polynomials and every \(D\), \(C_D(\Gamma^A)=C_D(\Gamma)^A\). In particular the two systems have the same refutation degree.

Proof. \(f\mapsto f^A\) is a ring automorphism of the functions on the cube. It does not raise degree, since each coordinate of \(A\) is an affine polynomial, and the same holds for \(A^{-1}\), so it preserves degree; hence it maps axioms of degree at most \(D\) to axioms of degree at most \(D\). \(C_D(\Gamma)\) is the least space containing those axioms and closed under \(q\mapsto x_iq\) for \(q\) in it of degree at most \(D-1\). If \(q^A\in C_D(\Gamma^A)\) has degree at most \(D-1\), then \((x_iq)^A=x_i^Aq^A\), and \(x_i^A\) is a constant plus a sum of variables, so \((x_iq)^A\) is a combination of \(q^A\) and of products \(x_jq^A\), all in \(C_D(\Gamma^A)\). By induction \(C_D(\Gamma)^A\subseteq C_D(\Gamma^A)\); the reverse inclusion is the same statement for \(A^{-1}\) and \(\Gamma^A\). \(\square\)

So a system of rows on forms all taken from one basis is a system of rows on variables, and the theorems for variables apply to it in that basis; and any \(\mathbb F_2\)-basis of \(\mathbb F_{2^n}\) may be used to speak of degree there.

The family

Let \(p=n+1\) be prime with \(2\) a primitive root modulo \(p\), and \(\zeta\in\mathbb F_{2^n}\) of order \(p\); it exists because \(p\) divides \(2^n-1\), and its minimal polynomial is the \(p\)-th cyclotomic polynomial, irreducible of degree \(n\) because \(2\) has order \(n\). So \(\zeta,\ldots,\zeta^n\) is a basis and \(\sum_{i\in\mathbb Z_p}\zeta^i=0\). The map \(y\mapsto\sum_{i\in\mathbb Z_p}y_i\zeta^i\) from \(\mathbb F_2^{\mathbb Z_p}\) onto \(\mathbb F_{2^n}\) has kernel spanned by the all-ones vector: points of the field are two-colourings of \(\mathbb Z_p\) up to complementation. Multiplication by \(\zeta\) shifts the indices by one and Frobenius multiplies them by two. Since \(2\) generates \(\mathbb Z_p^*\), the group \(\Gamma_p\) they generate acts as all maps \(i\mapsto ai+b\), \(a\ne0\): order \(n(n+1)\), sharply two-transitive on \(\mathbb Z_p\). Linear forms on the field are the sets of even size, \(y\mapsto\sum_{i\in S}y_i\).

Proposition (cyclotomic orbit cover). With these \(n,p\) (so \(n\ge4\)): (a) if the \(\Gamma_p\)-orbits of \(m\) subspaces of codimension \(w\) cover \(\mathbb F_{2^n}\), then \(2^w\le mn(n+1)\); (b) for every \(w\) with \(2^w\le n+1\) there are \(2n\) linear subspaces of codimension \(w\) whose orbits cover \(\mathbb F_{2^n}\).

Proof. (a) There are at most \(mn(n+1)\) rows, each with \(2^{n-w}\) points. (b) Let \(y\ne0\). The translations form a subgroup of prime order \(p\), and a translation fixing a colouring up to complementation fixes it, because it has odd order \(p\) and so cannot swap the colouring with its complement; a colouring fixed by a nontrivial translation is constant, that is, \(y=0\). So the orbit \(O\) of \(y\) has \(N\ge p\) points, all nonzero. Let \(V\) be a uniformly random subspace of codimension \(w\), and \(X=|O\cap V|\). For a nonzero point, \(\Pr[o\in V]=\pi=(2^{n-w}-1)/(2^n-1)\ge2^{-w}-2^{-n}\); for two distinct nonzero points, which are linearly independent over \(\mathbb F_2\), \(\Pr[o,o'\in V]=\pi(2^{n-w}-2)/(2^n-2)\le\pi^2\). So \(\mathbb E X^2\le\mathbb E X+(\mathbb E X)^2\) and \(\Pr[X>0]\ge\mathbb E X/(1+\mathbb E X)\). Here \(\mathbb E X=N\pi\ge p2^{-w}-p2^{-n}\ge1-(n+1)2^{-n}\ge1/2\) for \(n\ge3\), so \(\Pr[X>0]\ge1/3\). The orbit of \(V\) contains \(y\) exactly when \(V\) meets \(O\). For \(2n\) independent subspaces, \(y\) is uncovered with probability at most \((2/3)^{2n}<2^{-n}\), and there are fewer than \(2^n\) nonzero points; the point \(0\) lies in every subspace. \(\square\)

Part (b) uses only that orbits have at least \(p\) points, which the translations alone give: their orbits already cover, with \(2n(n+1)\) rows. Frobenius, the multipliers and two-transitivity are not used in the proposition; they are part of the family, not of its existence proof.

What can and cannot be said about its degree

The system of (b) has rows of width \(w\le\log_2(n+1)\), at most \(2n^2(n+1)\) of them, and free dimension \(n\), so its parameters are admissible for the family statement with any deficit. Checked against the recorded ceilings: the symmetric system ceiling needs each axiom symmetric and here only the set of axioms is invariant, under a group that is two-transitive and not more; the transversal rank ceiling needs forms of small rank making every row affine, and generic rows of width \(w\) need rank near \(n\); the counting proposition of the preceding entry needs about \(n^{w}\) rows; a group inside a subfield would put all rows on few forms, as the reviewer of the review noted, and here the group generates the whole field. No proved ceiling applies that I can see. A count does bear on it, as the reviewer points out: at degree \(D\) the multiples of one row of width \(w\) span at most \(\binom{n-w}{\le D-w}\) dimensions, so if the \(M\) rows behaved generically their multiples would span everything of degree at most \(D\) once \(M\) is about \((n/D)^w\); with \(M=2n^3\) and \(w=\log_2n\) that is \(D\approx n/8\). This is a prediction under generic rank, not a ceiling, but it says that this family reaches near half only through a large rank deficiency. No lower bound applies either: nothing recorded uses invariance, and each point lies on average in \(2n^2(n+1)2^{-w}\) rows, about \(2n^2\) at the largest \(w\) and more below, far more than a minimal cover needs, which in the samples of the small covers entry went with degree \(w+1\). The existence proof takes random base subspaces; the family that matters is the one with the fewest base subspaces, or with base subspaces defined by the arithmetic of \(\mathbb Z_p\), and neither is examined here.

So a candidate needs \(sw\gtrsim n\log(M/2^w)\), for example \(w,s\sim n^{0.6}\), or a rank deficiency forced by its structure.

A matching of disjoint pairs is untested.

The reviewer's counting threshold, if it becomes a statement, would bear on the specification directly: it favours width and deficit both of order \(n^{0.6}\) over logarithmic width.

9 October 2026 — Two counts for covers: the static span bound, the series as the wrong model for subspace rows, and the orbit covers far below half by both

One small working proof and one computation; corrects the reading of the series count in the fifth review: it models generic polynomials, not subspace rows. Queue development of a chosen check while draining. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort low).

Chosen. The queued check asking to replace the dimension count by the semi-regular series for parity-row systems bears on the family statement through the question which systems of rows leave room for a barrier near half; it comes before the head because the preceding entry's reviewer raised exactly this count, and the check on rows on linear forms has used its spell.

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement: the reviewer of the preceding entry suggested that generic rank leaves room near \(n/2-s\) only if the number of rows is at most about \(2^we^{2sw/n}\), favouring widths of order \(n^{0.6}\). Is that a statement, and what does it say about candidates?

New mathematics. Four points. (1) Large width is not an option: a cover by \(M\) subspaces has \(\sum_r2^{-w_r}\ge1\), so rows of codimension above \(\log_2M+t\) cover less than a fraction \(2^{-t}\); and a cover that is not odd has \(\sum_r2^{-w_r}\ge1+2^{-w}\). (2) The reviewer's count is a rigorous bound on the dimension of the static span: the multiples of one subspace row within degree \(D\) have dimension exactly \(\binom{n-w}{\le D-w}\), so the static span is proper below the least \(D\) with \(M\binom{n-w}{\le D-w}\ge\binom n{\le D}\); it bounds neither the closure nor the degree. (3) The series \((1+z)^n/\prod(1+z^{w_r})\), which the fifth review used for covers, is the count for generic polynomials of degree \(w\) and is the wrong model for subspace rows, whose multiples are about \(2^{w-1}\) times fewer near the middle; my first draft of this entry had it the other way round and the reviewer corrected it. That review's figure of \(0.35n\) for covers at covering sum one is therefore withdrawn as a prediction about covers: at covering sum one the static span is proper by dimension at every degree below \(n\). (4) At the parameters of the orbit covers the two counts agree: about \(0.1n\) for the proved covers and \(0.2n\) for one orbit at \(n=508\).

Goal progress. Unchanged. No constraint on candidates is proved beyond the elementary lemma and the dimension bound; the invariant family is not excluded and nothing supports it; a recorded reason for setting barely covering systems aside is withdrawn. The required implication is as before.

General statement. lem:cover-sum-gap holds for every cover of \(\mathbb F_2^n\) by affine subspaces. The series values are ex:orbit-cover-series-index, a statement about power series only.

The elementary constraints

Lemma (cover sum gap). Let affine subspaces \(V_1,\ldots,V_M\) of codimensions \(w_r\le w\) cover \(\mathbb F_2^n\), with indicator polynomials \(R_r\). (a) \(\sum_r2^{-w_r}\ge1\), and the rows of codimension greater than \(\log_2M+t\) cover fewer than \(2^{n-t}\) points. (b) \(g=1+\sum_rR_r\) is the indicator of the set \(E\) of points lying in an even number of rows, it has degree at most \(w\), and for \(D\ge w\), \(1\in C_D\) exactly when \(g\in C_D\). (c) If \(E\) is empty, \(1=\sum_rR_r\) is a refutation of degree \(w\). (d) Otherwise \(|E|\ge2^{n-w}\) and \(\sum_r2^{-w_r}\ge1+2^{-w}\).

Proof. (a) Count points with multiplicity; at most \(M\) rows of codimension above \(\log_2M+t\) have fewer than \(2^{n-t}/M\) points each. (b) Over \(\mathbb F_2\), \(\sum_rR_r(x)\) is the parity of the number of rows through \(x\); the rows are axioms of degree at most \(w\le D\). (c) is (b) with \(g=0\). (d) A nonzero multilinear polynomial of degree at most \(w\) is nonzero on at least \(2^{n-w}\) points; every point of \(E\) lies in at least two rows, so the count with multiplicity is at least \(2^n+|E|\). \(\square\)

Part (b) restates the task: refuting a cover is deriving the indicator of its evenly covered set, a polynomial of degree at most \(w\) supported on a set of density at most \(\sum_r2^{-w_r}-1\). Together with the recorded remark that the static degree is at most the largest codimension of a nonempty intersection of rows, this is all that counting gives rigorously here.

The two counts

Static span bound. For a subspace row \(R\) of codimension \(w\), \(Rq\) depends only on the restriction of \(q\) to the subspace, and within degree \(D\) the multiples \(Rq\), \(\deg q\le D-w\), form a space of dimension \(\binom{n-w}{\le D-w}\): after an affine change of coordinates \(R=x_1\cdots x_w\) and the multiples are \(x_1\cdots x_w\) times the polynomials of degree at most \(D-w\) in the other variables. So the span of all such multiples of \(M\) rows has dimension at most \(M\binom{n-w}{\le D-w}\). This is a bound on the static span only: the closure \(C_D\) may be larger, and a proper span may contain \(1\).

The series. \((1+z)^n/\prod_r(1+z^{w_r})\) is the semi-regular count for polynomials of degree \(w_r\) over \(\mathbb F_2\) with the field equations. A subspace row is never of that kind for \(w\ge2\): its top form is a product of linear forms \(l_1\cdots l_w\), and \(l_1\) annihilates it in degree \(w+1\) without lying in the ideal; correspondingly its multiples are far fewer than a generic polynomial's, which is nonzero on half the cube. So the series overestimates what subspace rows span, and its index is not a prediction for covers. The fifth review's statement that barely covering systems sit near \(0.35n\) "within the semi-regularity hypothesis" stands as a statement about that series and is withdrawn as a reason to set such covers aside; this entry is the correcting record.

What the bound says. Near \(D=n/2-s\) the ratio \(\binom n{\le D}/\binom{n-w}{\le D-w}\) is about \(2^we^{2sw/n+w^2/2n}\). With logarithmic \(w\), forced in measure by the lemma, the static span is proper by dimension near half only when the covering sum is \(1+O(sw/n)\); with \(s\le n^{1-\epsilon}\) that is a cover in which all but a fraction \(n^{-\epsilon}\log n\) of the points lie in exactly one row, while by part (d) of the lemma a non-odd cover has excess at least \(2^{-w}\), which is \(n^{-c}\) for \(w=c\log_2n\). The window is not empty. Both ends are easy cases: a partition has excess zero and degree \(w\); large excess fills the static span. Whether a cover inside the window can have a barrier near half is exactly as open as before; what changed is that the recorded heuristic reason against it is gone, and that for larger excess a barrier would need the static span to be proper although the dimension count allows it to be everything.

Both counts at the orbit parameters

Test design. Hypothesis: at the parameters of prop:cyclotomic-orbit-cover, \(w=\lfloor\log_2(n+1)\rfloor\), the series index over \(n\) is well below one half for \(M=n(n+1)\), one orbit, and for \(M=2n^2(n+1)\), the proved covers. Sizes: \(n=10,12,18,28,60,130,268,508\), all with \(n+1\) prime and \(2\) a primitive root, asserted in the script. A value near one half would have refuted it. Exact integer arithmetic, with the function of the fifth review's script. The static span bound, the least \(D\) at which the dimension count stops forcing a proper span, is computed alongside; "one orbit" means \(M=n(n+1)\) rows, an upper bound for an orbit, and single-orbit covers are not known to exist.

For the orbit family the dimension count thus allows the static span to be everything from about \(0.1n\) to \(0.2n\) on; a barrier near half would need it to stay proper far beyond. Specification decision. No change. Considered and rejected: admitting only widths of order \(n^{0.6}\); by (a) of the lemma uniformly wide rows cannot form a cover of polynomial size; wide rows may serve only for a residual fraction of the points. Considered and left open: restricting candidates to covers with covering sum \(1+O(n^{-\epsilon}\log n)\); it is suggested by a dimension count on the static span, which is not a necessary condition for a barrier.

Verification gate. One fresh-context medium reviewer found the lemma and all table entries of the first draft correct and its account of the two counts wrong: the series is the semi-regular count for generic polynomials, a subspace row is never semi-regular for width at least two, and the reviewer's count is a rigorous bound on the static span. The section, the title, the summary and the conclusions are rewritten accordingly, the fifth review's reading is corrected here, and the span bound was then computed alongside the series (its values for small \(n\) agree with the reviewer's hand values \(4,6,7\)). Further corrections applied: what is separated at which size; single-orbit covers are not known to exist; "carried" is in measure. The rewritten section was not re-read by the reviewer. Record: review.txt.

Follow-up. Closed: falsified. The check proposed to replace the dimension count by the semi-regular series for parity-row systems; the series is not the count for rows on linear forms, whose multiples have dimension \(\binom{n-w}{\le D-w}\), and the dimension count is the correct bound on the static span. Its calibration against random 3-CNF was not carried out and is not needed for this conclusion. What follows from the entry goes on under the check on rows on linear forms and its queued build: the exact static span and closure of orbit covers at \(n=18\), and covers with covering sum barely above one.

Reviewer's suggestions, unverified

  • An extremality of generic forms in the manner of Fröberg would say generic polynomials have the largest ideal in each degree, so structure can only delay filling; it bounds the refutation degree in neither direction, since a refutation can come before filling, as for a partition. It knows no class of systems proved to exceed the series index.
  • If the evenly covered set \(E\) is a subspace of codimension at most \(w\), restricting to it gives a cover whose rows sum to zero, and the degrees differ by at most \(w\); so totally even covers are a reduced case, and one can build covers recursively so that \(E\)'s induced cover is of the same kind in dimension \(n-w\), at a cost of at most \(w\) per level. Whether degree accumulates along the recursion is open.
  • A count for random subspace rows is the right generic model and is missing.

Process assessment. My first draft called the reviewer's count wrong and the recorded series right; it was the reverse, and the error went back to the fifth review, where the series was applied to covers without asking whether subspace rows are generic for it. The reviewer of that review did not catch it either. A heuristic model needs its hypothesis checked on the simplest instance, here one row, before its numbers are used to set a class of candidates aside.

9 October 2026 — A single-orbit cover at \(n=18\) has the largest static span the count allows and refutation degree exactly six; at \(n=10\), degree four

Finite check at two sizes; at these sizes invariance under the affine group produces no rank deficiency. It does not decide larger sizes. Queue development of a chosen build while draining. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort low).

Chosen. The queued build on orbit covers bears on the family statement as the test of the one candidate family defined so far; it comes before the head because the goal-level review named this computation as the step after existence.

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement: the static span bound allows the span of the multiples of the rows of an orbit cover to be everything from about \(0.2n\) on. Does the symmetry keep it proper beyond that, which a barrier near half would need, or does the family behave as the count allows?

New mathematics. At \(n=10\), \(w=3\) and at \(n=18\), \(w=4\) a single orbit of a random subspace covers the space, with \(110\) and \(342\) rows. At \(n=18\) the static span has rank exactly the count's bound at degrees four and five, \(342\) and \(5130\), and is the whole space of dimension \(31180\) at degree six, where the bound first exceeds the dimension; so \(1\) is a combination of multiples of rows of degree six. The span at degree five contains nothing of lower degree beyond the rows, so it is the closure and the refutation degree is exactly six. At \(n=10\) the span is everything at degree four, the exact refutation degree is four, and at degree three the \(110\) rows have five dependencies, which the reviewer traced to the particular base subspace. Before this I looked for a family with covering sum barely above one and found none; that attempt is described below.

Goal progress. Unchanged. The one candidate family shows generic behaviour at the two sizes computed; nothing is proved about it, and the required implication is as before.

General statement. The family is that of prop:cyclotomic-orbit-cover; the hypothesis tested, that its static span stays proper beyond the degree at which lem:cover-sum-gap's dimension count allows it to be everything, is refuted at the two sizes by ex:orbit-cover-static-span. No all-parameter statement is proved; that orbit covers have nearly the largest possible static span at every size is an untested hypothesis beyond these sizes.

Test design, before the run

Hypothesis in the family's favour: for a covering orbit, \(1\notin S_D\) at the least \(D\) with \(M\binom{n-w}{\le D-w}\ge\binom n{\le D}\), where \(S_D\) is the span of \(mR\), \(R\) a row and \(m\) a monomial of degree at most \(D-w\). Sizes: \(n=18\) is the smallest at which the three values to be told apart differ, \(w+1=5\), the count's degree \(6\), and \(n/2=9\); \(n=10\) serves as control against the exact kernel, since there the count's degree equals \(w+1=4\). Outcomes: \(1\in S_6\) at \(n=18\) refutes the hypothesis at that size; \(1\notin S_6\) with rank below the dimension would be the deficiency sought. Since \(S_D\subseteq C_D\), \(1\in S_D\) gives refutation degree at most \(D\).

The hypothesis is refuted at both sizes. At \(n=18\) the rows' multiples are linearly independent through degree five and span everything at degree six: the largest span the count allows at every degree. The refutation degree there is exactly six: the part of \(S_5\) of degree at most four has rank \(342\), the rank of \(S_4\), so every element of \(S_5\) of degree at most four is a combination of rows, \(S_5\) is closed under multiplication by variables within degree five, hence \(C_5=S_5\), which does not contain \(1\). The reviewer found this with an added count, which is now in the program. At \(n=10\) the same count gives \(C_3=S_3\) and degree exactly four, as the exact kernel of the small covers entry gives for the same cover. At \(n=10\), degree three, the rank is \(105\) and not \(110\): the reviewer computed the kernel and found the five relations \(\sum_bR_{a,b}=\sum_bR_{-a,b}\), one for each pair \(\pm a\), and that seven of eight other random bases do not have them; they belong to this base, not to orbits. The cover was found at the first random subspace at both sizes.

What this says. The symmetry does not by itself make the span small: at \(n=18\) the orbit cover has the largest span a system of subspace rows can have, and at \(n=10\) it falls short by five dimensions at one degree for a reason special to the base. If that persists, the refutation degree of single-orbit covers follows the count, about \(0.2n\), and the proved covers with more base subspaces lie lower. What it does not say: two sizes decide nothing about growth, and base subspaces chosen by the arithmetic of \(\mathbb Z_p\), not at random, were not examined. The series is stopped: the next admissible size is \(n=28\), where the elimination at the count's degree seven has dimension about \(1.7\) million, and the question the sizes could answer, whether invariance alone gives deficiency, is answered at the sizes that can test it.

The attempt on covers with covering sum barely above one

The next step named such covers. A cover in which every point lies in at most \(c\) rows is refuted in degree \(cw\): expand \(\prod_r(1+R_r)=0\), in which products of more than \(c\) rows vanish. So a barrier at \(D\) needs a point in at least \(D/w\) rows whose forms have joint rank at least \(D\), as the recorded remark on intersections says, while the average multiplicity is \(1+o(1)\). I tried the simplest shape: about \(n/2w\) rows through the origin on disjoint blocks of coordinates, the rest covered by shallow rows with small overlap. The overlap is small enough for the window when \(2^w\ge n^2\). But the shallow rows together with the block rows are again an arbitrary system of rows on forms, a formula in the forms, and I found no choice for which a lower bound is in reach or for which the block rows are needed in an essential way; when the shallow rows form a partition they refute alone. No family and no statement came of it.

Checks, scope and verification

Controls: at \(n=10\) its first degree with \(1\) in the span, four, equals the exact refutation degree from the earlier kernel for the same cover (cover, output "4 0": degree four, and the flag says the cover is not minimal); the rank at the lowest degree is at most the number of rows, and the full rank at the top degree equals \(\binom n{\le D}\). Outputs: span-n10.jsonl, span-n18.jsonl. The run at \(n=18\) took 130 s; it was run twice, the second time with the count of the last column.

Scope. One random base subspace at each of two sizes, seed 1. At \(n=18\) the closure is known at degree five only through the count described above.

Specification decision. No change. Invariance under the affine group of \(\mathbb Z_p\) is not added to the specification: at the sizes tested it does not produce what a candidate needs.

One fresh-context medium reviewer checked the program's group action, canonical forms, cover test, row expansion, indexing, accumulation of the span, the criterion for \(1\) and the arithmetic, and recomputed the rank \(105\) at \(n=10\) from truth tables. Corrections applied: the degree at \(n=18\) is exactly six, by a count the reviewer made on a scratch copy and which I added to the program and reran; the claim of generic behaviour is restricted to \(n=18\) and the five relations at \(n=10\) are described; the obstacle at \(n=28\) is the elimination; the control's cover file and flag are recorded; the program now checks that \(2\) is a primitive root; undone work is listed as a sub-idea. Record: review.txt.

Decide whether \(p\) translates can cover when \(2^w\le p\), by proof or by enumeration at \(p=11,13,19\); if a cover exists, the dimension count keeps its static span proper far beyond half, and its degree is the next thing to compute.

9 October 2026 — Translates of a multiplier-invariant subspace do not cover with covering sum below two, at \(p=13\) and \(19\); in that range they miss about \(e^{-p/2^w}\) of the points

Finite check refuting the candidate at the two sizes that test it, with a counting lemma that is too weak to prove it in general. Queue development of a chosen check while draining. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort low).

Chosen. The queued check on covers by translates bears on the family statement as the first candidate with covering sum barely above one, the window the dimension count leaves open; it comes before the head because the preceding entry named it.

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement: for \(p=n+1\) prime with \(2\) a primitive root and a subspace \(V\) of codimension \(w\) invariant under all multipliers, can the \(p\) translates of \(V\) cover the space when \(p/2<2^w<p\)?

New mathematics. Not at the sizes examined. The invariant subspaces of codimension \(w\) correspond to the divisors of degree \(w\) of \(x^n-1\) over \(\mathbb F_2\). At \(p=13\), \(w=3\), both miss about \(18\%\) of the points; at \(p=19\), \(w=4\), both miss about \(29\%\); at \(p=11\) there is no invariant subspace of codimension three. The missed fractions are close to \(e^{-p/2^w}\), what independent random rows would miss. A counting lemma gives a necessary condition for covering that turns out to be the first-moment bound \(p>2^w\) again. One exact case exists, \(p=5\), \(w=2\): the five translates of the subfield of four elements partition the nonzero elements of the field of sixteen.

Goal progress. Unchanged. A candidate inside the window is excluded at two sizes; no family is obtained and the required implication is as before.

General statement. lem:translate-cover-count holds for every such \(p\) and every subspace, invariant or not. The hypothesis that translates cover in the window is refuted at \(p=13,19\) by ex:translate-cover-enumeration; that they never do for \(p>5\) is an untested hypothesis beyond these sizes, and the lemma does not prove it.

Setting and the attempt at a proof

As in the orbit covers entry, the space is \(F=\mathbb F_{2^n}\) with \(\zeta\) of order \(p\); translation is multiplication by \(\zeta\) and the multipliers are the powers of Frobenius. A subspace is invariant under all multipliers exactly when it is a Frobenius submodule; \(F\) has a normal basis, so it is a free module of rank one over \(\mathbb F_2[x]/(x^n-1)\), and its submodules of codimension \(w\) are the images of the divisors \(g\) of \(x^n-1\) of degree \(w\). The orbit of such a \(V\) under the whole group is \(\{\zeta^bV\}\), at most \(p\) rows.

Lemma (translate cover count). Let \(V\subseteq F\) be an \(\mathbb F_2\)-subspace of codimension \(w\) and \(\mu\) the group of \(p\)-th roots of unity. (a) \(\bigcup_b\zeta^bV=F\) exactly when \(y\mapsto y^p\) maps \(V\setminus0\) onto the group of \(p\)-th powers, which has \((2^n-1)/p\) elements. (b) The number of nonzero points covered is at most \(p(2^{n-w}-1)-\sum_{d\ne0}(|V\cap\zeta^dV|-1)\le p(2^{n-w}-1)-(p-1)(2^{n-2w}-1)\). (c) So covering requires \(p(2^{n-w}-1)-(p-1)(2^{n-2w}-1)\ge2^n-1\).

Proof. (a) \(x\in\zeta^bV\) for some \(b\) exactly when the coset \(x\mu\) meets \(V\), and \(x\mu\mapsto x^p\) is a bijection from the cosets of \(\mu\) in \(F^*\) to the \(p\)-th powers. (b) For \(x\ne0\) let \(N(x)\) be the number of \(b\) with \(x\in\zeta^bV\). Then \(\sum_xN(x)=p(2^{n-w}-1)\) and \(\sum_xN(x)(N(x)-1)=\sum_{b\ne b'}(|\zeta^bV\cap\zeta^{b'}V|-1)=p\sum_{d\ne0}(|V\cap\zeta^dV|-1)\). Since \(N\le p\), \(N-1\ge N(N-1)/p\) where \(N\ge1\), so the number of covered points is \(\sum N-\sum_{N\ge1}(N-1)\le\sum N-\tfrac1p\sum N(N-1)\). Each \(V\cap\zeta^dV\) has codimension at most \(2w\). (c) follows. \(\square\)

The condition in (c) is equivalent to \(p\ge2^w+1\) exactly, as the reviewer computed: it is the first-moment bound and excludes nothing new. Equality \(p=2^w+1\) with \(2\) a primitive root forces \(p\in\{3,5\}\), and \(p=5\) is the exact case below. A proof that translates do not cover in the window would need the distribution of \(N\) and not only its first two moments; I do not have one.

The enumeration

Test design. Hypothesis: for some invariant \(V\) of codimension \(w\) with \(p/2<2^w<p\) the translates cover. Sizes: the admissible \(p\le19\) other than \(3\), that is \(5,11,13,19\) (at \(p=3\) the window is \(w=1\), which covers); the window is \(w=2\) at \(p=5\), \(w=3\) at \(11\) and \(13\), \(w=4\) at \(19\). All divisors of every degree with \(2^w<p\) are enumerated, so larger covering sums serve as controls: \(w=1\) must cover, since some translate of any point has trace zero. A single cover in the window at \(p\ge11\) would confirm the hypothesis.
