That is a spread, exact because \((2^m-1)p=2^n-1\). A proper spread has rows of dimension \(m\) dividing \(n\), so of codimension at least \(n/2\), and at least \(2^{n/2}+1\) of them: not polynomially many. Script translate_covers.py, output translate-covers.jsonl; the script asserts that each kernel has dimension \(w\) and is invariant under doubling. The kernel of \(g(T)\) on forms may correspond to the reciprocal divisor on \(F\); all divisors in the table are self-reciprocal. Every uncovered count is divisible by \(p\), as part (a) requires.

A remark I drew from this in the draft was false, and the reviewer's counterexample is worth keeping. I had written that a cover with covering sum \(1+o(1)\) cannot consist of shallow rows through one point. It can: take a spread of \(2^w+1\) subspaces of dimension \(w\) in \(\mathbb F_2^{2w}\) and pull it back along a quotient map from \(\mathbb F_2^n\). That gives \(2^w+1\) subspaces of codimension \(w\) through \(0\), pairwise meeting in one common subspace \(U\) of codimension \(2w\), covering everything with covering sum \(1+2^{-w}\): the equality case of part (b), with \(N=1\) off \(U\) and \(N=2^w+1\) on it, and of part (d) of the cover sum gap. It depends on \(2w\) forms only and so is refuted in degree at most \(2w+w\) by the transversal rank ceiling. Two subspaces of codimension \(w\) through a point share a fraction at least \(2^{-w}\) of each, and that is all that is true.

Reviewer's suggestions, unverified

  • A partial proof of non-covering: a singleton colouring is uncovered exactly when some form of \(L\) contains \(0\), which holds exactly when \((x+1)^{2^k}\) divides \(g\), \(2^k\) the power of two in \(n\); it matches the three table rows with misses outside the window and predicts none at \(5\) or \(13\); colourings of weight two and three might settle the other divisors. Record. Searched "translate cover singleton colouring divisor" and this notebook: nothing recorded on translate covers before this entry.
  • Candidates for the remaining shape: the lifted spread above, a function of \(2w\) forms; the cosets of a Hamming code, an exact partition of codimension \(\log_2(n+1)\) that is a parity decision tree; irreducible subcube partitions and affine vector space partitions (Filmus and others; Bamberg, Filmus, Ihringer and Kurz), which are exact, so that no barrier can come from an unevenly covered set. Record. Searched "irreducible subcube partition affine vector space partition", "spread subspaces partition lifted junta", "Hamming code cosets perfect code partition": matches only in other threads (junta residues, code balls); this notebook mentions none of them. By lem:cover-sum-gap (c) every exact partition is refuted in degree \(w\), so these are not candidates.

Specification decision. No change. Considered: requiring candidates to have covering sum \(1+o(1)\). It is suggested only by a dimension count on the static span, which is not a necessary condition for a barrier; not adopted.

Verification gate. One fresh-context medium reviewer checked the module statement, the lemma, the script and all fifteen table rows by hand, and found them correct. Corrections applied: the paragraph claiming that covering sum near one excludes shallow rows through a point was false, by the lifted spread, and is replaced by that example; part (c) is exactly the first-moment bound; the sentence on spreads is corrected; \(p=3\) is mentioned; the title is restricted to the window; the reciprocal divisor is noted; the lemma does not use invariance. The reviewer did not rerun the script. Record: review.txt.

9 October 2026 — The parity chain ceiling holds for labels that read linear forms; the colouring screen sharpened from homology to chains

Working proof of one extension of the lead's theorem, and a sharper form of its colouring screen; the lead stays open, its lower-bound direction untried. Queue development of the head while draining. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort low).

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement: the queue's head, the Fan parity and graph topology lead, produced a ceiling from antipodal chain certificates and a homology screen for colouring systems. Does it still bear on the family statement, in particular for systems of rows on linear forms, which the route has moved to since?

New mathematics. The parity chain ceiling extends from labels reading \(b\) Boolean bits to labels reading \(b\) linear forms, with rows on forms in place of clauses, in the multilinear calculus: degree at most \(b(m+1)\). So topological certificates of this kind give low-degree refutations in the hidden-subspace form as well, and the homology screen for colourings is unaffected by auxiliary affine equations. The colouring screen is also recorded in its sharper form: existence of the chains themselves, one linear system, already gives the ceiling.

Goal progress. Unchanged. An upper-bound tool is extended to the setting of the last entries; it excludes candidates and supplies none, and the required implication is as before.

General statement. prop:form-label-chain-ceiling holds for every complex, chain system and labelling satisfying its hypotheses; cor:colouring-chain-screen for every graph and number of colours.

The extension

Setting of the chain compiler: a finite simplicial complex \(K\) with a simplicial involution \(\tau\), and chains \(c_j\in C_j(K;\mathbb F_2)\), \(0\le j\le m\), with \(\operatorname{aug}(c_0)=1\) and \(\partial c_j=(1+\tau)c_{j-1}\). Let \(\Gamma\) be a system of rows on linear forms on \(\mathbb F_2^n\): each row forbids one tuple of values of its linearly independent forms, and its polynomial is the corresponding product of affine forms.

Proposition (form label chain ceiling). For each vertex \(u\) of \(K\) let a label \(L_u\in\{\pm1,\ldots,\pm m\}\) be a function of the values of at most \(b\ge1\) linear forms, a set \(F_u\), with \(L_{\tau u}=-L_u\). Suppose that whenever the labels at an edge \(uv\) are opposite at a point, the point violates a row of \(\Gamma\) whose forms lie in the span of \(F_u\cup F_v\). Then \(1\) is a combination of multiples of row polynomials in which every multiple is a product of at most \(b(m+1)\) affine forms; in particular \(\Gamma\) is refuted in the multilinear calculus in degree at most \(b(m+1)\).

Proof. The argument of the parity chain ceiling uses the bits only in its local compilation step; the parity identity for alternating simplices and the chain summation are statements about label values. So it suffices to redo that step, for the parity identity on simplices of dimension \(1\le j\le m\); an opposite pair of labels in a simplex sits on one of its edges. Fix a simplex \(\sigma\) of dimension \(j\le m\) and let \(W\) be the span of the forms read at its vertices, with basis \(g_1,\ldots,g_r\), \(r\le b(j+1)\). The difference of the two sides of the parity identity on \(\sigma\) is a function \(\delta\) of the values of \(g_1,\ldots,g_r\), and it vanishes at every point that violates no row with forms in the span of two vertices' forms, hence at every point violating no row with forms in \(W\). Write \(\delta=\sum_a\delta(a)\,\mathbf 1[g=a]\) over the value tuples \(a\) with \(\delta(a)\ne0\). For such \(a\), the points with \(g=a\) violate a row \(R\) with forms \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_k\in W\), and since the \(\lambda\)'s are functions of \(g\), the whole flat \(\{g=a\}\) lies in the forbidden flat of \(R\). Extend \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_k\) to a basis \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_k,h_1,\ldots,h_{r-k}\) of \(W\); the flat \(\{g=a\}\) is given by the forbidden values of the \(\lambda\)'s and some values \(e_i\) of the \(h\)'s, so \(\mathbf 1[g=a]=R\cdot\prod_i(h_i+e_i+1)\), a multiple of the row polynomial that is a product of \(r\le b(j+1)\) affine forms. Thus each local identity is a combination of such multiples, as functions and therefore as multilinear polynomials. Summing along the chains as in the original proof gives \(1\) as a combination of multiples, each a product of at most \(b(m+1)\) affine forms; its multilinear reduction has degree at most \(b(m+1)\), and each multiple \(R\prod(h_i+e_i+1)\) is derivable from \(R\) within that degree by multiplying by one affine form at a time. \(\square\)

For bits this is the original theorem, with the \(g\)'s variables. The one change is the cofactor: with variables it lives on the coordinates outside the clause, here on a complement of the row's forms inside \(W\).

Corollary (colouring chain screen). Let \(G\) have an edge, \(c\ge2\), \(b=\lceil\log_2c\rceil\), and let \(B_0(G)\) be the complex of the homology screen with its sign-swapping involution. If chains \(c_0,\ldots,c_c\) on \(B_0(G)\) with \(\operatorname{aug}(c_0)=1\) and \(\partial c_j=(1+\tau)c_{j-1}\) exist, the compact \(b\)-bit \(c\)-colouring system of \(G\), with any auxiliary affine equations, is refuted in degree at most \(b(c+1)\). Whether they exist is one linear system over \(\mathbb F_2\) of size polynomial in \(|V(G)|\) for fixed \(c\).

Proof. This is the last paragraph of the proof of the neighbourhood homology ceiling, which uses the homology hypothesis only to produce the chains: label \((v,\pm)\) by plus or minus the colour of \(v\), read from \(b\) bits, and apply the chain ceiling with \(m=c\). Added affine equations are further axioms and do not raise the degree. The unknowns are the coefficients of the chains on faces of dimension at most \(c\), of which there are \(O(|V(G)|^{c+1})\). \(\square\)

The reviewer pointed out that this is sharper than the recorded screen: the chains need only an equivariant chain map from a sphere of dimension \(c\), not vanishing homology, and the Kneser corollary already used chains without that hypothesis. For four colours a candidate must therefore admit no such chains through \(m=4\) on \(B_0(G)\), which implies the homology condition and is checkable for a given graph.

Where the lead stands

Its results are upper bounds and one witness: thm:parity-chain-degree-ceiling, cor:neighborhood-homology-ceiling, cor:kneser-parity-ceiling for full Kneser graphs, and prop:high-girth-homology-witness, that the screen is not vacuous; now also the two statements above. The source it was meant to test, edge-minimal cores of Kneser graphs, was bounded afterwards by the independent colour ceiling at \(3v/8+o(v)\), through their independence number. For the systems of rows on forms of the last entries the proposition makes the mechanism available, but it needs a complex, chains and a labelling, and I know of none for the covers studied in this block.

One direction of the lead was never attempted: the review that queued it said that the absence of a chain certificate would direct a lower-bound attempt. Absence of chains says only that this particular certificate fails. Whether an obstruction to the chains can be turned into a property of the closure, a standard monomial or a dual witness, is untried, and it is the reason the lead is not closed here.

Reviewer's suggestions, unverified

  • Tucker and Borsuk–Ulam search problems, octahedral Tucker included, are complete for the class of parity arguments, and totality in that class corresponds to low-degree Nullstellensatz over \(\mathbb F_2\); so principles of this kind with locally read labels are expected to be easy over \(\mathbb F_2\), and the proposition is the query form of that fact. Record. Searched "Tucker Borsuk-Ulam PPA Nullstellensatz octahedral": one unrelated match in the cube thread; this notebook has no claim on such principles.
  • Hardness of parity principles is known in odd characteristic only; octahedral Tucker has far more table bits than its ceiling; Kneser–Lovász formulas have known hardness only through the pigeonhole principle, far below half the variables; Schrijver graphs map to a Kneser graph that the independent colour ceiling already bounds. Record. Searched "Kneser Lovasz formulas truncated Tucker Frege proofs" and "Schrijver graph stable Kneser": cor:kneser-core-degree-ceiling is the recorded bound for Kneser cores; Schrijver graphs are not mentioned in this notebook.

Specification decision. No change. For four-colour candidates the homology screen is replaced by the sharper chain screen: no chains through \(m=4\) on \(B_0(G)\), with any auxiliary affine equations. It follows from the degree hypothesis and is checkable; whether it is binding beyond the homology screen is not known. No condition is added for covers, the proposition having no instance among them.

Verification gate. One fresh-context medium reviewer read the original theorem's proof and found no gap in the proposition: the bits enter only in the local step, the edge hypothesis suffices, the cofactor has the stated number of factors and the degree is right. Corrections applied: a remark deriving the proposition from affine invariance was wrong as stated and is removed; the bound for Kneser cores is quoted with its error term; the closure was premature and is withdrawn; the sharper chain screen it pointed out is stated as a corollary, whose proof is a paragraph of the recorded one and was not separately reviewed; the merge of the child check is dropped. Record: review.txt.

Follow-up. Continuing. First entry on the lead in this spell. Next attempt on it: the untried direction, what an obstruction to the chains on \(B_0(G)\) says about the closure of the colouring system, starting from the smallest graph on which the chain system has no solution.

9 October 2026 — Graphs without \(K_{2,3}\) have no chains: the topological screen binds only dense local structure, and its failure says nothing about hardness

Working proof, resting on one imported theorem read at its source; the lead's lower-bound direction is closed by it. Queue development of the head while draining. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort low).

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement: the colouring chain screen says a four-colour candidate must admit no chains through \(m=4\) on \(B_0(G)\). Which graphs admit none, and does an obstruction to the chains say anything about the closure of the colouring system?

New mathematics. A graph with no complete bipartite subgraph \(K_{\ell,m}\) has no chains through \(\ell+m-1\) on \(B_0(G)\). So every graph without \(K_{2,3}\), in particular every graph without four-cycles, passes the four-colour chain screen, whatever its chromatic number. Among such graphs are non-four-colourable families refuted in constant degree. Hence the absence of chains carries no information on the degree, and the screen constrains only graphs that contain \(K_{2,3}\).

Goal progress. Unchanged. The scope of one screen is determined and a hoped-for lower-bound direction is closed; no family and no method, and the required implication is as before.

General statement. prop:bipartite-free-chain-bound holds for every graph and all \(\ell,m\ge1\).

Imported statement

Csorba, Lange, Schurr and Wassmer, Box complexes, neighborhood complexes, and the chromatic number (arXiv math/0310339; Sections 2, 4 and the statement of Section 5 read by me, not redistributed). With \(B(G)=\{A\uplus B:\ A,B\in N(G),\ G[A;B]\text{ complete bipartite}\}\) and \(L(G)\) the Lovász complex: the halved doubled Lovász complex, a subcomplex of the shore subdivision of \(B(G)\), is a strong \(\mathbb Z_2\)-deformation retract of \(B(G)\) (their Theorem 3) and is \(\mathbb Z_2\)-isomorphic to \(L(G)\) (their Theorem 2); and if \(G\) contains no \(K_{\ell,m}\) then \(\dim L(G)\le\ell+m-3\) (second proof of their Theorem 1). From this I use only an equivariant continuous map from \(B(G)\) to \(L(G)\) and the dimension, not the index. The source takes freeness of the actions as part of its notion of a \(\mathbb Z_2\)-space; it holds because \(G\) has no loops: \(A\cap CN(A)=\emptyset\) for nonempty \(A\), so no simplex \(A\uplus B\) has \(A=B\) and no chain of closed sets contains both \(A\) and \(CN(A)\).

The bound

Lemma (dimension bound for chains). Let \(X\) be a simplicial complex of dimension \(d\) with a simplicial involution \(\tau\) that fixes no nonempty simplex setwise (equivalently, acts freely on points). There are no chains \(c_0,\ldots,c_{d+1}\) with \(\operatorname{aug}(c_0)=1\) and \(\partial c_j=(1+\tau)c_{j-1}\).

Proof. \(c_{d+1}=0\), so \((1+\tau)c_d=0\). No simplex is fixed, so an invariant chain is \((1+\tau)e\) for some chain \(e\): \(c_d=(1+\tau)e_d\). Suppose \(c_j=\partial e_{j+1}+(1+\tau)e_j\), which holds for \(j=d\) with \(e_{d+1}=0\). Then \((1+\tau)c_{j-1}=\partial c_j=(1+\tau)\partial e_j\), so \(c_{j-1}+\partial e_j\) is invariant and \(c_{j-1}=\partial e_j+(1+\tau)e_{j-1}\). At \(j=0\): \(\operatorname{aug}(c_0)=\operatorname{aug}(\partial e_1)+\operatorname{aug}((1+\tau)e_0)=0\). \(\square\)

Proposition (bipartite-free chain bound). If \(G\) contains no \(K_{\ell,m}\) as a subgraph, there are no chains through \(\ell+m-1\) on \(B_0(G)\). In particular a graph without \(K_{2,3}\) admits none through \(4\) and passes the four-colour chain screen.

Proof. \(B_0(G)\) is the union of \(B(G)\) and the two full simplices \(\Delta^+,\Delta^-\) on the positive and the negative vertices: a simplex \(A^+\cup B^-\) with both sides nonempty has \(A\subseteq CN(B)\), \(B\subseteq CN(A)\), so both sides lie in \(N(G)\) and it is in \(B(G)\). \(\Delta^\pm\) meets \(B(G)\) in the shore, a copy of \(N(G)\), and \(\Delta^+\cap\Delta^-=\emptyset\). Let \(Y\) be the suspension of \(L(G)\) with the involution that acts on \(L(G)\) and swaps the two apexes; triangulated as the join with two points, it is a free simplicial \(\mathbb Z_2\)-complex of dimension at most \(\ell+m-2\). The retraction \(B(G)\to L(G)\) is equivariant; compose with the inclusion of the equator. On \(\Delta^+\) extend the resulting map of the shore into the cone of \(Y\) over the positive apex, which is contractible; define the map on \(\Delta^-\) by applying \(\tau\). This gives a continuous equivariant map \(B_0(G)\to Y\). The involution of \(B_0(G)\) is free, since the two sides of a simplex are disjoint; for a free action on the source, the map has an equivariant simplicial approximation from an iterated barycentric subdivision of \(B_0(G)\) to \(Y\): choose the approximation on one vertex of each orbit by the star condition and extend by \(\tau\). Subdivision is an equivariant chain map preserving augmentation, and so is a simplicial map; so chains through \(k\) on \(B_0(G)\) give chains through \(k\) on a free complex of dimension at most \(\ell+m-2\). By the lemma \(k\le\ell+m-2\). \(\square\)

No information on the degree

Corollary. For every \(N\) there is a graph on at least \(N\) vertices that is not four-colourable, has no chains through \(3\) on \(B_0(G)\), and whose two-bit four-colouring system is refuted in degree bounded independently of \(N\).

Proof. Let \(G_0\) be a non-four-colourable graph of girth at least five, which exists by the high girth witness or the classical theorem, and attach a path of \(N\) new vertices at one vertex. The result has no four-cycle, that is, no \(K_{2,2}\), and the proposition gives no chains through \(3\). Its system contains that of \(G_0\), which is refuted in degree at most \(2|V(G_0)|\). \(\square\)

So an obstruction to the chains is not a source of lower bounds: it is present in every graph of girth five, easy or not. The review that queued this lead expected that the failure of a topological certificate would direct a lower-bound attempt; what the failure shows is only that the graph has little complete bipartite structure. In the other direction the screen is real but narrow: it can exclude only candidates that contain \(K_{2,3}\) or \(K_{1,4}\), which is necessary and not sufficient; \(K_5\) is such a case.

Reviewer's suggestions, unverified

  • No real use of obstruction theory for lower bounds over \(\mathbb F_2\): mod-2 topological principles are parity arguments, which correspond to low-degree Nullstellensatz over \(\mathbb F_2\), so obstruction classes over \(\mathbb F_2\) are dual to the chain system and not to the closure. Record. Consistent with the corollary above; the preceding entry's search on Tucker-type principles found no claim in this notebook.
  • The one direction it can sketch is a mismatch of characteristic: principles certified by \(\mathbb Z_p\)-topology for odd \(p\), such as colourings of \(p\)-uniform Kneser hypergraphs, are counting arguments modulo \(p\), which need linear degree over \(\mathbb F_2\); the known dual witnesses there are algebraic, with constants far below one half. Record. Searched "counting principle mod p characteristic two linear degree Kneser hypergraph": thm:triple-colouring-degree-ceiling and prop:kneser-critical-core-witness bear on hypergraph and Kneser colourings; the notebook's modular sources and their ceilings are in the working context; nothing recorded combines \(\mathbb Z_p\)-topology with a degree bound.

Specification decision. The chain screen for four-colour candidates is kept and its scope stated: it is satisfied automatically by graphs without \(K_{2,3}\), and by those of maximum degree three, and needs checking only for the others. It follows from the degree hypothesis; it is not binding on sparse candidates such as the high girth witness.

Verification gate. One fresh-context medium reviewer read the source's text and found no break in the lemma, the proposition or the corollary; the bound agrees with the recorded controls, \(K_4\) failing at level four, the five-cycle at three, and \(K_5\) having chains through four. Corrections applied: the citation is to the halved doubled Lovász complex as the retract and its isomorphism with \(L(G)\); freeness is checked and not taken from the source; the lemma's hypothesis is stated as no fixed simplex; the approximation needs no subdivision of the target; the corollary gives no chains through three; the sentence on \(K_{2,3}\) is a necessary condition and the clause on Kneser graphs is dropped; the scope of the closing statement is narrowed to \(B_0(G)\) with colour labels. Unused: strength of the retraction; finiteness. Record: review.txt.

  • The lead's check asks for a different compact four-colour source meeting the independence threshold and the homology and local screens, or a replacement of the graph route. The search for such a graph is the standing four-colour check, to which the game value, the absence of bounded affine consequences and now the chain screen with its scope have been added; this item's wording is carried over to it so that the independence threshold and the topological screen stay in its statement. Follow-up. Closed: merged into entry-2026-10-08-four-colour-fibres:s1

Follow-up. Developed: the lead's ceilings and screens are thm:parity-chain-degree-ceiling, prop:form-label-chain-ceiling and cor:colouring-chain-screen; the scope of the screen and the failure of its lower-bound direction are prop:bipartite-free-chain-bound. No application to the open statement remains: for \(B_0(G)\) with colour labels the mechanism gives upper bounds only, and where it gives none it says nothing. Other complexes and labellings are not excluded by this; none is on record for a candidate.

Process assessment. The direction left untried for many entries took one cycle once the right source was read; its answer is negative and general. I recalled the source's theorem from memory before reading it and had the complex and the bound slightly wrong; the proof here uses what the text states.

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement: after six more research entries without goal progress, what did the block establish, what is the line stuck on, and what should be tested next?

The previous review's test was reported by the orbit covers entry and completed by the span computation: the invariant family exists and, at the sizes that can be computed, has the largest static span the dimension count allows and refutation degree six at \(n=18\). By that review's rule the alternative is closed in the forms tested.

General statement. The line's general claim is the open statement itself: polynomial-length literal CNFs with auxiliary affine equations over \(\mathbb F_2\), of free dimension \(n\), with no refutation at degree \(\lfloor n/2-s\rfloor\), \(s+w\le n^{1-\epsilon}\); by thm:near-half-frege-transfer this gives the goal. No registered claim asserts it.

Across the goal

  • Near-half Boolean PC family: open, status unchanged since the last goal-level review; six research cycles in this block, twenty-six since the transfer was proved.
  • Complete Frege transfer: working proof within stated limits; no cycle spent on it in this block; \(c_F\) still not computed.

The block's results, with claim IDs. The invariant family: lem:affine-coordinate-invariance, prop:cyclotomic-orbit-cover (existence), ex:orbit-cover-static-span (generic span, degree six at \(n=18\)), ex:translate-cover-enumeration with lem:translate-cover-count (no covers with covering sum below two at \(p=13,19\); the lifted spread). Counting for covers: lem:cover-sum-gap and ex:orbit-cover-series-index, with the correction that the semi-regular series is not a model for subspace rows, so that the fifth review's figure of \(0.35n\) for barely covering systems is withdrawn. Framework change in the block, at the user's direction (9 October 2026): reviewer suggestions are listed with the outcome of a record search, checked by the finisher. Three entries have been written under it.

Obstacle

Unchanged in substance: no lower-bound method over \(\mathbb F_2\) certifies degree beyond about a quarter of the free dimension for any polynomial-size family, and every structured candidate has fallen to an upper bound or behaves generically. What the block adds is a description of where a cover could be hard by dimension alone: the static span is forced to be proper near half only when the covering sum is \(1+O(sw/n)\), while exact partitions, covers of bounded multiplicity and the one known example in that window, the lifted spread, are easy. The line has no candidate in the window and no method outside it.

Architecture review

Necessary target. For every fixed depth: polynomially many clauses of width \(w\), auxiliary affine equations, free dimension \(n\to\infty\), and \(1\notin C_{\lfloor n/2-s\rfloor}\) over \(\mathbb F_2\), with \(s+w\le n^{1-\epsilon}\); for a single depth \(d\), \((s+w)(\log n)^{d+c_F-2}=o(n)\). One family suffices.

Extra requirements. The block's work on covers asked for the static span to be proper by dimension, which is more than the target: a proper closure may have a static span of full dimension count, and a barrier needs only \(1\notin C_D\). The window of covering sum near one is therefore a place where one argument is available, not a necessary condition; the specification was not changed for it. The reviewer asked whether the transfer could do with a static bound or a size bound in place of the degree bound. By the record it cannot use a static bound: the engine counts standard monomials of a closure that must be closed under multiplication. I did not re-read the transfer for this review, and the question whether a size bound could replace the degree bound is not answered here.

Independent alternative. The reviewer, given only the goal and the available results (review.txt, stage one), proposed block-field binomial systems: split the \(n\) bits into \(m=n/k\) blocks read as nonzero elements \(y_i\) of \(\mathbb F_{2^k}\); rows are the clauses of \(t\)-term multiplicative equations \(\prod y_i^{c_i}=g^b\), with \(tk=O(\log n)\) for polynomial size; bit-degree is the binary weight of exponents; binomial systems have binomial refutations (Buss, Grigoriev, Impagliazzo and Pitassi), so the degree is a combinatorial quantity without the loss of the expansion method; a typical monomial has weight about \(n/2\). Its own expected break: the refuter may steer through low-weight exponent vectors, and its estimate of the deficit is \(n(e^{-t/2}+2^{-k})\), which with \(tk=O(\log n)\) meets a single-depth condition at best. On the requirement it found nothing listed that refutes the statement, judged amplification from a constant fraction hopeless since every operation it knows gains at most half a degree per added variable, and listed the constructions that do not raise the ratio of degree to variables. These are the reviewer's statements, unverified by me.

Record search on the proposal, as the framework now requires. It is not new to the record as a question: the queue holds entry-2026-10-09-binomial-domain-rigidity:s1, "a nonlinear multi-variable encoding whose binomial structure survives the actual Boolean domain", and entry-2026-10-09-subspace-endpoint-review:s3, binomial systems over an extension field of \(\mathbb F_2\); neither was developed. thm:binomial-domain-rigidity excludes binomially spanned proper closures in two-state coordinates and does not apply to coordinates in a multiplicative group, where the domain equations are themselves binomial: in the coordinates \(z_{i,l}=y_i^{2^l}\), which mix the bits of a block, they are \(z_l^2=z_{l+1}\) and \(\prod_lz_l=1\). The recorded modular ceilings concern rows \(\sum a_ix_i\equiv b\) on Boolean \(x_i\), a different encoding.

Rank normalization. The dimension counts of the block compare the span of the rows' multiples with the space of polynomials of degree at most \(D\), in one space; the correction of the block was exactly that an earlier count had used the wrong model for one of the two. For the binomial proposal the question does not arise in that form: the closure is expected to be spanned by binomials, which is to be established, and its properness would then be a statement about walks on exponent vectors, not about dimensions.

Decision. Test the binomial proposal, through the two queued checks it coincides with. Compared with the work of this block it has what that work lacked: an exact description of the closure, so that a lower bound, if there is one, does not have to come from expansion; and its instances are not covers with special overlap but ordinary systems with a growing alphabet. The invariant family and the window for covers are not pursued further.

Decisive test. Next cycle, developing entry-2026-10-09-binomial-domain-rigidity:s1, chosen by bearing. The test is in two parts, and the reviewer corrected the second in a way that changes what is at stake.

The dictionary, to be proved. As the reviewer lays it out, unverified: over \(\mathbb F_{2^k}\) the \(z_{i,l}\) are an invertible linear recoding of the bits, so bit-degree is ordinary degree in \(z\), with affine invariance needed over the extension field; Booleanity has the same span as the binomial domain equations; the clauses of a row generate within degree \(tk\) all \(y^a(y^{jc}-\gamma^j)\) on its blocks; so the system is binomial in \(z\) and the theorem on binomial systems applies. The walk: states are vectors of residues modulo \(2^k-1\), with weight the binary weight of the representative in \([0,2^k-2]\); a step is \(a\to a+jc_r\) for any \(j\); a refutation at degree \(D\) is a walk from a state to itself with nonzero total charge all of whose states have weight at most \(D\).

The regime. My estimate of a ceiling from a well-chosen starting vector, a deficit of order \(n/\sqrt t\), was wrong outside \(t\ll k\): it used a large-deviation bound where it does not hold, and for \(t+1>k\) no starting value keeps all of a block's values below the median, so the strategy saves nothing. The designer therefore takes \(t\ge k\), for instance \(t\approx k\approx\sqrt{\log n}\), and the two heuristics then on the table, the zero start, which counts blocks inactive at the midpoint, and the mean-weight defect, give a deficit of about \(n2^{-\Theta(\sqrt{\log n})}\). That is not \(n^{1-\epsilon}\), but it satisfies \((s+w)(\log n)^{d+c_F-2}=o(n)\) for every fixed \(d\), and the goal allows the family to depend on the depth; here one family would even serve all depths. So, heuristically and with nothing proved, this is the first candidate in the notebook that no recorded ceiling or estimate excludes for the goal as stated. I record that as a reason to test it carefully, not as progress.

The test proper, for \(t\ge k\): prove the dictionary; then decide the lower-bound statement the reviewer names, that in every order of the rows the walk at its midpoint has a \(1-O(e^{-t/2})\) fraction of blocks active with residues of near-average weight, or find the refuter's strategy that defeats it. Outcomes: a strategy giving a deficit of order \(n/\operatorname{polylog}(n)\) or worse for every choice of \(t,k\) with \(tk=O(\log n)\) closes the proposal; a proof of the dictionary together with a walk lower bound within \(n2^{-\Theta(\sqrt{\log n})}\) of half would be the family for every fixed depth and would change the goal's status; a proved dictionary with the walk bound open leaves a precise combinatorial problem in place of the present search, and the next step is then exact computation at \(k=3\) with rows of at least six terms.

Falsification attempt on this line

  • A general ceiling below half would refute the line; none is known, and the block removed one heuristic that had pointed to one for covers.
  • The reviewer's structural worry: near half, dimension forces a proper span only in a window whose known members are easy. That is an argument about one method of proving properness, not about properness.
  • Amplification: if no operation raises the ratio of degree to variables, as the reviewer lists for parity lifting, gadget lifting, products and restriction, then a family at half must be built at half directly. Nothing in the record contradicts this, and it agrees with twenty-six entries of experience; it is not proved.
  • Evidence against the line remains a pattern in what was tried. Evidence for it: none.

9 October 2026 — Block-field binomial systems of small width are refuted in degree \(n/3+o(n)\): equivalences are derived where they are cheap and translated

Working proof of the ceiling \(\max\{w,n/3+k\sqrt m+5k+1\}\) for every such system of width \(w\); it closes the candidate the goal-level review selected, with a linear deficit. Queue development of a chosen check while draining. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort low).

Chosen. The queued check asking for a multi-variable encoding whose binomial structure survives the Boolean domain bears on the family statement as the candidate the goal-level review selected; it comes before the head because that review made it the decisive test.

Architecture test. The goal-level review asked for the dictionary between bit-degree and walks on exponent vectors, and then for the walk bound or the refuter's strategy, in the regime of rows with at least \(k\) terms. Outcome: the walk the review and its reviewer described, with a weight bound on every state visited, is the static picture. Polynomial calculus can do more: a derived equivalence between two monomials may be multiplied by variables, which moves both ends and forgets the path between them. With that, every block-field binomial system is refuted in degree \(\max\{w,\,n/3+O(k\sqrt m)\}\), \(w=kt\) the row width; in the review's regime \(tk=O(\log n)\) that is \(n/3+o(n)\). By the review's first outcome the proposal is closed: the deficit is linear.

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement: do block-field binomial systems have refutation degree near half their number of bits?

New mathematics. No: degree at most \(n/3+k\sqrt m+5k+1\), or the row width if that is larger, for every unsatisfiable system of this kind on \(m\) blocks of \(k\) bits, \(n=mk\). The proof derives, for each interval of rows of an inconsistent dependency, the equivalence between a monomial and its translate by the interval's sum at every pair of low weight, by induction on a binary splitting: a pair is joined at a base point where three monomials are simultaneously light, which exists with all three below \(n/3+k\sqrt m\), and is then carried to any other light pair by multiplying by variables.

Goal progress. Unchanged. The candidate is excluded with a proved linear deficit; no family is obtained and the required implication is as before.

General statement. prop:block-binomial-third-ceiling holds for every \(k\ge2\), every number of blocks and every unsatisfiable system of multiplicative rows.

The systems

Fix \(k\ge2\) (for \(k=1\) every system is satisfiable), \(K=\mathbb F_{2^k}\), \(q=2^k-1\), a generator \(g\) of \(K^*\) and a basis \(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_k\) of \(K\) over \(\mathbb F_2\). There are \(m\) blocks of \(k\) bits, \(n=mk\); block \(i\) with bits \(b_{i,1},\ldots,b_{i,k}\) is read as \(y_i=\sum_j\alpha_jb_{i,j}\in K\). A row \(r\) has a set \(T_r\) of blocks, exponents \(c_r\in\mathbb Z_q^{T_r}\), extended by zero, and \(\gamma_r\in K^*\); its allowed set is \(R_r=\{y\in(K^*)^{T_r}:\prod_iy_i^{c_{r,i}}=\gamma_r\}\), assumed nonempty, and its axioms are the clauses forbidding each assignment of the bits of \(T_r\) outside \(R_r\), of width \(k|T_r|\). Every block lies in some row. Let \(w\) be the largest width. The system is unsatisfiable exactly when the linear system \(\sum_ic_{r,i}x_i=\log_g\gamma_r\) over \(\mathbb Z_q\) is inconsistent, and then there are, by duality for finite abelian groups (a vector outside a subgroup of \(\mathbb Z_q^M\) is separated from it by a character, and characters of \(\mathbb Z_q^M\) are given by vectors \(J\)), \(J_r\in\mathbb Z_q\) with \(\sum_rJ_rc_r=0\) and \(\prod_r\gamma_r^{J_r}\ne1\).

For a residue \(a\in\mathbb Z_q\) let \(\operatorname{wt}(a)\) be the binary weight of its representative in \([0,q-1]\), and for \(a\in\mathbb Z_q^m\) the sum over blocks. Note \(\operatorname{wt}(-a)=k-\operatorname{wt}(a)\) for \(a\ne0\).

The ceiling

Proposition (block binomial third ceiling). Every unsatisfiable system as above is refuted, in the multilinear calculus over \(\mathbb F_2\) with Boolean axioms, in degree at most \(\max\{w,\ \lceil n/3+k\sqrt m\rceil+5k+1\}\).

Proof. Coordinates. Work over \(K\) in the ordinary polynomial ring in the bits, and let \(S_D\) be the least \(K\)-space of polynomials of degree at most \(D\) containing the axioms and the Boolean axioms of degree at most \(D\) and closed under multiplication by a variable from degree at most \(D-1\). If \(1\in S_D\) then \(1\in C_D\) over \(\mathbb F_2\): multilinear reduction turns an ordinary derivation into a multilinear one without raising degree, and \(C_D\otimes K\) contains the axioms and is closed under the rule, so it contains the closure over \(K\); an \(\mathbb F_2\)-linear functional on \(K\) with value \(1\) at \(1\) then takes \(1\in C_D\otimes K\) to \(1\in C_D\). Throughout, a function of the bits of degree at most \(d\) has a polynomial in the \(z\)'s of degree at most \(d\), which differs from its multilinear polynomial in the bits by Boolean-axiom multiples of degree at most \(d\). Put \(z_{i,l}=\sum_j\alpha_j^{2^l}b_{i,j}\), \(0\le l<k\). The matrix \((\alpha_j^{2^l})\) is invertible, so the \(z\)'s are a linear change of variables: degrees are the same, and \(S_D\) is closed under multiplication by each \(z_{i,l}\). On Boolean points \(z_{i,l}=y_i^{2^l}\). In characteristic two \(z_{i,l}^2-z_{i,l+1}=\sum_j\alpha_j^{2^{l+1}}(b_{i,j}^2-b_{i,j})\), indices of \(l\) modulo \(k\), so these binomials lie in \(S_D\) for \(D\ge2\).

A monomial in the \(z\)'s is, as a function, \(\prod_iy_i^{E_i}\) with \(E_i=\sum_le_{i,l}2^l\), and its degree is \(\sum e_{i,l}\). For \(a\in\mathbb Z_q^m\) let \(y^a\) be the squarefree monomial whose block exponents are the representatives in \([0,q-1]\); its degree is \(\operatorname{wt}(a)\). Write \(a\approx_cb\) when \(y^a-cy^b\in S_D\); this relation is transitive, with labels multiplying, and symmetric with the label inverted.

Normal form. If \(M\) is a monomial of degree at most \(D\) whose block exponents are congruent to \(a\) modulo \(q\), then \(M-y^a\in S_D\). Indeed, using \(z_l^2\to z_{l+1}\), each use a multiple of a domain binomial of degree at most \(\deg M\), \(M\) reduces to a squarefree monomial, of no larger degree, with exponents in \([0,q]\) congruent to \(a\). A block with exponent \(q\), all \(k\) variables present, lies in some row \(r\); the function \(\prod_{l}z_{i,l}-1\) vanishes on \(R_r\), so it is a combination of the row's clause polynomials modulo Boolean axioms within degree \(w\le D\), and its multiple by the rest of the monomial has the degree of the monomial; this replaces the exponent \(q\) by \(0\).

Row steps. For a row \(r\), \(j\in\mathbb Z_q\) and \(a\) with \(\operatorname{wt}(a),\operatorname{wt}(a+jc_r)\le D\): \(a+jc_r\approx_{\gamma_r^j}a\). On the blocks of \(T_r\) the function \(y^{(a+jc_r)|T_r}-\gamma_r^jy^{a|T_r}\) vanishes on \(R_r\), since there \(y^{jc_r}=\gamma_r^j\) and \(y_i^q=1\); so its polynomial in the \(z\)'s, of degree at most \(w\), is in \(S_D\), and multiplying by the variables of \(y^a\) outside \(T_r\) one at a time keeps the degree at most \(\max\{\operatorname{wt}(a),\operatorname{wt}(a+jc_r)\}\).

Translation. If \(a\approx_cb\) with \(\operatorname{wt}(a),\operatorname{wt}(b)\le D-1\), and \(e\) is \(2^l\) in one block and zero elsewhere, then \(a+e\approx_cb+e\). Multiply \(y^a-cy^b\) by \(z_{i,l}\): the result is in \(S_D\), and by the normal form its two monomials equal \(y^{a+e}\) and \(y^{b+e}\) modulo \(S_D\).

Three light monomials. For any \(A,B\in\mathbb Z_q^m\) there is \(x\) with \(\operatorname{wt}(x),\operatorname{wt}(x+A),\operatorname{wt}(x+B)\le n/3+k\sqrt m\). In one block, with \(\alpha=\operatorname{wt}(A_i)\), \(\beta=\operatorname{wt}(B_i)\), \(\chi=\operatorname{wt}(B_i-A_i)\), the three choices \(x_i=0,-A_i,-B_i\) cost, as triples of weights of \(x_i,x_i+A_i,x_i+B_i\), at most \((0,\alpha,\beta)\), \((k-\alpha,0,\chi)\), \((k-\beta,k-\chi,0)\). For any probability vector \(\lambda\) on the three coordinates, the combination of these three triples with weights \(\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3\) has \(\lambda\)-weighted cost \(k(\lambda_1\lambda_2+\lambda_1\lambda_3+\lambda_2\lambda_3)\le k/3\), the terms in \(\alpha,\beta,\chi\) cancelling; so for every \(\lambda\) some choice has \(\lambda\)-weighted cost at most \(k/3\), and by the minimax theorem there is a distribution on the three choices under which each of the three expected weights is at most \(k/3\). Choose the blocks independently from these distributions. Each of the three total weights is a sum of \(m\) independent variables in \([0,k]\) with mean at most \(n/3\), so it exceeds \(n/3+k\sqrt m\) with probability at most \(e^{-2}\), and \(3e^{-2}<1\).

Carrying a pair. Let \(V\in\mathbb Z_q^m\), \(D'\le D-5k-1\), and suppose \(x^*\approx_cx^*+V\) for one \(x^*\) with \(\operatorname{wt}(x^*),\operatorname{wt}(x^*+V)\le D'\). Then \(x\approx_cx+V\) for every \(x\) with \(\operatorname{wt}(x),\operatorname{wt}(x+V)\le D'\). Change the blocks from their values in \(x^*\) to those in \(x\) one block at a time, each by adding \(1\) repeatedly, applying the translation step at every addition. The two-dimensional vectors \(d_i=(\operatorname{wt}(x_i)-\operatorname{wt}(x^*_i),\ \operatorname{wt}(x_i+V_i)-\operatorname{wt}(x^*_i+V_i))\) have entries in \([-k,k]\); subtracting their mean gives vectors of sup-norm at most \(2k\) summing to zero, and by the Steinitz lemma, with constant two in the plane for any norm, the blocks can be ordered so that every partial sum of these is at most \(4k\) in each coordinate; so every partial sum of the \(d_i\) is within \(4k\) of the corresponding fraction of their total, and the two weights after any number of completed blocks are at most a convex combination of their values at \(x^*\) and at \(x\), plus \(4k\). So after any number of completed blocks both weights are at most \(D'+4k\), and during the change of one block at most \(D'+5k\le D-1\); the translation step applies throughout.

Induction. Order the rows of the dependency \(1,\ldots,M\), put \(V_{\sigma\tau}=\sum_{\sigma\le r<\tau}J_rc_r\) and \(c_{\sigma\tau}=\prod_{\sigma\le r<\tau}\gamma_r^{J_r}\), and let \(D'=\lceil n/3+k\sqrt m\rceil\), \(D=\max\{w,D'+5k+1\}\). Claim: for \(\sigma<\tau\) and every \(x\) with \(\operatorname{wt}(x),\operatorname{wt}(x+V_{\sigma\tau})\le D'\), \(x+V_{\sigma\tau}\approx_{c_{\sigma\tau}}x\). For \(\tau=\sigma+1\) this is a row step. Otherwise take \(\sigma<\rho<\tau\) and, by the three light monomials, \(x^*\) with \(x^*,x^*+V_{\sigma\rho},x^*+V_{\sigma\tau}\) of weight at most \(D'\). The claim for \((\sigma,\rho)\) at \(x^*\) and for \((\rho,\tau)\) at \(x^*+V_{\sigma\rho}\), both pairs light, give \(x^*+V_{\sigma\tau}\approx_{c_{\sigma\tau}}x^*\) by transitivity; carrying the pair gives the claim at every light \(x\). For \(\sigma=1,\tau=M+1\): \(V=0\), and at \(x=0\) the claim reads \(1-c\cdot1\in S_D\) with \(c=\prod\gamma_r^{J_r}\ne1\). \(\square\)

What it teaches

The static picture, a closed walk on exponent vectors all of whose states are light, was what the review's estimates analysed; its cost was thought to be near \(n/2\) for rows of many terms. The dynamic rule defeats it at a fixed price: only three monomials have to be light at once, the two ends of an interval and its splitting point, and three residues can always be shifted to average weight a third. Beyond the width \(w=kt\), which enters the bound as a floor, nothing in the argument uses the rows except that they generate the dependency: the choice of exponents and the structure of the dependency play no role, and the review's regime of rows with at least \(k\) terms is not needed. The same mechanism threatens any system whose closure is spanned by binomials in coordinates where degree is additive under a group structure, which is the setting in which exact lower bounds were hoped for. The constant one third is an upper bound; I have not looked for a matching lower bound, the proposal being closed either way.

For the line: this was the first candidate that no recorded ceiling excluded, and it survived one review. What excluded it is a ceiling that conditions on nothing and counts nothing, of a kind the record did not have: derive locally in the best coordinates, then move. Earlier candidates should be reread for it only where their closures are binomial; the modular sources of the record on Boolean variables are not of that form by thm:binomial-domain-rigidity.

Reviewer's suggestions, unverified

  • The constant one third: splitting an interval into more parts needs more monomials light at once and is worse; two monomials can be made light at about \(n/4\), so an improvement would need a way to join without holding the middle monomial; it sees no reason for a matching lower bound. Record. Searched "binomial ceiling translation equivalence three states third exponent weight Steinitz": lem:character-binomial-transport is the nearest recorded statement, on transporting binomials between charts; no recorded ceiling uses translation of derived equivalences.
  • Generality: the mechanism needs a binomial closure and a group acting by multiplication whose shifts recentre weight; with \(\mathbb Z_2\) in sign coordinates in characteristic other than two it would give about \(n/3\) for parity systems, a consistency check outside this goal; for Boolean monomials over \(\mathbb F_2\) multiplication is idempotent and only enlarges supports, so it does not transfer to covers or formulas. Record. Searched "XOR system Fourier sign coordinates odd characteristic degree third ceiling parity": thm:coset-character-degree-ceiling is a recorded ceiling in character coordinates in mismatched characteristic, by a different mechanism; nothing recorded states the parity case.

Specification decision. No change to the specification, which never admitted multi-bit alphabets as such. Recorded for future candidates: an encoding in which the closure is spanned by binomials on a product of cyclic groups of order \(2^k-1\) is excluded with deficit at least \(n/6-o(n)\) whenever the row width is at most \(n/3\) and the number of blocks grows.

Verification gate. One fresh-context medium reviewer checked ten steps separately by hand and could not break the proposition: the systems, the two reductions to \(\mathbb F_2\), the normal form, the row steps, the translation step, the three light monomials with the cancellation and the minimax step, the carrying of a pair, the induction including the root, and the final bound. Corrections applied: the certificate of inconsistency over \(\mathbb Z_q\) is justified by character duality and not by injectivity alone; the descent from \(K\) and the cost of multilinear reduction are stated; the Steinitz step is derived with its constant; \(k\ge2\); the title, summary and discussion state the dependence on the width, which I had denied. Unused: nonemptiness of the allowed sets; the regime of many terms. Record: review.txt.

Follow-up. Closed: falsified. The encoding the check asked for exists, its binomial structure does survive the Boolean domain, and it is refuted in degree \(n/3+o(n)\) by prop:block-binomial-third-ceiling; it cannot serve the family statement.

Process assessment. Both the reviewer and I analysed this candidate for a whole review as a walk with every state bounded, the static span, in an entry that elsewhere distinguishes the static span from the closure. I found the error only when I tried to write the dictionary as a proof and the closure refused to be spanned by multiples of generators. A candidate should be handed to a proof of its simplest claimed property before estimates about it are compared.

No new result: bookkeeping from a recorded lemma, a record search, and the closure of two checks that later entries answered. Queue development of a chosen lead while draining. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort low).

Chosen. The affine restriction lead bears on the family statement as the origin of its hidden-subspace form and as the one recorded source of method not yet reread against it; it comes before the head because the preceding entry's proposition answers one of its checks.

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement: the lead proposed to choose the subspace in the analysis, hard at half the dimension of some subspace and not of the whole cube. Its first use was adopted as the free-dimension endpoint. Does it give a way to produce a family, by restricting a formula that is hard at a smaller fraction?

New mathematics. Nothing new is proved. From the recorded case split, lem:term-value-case-split, adding an affine equation with a suitably chosen right-hand side lowers the refutation degree by at most one; so restricting to a subspace of codimension \(r\) with degree drop \(\delta\le r\) changes the deficit from \(s\) to \(s-r/2+\delta\). A subspace helps exactly when the drop is below half the codimension. Whether any hard formula admits such restrictions is the family statement again, for the restricted system. Two of the lead's four checks are answered by later entries and are closed below.

Goal progress. Unchanged. The lead's contribution to the statement, the free-dimension endpoint, was made when it was queued; this entry finds no method in it and no candidate.

General statement. The bookkeeping is a consequence of lem:term-value-case-split, which holds for every system and every Boolean-valued term; no further all-parameter statement is made.

The bookkeeping

Let \(\Gamma\) have free dimension \(n\) and refutation degree \(D\), deficit \(s=n/2-D\). For an affine form \(\ell\), if both \(\Gamma\cup\{\ell\}\) and \(\Gamma\cup\{\ell+1\}\) had refutations of degree \(B\), \(\Gamma\) would have one of degree \(B+1\), by the recorded lemma with a term of degree one: multiply one refutation by \(\ell+1\) and the other by \(\ell\) and add. So for one of the two values the degree is at least \(D-1\). After \(r\) independent equations with values so chosen the free dimension is \(n-r\) and the degree \(D-\delta\) with \(0\le\delta\le r\), and the deficit is \(s-r/2+\delta\). By affine invariance each step is the elimination of one coordinate.

So the lead's hope, start from a formula with degree \(cn\), \(c<1/2\), and find a subspace of dimension about \(2cn\) on which it is as hard, asks for about \((1-2c)n\) restrictions that cost no degree at all. That is the statement that the restricted system is hard at half its dimension; the lead moves the difficulty and does not reduce it. What it does give is the direction in which to look at any hard formula: for restrictions that are free.

Record search

The main notebook holds two statements on restrictions of the pigeonhole principle, found by searching "restriction affine equation case split degree drops": cor:safe-linear-systems-keep-base-hard, in which each equation of a safe linear system costs one full degree, the worst case of the bookkeeping; and conj:random-affine-conditioning-law, a conjecture fitted at small sizes over odd characteristic, by which random affine equations lower the degree in proportion to the dimension, so that the ratio of degree to dimension stays where it was. I read their registry summaries, not their proofs. Both say that for the pigeonhole principle restriction does not raise the ratio; neither is a statement over \(\mathbb F_2\) for a formula hard at a constant fraction of its dimension.

The lead's source, Itsykson and Sokolov on resolution over linear equations modulo two, I did not read: one retrieval attempt reached a different report. By a search result quoting later work, unverified, its lower bounds are for the tree-like system. Nothing in the record or in that description suggests a degree method there.

The lead's checks

  • Whether the immunity theorem holds for rows on linear forms with locally independent forms. Answered in the negative for the hypotheses tested: the leading-term step fails, and prop:rank-expansion-without-hardness, prop:three-family-odd-cover and prop:random-row-span refute the conclusion at widths one and two and uniformly in the number of rows; the remaining case, width three and more with a linear threshold, is carried by the check on rows on linear forms. Follow-up. Closed: merged into entry-2026-10-09-private-direction-projection:s1
  • Binomial systems over an extension field of \(\mathbb F_2\). Follow-up. Closed: falsified. prop:block-binomial-third-ceiling refutes every such system of small width in degree \(n/3+o(n)\).

The other two, on which parity-row systems arise from formulas and on a contracting step of the engine, are not touched here.

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement: the preceding entry reduced the lead to the question whether some restriction of a hard formula is free. Is it, for formulas known to be hard at a constant fraction, and what is left of the lead's two other checks?

New mathematics. None. Three observations from the record. A restriction raises the ratio of degree to dimension exactly when it loses less degree per dimension than the current ratio; a generic restriction to dimension \(d\) is free when the formula depends on at most \(d\) coordinates up to an affine change, and then the formula was a family padded with idle dimensions; for a formula that uses all its dimensions nothing recorded gives a free restriction, and the two recorded statements on the pigeonhole principle say there is none there. The lead's check on which systems arise from formulas is answered by prop:form-clause-encoding; its check on the engine's step is the question the thin-kernel review took up.

Goal progress. Unchanged. The lead is exhausted without a candidate or a method.

General statement. No new all-parameter statement; the entry rests on lem:term-value-case-split, prop:form-clause-encoding and thm:binary-approximator-rank.

When a restriction helps

With degree \(D\) in dimension \(n\) and a restriction of codimension \(r\) dropping the degree by \(\delta\), the ratio moves from \(D/n\) to \((D-\delta)/(n-r)\), which is larger exactly when \(\delta/r<D/n\). The worst case of the case split, \(\delta=r\), always lowers it. If the system is, after an affine change of coordinates, a system in \(n_0\) of the coordinates, a subspace of dimension \(d\ge n_0\) in general position restricts those coordinates to independent forms and the restricted system is the same system with \(d-n_0\) idle dimensions: \(\delta=0\). This is the projection away from irrelevant variables of the recorded normalization, and it produces a family only from a family. For a system that uses all its dimensions I know no restriction with \(\delta/r\) below the ratio. The main notebook's statements for the pigeonhole principle, which I have still read only in their registry summaries, give \(\delta=r\) for safe systems and, as a fitted conjecture in odd characteristic, \(\delta/r\) equal to the ratio for random equations: no gain in either.

The reading of the proofs announced in the last entry was not done: both statements are over other encodings and one over other fields, and neither outcome would bear on a formula over \(\mathbb F_2\) hard at a constant fraction. I record that as a choice.

Where half enters

The lead's fourth check asked to make rigorous, or to beat, the heuristic that one step of the engine contracts too little below half. Rereading thm:binary-approximator-rank: the gain of a round is \(\tfrac12c_P(K-d)\), and the only general bound relating it to \(c_P(K)\) is the monotonicity of the normalized rank, \(c_P(K-d)\ge\frac{N_n(K-d)}{N_n(K)}c_P(K)\), which at \(K=\alpha n\), \(\alpha<1/2\), is about \((\alpha/(1-\alpha))^d\) and, with \(d\) polylogarithmic and at most \((D-K)/d\) rounds, is too small. The bound is an equality when the standard monomials below the cutoff are all monomials, so no choice of \(q\) helps in general; it is beaten exactly when the standard monomials are thin at the top, which is the alternative endpoint of the thin-kernel review, proved as a transfer in thm:level-size-degree-transfer and parked for want of a system with such a closure. So the check has been answered as far as the record goes: half is forced for closures with full levels and not for thin ones, and the open question is the existence of a thin proper closure, not the choice of \(q\).

The lead's checks

  • Which parity-row systems arise as restrictions of bounded-width formulas, and whether structured ones with many relations among multiples of rows are among them. All systems of clauses on affine forms of width \(w\) arise, by prop:form-clause-encoding, at the cost of the width; the structured systems of the later entries, the three-family cover and the orbit covers, are instances. Follow-up. Closed: superseded by prop:form-clause-encoding, which answers it.
  • The engine's step below half. Follow-up. Closed: superseded by thm:level-size-degree-transfer and the thin-kernel review, which state exactly when the step contracts faster.

Specification decision. No change. The observation on idle dimensions adds nothing to the specification, which already counts the free dimension after projection.

Verification gate. No new statement is made, so no reviewer was used. Reread in this cycle: the statement and proof of thm:binary-approximator-rank in full, the passage "Why half stays" of the review that queued the lead, and the lead's checks. Not reread: the proofs of the two main-notebook statements on restrictions.

Follow-up. Developed: the lead's contribution is the free-dimension endpoint, recorded in the transfer; its checks are answered by prop:form-clause-encoding, prop:block-binomial-third-ceiling, thm:level-size-degree-transfer and the results on rows on forms. No application to the open statement remains beyond those.

Process assessment. Two housekeeping entries in a row. They removed six queue items and produced no mathematics; the rereading of the rank theorem was the useful part, because it states once more that the only recorded way around half is a thin closure, and that endpoint has been parked since before the transfer was proved. The next review should ask whether the tools of the last twenty entries say anything about it.

9 October 2026 — For small width the binomial ceiling is a quarter, by joining one row at a time; and what a thin proper closure would ask of a binomial system

Working proof of a sharper ceiling for block-field binomial systems; the reading of the thin-closure endpoint against these systems is a discussion without a result. Queue development of a chosen bridge while draining. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort low).

Chosen. The bridge on vanishing ideals of small point sets belongs to the thin-closure endpoint, the only recorded alternative to half the free dimension in the family statement; it comes before the head because the preceding entry located the half requirement in exactly the bound that endpoint replaces, and the binomial closures of the last entries are the first closures whose standard monomials are understood.

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement: the thin-closure endpoint asks for a closure that is proper at \(D\) and whose standard monomials just below a cutoff \(K\) number at most \(\binom Xj\) with \(X\) about \(2K\). For block-field binomial systems the standard monomials are classes of exponent vectors under derivable translations. Can such a closure be thin and proper below the ceiling?

New mathematics. One result. The ceiling of the third ceiling entry improves, when the width is below about \(n/12\), to a quarter: degree at most \(\lceil n/4+k\sqrt m\rceil+w+5k+1\), so that the two bounds together give the smaller of this and the third ceiling. Joining the rows of the dependency one at a time needs only two monomials light at once, the base and its translate by a prefix sum, the next prefix differing in one row; and two residues can be shifted to average weight a quarter. On the question itself there is no result: a discussion below says what thinness would require, in terms of boxes of exponent vectors; my expectation about which boxes are the obstacle was wrong, as the reviewer showed, and nothing is proved.

Goal progress. Unchanged. A recorded ceiling is sharpened for a class already excluded, and the alternative endpoint is not decided for it.

General statement. prop:block-binomial-quarter-ceiling holds for every \(k\ge2\) and every unsatisfiable block-field binomial system.

The quarter ceiling

Setting and notation of the third ceiling entry: \(m\) blocks of \(k\) bits, \(n=mk\), \(q=2^k-1\), rows of width at most \(w\), a dependency \(\sum_rJ_rc_r=0\) with \(\prod\gamma_r^{J_r}\ne1\) over rows ordered \(1,\ldots,M\), the space \(S_D\), the relation \(a\approx_cb\), and from its proof the row steps, the translation step and the carrying of a pair, which are used unchanged.

Proposition (block binomial quarter ceiling). Every unsatisfiable block-field binomial system is refuted, in the multilinear calculus over \(\mathbb F_2\), in degree at most \(\lceil n/4+k\sqrt m\rceil+w+5k+1\). This is \(n/4+o(n)\) when \(w=o(n)\) and the number of blocks grows.

Proof. Two light monomials. For any \(A\in\mathbb Z_q^m\) there is \(x\) with \(\operatorname{wt}(x),\operatorname{wt}(x+A)\le n/4+k\sqrt m\). In one block with \(\alpha=\operatorname{wt}(A_i)\), the choices \(x_i=0\) and \(x_i=-A_i\) cost at most \((0,\alpha)\) and \((k-\alpha,0)\); taking the second with probability \(\alpha/k\) gives both expected weights at most \(\alpha(k-\alpha)/k\le k/4\). Choosing the blocks independently, each total exceeds \(n/4+k\sqrt m\) with probability at most \(e^{-2}\), and \(2e^{-2}<1\).

Induction on prefixes. Let \(P_\tau=\sum_{r\le\tau}J_rc_r\), \(\theta_\tau=\prod_{r\le\tau}\gamma_r^{J_r}\), \(D_0=\lceil n/4+k\sqrt m\rceil\), \(D'=D_0+w\), \(D=D'+5k+1\), which is at least \(w\). Claim: for \(1\le\tau\le M\) and every \(x\) with \(\operatorname{wt}(x),\operatorname{wt}(x+P_\tau)\le D'\), \(x+P_\tau\approx_{\theta_\tau}x\). For \(\tau=1\) this is a row step. For \(\tau>1\) take \(x^*\) with \(\operatorname{wt}(x^*),\operatorname{wt}(x^*+P_{\tau-1})\le D_0\). Since \(P_\tau-P_{\tau-1}=J_\tau c_\tau\) is supported on the blocks of row \(\tau\), which have at most \(w\) bits, \(\operatorname{wt}(x^*+P_\tau)\le D_0+w=D'\). The claim for \(\tau-1\) at \(x^*\) and the row step for row \(\tau\) at \(x^*+P_{\tau-1}\), both of whose ends have weight at most \(D'\le D\), give \(x^*+P_\tau\approx_{\theta_\tau}x^*\) by transitivity; the carrying of a pair, used with the two ends exchanged by symmetry of the relation and needing \(D'\le D-5k-1\), gives the claim at every \(x\) with both weights at most \(D'\). For \(\tau=M\), \(P_M=0\) and at \(x=0\) the claim reads \(1-\theta_M\in S_D\) with \(\theta_M\ne1\). \(\square\)

The earlier proof split intervals in the middle and so held three unrelated monomials at once. Nothing forces that: the dependency is a sum, and a sum can be built one term at a time. A quarter is the right constant for a lemma about two monomials, by the reviewer's example: for \(k\) even and \(A_i=q/3\), the pattern \(0101\ldots\), every shift costs \(k/4\) on average. For typical residues other shifts should cost less, about \(k/6\) each by the non-adjacent form; that is the reviewer's estimate and is not proved here.

The thin endpoint for binomial closures: a discussion

This section proves nothing. The endpoint asks for a closure proper at \(D\) whose quotient has at most \(\binom Xj\) dimensions in degree \(j\) just below a cutoff \(K\), \(X\) about \(2K\); for these systems \(K\) is below the refutation degree, hence below about \(n/4+k\sqrt m+w\). The level sizes \(\dim V_j/(C_D\cap V_j)\) do not depend on the coordinates or on the field, since \(S_D=C_D\otimes K\): one inclusion is in the third ceiling entry and the other holds because \(S_D\) contains the axioms and is closed under the rule. I expect, and have not written out, that in the \(z\)-coordinates \(S_D\) is spanned by binomials and monomials, so that the quotient has one dimension for each class of monomials that is not killed by carrying two labels; the classes live on exponents in \([0,q]\) per block, not on residues.

The recorded shattering bound is for bit variables. The same count in the \(z\)-coordinates says: if the lowest \(s_i\) bits of block \(i\) are taken, with \(\sum s_i\) above about \(2K\), then some monomial of degree at most \(K\) with exponents in the box \(\prod[0,2^{s_i})\) is not standard. That is all it says; the monomial may be killed, or lowered to a monomial outside the box. I had read it as requiring a derivable translation inside every such box and had guessed that boxes spread thinly over all blocks are the obstacle. The reviewer points out that this is wrong: a multiple \(jc_r\) of one row is zero outside its \(t\) blocks, so being spread costs nothing; what matters is the fraction \(s/k\) of bits taken in the row's blocks. By Dirichlet's theorem some multiple of a row has all entries below \(q^{1-1/t}\), so boxes with \(s\ge k(1-1/t)\) are hit by one row step, while generic rows of three or more terms have no multiple below \(2^{k/2}\). On that reading the largest unshattered boxes have about \(n(1-1/t)\) bits and thinness would need \(K\) of at least about \(n/4\), at or above the ceiling. This is the reviewer's estimate, unverified, and it uses only single rows; combinations of rows give shorter vectors, and whether those are derivable below the ceiling is open.

So the endpoint is neither attained nor excluded for these systems, and the one estimate available points against it.

Reviewer's suggestions, unverified

  • The quarter is optimal for the two-monomial lemma, by \(A_i=q/3\); typical residues cost about \(k/6\) each. Record. Searched "signed digit non-adjacent form weight residue shift": matches only in the cube thread; nothing recorded here on weights of shifted residues beyond the two ceiling entries.
  • Small multiples of one row hit boxes with \(s\ge k(1-1/t)\); by Minkowski the row lattice has a vector of sup-norm at most \(q^{1-\operatorname{rank}/m}\), so short global translations exist and only their derivability is open; rows short enough to hit small boxes have light prefix sums and cheap refutations, heuristically. Record. Searched "Dirichlet simultaneous approximation short lattice vector Minkowski sup-norm": matches only in the cube thread; this notebook has no statement on short vectors of row lattices.

Specification decision. No change. The exclusion recorded for binomial encodings is sharpened: deficit at least \(n/4-o(n)\) for small width.

Verification gate. One fresh-context medium reviewer checked the two changed steps against the recorded proof and found the proposition correct: the two-monomial lemma with its degenerate case, the induction on prefixes, and the use of the recorded lemmas within their hypotheses. Corrections applied: a notation clash between the prefix label and the row vector; symmetry in the use of the carrying step; the redundant outer maximum; the statement that the bound improves the recorded one only for width below about \(n/12\). In the discussion it found one unrecorded fact stated as known, now marked as expected, two overstated consequences of the shattering bound, now corrected, and a wrong dichotomy, now replaced by its remark. Unused: nonemptiness of allowed sets. Record: review.txt.

Follow-up. Continuing. First entry on this bridge in this spell. Next attempt on it: measure, for explicit small binomial systems, the level sizes of proper closures against \(\binom{2K}{j}\) by exact computation of its closure's level sizes, since the closure is a graph on exponent vectors with the translation rule and can be computed without polynomial arithmetic.

Sub-ideas

  • A closure computation for block-field binomial systems on exponent vectors: classes of weight at most \(D\) under row steps, transitivity and translation by a bit when both ends have weight at most \(D-1\); output the refutation degree and the level sizes of proper closures, to compare with \(\binom{2K}{j}\) and with the quarter ceiling, at \(k=3,4\) and four to six blocks.

Process assessment. The quarter came from asking, while reading the thin endpoint, which translations are derivable below the ceiling, and noticing that the ceiling's own recursion was wasteful. The reviewer of the last entry had said an improvement would need a join that does not hold the middle monomial; joining one row at a time is that. The discussion is recorded as a discussion; its first draft contained a guess about spread boxes that one line of the reviewer's disposed of.
