9 October 2026 — Binomial closures are labelled classes of exponent vectors; at every size that can be enumerated the systems fall at their width, so no proper closure is there to measure

Working proof of the description of the closure; finite check on 27 systems, all refuted at their width, with a kernel whose validation has no discriminating power. Queue development of a chosen bridge while draining. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort low).

Chosen. Second entry on the thin-closure bridge, which bears on the family statement through its alternative endpoint; it comes before the head because the preceding entry left a claim about these closures unwritten and a computation resting on it queued.

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement: is the degree-\(D\) closure of a block-field binomial system spanned by binomials and monomials, so that it can be computed on exponent vectors; and what are the level sizes of a proper closure, compared with the thin endpoint's \(\binom{2K}{j}\)?

New mathematics. The first part is proved: for \(D\ge\max\{w,2\}\) the closure is the span of the binomials and monomials given by the least labelled equivalence on exponent vectors of weight at most \(D\) generated by row steps and by translation of pairs of weight at most \(D-1\), with inconsistent classes dead; refutation is death of the zero vector, and the level sizes are the numbers of live classes by least weight. The second part has no answer: a kernel computing this was written, and on all 27 systems run, random and of flow type, with \(q^m\) up to \(4.3\cdot10^7\), the system is refuted at its width, the least degree at which its axioms exist. A proper closure above the width needs prefix sums of weight above the width in every order, and such systems are beyond enumeration.

Goal progress. Unchanged. The alternative endpoint is not decided for binomial systems; a tool to decide it exists and cannot reach the sizes where the question is not vacuous.

General statement. lem:binomial-closure-classes holds for every \(k\ge2\), every block-field binomial system, satisfiable or not, and every \(D\ge w\).

The closure

Setting, notation and the lemmas named normal form, row steps and translation are those of the third ceiling entry: \(m\) blocks of \(k\) bits, \(q=2^k-1\), rows \((T_r,c_r,\gamma_r)\) of width at most \(w\), the \(K\)-space \(S_D\subseteq K[z]_{\le D}\), and for a monomial \(M\) in the \(z\)'s the vector \(a(M)\in\mathbb Z_q^m\) of its block exponents modulo \(q\), with \(\operatorname{wt}(a(M))\le\deg M\) since the binary weight of the representative in \([0,q-1]\) is the least number of powers of two with that sum modulo \(q\). Let \(\Omega_D\) be the set of \(a\) with \(\operatorname{wt}(a)\le D\).

Let \((\approx,\Delta)\) be the least pair of a family of relations \(a\approx_cb\) on \(\Omega_D\), \(c\in K^*\), and a set \(\Delta\subseteq\Omega_D\) of dead vectors such that: \(\approx\) is reflexive with label \(1\), symmetric with the label inverted and transitive with labels multiplied; \(a+jc_r\approx_{\gamma_r^j}a\) whenever both lie in \(\Omega_D\); \(a\approx_cb\) with \(a,b\in\Omega_{D-1}\) gives \(a+e\approx_cb+e\) for every \(e\) equal to a power of two in one block; \(a\approx_ca\) with \(c\ne1\) puts \(a\) in \(\Delta\); \(\Delta\) is a union of classes; and \(a\in\Delta\cap\Omega_{D-1}\) gives \(a+e\in\Delta\).

Lemma (binomial closure classes). Let \(D\ge w\); then \(D\ge2\), since every block lies in a row and \(w\ge k\). Then \(S_D\) is spanned by the binomials \(M-y^{a(M)}\) for monomials \(M\) of degree at most \(D\), the binomials \(y^a-cy^b\) with \(a\approx_cb\), and the monomials \(y^a\), \(a\in\Delta\). Consequently \(1\in C_D\) if and only if \(0\in\Delta\), and for \(j\le D\) the dimension of \(V_j/(C_D\cap V_j)\) over \(\mathbb F_2\) is the number of classes outside \(\Delta\) containing a vector of weight at most \(j\).

Proof. Spaces of binomials. In a vector space with a basis of monomials, let \(W\) be spanned by some binomials \(M-cM'\), \(c\ne0\), and some monomials. Join \(M,M'\) for each binomial; call a component dead if it contains a spanning monomial or a closed walk whose labels do not multiply to \(1\), and live otherwise. On a live component there is \(\phi\ne0\) with \(\phi(M)=c\phi(M')\) along every binomial, and \(W\) is the sum of the span of the monomials of dead components and, for each live component, the hyperplane \(\{\sum\lambda_MM:\sum\lambda_M\phi(M)=0\}\) of its span. Hence, for any set \(U\) of monomials, \(W\cap\operatorname{span}U\) is spanned by the monomials of \(U\) in dead components and the binomials \(M-(\phi(M)/\phi(M'))M'\in W\) with \(M,M'\in U\) in one live component.

Binomial generators. The functions on the bits of \(T_r\) have as a basis the squarefree monomials in the \(z\)'s of those blocks: every polynomial reduces to a combination of them by \(z_{i,l}^2\to z_{i,l+1}\), and their number is the dimension. Write them \(y^E\), \(E\in[0,q]^{T_r}\). The functions vanishing on \(R_r\) are spanned by binomials \(y^E-cy^{E'}\): those vanishing where no \(y_i\) is zero, by \(y^E-y^{E'}\) with \(E'\) obtained from \(E\) by changing one exponent \(0\) to \(q\); those supported there and vanishing on \(R_r\), which is nonempty by hypothesis and so a coset of the kernel of the character \(y^{c_r}\), by \(y^E-\gamma_r^jy^{E'}\) with \(E,E'\in[1,q]^{T_r}\) and \(E\equiv E'+jc_r\); and \(f=f(1-\prod_iy_i^q)+f\prod_iy_i^q\). Let \(G\) consist of these binomials, as squarefree polynomials in the \(z\)'s of degree at most \(w\), and of the \(z_{i,l}^2-z_{i,l+1}\). The degree-\(D\) closure of \(G\) is \(S_D\): the \(z_{i,l}^2-z_{i,l+1}\) and the Boolean axioms span the same space; a clause polynomial of row \(r\) differs from its squarefree form in the \(z\)'s by a polynomial of degree at most \(w\) vanishing on the cube, a combination of multiples of Boolean axioms within degree \(w\), and that form is a combination of the binomials; and conversely each binomial of \(G\) is, in the same way, a combination of the clause polynomials of its row modulo such multiples.

The span. Let \(S'\) be the span in the statement. It lies in \(S_D\), by the normal form, row step and translation lemmas and because \(y^a-cy^a\in S_D\) with \(c\ne1\) gives \(y^a\in S_D\), and then \(z\,y^a\in S_D\) for \(\operatorname{wt}(a)\le D-1\), which is \(y^{a+e}\) modulo \(S_D\). It contains \(G\): the two monomials of \(z_{i,l}^2-z_{i,l+1}\) and of a binomial of the first kind have the same \(a\); those of a binomial of the second kind have vectors \(a,a+jc_r\) of weight at most \(w\le D\) and label \(\gamma_r^j\), a row step. It is closed under the rule: \(S'\) is a space of binomials whose components are, through \(M\mapsto a(M)\), the classes of \(\approx\), dead exactly when in \(\Delta\); by the first step, \(S'\cap K[z]_{\le D-1}\) is spanned by monomials \(M\) with \(a(M)\in\Delta\) and binomials \(M-cM'\) with \(a(M)\approx_ca(M')\), all of degree at most \(D-1\), so that \(a(M),a(M')\in\Omega_{D-1}\); multiplying by \(z_{i,l}\) gives a monomial with vector \(a(M)+e\in\Delta\), respectively a binomial with \(a(M)+e\approx_ca(M')+e\). So \(S_D\subseteq S'\).

Consequences. \(1=y^0\in S_D\) exactly when \(0\in\Delta\), and \(1\in S_D\) exactly when \(1\in C_D\): one direction is in the third ceiling entry, the other holds because \(S_D\) contains the multilinear closure, a multilinear step being a multiplication followed by subtraction of Boolean multiples of no larger degree. With that, \(S_D\cap(V_D\otimes K)=C_D\otimes K\): the left side contains the right, and reduction, the identity on multilinear polynomials, maps \(S_D\) into \(C_D\otimes K\). Also \((C_D\otimes K)\cap(V_j\otimes K)=(C_D\cap V_j)\otimes K\), extension of scalars commuting with intersections. By the first step the dimension of \(K[z]_{\le j}/(S_D\cap K[z]_{\le j})\) is the number of live components containing a monomial of degree at most \(j\), that is, classes outside \(\Delta\) with a vector of weight at most \(j\). Multilinear reduction maps \(S_D\) onto \(C_D\otimes K\) and \(S_D\cap K[z]_{\le j}\) onto \((C_D\cap V_j)\otimes K\), its kernel within degree \(j\) lying in \(S_D\); so the dimension equals that of \(V_j/(C_D\cap V_j)\). \(\square\)

Unsatisfiability is not used. Nonemptiness of the allowed sets is used in the second step and that every block lies in a row in the normal form; the reviewer notes that the second step also holds for an empty allowed set, the binomials then killing every character.

The computation

Prediction counted before the run. The thin endpoint at a cutoff \(K\) allows about \(\binom{2K}{j}\) classes of least weight \(j\) just below \(K\); for \(k=2\), fifteen blocks and \(j=6\) there are \(\binom{15}{6}2^6=320320\) vectors against \(\binom{13}{6}=1716\), so the comparison would have been decisive in either direction. It needs a closure that is proper at some \(D\ge w\).

The kernel binomial_closure.c computes \((\approx,\Delta)\) by a labelled union-find on \(\Omega_D\) with the translation rule iterated to a fixed point, and reports the least \(D\ge w\) with \(0\in\Delta\) and the level sizes one degree below. Two generators: random rows on \(t\) distinct blocks with random exponents and right sides, \(R=m+1\) rows; and flow conservation on a random connected \(t\)-regular graph, blocks the edges and rows the vertices with exponents \(\pm1\), right sides of nonzero total, where the sum of all rows is the only dependency. Unsatisfiability is asserted by brute force. Outcome, from series.jsonl:

generator\(k\)blocksterms\(n\)\(w\)systemsdegree
random24, 528, 10474
random26, 12312, 24656
random372, 3216, 946, 9
flow, cubic26, 9, 12, 15312 to 30696
flow, 4-regular216432828

Every system is refuted at its width. Since every axiom has degree equal to the width of its row, this is the least possible value, and there is no proper closure at any \(D\ge w\) whose levels could be reported. For the thirteen systems with \(k=2\) and at most twelve bits the degree agrees with the reference tools/truncated_buchberger.py on the clause polynomials. As the reviewer showed, this comparison has no discriminating power: in ten of them \(m\le w\), so every vector is light and row steps alone close the dependency, and the other three are forced by a short argument of the same kind. The kernel is therefore checked by the reviewer's reading of its code, which found no path declaring refutation too early, and not by a test; its level output was never produced, and I did not run it with translation disabled to see where that rule matters. Dead classes are not merged under translation, which does not affect the two outputs.

Why. A refutation at degree \(D\ge w\) exists as soon as the rows of a dependency can be ordered so that all prefix sums have weight at most \(D\), by row steps alone. For flow systems the prefix sums are supported on cuts, of weight one or \(k-1\) per edge; the outcome shows that each graph of the run has an order whose cuts fit. A proper closure at \(D>w\) needs graphs whose cuts exceed the width in every order, or rows whose prefix sums are heavy, and the translation rule only lowers the degree further. I have not determined the least size at which the degree exceeds the width; for cubic flow systems at \(k=2\) it needs at least a graph with no order of cut width six. Enumeration of \(\Omega_D\) is the wrong tool for the question; a method that follows only the classes near a given vector would be needed.

The bridge's sub-idea

  • The closure computation on exponent vectors. Follow-up. Developed: built, at research/provenance/near-half-binomial-closure-20261009/binomial_closure.c; not validated by a discriminating test, and unable to reach a proper closure above the width for unsatisfiable systems.

9 October 2026 — Light vectors are live and levels dominate coset leaders; the bound is too weak to decide thinness, and the kernel now agrees with the reference on level sizes

Working proof of a lower bound on the level sizes of proper binomial closures, with a negative assessment of its use; validation evidence for the closure kernel. Queue development of a chosen bridge while draining. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort low).

Chosen. Third entry on the thin-closure bridge, bearing on the family statement through its alternative endpoint; it comes before the head because the preceding entry left a lower bound to prove and a validation owed.

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement: with closures of block-field binomial systems described as classes of exponent vectors, can the level sizes of a proper closure be bounded from below well enough to decide whether they can be as small as the thin endpoint asks?

New mathematics. A lemma, following the reviewer's suggestion of the last entry: at a proper \(D\) every vector of weight at most \(D-k+1\) is live, classes lie in cosets of the row lattice \(L\), and so for \(j\le D-k+1\) the level of degree \(j\) has at least as many standard monomials as there are cosets of \(L\) of least weight \(j\); the least weights of cosets fill an interval. The bound does not decide thinness for any family I can evaluate: for flow systems the lattice has \(q^{V-1}\) elements, which is far more than the ratio the endpoint constrains, and for lattices of full rank the bound is empty. What thinness asks is derivability of translations within weight \(D\), and the coset count does not see it.

Goal progress. Unchanged. A necessary condition for the alternative endpoint on binomial systems, satisfied trivially in the cases of interest.

General statement. lem:binomial-coset-level-bound holds for every block-field binomial system and every \(D\ge w\) at which the closure is proper.

The bound

Setting and notation of lem:binomial-closure-classes: the relation \(\approx\) and the dead set \(\Delta\) on \(\Omega_D\), \(D\ge w\). Let \(L\subseteq\mathbb Z_q^m\) be the subgroup generated by the rows \(c_r\); for a coset let its least weight be the least \(\operatorname{wt}\) of its elements, \(\ell_j(L)\) the number of cosets of least weight \(j\), and \(\rho(L)\) the largest least weight. Let \(b_j\) be the number of classes outside \(\Delta\) whose least weight is \(j\); by that lemma \(b_j=\dim V_j/(C_D\cap V_j)-\dim V_{j-1}/(C_D\cap V_{j-1})\), with \(V_{-1}=0\).

Lemma (binomial coset level bound). Let \(D\ge w\) and \(0\notin\Delta\). Then (1) no vector of weight at most \(D-k+1\) is in \(\Delta\); (2) \(a\approx_cb\) implies \(a-b\in L\); (3) for \(j\le D-k+1\), \(b_j\ge\ell_j(L)\), and the number of live classes with a vector of weight at most \(j\) is at least the number of cosets of \(L\) meeting \(\Omega_j\); (4) \(\ell_j(L)\ge1\) for every \(0\le j\le\rho(L)\).

Proof. (1) Let \(a\in\Delta\) with \(\operatorname{wt}(a)\le D-k+1\). Take a block with \(a_i\ne0\), of weight \(\alpha\ge1\), and add to it, one at a time, the \(k-\alpha\) powers of two absent from the binary expansion of \(a_i\). Before the last addition the block has weight at most \(k-1\) and the vector weight at most \(\operatorname{wt}(a)-\alpha+k-1\le D-1\), so each addition is a translation of a dead vector of weight at most \(D-1\) and its result is dead; the last addition makes the block \(q\equiv0\) and the weight \(\operatorname{wt}(a)-\alpha\). Repeating over the blocks, with weights only smaller, gives \(0\in\Delta\). (2) Row steps relate vectors differing by a multiple of a row, translation adds the same vector to both sides, and reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity preserve the property. (3) By (2) every class lies in one coset. A coset of least weight \(j\le D-k+1\) has an element \(a\) of weight \(j\), which is live by (1); its class has no lighter element, so it is counted in \(b_j\), and different cosets give different classes. The cumulative statement is the same argument for cosets meeting \(\Omega_j\). (4) If a coset has least weight \(\rho\ge1\), attained at \(a\), remove one power of two from a block of \(a\): the result \(a'\) has weight \(\rho-1\), and its coset has least weight at least \(\rho-1\), since an element \(l\) of it gives \(l+e\) in the coset of \(a\) with \(\operatorname{wt}(l+e)\le\operatorname{wt}(l)+1\). Descend. \(\square\)

Unused: nothing in the proof uses unsatisfiability beyond \(0\notin\Delta\), which for an unsatisfiable system is properness and for a satisfiable one always holds.

What it gives for the thin endpoint

The endpoint asks for \(b_j\le\binom Xj\), \(X\) about \(2K\), from some \(j\) just below a cutoff \(K\); the standard monomials of degree at most \(D\) under a degree-compatible order are closed under taking divisors, a leading monomial of degree below \(D\) having its multiples among the leading monomials, so by the Kruskal–Katona bound on lower shadows such a bound at one level propagates to higher levels, not to lower ones. So the lemma yields the necessary condition \(\ell_j(L)\le\binom Xj\) for those \(j\) up to \(D-k+1\). I can evaluate neither side usefully.

  • Flow systems on a connected \(t\)-regular graph with a consistent orientation: \(L\) is the cut lattice, of \(q^{V-1}\) elements, at most \(2^{2n/t}\). Vectors supported on the \(m-V+1\) edges outside a spanning tree lie in different cosets, a cut vanishing on a spanning tree being zero, so the cosets meeting \(\Omega_j\) number at least \(\sum_{i\le j}k^i\binom{m-V+1}{i}\). This is a cumulative count, and the endpoint bounds single levels from some level on while leaving the lower ones free, so the two are not comparable: the count could sit entirely in levels below the window. A bound on \(\ell_j\) itself is needed, and I did not obtain one; the reviewer proposes one below.
  • Overdetermined systems with \(L=\mathbb Z_q^m\): one coset, \(\ell_0=1\), and the bound is empty.

In both cases what decides the level sizes is which lattice translations are derivable within weight \(D\), and the lemma uses none of that. It is a correct statement that does not bear on the question; I record it because the last entry named it as the next attempt.

Whether proper closures above the width exist at all for these systems: by a search summary of Buss, Grigoriev, Impagliazzo and Pitassi's paper, which I have not read, Tseitin systems modulo \(p\) on an \(r\)-regular graph of expansion \(\epsilon\) have no refutation of degree below \(\epsilon V/8\) over a field of other characteristic, in multiplicative variables. At \(k=2\) the flow systems are such systems over \(\mathbb F_4\), and under the substitution \(z_{i,0}=y_i\), \(z_{i,1}=y_i^2\) a step of ours should be at most two of theirs, so that our degree is at least half of theirs, up to an additive term of the order of the width for deriving each side's axioms; that step is not written out, and the constant is from the summary. On that reading proper closures above the width exist for large expanders, far beyond enumeration, and the thin question concerns them.

Validation of the kernel

The kernel of the last entry gained a mode for satisfiable systems, with right sides from a planted solution, reporting for each \(D\ge w\) the cumulative numbers of live classes by weight. For eight systems at \(k=2\), \(n=8\) and \(10\), rows of two or three terms, and each \(D\) from \(w\) to \(w+3\), these numbers agree with the numbers of standard monomials of the degree-\(D\) closure computed by tools/truncated_buchberger.py from the clause polynomials: 32 comparisons, no mismatch, no dead vector (validation.txt, from satisfiable.jsonl). Its strength: the level output is exercised and the values are not all trivial, one system having cumulative counts \(1,7,9\): six classes of least weight one, two of least weight two. Its limit: in every case the counts are the same for all four values of \(D\), from which I infer, without having printed the number of solutions, that the closure at \(D=w\) is already the full ideal within these degrees; so the comparison does not show the translation rule doing work that row steps could not; the kernel remains unchecked in a case where the degree matters.

  • Validate the kernel on satisfiable systems. Follow-up. Developed: done as far as feasible sizes allow, evidence in research/results/near-half-coset-level-bound-20261009/validation.txt; 32 agreements, with the limit stated above.

Reviewer's suggestions, unverified

  • The least-weight distribution of the cut lattice can be bounded on expanders. At \(k=2\), \(\operatorname{wt}(a+\delta f)\ge\operatorname{wt}(a)+|\partial f\setminus\operatorname{supp}a|-|\partial f\cap\operatorname{supp}a|\), so \(a\) is the unique lightest element of its coset when its support holds fewer than half the edges of every cut; for a subgraph \(H\) of maximum degree below half the edge expansion every vector supported on \(E(H)\) is such, giving \(\ell_j\ge2^j\binom{|E(H)|}{j}\) for \(j\le D-1\), with \(|E(H)|\) about \(n/8\) on near-Ramanujan graphs. Against \(\binom{2K}{j}\) this would exclude the thin endpoint for these systems when \(K\) is below about \(n/8\) and leave it open above. It may fail for potentials \(f\) with many values, for \(k>2\), where \(\operatorname{wt}(-a)\ne\operatorname{wt}(a)\), and for cubic graphs. Record. Searched "unique coset leader edge expansion cut subgraph low degree": the matches (gadget ring screens, a conjunction quotient rank theorem, an input sector collapse, a cube lemma) are on other objects; no statement on least weights in cosets of a cut lattice is recorded.

Specification decision. No change. The lemma constrains the alternative endpoint for one class of systems and gives no property a candidate for the family statement could be required to have.

Verification gate. One fresh-context medium reviewer checked the four parts of the lemma and found them correct, including the threshold \(D-k+1\) and the subadditivity of the weight modulo \(q\). Corrections applied: the range of the cumulative clause; the shadow direction and the reason the family is closed under divisors; the size of the cut lattice; a false sentence that counting gives only the volume bound, replaced by the spanning-tree count and the reason it is not comparable with the endpoint; the direction and additive term of the comparison with the Tseitin bound; a misreading of cumulative counts as levels; and an unshown claim about the number of solutions, now marked as inferred. It confirmed eight systems and 32 comparisons against the saved output. Unused: \(D\ge w\) beyond the cited lemma. Record: review.txt.

Follow-up. Continuing. Third entry on this bridge in this spell. Next attempt on it, after the scheduled review: verify the reviewer's bound on least weights for the cut lattice of an expander, which with the lemma would exclude the thin endpoint for flow systems below a cutoff of about \(n/8\); and read the Tseitin bound's proof, which constructs a proper closure and therefore describes its live classes above that.

Process assessment. Three entries on binomial closures have produced a description, a kernel and a bound, and none touches the question they were for. The object is now understood well enough to see why: the question is about derivability within a weight budget, and each tool so far counts something coarser. The one source that constructs a proper closure for these systems is the Tseitin lower bound, which I have cited from a search summary and should have read first.

9 October 2026 — Goal-level review: level selection cannot replace the binomial rate, barely covering systems are as hard as arbitrary covers, and the engine's own families are the next test

Goal-level route review: one open statement, unchanged across thirty-three research entries. No outside leads or bridges while the queue drains. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort low).

Question. Six research entries since the last review closed its candidate and left the family statement where it was. What does the block teach about the line, is there a different architecture, and which test comes next?

Architecture test. The last review's decisive test, the block-field binomial candidate, was reported in the third ceiling entry: refuted, and since sharpened to a quarter.

New mathematics. One lemma, found by the reviewer in answering the test this review first proposed: a cover whose evenly covered set lies in a subspace \(U\) cut out by forms has refutation degree between that of its restriction to \(U\) and that plus \(w\), when the latter is at least \(w\); and any cover of a subspace of codimension \(w\) extends, by a partition of the complement, to a cover of the whole space with covering sum \(1+2^{-w}(\Sigma-1)\) and at least the same degree. So covers that barely cover are exactly as hard as arbitrary covers in \(w\) fewer dimensions, and the static dimension count, which leaves room near half only for them, constrains nothing. Besides this, two readings of the recorded size bound, made to assess the reviewer's independent proposal: the cutoff \(K\) is already free in it, and choosing it by pigeonhole guarantees only the rate the binomial ratio already has at a constant \(K/n\); what the engine needs is that the counts grow by a factor \(1+o(1)\) per degree below the cutoff.

Goal progress. Unchanged. The six entries produced two ceilings, a description of binomial closures, a lower bound on their levels and the closure of one lead; none bears on the existence of a family, and the alternative endpoint is undecided for the one class where closures are now computable in principle.

General statement. The line's claim is the family statement, thm:near-half-frege-transfer being its use; the block's all-parameter results are prop:block-binomial-third-ceiling, prop:block-binomial-quarter-ceiling, lem:binomial-closure-classes and lem:binomial-coset-level-bound; this review adds lem:barely-covering-padding, for every cover of \(\mathbb F_2^n\) by affine subspaces.

Across the goal

  • Near-half Boolean PC family. Open, as at every review. Since the last one: block-field binomial systems, the first candidate no recorded ceiling excluded, are refuted in degree \(\min\{n/3,n/4+w\}+o(n)\); the affine restriction lead is closed, its contribution being the free-dimension endpoint; binomial closures are labelled classes of exponent vectors, and at sizes that can be enumerated every such system falls at its width.
  • Complete Frege transfer. Working proof within its recorded limits; untouched in this block. The constant \(c_F\) is still not computed.

Obstacle

Unchanged in substance and sharper in form. The engine needs, at some cutoff \(K\) below the barrier, that every down-closed family of standard monomials it meets grows slowly across a window of polylogarithmic width: by a factor \(1+o(1)\) per degree at two levels, and correspondingly less with more. For subsets of an \(n\)-set this happens only near \(n/2\); for a family with at most \(\binom Xj\) sets per level, only near \(X/2\). Either way the closure must be proper beyond half of a dimension in which its standard monomials live, and no lower-bound method for \(\mathbb F_2\) is known to pass a quarter. Each structured candidate has fallen to a ceiling whose mechanism was not among those listed when it was proposed: this time, deriving an equivalence where two monomials are light and carrying it by multiplication.

Architecture review

Necessary target. As stated in Open statements: literal CNFs of polynomial length with auxiliary affine equations, of free dimension \(n\), with no refutation at \(\lfloor n/2-s\rfloor\), \(s+w\le n^{1-\epsilon}\), or \((s+w)(\log n)^{d+c_F-2}=o(n)\) for one depth. This is sufficient and not shown necessary for the goal. Read through the size bound's proof, what the engine uses is weaker than the barrier's position: a cutoff \(K\) with \(K+n^{o(1)}\le D\) and slow growth of the counts just below \(K\).

Extra requirements. Two were examined. That the cutoff sit next to the barrier is not required by the proof; it is a consequence of using the ambient binomial ratio, which is close to one only near \(n/2\), together with the ceiling \(n/2\) one expects for \(D\). That the slow growth hold for every down-closed subfamily is required as the proof stands, since nothing is known about which subfamilies the engine's prefactors produce; the thin endpoint is a sufficient condition under which the worst subfamily is harmless, and its necessity is not shown. Control of the prefactors would be a weakening; the decisive test below takes it up.

Independent alternative. Before seeing this route the review's medium reviewer received the goal and the available results (stage-one-brief.txt) and proposed three things (independent-review.txt). (A) Choose the cutoff per proof by pigeonhole over levels, accepting a ratio \(1/t\), so that a barrier at any linear or polynomial degree would do; it expected a hidden budget, since the proposal would turn known linear bounds into the goal. Audited below: the hidden budget is the rate itself. (B) Read the thin endpoint as near-half in the Kruskal–Katona dimension \(X_j\) of the levels, and test \(D\) against \(X_K/2\); adopted as a formulation, with the remark that a general bound \(D\le X_K/2+O(w)\) would end that endpoint and is of the same kind as the unproved half ceiling for the cube. (C) Evidence against the approach: ceilings at a third or less for every structured family, methods stopping at a quarter, and the hereditary condition under restriction; it would spend a cycle on a general ceiling \((1/2-c)n\) for polynomially many rows. The record's attempt at such a ceiling failed at its base case, so this review first chose the part of it for which there seemed to be a counting reason, the barely covering systems; that test is answered below, in the negative.

Audit of (A). In cor:bounded-depth-size-bound the levels have shifts \(\Delta_0=1\), \(\Delta_i=\Delta_{i-1}t_i\) with \(t_i=\lceil\ln(\ell n^A)/\eta_i\rceil+1\) and \(\eta_i=\eta_K(\Delta_{i-1})\), the transfer theorem's rate, for which the corollary uses the lower bound \(\tfrac14\rho^{2\Delta_{i-1}}\); the only conditions on \(K\) are \(\Delta\le K\) and \(K+\max\{4\Delta,\Delta+w\}\le D\). So \(K\) may be any level, and the proposal's freedom is already there. Pigeonhole over the \(J=\lfloor(D-K_0)/\Delta\rfloor\) levels \(K_0+i\Delta\) gives a level with ratio at least \((c(K_0)/c(D))^{1/J}\ge2^{-n/J}\), about \(2^{-n\Delta/(D-K_0)}\), which is \(\exp(-\Theta(\Delta))\) when \(D-K_0\) is of order \(n\) and worse otherwise. Nothing better can be guaranteed: on the cube, \(c=N_n\) with \(D\le\alpha n\), \(\alpha<1/2\), has every such ratio of order \((\alpha/(1-\alpha))^{\Delta}\). The engine's counts also change with the prefactor from round to round, which weakens selection further: each family has few bad levels, but over the families of a proof no common good level need exist, and a random level is good only for a fraction of them at the same rate. With a rate \(e^{-\gamma\Delta}\), \(\Delta_1\) is of order \(A\log n\) and \(\eta_2\) a negative power of \(n\) with exponent proportional to \(\gamma A\), so that the second shift exceeds \(D-K\) unless \(\gamma A\) is below a small constant. At two levels the proof therefore needs \(\gamma=o(1)\) to serve every \(A\). That is the plateau, and it is where half enters; level selection does not produce it. With the ambient binomial ratio and a barrier at \((1/2-\epsilon)n\), small constant \(\epsilon\), \(\gamma\) is about \(4\epsilon\), and two levels exclude sizes \(n^A\) only for \(A\) of order \(1/\epsilon\), a fixed polynomial bound.

Rank normalization. The reviewer's (B) is this question answered for the thin endpoint: losses and survivors are both counted among the standard monomials, whose levels have a dimension \(X\) of their own, and the engine's rate is a relative contraction in that count. The endpoint is then "proper beyond \(X/2\)", the same phenomenon as near-half in a different quotient; it helps only if structure lowers \(X\) without lowering \(D\); the record has no example where that happens, product frames being the one case examined.

Decision. Retain the family statement with its two endpoints. Drop level selection. As a judgment, not an exclusion: stop developing binomial closures as a route to the thin endpoint beyond the two items already named for the bridge, since by the ceilings these systems can serve only that endpoint and only below \(\min\{n/3,n/4+w\}+o(n)\). Drop the static dimension count as a guide to candidates. Test next the one requirement this review found unexamined: which families the engine's prefactors actually produce.

Decisive test. The engine's own families. In thm:binary-approximator-rank the count \(c_P(k)\) is the codimension in \(V_k\) of \(Z_P(k)=\{f:Pg_if\in C_D\text{ for all }i\}\), a space containing \(C_D\cap V_k\) and closed under multiplication by variables below the cutoff; the plateau is needed for these spaces and not for arbitrary down-closed subfamilies of the standard monomials. Next cycle: describe \(Z_P(K)\) for the prefactors the proof produces, products of \(1+q\) with \(q\) in the span of the inputs, and decide whether its standard monomials can be an arbitrary down-closed subfamily. If one explicit prefactor yields a family as bad as the worst, the thin condition is necessary for the method as well as sufficient, and the alternative endpoint stands as stated. If the families are constrained, for instance to those of closures of larger systems, the statement to be proved changes to a plateau for those, which may hold at a cutoff where the ambient ratio fails.

The barely covering test, answered

This review's first choice of test was: for a cover whose evenly covered set \(E\) has small measure, bound the degree by \(w\) plus the degree of the system restricted near \(E\), and ask whether the restricted system is again barely covering. The reviewer answered both parts in stage two; I checked the arguments and record them.

Lemma (barely covering padding). Let rows \(\mathbf 1_{A_r}\) of codimension at most \(w\) cover \(\mathbb F_2^n\), let \(E\) be the set of points in an even number of the \(A_r\), and let \(U\supseteq E\) be an affine subspace, the common zero set of affine forms \(l_1,\ldots,l_c\). Let \(d\) be the refutation degree of the rows and \(d_U\) that of the rows together with the \(l_i\). Then \(d_U\le d\le\max\{d_U,w\}+w\). Conversely, if \(U\) has codimension \(w\) and \(\mathcal C\) is any cover of \(U\) by affine subspaces of \(U\), with covering sum \(\Sigma\) inside \(U\), then \(\mathcal C\) together with the \(w\) subspaces \(\{l_1=\cdots=l_{i-1}=0,\ l_i=1\}\) covers \(\mathbb F_2^n\) with covering sum \(1+2^{-w}(\Sigma-1)\) and refutation degree at least that of \(\mathcal C\) as a cover of \(U\).

Proof. Adding axioms does not raise the degree, so \(d_U\le d\). Over \(\mathbb F_2\) the sum of the rows is \(1+g\) with \(g=\mathbf 1_E\), of degree at most \(w\), and \(g\,l_i=0\) as a function, hence as a multilinear polynomial. Multiply every line of a refutation of the rows and the \(l_i\) of degree \(d_U\) by \(g\): the axioms \(l_i\) become zero, the rows become multiples of rows of degree at most \(2w\), and the last line becomes \(g\). So \(g\) is derived from the rows in degree \(\max\{d_U,w\}+w\), and \(1=g+\sum_r\mathbf 1_{A_r}\). For the converse, the \(w\) subspaces partition the complement of \(U\), of measure \(1-2^{-w}\), and the members of \(\mathcal C\) have total measure \(2^{-w}\Sigma\); restricting to \(U\) by adding the \(l_i\) makes the partition rows zero and leaves \(\mathcal C\). \(\square\)

What it teaches. Covering sum close to one is no restriction: every cover in dimension \(n-w\) appears, with its degree, among the barely covering systems in dimension \(n\). The static span is proper by dimension for all of them, which shows only how weak that count is; the recorded remark that room near half exists "exactly when the covering sum is \(1+O(sw/n)\)" is a statement about the count and says nothing about which systems can be hard. The recursion gains nothing either: rows inside \(U\) have their width increased by \(w\), so nesting accumulates width and not degree. The window \(1+O(sw/n)\) in the earlier draft of this test came from the static span bound, not from lem:cover-sum-gap.

Falsification attempt on this line

The claim: some polynomial-size family is hard near half of its free dimension, or has a proper closure that is thin below its cutoff. Three attacks. A general ceiling below half would refute the first form; none is known, and the recorded attempt failed. The hereditary condition: by lem:term-value-case-split, if a system of free dimension \(n\) has no refutation at \(n/2-s\), then for any \(r\) independent affine forms some assignment of values leaves a system of dimension \(n-r\) with no refutation at \((n-r)/2-(s+r/2)\); so near-half hardness passes to a coset of every subspace of small codimension, and a family for which some few forms make every coset easy is excluded. I have not checked the recorded candidates against this condition; it is satisfied by any family that is hard for a global reason, so it is a screen and not evidence either way. Third, the thin form: for flow systems the reviewer of the last entry gave an unverified bound that would exclude it below \(n/8\). The claim survives, as before, because nothing is proved in either direction.

Checks, scope and verification

Scope. Entries covered: the third and quarter ceilings, the affine restriction lead and its closure, binomial closures and the coset level bound. Reread for this review: the proof of cor:bounded-depth-size-bound in full, the statement and proof of thm:binary-approximator-rank earlier in this session, the summaries of the splitting ceiling attempt and of the entry on counts for covers.

Follow-ups whose status changed. The affine restriction lead and its four checks are closed or developed; the binomial check of the domain rigidity entry is closed by the third ceiling; the thin-closure bridge continues with two named items.

Verification gate. The review's single medium reviewer worked in two stages. Stage one is described under Independent alternative. In stage two it found the audit of its proposal sound, with corrections applied: the rate's definition and exponent, the range in which the pigeonhole rate is \(\exp(-\Theta(\Delta))\), the cube as the justification that nothing better is guaranteed, and the effect of changing prefactors. It corrected "exactly" to "sufficient" for the thin condition, removed an unsupported sentence on definitions of variables and a wrongly quantified sentence on cosets, and narrowed the title and the decision on binomial closures. It answered the decisive test first proposed here by the two arguments recorded as the padding lemma, which I checked line by line and which no second reader has seen, and proposed the test now adopted. Not read by the reviewer: the transfer theorem's definition of its rate. Records: review.txt, independent-review.txt.

Process assessment. In all six entries the reviewer removed or reversed something I had stated: a general claim in the ceiling's discussion, the range in which the quarter beats the third, a guessed dichotomy, a validation that tested nothing, a sentence contradicted by our own record, a cumulative count read as a level; and in this review the decisive test I chose was answered by the reviewer in three lines. Three habits follow and are carried forward: hand a candidate to a proof of its simplest property before estimates about it are compared; before a computation, count not only its prediction but whether any reachable instance is non-vacuous; read a source before building on a summary of it. The reviewer's help has been worth more than its error-checking in this block: the quarter, the satisfiable validation and the coset bound all came from its suggestions. The queue has 48 items and has fallen by five in this block through closures of answered checks; at this rate it does not reach ten, and most of its items predate the transfer.

Decision. Core: the first open statement, the near-half Boolean PC family, is worked next by the decisive test above on the families the engine's prefactors produce. No publication, stopping or Lean work follows from this review.

9 October 2026 — The engine's families are truncated colons and include the closure's own; in the series model for generic rows the levels grow up to the first zero, so nothing is thin below half

Working proof of an elementary description of the engine's families; finite check on six power series, a statement about series and not about systems. Queue development of a chosen check while draining. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort low).

Chosen. The check on the thin endpoint from the thin-kernel review bears on the family statement through its alternative endpoint, and the goal-level review made the question behind it its decisive test; it comes before the head for that reason.

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement: the engine needs slow growth of the counts \(c_P\) below the cutoff. Which families of standard monomials do these counts come from, can they be arbitrary down-closed subfamilies of the closure's, and is the resulting requirement weaker than the thin condition?

Architecture test. Outcome of the decisive test of the review: the families are constrained, and the constraint does not help. They are the standard monomials of truncated colon spaces \((C_D:Pg_i)\), which contain \(C_D\); but whenever the inputs generate \(1\) in low degree and the product is empty, the family is the closure's own, so any rate that holds for all families holds for the closure's own counts \(h_k=\dim V_k/(C_D\cap V_k)\). A rate better than the ambient binomial one therefore changes the requirement in form, to a plateau of \(h\) and of its localizations, and not in difficulty: in the one model available for levels of generic systems they grow by large factors up to the last degree before the first zero.

New mathematics. A lemma of two lines describing the families, with the consequence above. And a computation on series: for \((1+z)^n/(1+z^k)^m\) at \(n=256\), the coefficients below the first non-positive one increase up to its predecessor in the three cases at threshold density, by factors of two to about five per degree at the end, and are within a factor two of their maximum in a fourth, and their Kruskal–Katona dimension there is between \(0.75n\) and \(0.96n\) against \(2j\) between \(0.1n\) and \(0.55n\). Before the run I expected the opposite, a decline before the zero that would have made generic systems thin just below their regularity at any density; that expectation is refuted for these series.

Goal progress. Unchanged. Any improvement of the engine's rate over the ambient one is shown to need a plateau of the closure's own counts, and the only model of generic levels has none below half.

General statement. lem:engine-colon-families holds for every Boolean system over \(\mathbb F_2\), every cutoff and every prefactor within the degree conditions of thm:binary-approximator-rank.

The families

Notation of thm:binary-approximator-rank: \(C_D\) the closure, \(g_1,\ldots,g_s\) of degree at most \(d\), \(P\) of degree \(a\), \(a+k+d\le D\), \(Z_P(k)=\{f\in V_k:Pg_if\in C_D\text{ for all }i\}\), \(c_P(k)=\dim V_k/Z_P(k)\), and \(h_k=\dim V_k/(C_D\cap V_k)\).

Lemma (engine colon families). (1) \(Z_P(k)=\bigcap_i(C_D:Pg_i)\cap V_k\), where \((C_D:u)=\{f:uf\in C_D\}\); it contains \(C_D\cap V_k\), and \(c_P(k)\) is the rank of \(f\mapsto([Pg_if])_i\) from \(V_k\) to \((V_D/C_D)^s\). (2) For a degree-compatible order the standard monomials of \(Z_P(k)\) form a subfamily, closed under divisors, of the standard monomials of \(C_D\cap V_k\), and \(c_P(k)\le h_k\). (3) If \(P=1\) and \(\sum_iu_ig_i=1\) with \(\deg u_ig_i\le e\), then \(Z_P(k)=C_D\cap V_k\) and \(c_P(k)=h_k\) for \(k\le D-\max\{d,e\}\). (4) Hence, for any \(\theta\) and \(K+\max\{d,e\}\le D\): if \(c_P(K-d)\ge\theta\,c_P(K)\) holds for \(P=1\) and all such inputs, then \(h_{K-d}\ge\theta\,h_K\).

Proof. (1) is the definition; \(C_D\cap V_k\subseteq Z_P(k)\) by multiplication within degree \(a+d+k\le D\). (2) A larger space has more leading monomials, so fewer standard ones; closure under divisors is in the proof of the monotone normalized rank lemma. (2) also uses \(a+k+d\le D\), for closure under divisors. (3) If \(g_if\in C_D\) for all \(i\), then \(f=\sum_iu_i(g_if)\in C_D\) by multiplication within degree \(e+k\le D\); conversely \(f\in C_D\cap V_k\) gives \(g_if\in C_D\). (4) Apply the hypothesis to such inputs. \(\square\)

The inputs \(\{1\}\) alone are a degenerate case of the rank theorem, as the reviewer notes, and a proof could treat them separately; \(\{x_1x_2,1+x_1,1+x_2\}\) generates \(1\) in degree two without containing it. In the rank theorem itself the rate \(\theta=N_n(K-d)/N_n(K)\) holds unconditionally, so (4) constrains nothing there; it constrains any attempt to use a better rate, as thm:level-size-degree-transfer does under the thin hypothesis. I did not reread that theorem's proof for this entry.

Reading. The engine does not meet arbitrary subfamilies: it meets the closure's own family and those of its colons by polynomials \(Pg\) of degree at most \(a+d\). When \(u=Pg\) is the indicator of a subcube the colon \((C_D:u)\) contains the closure of the restricted system at degree \(D-\deg u\), so these are localizations of the system to regions cut out by low-degree polynomials. A region of low degree is large, and a small substructure cannot be isolated by one; but the first family is the whole, and a rate sufficient at two levels means for it a plateau: \(h\) growing by a factor \(1+o(1)\) per degree below the cutoff, as computed in the review. The thin condition implies this for all the families at once. The plateau of \(h\) alone is weaker than thinness only in a contrived way: with minimal shadows the lower levels of a thick top level sum to less than it, so a plateau without thinness needs lower levels that are large for another reason, such as being full on many more points. I do not claim a plateau is necessary for every proof by this engine: (4) concerns rates that hold for all families, not the true gain of a round.

Do generic levels plateau below half?

Prediction, stated before the run. If the levels of a closure followed a series whose coefficients decline to zero at the index of regularity, the levels just below it would be small against the cumulative count, \(h\) would plateau there, and the Kruskal–Katona dimension \(X_j\) would fall to about \(2j\); then generic overdetermined systems would meet the alternative endpoint at any density. The test: compute, for \(S(z)=(1+z)^n/(1+z^k)^m\), the coefficients \(a_j\) below the first non-positive one at index \(D^*\), their mode, and \(X_j\), the least \(X\) with \(\binom Xj\ge a_j\). The outcome could go either way: for \(m=0\) the series is the cube's and is thin exactly near \(n/2\).

\(k\)\(m\)\(D^*\)mode\(X_j/2j\) at \(j=D^*-1\)\(\log_2\) of last two coefficients

All at \(n=256\); the first three rows are at the density \(m=\lceil\ln2\cdot2^kn\rceil\) of the first-moment bound, above which random rows are unsatisfiable (series.json, by series_thinness.py, exact integers). In the three dense cases the coefficients increase up to \(D^*-1\) and then change sign at once; at \(m=64\) they peak three degrees before and have declined by a factor of about \(1.9\). At the sampled degrees and the last four below \(D^*\), the ratio \(X_j/2j\) decreases with \(j\) and stays above \(1.5\) in these four cases; the window with \(X_j\le2j+2\) ending at \(D^*-1\) is empty. The output stores \(X_j\) at sampled \(j\) only. The engine's cutoff lies below the barrier by the product degree, not at \(D^*-1\); the conclusion is the same, the growth holding throughout. It is nonempty only in the two sparse cases, near \(j=n/2\). The prediction is refuted for these series: there is no decline before the first zero, and no plateau.

Scope. This is a statement about six series at one \(n\). It says nothing about a system unless its levels follow the series; for rows that are indicator polynomials of subspaces the record shows the series is the wrong model, and for products of affine forms the record's conjecture concerns the degree only. As far as the model goes it says that a generic system's closure, just below the degree where it stops being proper, has levels still growing by a factor of two or more, so it meets neither the plateau nor the thin condition away from \(n/2\).

The queued check

The check asked whether level sizes at most \(\binom Xj\) below the cutoff force a refutation at about \(X/2\). Not decided. What this entry adds is on the other side: the model in which levels are known gives no thin closure below half, and the proof needs at least a plateau of \(h\).

Reviewer's suggestions, unverified

  • Why the coefficients rise to the first zero: the first non-positive index is where two saddle points coalesce, and there \(a_j\approx z_0^{-j}(j^*-j)\) with \(z_0<1\) constant at fixed \(m/n\), so the mode is within \(O(1)\) of \(D^*\) at every \(n\); a decline appears only as \(m/n\to0\). Record. Searched "saddle points coalesce Airy index of regularity asymptotics series": the record has the exact values of ex:covering-series-index and ex:orbit-cover-series-index and a queued check asking for these asymptotics; no derivation is recorded.
  • An exact plateau forces collapse: if \(h_K=h_{K-1}\) and \(D\) is at least about \(3K\) plus the axiom degree, no standard monomial has degree \(K\) or more, the quotient \(V_{K-1}/(C_D\cap V_{K-1})\) is a nonzero finite Boolean ring satisfying the axioms, and it has a point, contradicting unsatisfiability; a flat-extension argument. It does not cover an approximate plateau, where the top level is small and nonzero, which is the case the engine needs. Record. Searched "flat extension exact plateau finite Boolean ring point collapse": no recorded statement of this kind; the kernel dimension lemma gives only that a proper closure has a standard monomial on \(D-1\) coordinates.

Specification decision. No change to the specification. For the alternative endpoint a condition implied by any rate better than the ambient one is recorded, slow growth of the closure's own counts below the cutoff, which a candidate offered for that endpoint should be tested against first, being cheaper to estimate than the thin condition.

Verification gate. One fresh-context medium reviewer found parts (1) to (3) of the lemma correct and required part (4) restated: in the rank theorem the rate holds unconditionally, so nothing is required there; the statement is now an implication for any rate, with the degenerate input \(\{1\}\) replaced by inputs generating \(1\). It corrected a wrong reason for "weaker than thinness", the degree in the subcube inclusion, the upper figure \(0.97n\), two growth factors, a claim about all degrees where the output holds samples, and the description of the density. It checked the script against its description and every table entry against the saved output by reading, and ran nothing. Not checked: the use of the bound in thm:level-size-degree-transfer. Record: review.txt.

Follow-up. Continuing. First entry on this check in this spell. Next attempt on it: the check as posed, starting from the reviewer's argument that an exact plateau forces a point, and asking how far an approximate plateau can sit below the barrier; and the plateau for the one structured class at hand, flow systems of an expander, where the levels are live classes and the reviewer's bound on least weights, if verified, gives their growth.

Process assessment. The prediction was written down before the run and failed cleanly, in under a second of computation; that is the cheapest decisive test of this session, and it came from asking what the proof's first round needs and not what its worst case could be. The record already held series computations for covers; none had been read for the shape of the coefficients below the zero.

9 October 2026 — An exact plateau is already excluded by the kernel dimension theorem; a thin proper closure has levels between two cubes; derived affine consequences count in the free dimension

Working proof of a small refinement on the free dimension; the rest reads recorded results against the queued check, closed in one case as a restatement and carried on in the other. Queue development of a chosen check while draining. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort low).

Chosen. Second entry on the thin-endpoint check, bearing on the family statement through its alternative endpoint; it comes before the head because the preceding entry left a reviewer's argument on it to verify.

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement: the reviewer argued that an exact plateau, no standard monomial of degree \(K\), forces a solution when \(D\) is about \(3K\). Is that right, what does it give for an approximate plateau, and does thinness below the cutoff force a refutation at about half its Kruskal–Katona dimension, as the queued check asks?

New mathematics. One lemma, a refinement already implicit in the rank theorem's proof: affine elements of the closure may be added to the auxiliary equations without changing the closure, so the free dimension in the transfer may be taken as the number of standard variables of the closure, \(b_1\); thinness at level one is thereby the same as a smaller free dimension. The rest is assembly. The reviewer's argument is correct and is superseded by thm:truncated-kernel-dimension, which gives \(b_j\ge\binom{D-1}j\) for every \(j\le D-1\) at a proper \(D\) and so excludes an exact plateau below \(D\) with no condition \(D\ge3K\). With the thin condition the levels just below the cutoff lie between those of a cube on \(D-1\) points and a cube on about \(2K\) points, so thinness with \(X\le D-2\) at any level already refutes. Counting gives no obstruction to an approximate plateau: the lower profile itself has one above \((D-1)/2\). And the queued check is implied by the half ceiling in the free dimension when \(X\) is at least the number of standard variables, and is a stronger, separate question when it is smaller.

Goal progress. Unchanged. The alternative endpoint is located more exactly and is not decided.

General statement. lem:derived-affine-dimension holds for every Boolean system over \(\mathbb F_2\) and every \(D\ge1\) with \(1\notin C_D\).

Derived affine consequences

Lemma (derived affine dimension). Let \(\mathcal Q\) contain the Boolean axioms, \(D\ge1\), \(1\notin C_D(\mathcal Q)\), and let \(A=C_D(\mathcal Q)\cap V_1\). Then \(C_D(\mathcal Q\cup A)=C_D(\mathcal Q)\); \(A\) is a consistent set of affine polynomials; and for a degree-compatible order the number \(b_1\) of standard monomials of degree one equals \(v-\operatorname{rank}A\), \(v\) the number of variables and the rank that of the linear parts. Consequently thm:binary-approximator-rank holds for \(C_D\) with \(n=b_1\), in the range \(K\le b_1\), and the hypothesis of thm:near-half-frege-transfer holds for the formula with auxiliary equations \(\Lambda\cup A\), free dimension \(b_1\) and any degree \(D'\le D\): the free dimension may be counted after all affine consequences derivable within degree \(D\). Here \(A\) and \(b_1\) depend on \(D\); the transfer then needs \(\lfloor b_1/2-s\rfloor\le D\), and its deficit condition and its size bound are in terms of \(b_1\).

Proof. \(C_D(\mathcal Q)\) contains \(\mathcal Q\cup A\) within degree \(D\) and is closed under the rule, so it contains \(C_D(\mathcal Q\cup A)\); the other inclusion is monotonicity. \(A\) is a subspace not containing \(1\), so the system \(\{a=0:a\in A\}\) has no combination equal to \(1\) and is consistent. The leading monomials of degree one of elements of \(C_D\) are those of the nonzero elements of \(A\) whose linear part is nonzero, since an element with leading monomial of degree one has degree one; a reduced basis of \(A\) has one pivot variable per element, the pivots being the largest variables of their rows, so there are \(\operatorname{rank}A\) of them. The rank theorem is stated for any consistent set of affine elements of the system; apply it to \(\mathcal Q\cup A\), whose closure is the same; any affine axioms \(\Lambda\) lie in \(A\), so the rank is that of \(A\). As the reviewer notes, the theorem's proof uses the affine set only to place the pivot variables among the leading monomials of \(C_D\cap V_1\), so the lemma states what that proof already gives; any degree-compatible order serves. For the transfer, \(C_{D'}(\mathcal Q\cup A)\subseteq C_D(\mathcal Q)\) does not contain \(1\), and its auxiliary equations need not belong to the formula. \(\square\)

Use. A system need not display its affine structure: if PC derives affine relations within the barrier degree, they lower \(n\) and with it the degree that counts as half. This is the level-one case of thinness, \(b_1\le X\), and it shows that the thin endpoint and the free-dimension endpoint are one family of conditions: at level one it is the free dimension, at level \(j\) the Kruskal–Katona dimension of the standard monomials of degree \(j\).

Exact and approximate plateaus

The reviewer's argument, checked. If no monomial of degree \(K\) is standard, every polynomial of degree at most \(D\) reduces modulo \(C_D\) into \(V_{K-1}\), by replacing a factor of degree \(K\) of each monomial and multiplying back, within degree \(D\). For \(D\ge3K-3\) the product of representatives makes \(V_{K-1}/(C_D\cap V_{K-1})\) a commutative ring: products of two representatives have degree at most \(2K-2\), and associativity needs a third factor, degree \(3K-3\). It is generated by idempotents, the classes of the variables, the axioms vanish in it, and a nonzero finite Boolean ring has a homomorphism to \(\mathbb F_2\), a solution. For \(K=1\) the generators are constants. So if the axioms of degree at most \(D\) are unsatisfiable, an exact plateau at \(K\le(D+3)/3\) forces \(1\in C_D\).

The record has more. By thm:truncated-kernel-dimension, a proper closure at \(D\ge2\), when the axioms of degree at most \(D\) are unsatisfiable, has a set of \(D-1\) variables all of whose monomials are standard, so \(b_j\ge\binom{D-1}j\) for all \(j\le D-1\): no exact plateau anywhere below \(D\). The theorem is applied to the multilinear part of \(C_D\), whose standard monomials are those of \(C_D\), all squarefree for \(D\ge2\).

For the thin endpoint this pins the levels in the window: \(\binom{D-1}j\le b_j\le\binom Xj\), with \(X\) about \(2K\) and \(K<D\). A thin proper closure is one whose standard monomials just below the cutoff are, in number, those of a cube of dimension between \(D-1\) and about \(2K\), whatever the number of variables; and since a bound \(\binom Xj\) at one level passes to all higher levels, thinness with \(X\le D-2\) at any level \(1\le j\le D-1\) forces \(1\in C_D\). The open range is \(D-1\le X\), up to about \(2K\). For an approximate plateau, in the sense of the review's audit, growth of the cumulative counts by a factor \(1+o(1)\) per degree, there is no obstruction by counting: the lower profile \(b_j=\binom{D-1}j\) has \(b_K/h_{K-1}=O(D^{-1/2})\) for \(K\ge(D-1)/2\), and \(K\le D-n^{o(1)}\) leaves that room. Whether a closure can be that close to its lower profile is the question; the series of the last entry are far from it, their levels being those of nearly the full ambient cube.

The queued check

  • Whether level sizes at most \(\binom Xj\) just below the cutoff force \(1\in C_D\) for \(D\ge X/2+c\). For \(X=n\) the hypothesis is empty and the statement is that every unsatisfiable system is refuted at \(n/2+c\), the half ceiling, for which the recorded attempt found no proof even with the width added. For \(b_1\le X<n\) it is implied by the half ceiling in the free dimension \(b_1\), substituting the pivot variables within degree \(D\) by the lemma above, and equals it at \(X=b_1\). For \(X<b_1\), thinness at high levels only, it is a stronger and separate statement, which the first draft of this entry overlooked; the reviewer's padding example below shows the case is not empty. Interpolation on the standard family gives only the exact case. Outcome: a restatement of the open half-ceiling question in the case \(b_1\le X\); the case \(X<b_1\) is queued below.

Reviewer's suggestions, unverified

  • The case \(X<b_1\) is not empty: pad a hard system \(G\) on \(m\) variables with \(N\) variables \(z\) and axioms \(z_iz_j\); then \(b_j=b_j(G)+N\,b_{j-1}(G)\), at most \(\binom{m+O(\log N)}j\) near \(j=m/2\), while \(b_1=m+N\). Setting \(z=0\) reduces this instance to the half ceiling for \(G\), so it is no counterexample, and no general reduction is visible. Record. Searched "derived affine consequences free dimension closure degree one standard variables" and "thin levels padding quadratic": the product-tree frame and the shattered dimension bound are the recorded neighbours; this padding is not recorded.
  • A recollection, marked uncertain by the reviewer, of an upper bound of about \(\lceil n/2\rceil+1\) on degree for Boolean systems in the context of Impagliazzo, Pudlák and Sgall. Record. Already examined: the review that read that paper found its ceiling \(n/2+1\) special to one linear axiom over large characteristic and void over \(\mathbb F_2\); no general ceiling is in it.

Sub-ideas

  • For a closure whose levels just below the cutoff are at most \(\binom Xj\) with \(X\) smaller than its number of standard variables \(b_1\): find a reduction to a system of free dimension about \(X\), or a system for which none exists; the padding by pairwise annihilating variables is the first example and reduces trivially.

Specification decision. One counting allowed, with the witness unchanged: the free dimension of a candidate may be counted as the number of standard variables of its closure at the barrier degree, that is, after derived affine consequences. This can only lower \(n\); it loosens the degree a candidate must reach and tightens the deficit condition and the size conclusion, which are then in terms of the smaller number. It is optional, and the guarded witness, with no such structure recorded, is as it was.

Verification gate. One fresh-context medium reviewer found the lemma and the plateau argument correct and the closing of the check too broad. Corrections applied: the lemma is labelled a refinement of what the rank theorem's proof already gives, with its range, its dependence on \(D\) and the rank of \(\Lambda\cup A\) stated; unsatisfiability is required of the axioms of degree at most \(D\); the kernel theorem is applied to the multilinear part; the sandwich's consequence and the correct bounds \(D-1\) and \(2K\) are stated; the check is closed only for \(b_1\le X\) and the other case queued; the direction of the specification remark is corrected. Not checked by the reviewer: that the ratio \(O(D^{-1/2})\) meets the audit's definition of a plateau, which I state above. Record: review.txt.

Follow-up. Closed: restatement in the case stated in the list above, with the remaining case queued as a check. The plateau question, how close a proper closure can be to the lower profile of the kernel dimension theorem, is carried to the next review as the sharpest form of the alternative endpoint.

Process assessment. The reviewer's flat-extension argument was correct and the record already had a stronger statement, which a search for "standard monomial" and "proper closure" before adopting it as the next step would have shown; the search rule for suggestions was applied to the wrong words. And I closed the check too broadly in the draft, missing the one case that is specific to thinness. Two entries after the review, the alternative endpoint is described from both sides and no system is nearer to meeting it.

9 October 2026 — In five computed systems the static row span of random half-tables contains one from the degree where the dimension count is reached; if that persists, the random-table source falls at about \(0.15v\)

Working proof of an exact dimension formula and an inclusion; finite check on five random systems at three sizes; the asymptotic reading is a calculation under an unproved hypothesis. Queue development of the head while draining. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort low).

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement: the queue's head is the random-table source of the first sessions, rows on \(k=\lceil2\log_2v\rceil\) variables each allowing a random half of the assignments, \(m=v+k\) rows, with a recorded ceiling above \(v/2\) and a queued test never carried out: is \(1\) in the span \(K_D\) of the degree-\(D\) parts of the row cylinder ideals? What does a dimension count predict, and is the prediction right at sizes that can be computed? The runs use \(k=v/2\) and \(m=3k\) at \(v=12,14,16\); the source's own width \(\lceil2\log_2v\rceil\) is \(8\) at all three, so only \(v=16\) has the source's parameters.

New mathematics. A proposition: the degree-\(D\) part of the ideal of a row cylinder has dimension \(\sum_i(\binom ki-b_i(R))N_{v-k}(D-i)\), \(b_i\) the level sizes of the allowed set, and \(K_D\) lies in the closure \(C_{\max\{k,D\}}\). A computation: for five random half-table systems, \(v=12,14,16\), the constant \(1\) lies in \(K_D\) exactly from the least \(D\) at which the sum of the row dimensions reaches \(\dim B_{\le D}\): \(D=4,5,5\). A calculation from the formula: that threshold is at \(\alpha v\) with \(4\alpha(1-\alpha)=2^{-2/c}\) for width \(c\log_2v\), that is \(0.146v\) at \(c=2\) and \((1/2-0.59/\sqrt c)v\) for large \(c\). It bounds the refutation degree only under the hypothesis that \(1\) enters \(K_D\) once the count exceeds the dimension by a constant factor, which is observed at three small sizes and not proved.

Goal progress. Unchanged. Nothing is refuted at the sizes computed, where the width equals \(v/2\) and the bound of the proposition is \(v/2\) itself; what is observed is that the span behaves as the count predicts. If that hypothesis holds at large sizes, the oldest surviving candidate of the notebook is refuted at a constant fraction below half at every polynomial length. No family is gained.

General statement. prop:table-row-span holds for every row on \(k\) of \(v\) Boolean variables with any allowed set, and every \(D\).

The row span

Setting. \(B\) is the multilinear algebra on \(v\) variables over \(\mathbb F_2\), \(B_{\le D}\) its part of degree at most \(D\), \(N_u(j)=\sum_{i\le j}\binom ui\). A row has a scope of \(k\) variables and an allowed set \(R\subseteq\{0,1\}^k\); its axioms are the clause polynomials of the assignments outside \(R\); \(J\) is the ideal of functions vanishing on \(R\times\{0,1\}^{v-k}\). For a degree-compatible order on the monomials of the scope let \(b_i(R)\) be the number of standard monomials of degree \(i\) of the ideal \(I(R)\) of functions on the scope vanishing on \(R\); \(\sum_ib_i(R)=|R|\). For rows \(1,\ldots,m\) put \(K_D=\sum_a(J_a\cap B_{\le D})\).

Proposition (table row span). (1) \(\dim(J\cap B_{\le D})=\sum_{i=0}^k\bigl(\binom ki-b_i(R)\bigr)N_{v-k}(D-i)\). (2) \(J\cap B_{\le D}\subseteq C_{\max\{k,D\}}\), the polynomial calculus closure of the row's axioms and the Boolean axioms; hence \(K_D\subseteq C_{\max\{k,D\}}\) for the system, and \(1\in K_D\) gives a refutation of degree \(\max\{k,D\}\). (3) If \(\sum_a\dim(J_a\cap B_{\le D})<\dim B_{\le D}\), then \(K_D\ne B_{\le D}\).

Proof. (1) Write \(f\in B\) as \(\sum_Tg_Tm_T\), \(m_T\) the monomials in the other \(v-k\) variables and \(g_T\) polynomials in the scope. Then \(f\in J\) exactly when every \(g_T\in I(R)\), fixing the other variables in all ways; and \(\deg f=\max_T(\deg g_T+|T|)\), monomials of the two groups having disjoint supports. So \(J\cap B_{\le D}=\bigoplus_T(I(R)_{\le D-|T|})\,m_T\), and \(\dim I(R)_{\le j}=\sum_{i\le j}(\binom ki-b_i(R))\), the non-standard monomials of degree at most \(j\) being the leading monomials of a basis. Summing over \(T\) and exchanging the sums gives the formula. (2) Each \(g_T\in I(R)\) is, as a multilinear polynomial, a combination of the clause polynomials of the row, so it lies in \(C_k\); multiplying by the variables of \(m_T\) one at a time keeps the degree at most \(\max\{k,\deg g_T+|T|\}\le\max\{k,D\}\). (3) Dimension. \(\square\)

The count. Let \(\Sigma_D=\sum_a\dim(J_a\cap B_{\le D})\). The hypothesis used below, called the unit hypothesis, is: \(1\in K_D\) once \(\Sigma_D\ge(1+\epsilon)\dim B_{\le D}\). It is weaker than general position of the rows, which the data do not show: at the threshold \(K_D\) is never the whole space. For \(D=\alpha v\), \(\alpha<1/2\) fixed and \(k=O(\log v)\), \(N_{v-k}(D-i)/N_v(D)=\alpha^i(1-\alpha)^{k-i}(1+O(k^2/v))\), so \(\dim(J\cap B_{\le D})/\dim B_{\le D}\) is \(\rho_R(\alpha)=\sum_i(\binom ki-b_i(R))\alpha^i(1-\alpha)^{k-i}\) up to that factor, the \(\alpha\)-biased weight of the non-standard monomials. For a random half-table the levels are full below about \(k/2\) and empty above, by the recorded erasure estimate, with a transition of width \(O(\sqrt k)\); so \(\rho_R(\alpha)\) is the probability that a binomial \((k,\alpha)\) variable exceeds \(k/2\), which is \((4\alpha(1-\alpha))^{k/2}\) up to factors polynomial in \(k\) and \(e^{O(\sqrt k)}\), all \(v^{o(1)}\). With \(m=v^{1+o(1)}\) and \(k=c\log_2v\) the threshold \(\sum_a\rho_{R_a}(\alpha)=1\) is at \(4\alpha(1-\alpha)=2^{-2/c}\), up to \(o(1)\) in \(\alpha\). At \(c=2\), \(\alpha=(1-2^{-1/2})/2=0.146\); for large \(c\), \(1/2-\alpha\) is about \(\sqrt{2\ln2/c}/2=0.59/\sqrt c\), and the formula has \(m2^{k-1}\) clauses, about \(v^{c+1}\). This is arithmetic from (1) and the level sizes; with (2) it bounds the refutation degree by the threshold only under the unit hypothesis.

The computation

Prediction counted before the run. Under the unit hypothesis, \(1\in K_D\) from the least \(D\) with \(\Sigma_D\ge\dim B_{\le D}\): by (1), with the full levels \(1,k,\ldots\) below half, \(D=4\) at \(v=12\), \(k=6\), \(m=18\); \(D=5\) at \(v=14\), \(k=7\), \(m=21\) and at \(v=16\), \(k=8\), \(m=24\). If the source were hard near half, \(1\notin K_D\) up to about \(v/2\), that is \(6,7,8\). Below the threshold \(K_D\) is proper by (3), which does not by itself exclude \(1\). At these sizes the width \(k\) is at least \(v/2\), so the computation tests the span and not the refutation degree, which (2) bounds only by \(\max\{k,D\}\).

In all five systems \(1\) enters the span at the predicted degree; the span is then within one percent of the whole space at \(v=12,14\) and within three percent at \(v=16\), and one degree later, where computed, equals it in two systems and is one dimension short in a third. What it says about the source and its queued checks

The recorded ceiling for this source, \(v/2+3v/\sqrt k\), is above half and left it standing. Under the unit hypothesis, (2) puts its refutation degree at most at about \(0.146v\), and no choice of the constant in the width brings a random-table source within \(o(v)\) of half at polynomial length: the deficit is of order \(v/\sqrt c\) at length \(v^{c+1}\). A proper multiplication-closed space at a cutoff \(D\ge k\) contains \(K_D\) and so cannot exist once \(1\in K_D\). For any table, \(\rho_R(1/2)\) is the forbidden fraction, so the sum at half is the covering sum; below half \(\rho_R(\alpha)\) weights non-standard monomials of low degree most, and among tables of a given size it is least when the non-standard monomials are those of highest degree. What the count gives is a necessary condition under the unit hypothesis: where \(\sum_a\rho_{R_a}(\alpha)\) exceeds one, a hard system must keep \(1\) out of a span that the dimensions would fill.

9 October 2026 — Where one enters the row span follows the level form of the count in nine systems; the product series of table rows has an index that depends on the width and approaches half slowly

Working proof of a lemma on the codimension of the row span; a conjecture with small computed evidence that does not test its higher-order terms; finite check on series. Queue development of the head while draining. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort low).

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement: the preceding entry left a hypothesis, that \(1\) enters the row span \(K_D\) of a random-table system once the first-order count exceeds the dimension. Is the reviewer's lemma on top coefficients right, what does it say about that hypothesis, and is there a better model of the degree at which \(1\) enters?

New mathematics. The lemma holds: a set \(S\) of size \(D\) meeting every scope in fewer variables than the least degree of that row's ideal gives a functional vanishing on \(K_D\), so the span is far from the whole space wherever such sets exist. A model: the series \((1+z)^v\prod_a\bigl(h_a(z)/(1+z)^k\bigr)\), \(h_a\) the level polynomial of row \(a\), which treats the rows as independent conditions. In all nine systems computed, at five parameter sets, \(1\) enters \(K_D\) exactly at the index \(D^*\) of its first non-positive coefficient; at those sizes \(D^*\) is decided by the first-order term taken level by level, so the evidence tests that form of the count against the cumulative form of the last entry, and not the higher-order terms. The series itself, computed exactly: at fixed width its index over \(v\) falls slowly with \(v\) and rises with the width, \(0.16v\), \(0.19v\), \(0.21v\), \(0.23v\) for widths \(12,16,20,24\) at \(v=2048\); the distance to half is \(0.74\sqrt{\ln k/k}\) to two digits at those four widths, the form the reviewer predicted.

Goal progress. Unchanged. Two readings of the last entry are withdrawn: the first-order figure \(0.146v\), and this entry's first draft, which took \(0.22v\) for a limit. As a statement about the series, the index of the random-table source tends to half with the width, with a deficit of order \(v\sqrt{\ln k/k}\), which at width \(O(\log v)\) is \(o(v)\) and far above \(v/\log v\). Whether the system follows the series is a conjecture, and a lower bound on refutation degree is not touched by any of this. No family is gained.

General statement. lem:top-coefficient-functionals holds for every system of table rows over \(\mathbb F_2\) and every \(D\). conj:table-series-unit-degree is a conjecture for random half-table systems.

Top coefficients

Setting of prop:table-row-span. For a row \(a\) let \(d_a\) be the least degree of a nonzero element of \(I(R_a)\).

Lemma (top coefficient functionals). Let \(|S|=D\) and let \(\lambda_S\) be the functional on \(B_{\le D}\) taking the coefficient of \(x_S\). If \(|S\cap\operatorname{scope}_a|<d_a\) for every row \(a\), then \(\lambda_S\) vanishes on \(K_D\). Hence the codimension of \(K_D\) in \(B_{\le D}\) is at least the number of such \(S\); these functionals vanish at \(1\) for \(D\ge1\).

Proof. By the proposition, \(J_a\cap B_{\le D}\) is spanned by products \(g\,m_T\), \(g\in I(R_a)\), \(m_T\) a monomial outside the scope, \(\deg g+|T|\le D\). The monomial \(x_S\) occurs in \(g\,m_T\) only if \(T=S\setminus\operatorname{scope}_a\) and \(x_{S\cap\operatorname{scope}_a}\) is a monomial of \(g\); then \(|S\cap\operatorname{scope}_a|\le\deg g\le D-|T|=|S\cap\operatorname{scope}_a|\), so \(g\) has degree \(|S\cap\operatorname{scope}_a|\ge d_a\). The functionals \(\lambda_S\) for different \(S\) are independent. \(\square\)

For random scopes a fixed \(S\) of size \(\alpha v\) meets a scope in a hypergeometric number of variables, and fails the hypothesis for row \(a\) with probability \(p_a=P(|S\cap\operatorname{scope}_a|\ge d_a)\), which is at least the \(\rho(\alpha)\) of the last entry and of its order when the table has the ideal levels; for tables with \(d_a\) below \(k/2\) it can be larger by a factor \(e^{O(\sqrt k)}\). Where \(\sum_ap_a\) is about one, a constant fraction of all \(D\)-sets qualify and \(K_D\) has codimension of the order of \(\binom vD\). So the rows are not in general position at scale, as the reviewer said; already at \((v,k,m)=(20,4,24)\) the span has codimension \(215\) and \(269\) at \(D=3\). This does not bear on \(1\).

The product series

The quotient of \(B\) by one row's ideal has the series \(h_a(z)(1+z)^{v-k}\), \(h_a(z)=\sum_ib_i(R_a)z^i\), counted by degree of standard monomials. If the rows imposed independent conditions, the quotient by the sum of their ideals would have the series \[S(z)=(1+z)^v\prod_a\frac{h_a(z)}{(1+z)^k}\] as long as its coefficients are positive; this is the analogue for table rows of the series of a semi-regular sequence, and it is a model, not a theorem. By the lemma it cannot describe the quotient \(B_{\le D}/K_D\) near its index at scale, where that quotient is large; it is offered only as a model of the degree at which \(1\) enters. Its first-order term is the level form of the last entry's count: the coefficient of \(z^D\) in \((1+z)^v-\sum_a(1+z)^{v-k}\sum_i(\binom ki-b_i)z^i\) is \(\binom vD-\sum_a\sum_i(\binom ki-b_i)\binom{v-k}{D-i}\), whose partial sums are \(\dim B_{\le D}-\Sigma_D\). Let \(D^*\) be the index of the first non-positive coefficient of \(S\).

Conjecture (table series unit degree). For random half-table systems with \(m\) at least \(v\) rows of width \(k=O(\log v)\), with \(D^*\) computed from the tables' actual level sizes: with high probability \(1\in K_D\) if and only if \(D\ge D^*\), up to an additive \(o(v)\).
