9 October 2026 — The saddle value of the product series: \(1/2-\ln k/k\) for clause rows at first-moment density, proved as a statement about a function; clause rows beat tables in the model

Working proof of an elementary two-sided bound on a saddle value; a conjecture linking it to the index of the series, with the exact indices on record as its evidence. Queue development of the head while draining. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort low).

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement: the preceding entry found the index of the product series of table rows to fit a form the reviewer derived and I had not verified. What is the derivation, what does it give for other rows, and which rows are best in the model? The test of the series' higher-order terms on a system, named as the next step, is not made here: no parameters were found at which it is both decisive and computable, and it stays queued.

New mathematics. The derivation is the usual one: the coefficients of \(S(z)=(1+z)^v(1-q(z))^m\) keep a real saddle point exactly while \(D\) is below the maximum of \(\Phi(z)=zS'(z)/S(z)\), so the first sign change is near \(v\max\Phi\), \(\Phi\) normalised by \(v\). For clause rows, \(q=\alpha^k\) with \(\alpha=z/(1+z)\), at the first-moment density \(m=2^kv\ln2\), the maximum is computed with explicit constants: \(1/2-\ln k/k-2\ln2/k\le\sup\Phi_k\le1/2-\ln k/k+0.77/k\) for \(k\ge9\). For half-tables the same calculation suggests \(1/2-(1+o(1))\sqrt{\ln k/(2k)}\), without bounded errors. The exact indices of the series lie above \(v\sup\Phi\) by \(0.009v\) to \(0.016v\) at \(v=2048\) in all eight cases computed, and approach it as \(v\) grows where that was computed. So in the model clause rows are better than tables; whether any row on \(k\) variables does better than order \(\ln k/k\) at a covering sum of order \(v\) is not settled here.

Goal progress. Unchanged. The best generic candidate found in the model at polynomial length, random clauses of width \(c\log_2v\) at first-moment density, has index \(v/2\) minus a deficit of order \(v\ln\ln v/\ln v\): admissible to the transfer at two levels, and short of three by the factor \(\ln\ln v\). This is a property of a series, linked to refutation degree by two unproved steps.

General statement. prop:clause-saddle-value holds for every \(k\ge9\). conj:product-series-index-formula is a conjecture about series, for every row type with level polynomial \(h\).

The saddle value

Let a row on \(k\) variables have level polynomial \(h\), put \(q(z)=1-h(z)/(1+z)^k\), and \(S(z)=(1+z)^v(1-q(z))^m\), the product series of \(m\) such rows. Write \(\alpha=z/(1+z)\), so that \(z\,\frac d{dz}=\alpha(1-\alpha)\frac d{d\alpha}\), and \[\Phi(\alpha)=\frac{zS'(z)}{vS(z)}=\alpha-\frac mv\,\frac{\alpha(1-\alpha)q'(\alpha)}{1-q(\alpha)} .\] The coefficient of \(z^D\) in \(S\) is a contour integral of \(S(z)z^{-D-1}\); its saddle points solve \(v\Phi=D\). For \(D\) below \(v\max\Phi\) there is a real positive one and the coefficient is positive to leading order; above, the saddle points are a complex pair and the coefficients oscillate. This is the heuristic by which the index of regularity of semi-regular sequences is located; to my recollection it is made rigorous for the series of quadratic and fixed-degree systems by Bardet, Faugère and Salvy, a source I have not reread for this entry, and not for these series.

Conjecture (product series index formula). For fixed \(k\), \(h\) and \(m/v\to\mu\), the index \(D^*\) of the first non-positive coefficient of \(S\) satisfies \(D^*/v\to\sup_{0<\alpha<1/2}\Phi(\alpha)\) as \(v\to\infty\), from above, whenever \(\Phi\) has an interior maximum on \((0,1/2)\); in general the supremum is to be read as the first critical value of \(\Phi\) on \(z>0\), and at low density, where there is none below \(1/2\), the conjecture says nothing.

Proposition (clause saddle value). For clause rows, \(h=(1+z)^k-z^k\), \(q=\alpha^k\), with \(\mu=2^k\ln2\): \[\Phi_k(\alpha)=\alpha-\ln2\cdot\frac{k(1-\alpha)(2\alpha)^k}{1-\alpha^k},\qquad \frac12-\frac{\ln k}k-\frac{2\ln2}k\ \le\ \sup_{0<\alpha<1/2}\Phi_k\ \le\ \frac12-\frac{\ln k}k+\frac{0.77}k\qquad(k\ge9).\]

Proof. The range \((0,1/2)\) is the relevant one: \(k(1-\alpha)/(1-\alpha^k)\ge1\), so for \(\alpha\ge1/2\), \(\Phi_k\le\alpha-\ln2\,(2\alpha)^k\le\alpha-2\alpha\ln2<0\). \(q'=k\alpha^{k-1}\), so \(\mu\alpha(1-\alpha)q'=\ln2\cdot k(1-\alpha)(2\alpha)^k\). Lower bound: at \(\alpha=1/2-\ln k/k\), which is positive, \((2\alpha)^k=(1-2\ln k/k)^k\le k^{-2}\), \(1-\alpha\le1\) and \(1-\alpha^k\ge1/2\), so the subtracted term is at most \(2\ln2/k\). Upper bound: put \(\alpha=1/2-\epsilon\). Since \(1-\alpha\ge1/2\) and \(1-\alpha^k\le1\), \(\Phi_k\le1/2-g(\epsilon)\) with \(g(\epsilon)=\epsilon+\tfrac{\ln2}2k(1-2\epsilon)^k\). If \(\epsilon\ge\ln k/k\), \(g\ge\ln k/k\). If \(\epsilon<\ln k/k\), then \(2\epsilon\le1/2\) for \(k\ge9\), so \(\ln(1-2\epsilon)\ge-2\epsilon-4\epsilon^2\) and \((1-2\epsilon)^k\ge e^{-2k\epsilon}e^{-4\ln^2k/k}\ge0.114\,e^{-2k\epsilon}\), as \(\ln^2k/k\le4/e^2\). So \(g(\epsilon)\ge\epsilon+Ake^{-2k\epsilon}\) with \(A=0.114\ln2/2\ge0.0395\); the right side is least where \(e^{-2k\epsilon}=1/(2Ak^2)\), with value \(\ln(2Ak^2)/(2k)+1/(2k)=\ln k/k+(\ln(2A)+1)/(2k)\ge\ln k/k-0.77/k\). \(\square\)

Half-tables, by the same steps and without constants. For a half-table of largest immunity \(q(\alpha)\) is the probability that a binomial \((k,\alpha)\) variable exceeds \(k/2\), up to the middle level; \(q'/q\) is about \(k(1-2\alpha)/(2\alpha(1-\alpha))\), and with \(\mu=1\) the subtracted term is about \(qk(1-2\alpha)/2\), smaller than \(\epsilon\) at the optimum only by a factor of order \(\ln k\). Setting the derivative to zero gives \(q\approx4\alpha(1-\alpha)/(k^2(1-2\alpha)^2)\), the reviewer's condition; with \(q\approx e^{-2k\epsilon^2}\) at \(\alpha=1/2-\epsilon\) this is \(2k\epsilon^2\approx\ln(4k^2\epsilon^2)\), so \(\epsilon=(1+o(1))\sqrt{\ln k/(2k)}\), and the subtracted term at the optimum is of smaller order. I have not bounded the errors.

Against the exact indices

The conjecture's evidence, from index-formula.txt, by index_formula.gp: the exact index at \(v=2048\) and the maximum of \(\Phi\) over a grid of step \(0.0005\) in \(\alpha\), for the level polynomials themselves.

For half-tables of width \(20\) the exact index at \(v=256,512,\ldots,8192\) is \(0.242,0.227,0.218,0.212,0.209,0.206\), from the last entry, decreasing toward the saddle value, which is \(0.2019\) at \(m/v=2068/2048\) and marginally different at \(m/v=1\); the other limits are not followed in \(v\). The ratio in the last column for half-tables grows slowly with \(k\), consistent with lower-order terms in \(\ln\ln k\) and not a test of the constant.

Which rows are best in the model

A system is unsatisfiable only if its rows cover, so \(m\,q(1/2)\ge1\); for random rows the first moment needs \(-m\ln(1-q(1/2))\ge v\ln2\), a covering sum of order \(v\). The index is where the subtracted term \(\frac mv\alpha(1-\alpha)q'\) becomes comparable with the distance of \(\alpha\) from half. For clauses \(q'=kq/\alpha\), and with a covering sum of order \(v\) the weight has to fall by a factor of order \(k^2\) below half, which costs \(\epsilon\) of order \(\ln k/k\): that is the proposition. For a general family of monomials \(U\) on \(k\) variables one has \(\frac d{d\alpha}\ln\mu_\alpha(U)\le k/\alpha\), which bounds how fast the weight can fall and is attained by the single top monomial; but the subtracted term involves \(q'\) itself, and I have no general lower bound for it. So "clauses are best" is the comparison of two computed cases and a plausible reason, not a result. The reviewer sketches a route to a general bound, recorded below.

Consequence in the model, for the best case found. At polynomial length a table or a clause has \(k=O(\log v)\), and random clauses have a deficit of order \(v\ln\ln v/\ln v\). The transfer's condition \((s+w)(\log n)^{\ell-2}=o(n)\) then holds at \(\ell=2\) and fails at \(\ell=3\) by the factor \(\ln\ln v\).

Smaller covering sums. For clauses with \(m=\Sigma2^k\), \(\Phi'(1/2)\) is about \(1-k^2\Sigma/v\). For \(\Sigma\) well below \(v/k^2\) the function has no maximum below \(1/2\), and the heuristic predicts a deficit of at most \(k\Sigma/2\), possibly none; between \(v/k^2\) and \(v\) the deficit is about \(v\ln(k^2\Sigma/v)/(2k)\). My draft had "of order \(k\Sigma\)" throughout, which the reviewer corrected. So in the model a covering sum below \(v/k^2\) would be enough. But random systems cannot have it, and the systems that do, such as those of lem:barely-covering-padding, have rows far from independent and are as hard as an arbitrary cover in fewer dimensions, not harder: there the model is wrong. The model thus places the requirement of the family statement between two regimes: generic rows, where the best case found has a deficit just above what three levels need, and covers of small covering sum, where the model does not apply and small covering sum forces dependence.

Limits. Everything in this section is about a series. Its relation to the row span is conj:table-series-unit-degree, whose evidence does not test the higher-order terms; its relation to refutation degree needs in addition that the closure does not refute before the span does, for which there is no method; and the known lower-bound methods reach about a quarter.

9 October 2026 — In the product model, rows on at most \(k\) variables, each forbidding at most half, with covering sum at least \(v/2\), have saddle function at most \(1/2-\ln k/(2k)+0.47/k\) below half; clauses are within a factor two of best

Working proofs of a power inequality for biased measures of up-sets and of a bound on the saddle function of the product series for all small row types; statements about a function. Queue development of the head while draining. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort low).

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement: the preceding entry computed the saddle value for clauses and for half-tables and could not say whether some other row type does better. Is there a bound for every row type?

New mathematics. Yes. For any rows on at most \(k\) variables, of any mixture of types, each forbidding at most half of its assignments, with covering sum at least \(v/2\), which random unsatisfiable systems need by the first moment, the saddle function of the product series satisfies \(\Phi(\alpha)\le1/2-\ln k/(2k)+0.47/k\) on \((0,1/2)\). The proof uses two facts about the \(\alpha\)-biased weight \(q\) of a family of monomials closed under multiples: \(q'\le kq/\alpha\), which is trivial, and \(\alpha q'\ge q\log_\alpha q\), which I derive from a power inequality \(\mu_{p^\theta}(U)\ge\mu_p(U)^\theta\) proved here by induction on the number of variables. With the clause value \(1/2-\ln k/k\) of the last entry, clauses are within a factor two of the best row type in the model.

Goal progress. Unchanged. In the product model, the saddle function of any system of rows on at most \(k\) variables, each forbidding at most half, with covering sum at least \(v/2\), stays \(\ln k/(2k)-0.47/k\) below half on \((0,1/2)\), whatever the rows. That is a theorem about the function and no longer a comparison of two cases. Read through the index conjecture, extrapolated to \(k=O(\log v)\) and assuming an interior maximum, it would mean a deficit of order at least \(v\ln\ln v/\ln v\), admissible to the transfer at two levels and at no more; it says nothing outside the model.

General statement. lem:biased-power-inequality holds for every family of subsets of a finite set closed under supersets and all \(0<p<1\), \(0<\theta\le1\). thm:saddle-deficit-bound holds for every \(k\ge2\) and every finite mixture of row types within its hypotheses.

Two facts about biased weights

For \(U\subseteq2^{[k]}\) and \(0<p<1\) let \(\mu_p(U)=\sum_{x\in U}p^{|x|}(1-p)^{k-|x|}\). Call \(U\) an up-set if it is closed under supersets; the non-standard monomials of an ideal, read as sets of variables, form one.

Lemma (biased power inequality). For an up-set \(U\), \(0<p<1\) and \(0<\theta\le1\): \(\mu_{p^\theta}(U)\ge\mu_p(U)^\theta\). Consequently \(t(p)=\ln\mu_p(U)/\ln p\) is nonincreasing in \(p\) where \(\mu_p(U)>0\), and \[p\,\frac d{dp}\mu_p(U)\ \ge\ \mu_p(U)\,\frac{\ln(1/\mu_p(U))}{\ln(1/p)} ,\] with the right side read as \(0\) for empty \(U\).

Proof. Induction on \(k\); for \(k=0\) both sides are \(0\) or \(1\). Let \(U_0,U_1\subseteq2^{[k-1]}\) be the sections of \(U\) without and with the element \(k\); both are up-sets and \(U_0\subseteq U_1\). Put \(a_i=\mu_p(U_i)\), \(b_i=\mu_{p^\theta}(U_i)\), so \(a_0\le a_1\) and \(b_i\ge a_i^\theta\) by induction. Then \(\mu_{p^\theta}(U)=(1-p^\theta)b_0+p^\theta b_1\ge(1-p^\theta)a_0^\theta+p^\theta a_1^\theta\) and \(\mu_p(U)=(1-p)a_0+pa_1\). If \(a_1=0\) there is nothing to prove; otherwise divide by \(a_1^\theta\) and put \(r=a_0/a_1\in[0,1]\): it suffices that \[G(r)=(1-p^\theta)r^\theta+p^\theta-\bigl((1-p)r+p\bigr)^\theta\ \ge0\qquad(0\le r\le1).\] \(G(0)=G(1)=0\). For \(\theta=1\), \(G\equiv0\). For \(\theta<1\), \(G''(r)=\theta(\theta-1)\bigl[(1-p^\theta)r^{\theta-2}-(1-p)^2((1-p)r+p)^{\theta-2}\bigr]\); the bracket is positive exactly when \(\bigl(r/((1-p)r+p)\bigr)^{2-\theta}<(1-p^\theta)/(1-p)^2\), and the left side increases with \(r\). So \(G\) is concave on an initial interval \([0,r_0]\) and convex on \([r_0,1]\), one of them possibly empty or the whole. On the convex part, \(G(r)\ge G(1)+G'(1)(r-1)\) and \(G'(1)=\theta(p-p^\theta)<0\), so \(G\ge0\) there; in particular \(G(r_0)\ge0\). On the concave part \(G\) is at least the smaller of its end values \(G(0)=0\) and \(G(r_0)\ge0\). If the whole interval is concave, the end values are \(0\) and \(0\). This proves the inequality. For \(p<p'<1\) take \(\theta=\ln p'/\ln p\): \(\ln\mu_{p'}\ge\theta\ln\mu_p\), and dividing by \(\ln p'<0\) gives \(t(p')\le t(p)\). Differentiating, \(t'(p)\le0\) reads \((\mu'/\mu)\ln p\le\ln\mu/p\), and dividing by \(\ln p<0\) gives the displayed inequality. \(\square\)

This is the edge-isoperimetric inequality for biased measures, known in the literature; I did not find it in the record and give the proof so that nothing is imported. The second fact needs no hypothesis on \(U\): \(\frac d{dp}\mu_p(U)=\sum_{x\in U}p^{|x|}(1-p)^{k-|x|}\bigl(|x|/p-(k-|x|)/(1-p)\bigr)\le(k/p)\mu_p(U)\), so for \(\alpha\le1/2\), \(\mu_\alpha(U)\ge\mu_{1/2}(U)(2\alpha)^k\).

The bound

Row types \(j=1,\ldots,J\); type \(j\) has an up-set \(U_j\) of non-standard monomials on at most \(k\) variables, \(q_j(\alpha)=\mu_\alpha(U_j)\), and \(m_j=\mu_jv\) rows. The product series is \(S=(1+z)^v\prod_j(1-q_j)^{m_j}\) and its saddle function, with \(\alpha=z/(1+z)\), \[\Phi(\alpha)=\alpha-\sum_j\mu_j\frac{\alpha(1-\alpha)q_j'(\alpha)}{1-q_j(\alpha)} .\]

Theorem (saddle deficit bound). Let \(k\ge2\), \(0<q_j(1/2)\le1/2\) for all \(j\), and \(\sum_j\mu_jq_j(1/2)\ge1/2\). Then for all \(0<\alpha<1/2\), \[\Phi(\alpha)\ \le\ \frac12-\frac{\ln k}{2k}+\frac{0.47}k .\]

Proof. Each \(q_j\) is nondecreasing, by the lemma. If \(\alpha\le1/4\), \(\Phi\le\alpha\le1/4\le1/2-\ln k/(2k)\), as \(\ln k/(2k)\le1/(2e)\). Let \(1/4\le\alpha<1/2\), \(\alpha=1/2-\epsilon\). By the lemma, \(\alpha q_j'\ge q_j\ln(1/q_j)/\ln(1/\alpha)\); here \(q_j(\alpha)\le q_j(1/2)\le1/2\), so \(\ln(1/q_j)\ge\ln2\), and \(\ln(1/\alpha)\le2\ln2\), \(1-\alpha\ge1/2\), \(1-q_j\le1\). So each term of the sum is at least \(\mu_jq_j(\alpha)/4\). By the second fact \(q_j(\alpha)\ge q_j(1/2)(2\alpha)^k\), the exponent \(k\) bounding the number of variables of every type. Hence the sum is at least \(\tfrac14(2\alpha)^k\sum_j\mu_jq_j(1/2)\ge\tfrac18(1-2\epsilon)^k\), and \(\Phi\le1/2-g(\epsilon)\), \(g(\epsilon)=\epsilon+\tfrac18(1-2\epsilon)^k\). If \(\epsilon\ge\ln k/(2k)\), \(g\ge\ln k/(2k)\). Otherwise \(2\epsilon<\ln k/k\le1/2\), so \((1-2\epsilon)^k\ge e^{-2k\epsilon-4k\epsilon^2}\ge e^{-\ln^2k/k}e^{-2k\epsilon}\ge0.58\,e^{-2k\epsilon}\), and \(g(\epsilon)\ge\epsilon+Ae^{-2k\epsilon}\) with \(A=0.0725\). Over all real \(\epsilon\) the right side is at least \(\ln(2Ak)/(2k)+1/(2k)=\ln k/(2k)+(\ln(2A)+1)/(2k)\ge\ln k/(2k)-0.47/k\). \(\square\)

Hypotheses. For rows forbidding at most half, the covering condition is what the first moment asks of random rows: \(\prod_j(1-q_j(1/2))^{m_j}\le2^{-v}\) with \(q_j(1/2)\le1/2\) gives \(\sum_j\mu_jq_j(1/2)\ge1/2\), since \(-\ln(1-q)\le2q\ln2\) there. For rows forbidding more than half the first moment allows a smaller covering sum, down to about \(v/k\), and the theorem as stated excludes them; the reviewer indicates below how the hypothesis on the rows can be dropped, the covering sum then being assumed directly. For a covering sum \(cv\) in place of \(v/2\) the constant \(0.47\) shifts by \(\ln(2c)/2\). The bound concerns rows with few variables: a row is whatever the model treats as one exact ideal, and a group of many clauses on a large common scope is outside it, the more so the larger the group, a single row for the whole formula making the model exact and the theorem empty.

Sharpness. For clauses the last entry's proposition gives \(1/2-\ln k/k\) up to \(O(1/k)\), so, as \(k\) grows, the best constant in front of \(\ln k/k\) over all row types lies between \(1/2\) and \(1\); the clause side is proved for \(k\ge9\). The loss of the factor two is in the step \(\ln(1/q_j)\ge\ln2\), which for clauses is far from sharp, \(\ln(1/q)\) being about \(k\ln2\) there; a row type with \(q\) near \(1/2\) at half and falling as fast as \((2\alpha)^k\) would be needed to approach \(1/2\), and the lemma forbids both together to some extent that I have not quantified.

What it says, within the model

Take rows on at most \(k=C\log_2v\) variables, as tables and clauses of polynomial length must be, with covering sum at least \(v/2\). This paragraph extrapolates: conj:product-series-index-formula is stated for fixed \(k\), one row type and a fixed density, and only when \(\Phi\) has an interior maximum below \(1/2\); here it is applied with \(k\) growing, mixtures, and densities growing with \(v\), and the theorem bounds \(\Phi\) only on \((0,1/2)\), so a system whose \(\Phi\) has no critical point there is not covered. With that said: if that conjecture and conj:table-series-unit-degree held for them, the unit would enter the row span, and a refutation of degree \(\max\{k,D\}\) would exist, by a degree \(D\) with \(v/2-D\) at least about \(v\ln k/(2k)\), of order \(v\ln\ln v/\ln v\). The transfer needs \((s+w)(\log n)^{\ell-2}=o(n)\): such a system could serve two levels and no more. So within the model the family statement at \(n^{1-\epsilon}\), or at any depth beyond the lowest, cannot be met by systems whose rows behave independently; it needs either rows with many variables that are not groups of independent small rows, or a covering sum far below \(v\), and for the second the record's only examples have dependent rows.

Limits, again. The theorem is about \(\Phi\). That the series index is near \(v\sup\Phi\) is a conjecture with evidence at eight points; that the unit enters the span at the index is a conjecture whose evidence does not test the series beyond first order; and an upper bound on refutation degree from the span is all that would follow. No lower bound is involved anywhere.

Reviewer's suggestions, unverified

  • Dropping the hypothesis on the rows: replace the two estimates on \(\ln(1/q)\) and \(1/(1-q)\) by \(q\ln(1/q)/(1-q)\ge q\) on \((0,1)\), and use \((1-\alpha)/\ln(1/\alpha)\ge0.54\) on \([1/4,1/2]\); each term is then at least \(0.54\mu_jq_j(\alpha)\), for any \(q_j<1\), and the constant \(0.47\) improves to about \(0.1\). Thresholds at level \(k-u\) behave like clauses on fewer variables and are worse. Record. Same search; no such second-order statement is recorded. Whether a family of monomials realises that profile is not known to me.

The lead and its check

  • Which families of monomials minimise the saddle deficit, and is \(\ln k/k\) the order of the best. Follow-up. Developed: thm:saddle-deficit-bound gives the order, between \(\ln k/(2k)\) and \(\ln k/k\), for all row types at covering sum at least \(v/2\); the exact constant is not determined.

The lead began as the random-table source with erasure capacity as its local input. Four entries have given: the exact count of a row's part and its inclusion in the closure; a lemma showing the span far from full; a conjecture that the unit enters at the series index, with evidence that does not reach beyond first order; and the saddle analysis, in which that source and every other system of small rows has a deficit of order at least \(v\ln k/(2k)\). The lead's other checks ask for a proper global space for the source near half; the model says there is none within \(o(v\ln\ln v/\ln v)\) of half, and nothing proved says so.

Specification decision. No change to the specification. The calibration of the last entry is now a theorem about the model: a candidate whose rows have at most \(k\) variables and whose covering sum is at least \(v/2\) has model deficit at least \((\ln k/(2k)-0.47/k)v\); a candidate claimed to do better must say which hypothesis it leaves, small covering sum or wide rows, before anything else is computed.

9 October 2026 — Goal-level review: the product series is exact through degree four on dense two-clause rows in seven systems; generic small rows fall short of three levels in the model; the next test is a proof of exactness in the first dependent case

Goal-level route review: one open statement, unchanged across thirty-nine research entries. One finite check made as the review's own test. No outside leads or bridges while the queue drains. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort low).

Question. Six research entries since the last review built a model, the product series of rows, and proved a bound inside it. Is the model right beyond the first-order count, which no run had tested; what does the block say about the line; and which test comes next?

Architecture test. The last review's decisive test, the families the engine meets, was reported in the colon families entry: they are truncated colons including the closure's own, and the requirement becomes a plateau of the closure's counts.

New mathematics. One computation, made here because every reading of the block depended on it. For random systems of products of two affine forms, at parameters where the product series and the first-order count disagree, the series is exact: at \((n,m)=(30,75)\) and \((28,70)\), two systems each, the quotient of \(B_{\le D}\) by the static span has dimension equal to the cumulative coefficient sum of \((1+z)^{n-2m}(1+2z)^m\) at \(D=3\) and \(D=4\), to the unit, and \(1\) is not in the span at \(D=4\), where the first-order count is negative and the second-order term makes the coefficient positive. In the three systems run where the coefficient at \(4\) is negative the span is the whole space, which is an observation about those three and not a rule. So for rows on dense forms of width two the model is exact through degree four at these sizes; what the degree-four lines test is one thing, that the only relations among the generators are the \(\binom m2\) trivial ones \(f_if_j\).

Goal progress. Unchanged. The block's theorem, that in the model every system of small rows with covering sum of order \(v\) has deficit at least of order \(v\ln k/k\), concerns rows on variables, where the span cannot follow the series near its index, so this check on dense rows supports the model's first two orders and not that theorem's application; it still says nothing about a family; the alternative endpoint is located and undecided; no lower-bound method beyond a quarter exists.

General statement. The line's claim is the family statement. The block's all-parameter results are lem:engine-colon-families, lem:derived-affine-dimension, prop:table-row-span, lem:top-coefficient-functionals, prop:clause-saddle-value, lem:biased-power-inequality and thm:saddle-deficit-bound; its conjectures are conj:table-series-unit-degree and conj:product-series-index-formula.

Across the goal

  • Near-half Boolean PC family. Open, as at every review. Since the last one: the engine's requirement is a plateau of the closure's own counts; a thin proper closure has levels between two cubes; the static row span of table systems has an exact count; in a model of independent rows, now checked through second order for one row type, small rows with covering sum of order \(v\) have deficit at least \((\ln k/(2k)-0.47/k)v\), enough for two levels of the transfer and for no more.
  • Complete Frege transfer. Working proof within its recorded limits; untouched. The constant \(c_F\) is still not computed, and it decides whether two levels correspond to any depth at all.

Obstacle

Two things, now separated. First, a lower-bound method: every recorded method is an expansion argument and certifies at most about a quarter of the dimension; the reviewer gives a reason, recorded below and not verified, why no expansion argument can pass a quarter in any family. Second, a candidate: in the one model that predicts degrees, rows that behave independently cannot be within \(o(v\ln\ln v/\ln v)\) of half at polynomial length; the ways out are subspace rows on dense forms, which by affine invariance have the same single-row profile as clauses and differ only in their dependencies; table rows of large scope, whose profile is different and which the saddle theorem does not cover; and covers of small covering sum, whose rows are dependent by necessity and whose only recorded examples reduce to smaller covers. The first obstacle is the binding one: even where the model allows a deficit \(o(v)\), nothing proves that a closure is proper beyond a quarter.

The review's test: the series beyond first order

Prediction, from the series itself. For rows that are products of two affine forms the single-row quotient is \((1+2z)(1+z)^{n-2}\) and the product series \((1+z)^{n-2m}(1+2z)^m\). At \((30,75)\) its coefficient at \(z^4\) is \(\binom{30}4-75\binom{28}2+\binom{75}2=1830\), positive only through the last term; at \((28,70)\) it is \(140\). The first-order count is negative at both. So the model says \(1\notin K_4\) and quotient dimensions \(4181\) and \(1933\); the first-order count says \(1\in K_4\).

Scope. Rows of width two on dense random forms, seven complete systems at degrees three and four and one at two and three; the degree-three lines are first order, the degree-four lines add one second-order term. Satisfiability is not asserted by the program; where the unit is in the span the system is unsatisfiable, and elsewhere nothing is claimed. Architecture review

Necessary target. Unchanged: literal CNFs of polynomial length with auxiliary affine equations, of free dimension \(n\), with no refutation at \(\lfloor n/2-s\rfloor\), \(s+w\le n^{1-\epsilon}\), or \((s+w)(\log n)^{\ell-2}=o(n)\) at \(\ell\) levels; sufficient, not shown necessary. The free dimension may be counted after derived affine consequences.

Extra requirements. The engine's rate needs a plateau of the closure's counts, and the thin condition is the sufficient form of it. The search has asked in addition that candidates be describable row by row with rows that can be analysed independently; the block shows that this, in the model, is what costs \(v\ln k/k\). That demand is not required by the target and should be dropped: a candidate must be dependent in a useful way.

Independent alternative. Before seeing this route the review's medium reviewer received the goal and the available results (stage-one-brief.txt) and answered that it finds no materially different architecture it can vouch for (independent-review.txt). It gave: a structural reason why expansion arguments stop at a quarter in any family, boundary of nearly \(n\) at set size \(r/2\) and near-disjointness at size \(r\) being incompatible; the remark that two levels is not a cheaper target, being already an open lower bound; a first proposal, dense rows, against which it set the dimension count, by which the span may be full at a linear deficit for a random cover, without proving that it is; a second, covers barely above covering sum one that are not paddings, with the test whether the evenly covered set always lies in one row's subspace; and for a constant-fraction engine, extension variables, with the expectation that their levels are too large. Its plain assessment: the goal is out of reach by this approach with present methods, and for it to work one needs both a cover with covering sum near one whose hardness is not inherited, or rows rich in relations without binomial structure, and a lower-bound method for \(\mathbb F_2\) that is not expansion-based. Compared with this route: its first proposal is the model's verdict reached by another count; its second is the small-covering-sum escape, whose first case the record already settles, a cover with sum below \(1+2^{-w}\) being odd; at equality the evenly covered set is one subspace covered exactly twice and the degree is at most \(2w\); the first unsettled case is an excess between \(2^{-w}\) and \(2^{1-w}\), where that set has one of the low-weight shapes and multiplicity four is possible; its assessment I share, with the difference stated under Decision.

Rank normalization. The model's deficit is measured against half of \(v\), the number of variables of the cube in which the rows live; the thin endpoint would measure against half of the Kruskal–Katona dimension of the closure's levels. For the row types computed the two do not differ: the levels of the series below its index are those of nearly the full cube, as the series entry found. Relative contraction is what the engine uses and is not at issue.

Decision. Retain the family statement. Accept as the working judgment that it is out of reach of the present methods, and direct the next cycles at the method and not at further candidates: the model is exact where it has been checked, and exactness of a series, which bounds the static span from above, gives a lower bound on refutation degree as soon as the closure equals the span, by a route that owes nothing to expansion. Drop independence of rows as a property sought in candidates. Keep the two escapes as the only places a candidate can come from.

Decisive test. Prove the series exact in the first dependent case, posed in the graded setting the reviewer proposes. In the associated graded ring \(A=\mathbb F_2[x]/(x_i^2)\) every linear form squares to zero, so \(A\) is invariant under all linear changes of coordinates; exactness of the graded series there implies both the cumulative count for the span and, below the index, that the closure equals the span, the criterion at a level \(D\) being \(K_D\cap B_{\le D-1}=K_{D-1}\), which necessarily fails at the index. For rows that are products of two linear forms, with all forms independent the ideal is monomial and the series is exact trivially. Next cycle: for \(m=n/2+1\) rows, one linear dependency among the \(2m\) forms, prove or refute that multiplication by the last row on the quotient by the others has the kernel the series predicts; then state what the argument needs for general excess. Run the single case \((20,64)\) at degree three as a control at the index. Outcomes: a proof gives a lower bound on refutation degree below the index for these systems by a method that is not expansion, small as the index is at width two, and turns the first obstacle into the question of extending it to wide rows; a counterexample at small excess shows the computed agreement to be a small-size effect. Caution, from the reviewer's memory and unverified: series of this kind are known to fail for generic quadrics in the exterior algebra and for powers of linear forms, so exactness may be special to products of two forms or to these sizes.

Falsification attempt on this line

The claim: some polynomial-size family is hard near half of its free dimension, or has a thin proper closure. Against it now: the model's theorem, by which no system of independent-like small rows qualifies, with the model exact where tested; the reviewer's argument that expansion cannot certify more than a quarter; and thirty-nine entries without a candidate that survives. For it: nothing beyond the absence of a general ceiling, which the record tried and could not prove. If the decisive test succeeds, it sharpens the claim's difficulty and not its truth: it would show, where the closure equals the span, that generic systems are as hard as the series says, which for small rows is not hard enough. The claim survives because the two escapes are not understood, not because anything supports it.

It proposed the graded form of the test, adopted. Not verified by anyone: its structural argument on expansion, and the literature caution. Records: review.txt, independent-review.txt.

The queue's head item, unread for thirty entries, held the test that started the block. 9 October 2026 — With one dependency among the forms, in general position, the product series is exact up to its first negative coefficient; in general exactness follows from one colon statement per row

Working proofs, in the graded ring: a recursion by which exactness of the series follows from a statement about one colon ideal per row, and exactness for two-form rows with a single linear dependency under an explicit position hypothesis. Queue development of a chosen check while draining. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort low).

Chosen. The queued check on relations among products of affine forms bears on the family statement through its first obstacle, the absence of a lower-bound method, and the goal-level review made the question behind it its decisive test; it comes before the head for that reason.

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement: the review found the product series of rows that are products of two forms exact through degree four in computed systems. In the graded ring, is it exact when the forms first become dependent, and what would exactness need in general?

Architecture test. Outcome of the decisive test of the review: proved in the first dependent case. For \(m\) rows on \(n=2m-1\) variables, the first \(m-1\) on disjoint pairs and the last in a stated position, the quotient has the series \(\bigl((1+2z)^m+z^{m+1}\bigr)/(1+z)\), which is the product series in every degree up to \(m\), where its first negative coefficient follows. In general, exactness of the series follows, row by row, from one statement: the colon of the earlier rows by the new one is generated, in the degrees in question, by the earlier rows and the two forms of the new one. The control run at the index gave what the reviewer predicted: a span that is not everything where the top coefficient is negative. So the required implication changes as the review said it would: from "no method" to "prove this colon statement for many rows", for which the first case gives the pattern and not yet an induction.

New mathematics. The ring \(\mathbb F_2[x]/(x_i^2)\) is the exterior algebra in characteristic two, a product of two forms is the two-vector of their plane, and its annihilator contains the plane. From this: a recursion \(H(n,m)=H(n,m-1)-z^2H(n-2,m-1)\) for the series whenever the colon statement holds, whose solution is the product series; and an explicit computation for one dependency, by splitting off the pairs untouched by the last row and using that multiplication by a linear form on an exterior algebra in characteristic two is exact. The same computation shows where exactness stops when the position hypothesis fails: at the number of pairs the last row meets, plus one.

Goal progress. Unchanged. A first statement of the kind the review asked for is proved, at one dependency and in general position, which over \(\mathbb F_2\) a random last row has only with probability \((3/4)^{m-1}\), typical rows being exact only through the number of planes they meet plus one; it bears on refutation degree only through the passage from the graded ideal to the closure, not made here, and at width two the degrees involved are a small fraction of \(n\) once the rows are many.

General statement. lem:decomposable-colon-recursion holds for every sequence of rows that are products of two linear forms; prop:one-dependency-series-exactness for every \(m\ge2\) under its position hypothesis, over any field of characteristic two.

The graded ring

Let \(F\) have characteristic two, \(V=F^n\) with coordinates \(x_i\), and \(A=F[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/(x_i^2)\), graded, \(\dim A_j=\binom nj\). Every linear form has square zero in \(A\), so \(A\) is the exterior algebra of the space of linear forms, which in characteristic two is commutative, and every invertible linear change of coordinates is an automorphism of \(A\). For linear forms \(\ell,\ell'\) the product \(\omega=\ell\ell'\) depends only on the plane \(W=\langle\ell,\ell'\rangle\), up to a nonzero scalar, and is zero when they are dependent. If \(W\) is a plane, choose coordinates with \(\ell=x_1\), \(\ell'=x_2\): then \(\omega A=x_1x_2A'\), \(A'\) the algebra on the other variables, and the annihilator of \(\omega\) is the ideal \((\ell,\ell')\). So \(\omega A\cong(A/(\ell,\ell'))(-2)\), with series \(z^2(1+z)^{n-2}\).

For planes \(W_1,\ldots,W_m\) with two-vectors \(\omega_i\) let \(I_m=(\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_m)\) and \(H_m(z)\) the Hilbert series of \(A/I_m\). The product series is \(P_{n,m}(z)=(1+z)^{n-2m}(1+2z)^m\).

Lemma (decomposable colon recursion). For each \(m\ge1\) and each degree \(j\), with \(\bar A=A/(\ell_m,\ell_m')\), the exterior algebra on \(n-2\) variables, and \(\bar I_{m-1}\) the image of \(I_{m-1}\) in it: \[\dim(A/I_m)_j=\dim(A/I_{m-1})_j-\dim(\bar A/\bar I_{m-1})_{j-2}+\dim\Bigl(\frac{(I_{m-1}:\omega_m)}{I_{m-1}+(\ell_m,\ell_m')}\Bigr)_{j-2}.\] Consequently, suppose that for every \(m'\le m\) and every set \(K\subseteq\{m'+1,\ldots,m\}\) the sum of the planes \(W_k\), \(k\in K\), is direct and meets each \(W_i\), \(i\le m'\), trivially, and that the last term vanishes for the configuration \(W_1,\ldots,W_{m'}\) taken modulo that sum, in degrees at most \(j-2|K|-2\). Then the coefficients of \(H_m\) through degree \(j\) are those of \(P_{n,m}\).

Proof. \((A/I_m)_j\) is the cokernel of multiplication by \(\omega_m\) from \((A/I_{m-1})_{j-2}\) to \((A/I_{m-1})_j\), whose kernel is \((I_{m-1}:\omega_m)/I_{m-1}\) in degree \(j-2\). That kernel contains \((I_{m-1}+(\ell_m,\ell_m'))/I_{m-1}\), since \(\ell_m\omega_m=\ell_m'\omega_m=0\), and \(A/(I_{m-1}+(\ell_m,\ell_m'))=\bar A/\bar I_{m-1}\). Counting dimensions gives the display. For the consequence: \(\bar I_{m-1}\) is generated by the images of the \(\omega_i\), which are two-vectors of planes in the \((n-2)\)-dimensional quotient space by the hypothesis, and induction on \(m\) through the configurations named applies with \(P_{n,m-1}-z^2P_{n-2,m-1}=(1+z)^{n-2m}(1+2z)^{m-1}\bigl((1+z)^2-z^2\bigr)=P_{n,m}\). \(\square\)

The last term of the display is what a proof of exactness has to kill: the new row must be a zero divisor on the quotient by the earlier ones only through its own two forms. It is injectivity of multiplication by \(\omega_m\) from \(\bar A/\bar I_{m-1}\) to \(A/I_{m-1}\). Only sufficiency is proved; the vanishing is equivalent to exactness for the new row once the earlier rows and their images are exact.

One dependency

Proposition (one dependency series exactness). Let \(n=2m-1\), \(m\ge2\), and let the space of linear forms be \(P_1\oplus\cdots\oplus P_{m-1}\oplus\langle t\rangle\) with planes \(P_i\). Let \(W_i=P_i\) for \(i<m\), and let \(W_m\) be a plane not contained in \(P=\bigoplus P_i\), so that \(W_m\cap P\) is a line \(\langle\lambda\rangle\), and suppose the component of \(\lambda\) in every \(P_i\) is nonzero. Then \[H_m(z)=\frac{(1+2z)^m+z^{m+1}}{1+z},\] which agrees with \(P_{n,m}=(1+2z)^m/(1+z)\) in every degree at most \(m\); the coefficients of \(P_{n,m}\) are positive through degree \(m\) and the next is \(-1\). If instead the component of \(\lambda\) is nonzero in exactly \(s\) of the planes, \(1\le s\le m-1\), then \(H_m=\bigl((1+2z)^m+z^{s+2}(1+2z)^{m-1-s}\bigr)/(1+z)\), agreeing with \(P_{n,m}\) exactly in degrees at most \(s+1\).

Proof. Choose \(\ell\in W_m\setminus P\) and change the coordinate \(t\) to \(\ell\), which fixes \(P\) and the \(\omega_i\), \(i<m\); then \(\omega_m=t\lambda\) up to a scalar. In \(P_i\), every pair of independent forms has the same product up to a scalar, so a basis \(u_i,v_i\) of \(P_i\) may be chosen with \(u_i\) the component of \(\lambda\) when it is nonzero; \(\omega_i=u_iv_i\). So \(A/I_{m-1}=Q\otimes F[t]/(t^2)\), \(Q=\bigotimes_{i<m}Q_i\), \(Q_i=F[u_i,v_i]/(u_i^2,v_i^2,u_iv_i)\) with basis \(1,u_i,v_i\), and \(\omega_m=t\sigma\), \(\sigma=\sum_{i\in S}u_i\), \(S\) the set of planes met, \(|S|=s\). Then \(\omega_m(A/I_{m-1})=t\,\sigma Q\), so \(\dim(I_m/I_{m-1})_j=\dim(\sigma Q)_{j-1}\). Split \(Q\) by the set \(T\subseteq S\) of factors in \(S\) taken as \(v_i\) and by the basis element taken in each factor outside \(S\): on such a summand \(\sigma\) acts as multiplication by \(\sum_{i\in S\setminus T}u_i\) on \(E=\bigotimes_{i\in S\setminus T}F[u_i]/(u_i^2)\), an exterior algebra on \(N=s-|T|\) variables, the terms \(u_i\) with \(i\in T\) killing \(v_i\). For \(N\ge1\) a change of coordinates makes this form a variable \(u\), and multiplication by a variable on \(E=F[u]/(u^2)\otimes E'\) has image \(uE'\), of series \(z(1+z)^{N-1}\); for \(N=0\) it is zero. Summing over \(T\) with \(|T|=r\le s-1\), weight \(z^r\), and over the factors outside \(S\), series \((1+2z)^{m-1-s}\): \[\sum_j\dim(\sigma Q)_jz^j=(1+2z)^{m-1-s}\sum_{r=0}^{s-1}\binom srz^r\,z(1+z)^{s-1-r}=(1+2z)^{m-1-s}\,\frac{z\bigl((1+2z)^s-z^s\bigr)}{1+z}.\] Hence \(H_m=(1+2z)^{m-1}(1+z)-z^2(1+2z)^{m-1-s}\bigl((1+2z)^s-z^s\bigr)/(1+z)\), which is the stated series, using \((1+z)^2-z^2=1+2z\). The difference from \(P_{n,m}\) is \(z^{s+2}(1+2z)^{m-1-s}/(1+z)\), whose lowest term is \(z^{s+2}\). For \(s=m-1\): the coefficients \(c_j\) of \(P_{n,m}\) are the dimensions of \((A/I_m)_j\) for \(j\le m\); \(c_m=\sum_i(-1)^{m-i}\binom mi2^i=1\) and \(c_{m+1}=-c_m=-1\). Since \(A/I_m\) is generated in degree one, \((A/I_m)_m\ne0\) forces \((A/I_m)_j\ne0\) for all \(j\le m\), so \(c_j>0\) there. \(\square\)

In the lemma's terms, the proposition says that for one dependency in general position the last term of the display vanishes below the top, where it is the class of \(v_1\cdots v_{m-1}\), and it shows what the term is otherwise: the part of the quotient on which \(\sigma\) is zero for want of a factor to act on.

Runs

From control-runs.jsonl, by the review's kernel, which works with affine forms in the Boolean ring and reports cumulative dimensions of the quotient by the static span. First dependent case with random forms over \(\mathbb F_2\), \((n,m)=(9,5)\) and \((11,6)\): the cumulative quotient equals the cumulative series through degree four, \(41,90,121\), respectively through degree five, \(61,172,301,364\); at \((9,5)\), degree five, it is \(121\) against \(122\). The proposition's series for \(m=5\) has coefficients \(1,9,31,49,31,1\), so the runs agree with it below the top degree. At the top the first is one short of the value for a last row meeting all four planes; I did not check which planes the random last row meets, whether the dependency is single, or whether the top forms are independent, so this is not a test of the top degree. The control at the index, \((20,64)\), two seeds: at degree three the top coefficient of the series is \(-12\), the span has rank \(1216\) of \(1351\), \(1\) is not in it, and the cumulative quotient is \(135\), which is the cumulative sum of the series including the negative coefficient; at degree four the span is everything. So the review's corrected sentence stands. At \((32,96)\), one system (run-n32.jsonl): at degree three the quotient is \(2513\), the cumulative series; at degree four the top coefficient is \(-1240\), \(1\) is in the span, and the span is not everything, its quotient being \(2112\). These runs compare the Boolean span with the series and not with a computed graded quotient.

These runs are evidence for the proposition's shape in the Boolean setting and are not registered as a separate check.

What general excess needs, and the queued check

For \(n=2m-2\), two dependencies, the same normalisation gives the last row as \(\bigl(\sum u_i\bigr)\bigl(\sum v_i\bigr)\) on \(Q\) alone, and the kernel of multiplication by it is no longer read off from a single linear form; that is the next case. For many rows the lemma reduces everything to the maximal rank statement, in the exterior algebra in characteristic two, for multiplication by a decomposable two-vector on the quotient by generic decomposable two-vectors. The review's caution applies: for generic two-vectors that are not decomposable the analogous series is reported to fail.

From graded to Boolean. The rows of a formula are products of affine forms in \(F[x]/(x_i^2-x_i)\); their top forms generate the ideal studied here, and the static span's associated graded space contains its part of degree at most \(D\), so the Boolean quotient is at most the graded one, with equality when every fall of degree has its top form in the graded ideal; falls there always are, a form times its own row. I have not proved equality in any case, and the runs do not show it, the graded quotient not having been computed.

  • Whether the linear relations of products of affine forms account for the excess of the computed degree over the index of the generic series at \(n=20\) and \(32\). The generic series ignores that a product of two forms is killed by each of them; the product series is the series of the recursion above and has index four at \((20,60)\) and at \((32,96)\). The static degree is four at both: at \(n=20\) by ex:two-clause-series-exactness with ex:parity-two-clause-static-degree, where the generic series gave three, and at \(n=32\) by the run above. This is consistent with the lemma and conditional on its colon statement, which is not proved for these systems. Outcome: answered at both sizes for the static degree.

Reviewer's suggestions, unverified

  • Two dependencies: when the last plane projects onto every \(P_i\), the quotient of \(Q\) by its two forms is the same family with one row fewer, so the lemma gives a self-similar induction and only injectivity of the last row from that quotient to \(Q\) remains; by the proposition the kernel of \(\lambda\) is \(\lambda Q\) plus the top class, so what is needed is exactness of the second form on \(Q/\lambda Q\) below the top. By hand the series is exact for \(m=2,3,4\): \(1+2z\); \(1+4z+3z^2\); \(1,6,11,4\). A general conjecture to aim at: exactness through the size of the smallest dependent set of planes. Record. Searched "exterior algebra characteristic two decomposable two-forms colon maximal rank Hilbert series": the matches are in the cube thread of the main notebook, on other algebras; nothing recorded on quotients of exterior algebras by decomposable two-vectors. This is the first check queued below.
  • Literature, from the reviewer's memory: no maximal-rank theorem known for products of linear forms; nearest are work on generic forms in exterior algebras, on semi-regularity in \(\mathbb F_2[x]/(x_i^2)\), and on Cartan homology of exterior face rings, \(Q\) being that of the boundary of the cross-polytope. Record. Same search; none of these sources is in the record or has been read here.

9 October 2026 — With two dependencies in general position the product series is exact through degree \(n/2\); the quotient by the independent rows is a tensor power of a module of the four-group

Working proof, in the graded ring, by the representation theory of \(F[\lambda,\mu]/(\lambda^2,\mu^2)\), confirmed by direct computation for up to seven pairs. Queue development of a chosen check while draining. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort low).

Chosen. The two-dependency check on exactness of the product series, queued by the preceding entry, bears on the family statement through its first obstacle, a lower-bound method that is not expansion; it comes before the head because it is the next case of the review's decisive test and the reviewer indicated a route.

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement: for \(m=n/2+1\) rows that are products of two linear forms, the first \(n/2\) on disjoint pairs and the last a plane projecting onto every pair, is the product series exact, and by what mechanism?

New mathematics. It is, through degree \(n/2\), with an exact formula beyond: the quotient has the series \(\bigl((1+2z)^m+(m-1)z^m+mz^{m+1}\bigr)/(1+z)^2\). The mechanism is not the one the reviewer sketched. The two forms of the last row generate a copy of \(R=F[\lambda,\mu]/(\lambda^2,\mu^2)\), the group algebra of the four-group in characteristic two, acting on the quotient \(Q\) by the earlier rows; each pair contributes the three-dimensional module \(R/(\lambda\mu)\), and \(Q\) is the tensor product of these. Such a tensor power is free except for one summand, the \(M\)-th cosyzygy of the trivial module, of dimension \(2M+1\); the last row \(\lambda\mu\) is the socle element of \(R\), which acts with rank one on each free summand and by zero on the rest. Counting free summands by degree gives the series.

Goal progress. Unchanged. The second case of the review's test is proved, in general position and in the graded ring. It suggests the language in which the general case should be put, restrictions of a module of an elementary abelian two-group to rank-two shifted subgroups, and does not give the general case.

General statement. prop:two-dependency-series-exactness holds for every \(M\ge1\) over every field of characteristic two, under its position hypothesis.

Statement

Setting of lem:decomposable-colon-recursion: \(A=F[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/(x_i^2)\), \(F\) of characteristic two, planes \(W_i\) of linear forms with two-vectors \(\omega_i\).

Proposition (two dependency series exactness). Let \(n=2M\), \(m=M+1\), let the space of linear forms be \(P_1\oplus\cdots\oplus P_M\) with planes \(P_i=W_i\), and let \(W_m\) be a plane whose projection to every \(P_i\) is an isomorphism. Then the Hilbert series of \(A/(\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_m)\) is \[\frac{(1+2z)^m+(m-1)z^m+mz^{m+1}}{(1+z)^2},\] which agrees with the product series \((1+2z)^m/(1+z)^2\) in every degree at most \(m-1=n/2\); the coefficient of the product series at \(z^m\) is \(-(m-1)\).

Proof

Normalisation. Let \(\lambda,\mu\) be a basis of \(W_m\) and \(u_i,v_i\) their components in \(P_i\), a basis of \(P_i\) by hypothesis; \(\omega_i=u_iv_i\) up to a scalar. So \(A/(\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_M)=Q=\bigotimes_{i\le M}Q_i\), \(Q_i=F[u_i,v_i]/(u_i^2,v_i^2,u_iv_i)\) with basis \(1,u_i,v_i\), graded with \(u_i,v_i\) in degree one, and \(\omega_m=\lambda\mu\) with \(\lambda=\sum u_i\), \(\mu=\sum v_i\). The series of \(Q\) is \((1+2z)^M\), and what is needed is \(\dim(\lambda\mu\,Q)_j\) for each \(j\).

The algebra \(R\). Let \(R=F[\lambda,\mu]/(\lambda^2,\mu^2)\), graded, with basis \(1,\lambda,\mu,\omega=\lambda\mu\) and series \((1+z)^2\). All modules are finite-dimensional and graded, maps of degree zero, \(X(-a)\) the shift with \(X(-a)_j=X_{j-a}\). \(Q\) is an \(R\)-module, \(\lambda\) and \(\mu\) acting by multiplication. On a tensor product \(X\otimes Y\) of \(R\)-modules let \(\lambda\) act by \(\lambda\otimes1+1\otimes\lambda\) and likewise \(\mu\); these square to zero in characteristic two and commute, so \(X\otimes Y\) is an \(R\)-module. With this, \(Q=Q_1\otimes\cdots\otimes Q_M\) as \(R\)-modules, each \(Q_i\cong\Omega:=R/(\omega)\).

(a) Free modules are injective, and \(\omega\) detects them. The form \(R\times R\to F\), the coefficient of \(\omega\) in the product, is nondegenerate, so \(R\) is a Frobenius algebra and free modules are injective. If \(x\in X\) is homogeneous with \(\omega x\ne0\), then \(a\mapsto ax\) is injective on \(R\), every nonzero ideal of \(R\) containing \(\omega\); its image \(Rx\cong R(-\deg x)\) is injective, hence a direct summand. Repeating, \(X=X_0\oplus\Phi\) with \(\Phi\) free and \(\omega X_0=0\), and \(\dim(\omega X)_j\) is the number of free generators of \(\Phi\) of degree \(j-2\).

(b) \(R\otimes X\) is free on \(1\otimes X\). Filter \(R\otimes X\) by the degree in \(X\): the submodules \(R\otimes X_{\ge d}\) are stable, and on the quotients \(\lambda,\mu\) act through the first factor alone, so the associated graded module is free on \(1\otimes X\); lifting a basis, \(R\otimes X\) is free with generators \(1\otimes x\), \(x\) in a homogeneous basis of \(X\), in the degrees of \(X\). The same holds for \(X\otimes R\).

(c) Cosyzygies of \(F\). Let \(\Omega^{-1}(X)\) be the cokernel of an injective hull \(X\to E(X)\); for any embedding of \(X\) in an injective module \(E\), \(E/X\cong\Omega^{-1}(X)\oplus\) injective, and \(\Omega^{-1}(X)\) has no free summand when \(X\) has none. Tensoring \(0\to F(-2)\to R\to\Omega\to0\), the first map \(1\mapsto\omega\), with \(X\) gives \(0\to X(-2)\to R\otimes X\to\Omega\otimes X\to0\), exact, with the middle term free by (b): the first map \(x\mapsto\omega\otimes x\) is \(R\)-linear because \(\lambda\omega=\mu\omega=0\). Hence \(\Omega\otimes X\cong\Omega^{-1}(X(-2))\oplus\) free. By (b), \(\Omega\otimes\) free is free. By induction on \(M\), starting from \(Q_1=\Omega=\Omega^{-1}(F(-2))\): \(Q\cong Y_M\oplus\) free, where \(Y_M\) is the \(M\)-th cosyzygy of \(F\) up to a shift and has no free summand; by (a), \(\omega Y_M=0\).

(d) The series of \(Y_M\). The minimal free resolution of \(F\) over \(F[\lambda]/(\lambda^2)\) is \(\cdots\to R_1(-2)\to R_1(-1)\to R_1\), one generator in each degree; \(R\) is the tensor product of two such algebras, and the tensor product of the two resolutions is the minimal resolution of \(F\) over \(R\), with \(i+1\) generators in step \(i\), all of degree \(i\). The \(M\)-th syzygy \(\Omega^M(F)\) therefore has series determined by exactness: \(\sum_{i<M}(-1)^i(i+1)z^i(1+z)^2=1-(M+1)(-z)^M+M(-z)^{M+1}\), so \(\Omega^M(F)\) has series \((M+1)z^M+Mz^{M+1}\). The graded dual \(\operatorname{Hom}_F(-,F)\) takes free modules to free modules, \(R\) being Frobenius, and minimal free resolutions to minimal injective ones, so the \(M\)-th cosyzygy of \(F\) is the dual of \(\Omega^M(F)\): it has dimension \(M\) in one degree \(a\) and \(M+1\) in degree \(a+1\). So the series of \(Y_M\) is \(Mz^a+(M+1)z^{a+1}\) for some integer \(a\).

Counting. By (a) and (c), \((1+2z)^M=(1+z)^2F_M(z)+Mz^a+(M+1)z^{a+1}\), where \(F_M\), with nonnegative coefficients, counts the free generators of \(Q\) by degree, and \(\dim(\omega Q)_j\) is the coefficient of \(z^{j-2}\) in \(F_M\). Divisibility by \((1+z)^2\) determines \(a\): at \(z=-1\), \((-1)^M+(-1)^a=0\); and the derivative at \(z=-1\), with \(\varepsilon=(-1)^M=-(-1)^a\), is \(\varepsilon(-2M-Ma+(M+1)(a+1))=\varepsilon(a+1-M)\), so \(a=M-1\). Hence \[F_M(z)=\frac{(1+2z)^M-Mz^{M-1}-(M+1)z^M}{(1+z)^2},\] and the series of \(Q/\omega Q\) is \((1+2z)^M-z^2F_M=\bigl((1+2z)^M((1+z)^2-z^2)+Mz^{M+1}+(M+1)z^{M+2}\bigr)/(1+z)^2\), which is the stated one with \(m=M+1\). Its difference from the product series is \(\bigl((m-1)z^m+mz^{m+1}\bigr)/(1+z)^2\), of lowest term \((m-1)z^m\); and \(Q\) vanishes in degree \(m\), so the coefficient of the product series there is \(-(m-1)\). \(\square\)

Direct check

Independently of the proof, check_two_dependencies.py computes the rank of multiplication by \(\sum_{i\ne j}u_iv_j\) on \(Q\) degree by degree for \(M\le7\), over \(\mathbb F_2\) (direct-check.txt): the ranks are the coefficients of \(F_M\) in every degree, for example \(1,12,59,150,201,120\) at \(M=7\); and the kernel on \(Q_d\) has the dimension of \(((\lambda,\mu)Q)_d\) for every \(d\le M-2\), hence equals it, the containment holding because \(\lambda\omega=\mu\omega=0\); this is the vanishing of the last term in the display of the colon recursion. The reviewer's hand values for \(m=2,3,4\) in the last entry are these. The matrices are defined over \(\mathbb F_2\), so the ranks hold over every field of characteristic two. Not tested by the script: the proof's prediction that the defect at \(d=M-1\) is exactly \(M\).

What the mechanism suggests

\(A\) itself is a group algebra: \(F[x]/(x_i^2)=F[(\mathbb Z/2)^n]\) with \(x_i=1+g_i\). A plane \(W\) of linear forms spans the group algebra of a rank-two shifted subgroup in the sense of the theory of rank varieties, its two-vector \(\omega\) is that subalgebra's socle element, and for any \(A\)-module \(X\) the dimension of \(\omega X\) is the number of free summands of the restriction of \(X\) to the shifted subgroup. So the last term of the colon recursion measures how far the restriction of \(A/I_{m-1}\) to the next plane is from what the restrictions of the two smaller quotients predict, and exactness of the series for many rows is a statement about restrictions of the cyclic modules \(A/I\) to generic rank-two shifted subgroups. In this entry's case the restriction is a cosyzygy of the trivial module plus a free module; in the one-dependency case it is a free module plus one copy of the periodic module \(R/(\lambda)\), shifted to the top degree, as the reviewer points out, so the non-free part has more than one shape. I have not read the source theory for this entry and take from it only the dictionary; whether its theorems on generic restrictions apply is the next question.

Limits. Position: the plane must project isomorphically onto every pair, which over \(\mathbb F_2\) a uniform random plane does for a given pair with probability \(6\cdot4^{n-2}/((2^n-1)(2^n-2))\to3/8\) (the reviewer's correction of my \(6/15\)), and for all \(M\) pairs with probability about \((3/8)^M\), so for random rows over \(\mathbb F_2\) this is not the typical case, and a field extension or the mixed cases are needed. Size: \(m=n/2+1\) rows, far from the \(m\ge2.41n\) of unsatisfiable systems. Setting: graded; nothing here passes to the Boolean closure.

Reviewer's suggestions, unverified

  • Semicontinuity: the rank of \(\omega_W\) on a fixed graded piece is lower semicontinuous in the plane \(W\), so one explicit plane, over any extension field, attaining the upper bound that the colon recursion allows would prove exactness for generic planes; the reviewer names work on modules over Grassmannians as the source. Record. Searched "semicontinuity rank Grassmannian generic plane restriction shifted subgroup free summands": no recorded statement on these quotients; the matches are unrelated results of the main notebook. The semicontinuity itself is elementary (a rank condition on a matrix polynomial in the plane's coordinates) and is the tool for the check queued below.
  • The stable theory (Dade's lemma, rank varieties, generic Jordan type) sees projectivity and stable type, not the degrees of free summands, so the grading must be carried by hand. Conjecture: for generic planes the restriction of \(A/I_{m-1}\) to \(W_m\) is free plus a part generated in degrees at least the product series' first non-positive degree minus two. First test: a second generic plane over \(\mathbb F_4\) or \(\mathbb F_8\), \(M=3,\ldots,6\), rank of its two-vector on \((Q/\omega Q)_d\) against \((1+2z)^{M+2}/(1+z)^4\). Record. Same search; nothing recorded. Queued below as the three-dependency check, replacing my plan to read the stable theory first.

Specification decision. No change to the accepted specification. This entry concerns what can be proved about systems whose rows are products of two forms, not a candidate family; the systems treated have \(n/2+1\) rows and are satisfiable, so no property of them can enter the specification, and nothing proved here weakens what a candidate must satisfy.

Verification gate. One fresh-context medium reviewer checked by hand the normalisation, the tensor action, the graded Frobenius splitting, the filtration argument for freeness of \(R\otimes X\), the linearity \(\lambda(\omega\otimes x)=\omega\otimes\lambda x\), the induction, the resolution series and the derivative computation, and the quotient series at \(M=1,2,3\); it read the script and matched its output to the entry. It found the proposition and proof correct. Corrections applied, all in commentary: the shape of the non-free part in the one-dependency case; the probability \(3/8\) in place of \(6/15\); the containment that turns equal dimensions into equal spaces; a sub-idea for planes of lower rank on some pairs. Unused: nonnegativity of \(F_M\) is stated and not needed. Its remark that \(a=M-1\) follows directly from the degrees of the cosyzygy agrees with the divisibility argument. Record: review.txt.

Follow-up. Developed: prop:two-dependency-series-exactness settles the two-dependency case in general position, with the direct check for \(M\le7\); the positions outside it are queued below.

Sub-ideas

  • Three dependencies by semicontinuity: for \(n=2M\), add a second plane over \(\mathbb F_4\) or \(\mathbb F_8\) and compute the rank of its two-vector on \((Q/\omega Q)_d\), \(M=3,\ldots,6\), against \((1+2z)^{M+2}/(1+z)^4\); one plane attaining the bound of lem:decomposable-colon-recursion proves exactness for generic planes at those sizes; then seek the general argument through \(0\to\omega Q\to Q\to Q/\omega Q\to0\) restricted to the new plane.

Process assessment. The reviewer's suggested route was exactness of one form on the quotient by the other; while trying it I saw that the two forms together are the four-group, after which the proof was bookkeeping with standard facts. Those facts are stated with their reasons and are the part a reader should check, in particular the freeness of \(R\otimes X\) and the identification of the non-free summand; the direct computation agrees in every degree for seven sizes, which protects the formula and not the argument.

9 October 2026 — For generic planes the product series is a lower bound as soon as examples attain it two variables down; exact for every number of rows up to eleven variables

Working proof of an induction that turns examples into lower bounds; finite check, with that lemma, of exactness for generic rows on at most eleven variables at every number of rows; a conjecture for all sizes. Queue development of a chosen check while draining. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort low).

Chosen. The three-dependency check on generic planes, queued by the two-dependency entry, bears on the family statement through its first obstacle, a lower-bound method that is not expansion; it comes before the head as the next step of the review's decisive test.

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement: beyond two dependencies, is the product series the Hilbert function of the quotient by generic products of two forms, and what would a proof need?

New mathematics. The reviewer's semicontinuity remark gives more than it asked for. An example bounds the generic quotient from above; the colon recursion bounds it from below by the generic quotients with one row fewer, on \(n\) and on \(n-2\) variables. Together: upper bounds on \(n-2\) variables, which examples give, imply the lower bound on \(n\) variables. So the inequality one would expect to be the hard half, that generic rows cannot do better than the series, follows from the existence of examples that do as well. With one example over \(\mathbb F_8\) for each of the 200 pairs \((n,m)\), \(n\le11\), \(\lfloor n/2\rfloor\le m\le\binom n2\), this proves that for generic planes over the algebraic closure of \(\mathbb F_2\) the quotient has the product series in every degree below its first non-positive coefficient, for every number of rows.

Goal progress. Unchanged. The obstacle "no method" now has a definite shape for rows of width two: a proof for all \(n\) needs only examples, one family of explicit planes attaining the series. But the statement is graded and generic over an extension field; random planes over \(\mathbb F_2\) itself fail it in about half the small cases run; and at width two the degrees are a small fraction of \(n\).

General statement. lem:generic-series-lower-bound holds for all \(n,m,j\); conj:generic-two-form-series is the all-parameter claim that the finite check supports.

Setting

\(F\) an algebraically closed field of characteristic two, \(A_n=F[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/(x_i^2)\), planes \(W_1,\ldots,W_m\) of linear forms with two-vectors \(\omega_i\), \(I=(\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_m)\), as in lem:decomposable-colon-recursion. Let \[g(n,m,j)=\min\dim(A_n/I)_j\] over all \(m\)-tuples of planes; for \(n<2\) there are no planes and \(g(n,m,j)=\binom nj\). For fixed \(j\) the dimension is \(\binom nj\) minus the rank of a matrix whose entries are polynomials in the coordinates of the planes, so the minimum is attained on a nonempty open subset of the irreducible variety \(\mathrm{Gr}(2,n)^m\), and for finitely many \(j\) simultaneously. An example over a subfield gives \(g(n,m,j)\le\) its value, rank being unchanged by field extension; this holds also when some generators of the example are zero or repeated, since replacing them by arbitrary planes enlarges the ideal. An infinite field would do in place of an algebraically closed one. \(P_{n,m}(z)=(1+z)^{n-2m}(1+2z)^m\), with coefficients \(P_{n,m}[j]\).

Lemma (generic series lower bound). (i) For \(m\ge1\), \(n\ge2\) and all \(j\): \(g(n,m,j)\ge g(n,m-1,j)-g(n-2,m-1,j-2)\). (ii) If \(n\ge2\), \(2m_0\le n\), \(m\ge m_0\) and \(g(n-2,m',j-2)\le P_{n-2,m'}[j-2]\) for every \(m_0\le m'<m\), then \(g(n,m,j)\ge P_{n,m}[j]\).

Proof. (i) By the display of the colon recursion, for every tuple with \(W_m\) a plane, \(\dim(A/I_m)_j\ge\dim(A/I_{m-1})_j-\dim(\bar A/\bar I_{m-1})_{j-2}\), where \(\bar A=A_{n-2}\) is the algebra of the quotient space by \(W_m\) and \(\bar I_{m-1}\) is generated by the two-vectors of the images of \(W_1,\ldots,W_{m-1}\). The first term on the right is at least \(g(n,m-1,j)\). The function sending a tuple to \(\dim(A/(I_{m-1}+(W_m)))_{j-2}=\dim(\bar A/\bar I_{m-1})_{j-2}\) is upper semicontinuous on \(\mathrm{Gr}(2,n)^m\) by the same rank argument, so it attains its minimum on a nonempty open set. That minimum is \(g(n-2,m-1,j-2)\): for fixed \(W_m\) every tuple of planes of the quotient space is an image, and \(g\) does not depend on the identification of that space with \(F^{n-2}\), which gives at most; a tuple with degenerate images has its image ideal inside that of a tuple of genuine planes, which gives at least (for \(n-2<2\) the image ideal is zero and the convention applies). It meets the open set where \(\dim(A/I_m)_j=g(n,m,j)\). On the intersection the inequality reads as claimed. (ii) For \(2m_0\le n\), generic planes are independent, the ideal is monomial in suitable coordinates and \(g(n,m_0,j)=P_{n,m_0}[j]\). Induct on \(m\) from \(m_0\) with (i) and \(P_{n,m}=P_{n,m-1}-z^2P_{n-2,m-1}\): \(g(n,m,j)\ge P_{n,m-1}[j]-P_{n-2,m-1}[j-2]=P_{n,m}[j]\). \(\square\)

The hypothesis of (ii) can hold only where \(P_{n-2,m'}[j-2]\ge0\). Since \(g\ge0\), the lemma gives nothing at degrees where the smaller series has gone negative; the statement that survives is about degrees below the index, the first \(j\) with \(P_{n,m}[j]\le0\).

Conjecture (generic two-form series). For all \(n\) and \(m\), \(g(n,m,j)=P_{n,m}[j]\) for \(j\) below the index of \(P_{n,m}\), and \(g(n,m,j)=0\) from the index on. By the lemma, the first part for all \(n\) follows from the upper bounds alone: it is enough to exhibit, for each \((n,m)\), planes whose quotient has dimension at most \(P_{n,m}[j]\) in each degree below the index, provided the degrees line up: \(j\) below the index of \(P_{n,m}\) must imply \(j-2\) below the index of \(P_{n-2,m'}\) for \(\lfloor n/2\rfloor\le m'<m\). That is a statement about the series alone, not proved here; the reviewer checked it arithmetically for all \(n\le24\) and \(m\le\binom n2\) without a violation.

The finite check

Prediction counted beforehand: for each \((n,m)\) the series has between one and five coefficients below its index beyond degree one, and a random example over \(\mathbb F_8\) either attains each of them or does not; the first run below shows that over \(\mathbb F_2\) examples frequently do not, so the test can fail.

two_form_full_range.m2 (Macaulay2) computes the Hilbert function of one random example over \(\mathbb F_8\) for every \(n=2,\ldots,11\) and every \(\lfloor n/2\rfloor\le m\le\binom n2\): 200 cases (full-range.txt). generic_exactness.py applies the lemma's rules mechanically, with two trivial upper bounds where no example was computed: no planes for \(n<2\), and \(h=1,n,0,\ldots\) for \(m\ge\binom n2\), generic two-vectors spanning the second exterior power (summary, table).

Outcome. In 199 of the 200 cases the example equals the series in every degree below the index and the lemma's chain of hypotheses is satisfied, so \(g(n,m,j)=P_{n,m}[j]\) there. The exception is \((5,3)\), where the random example has \(h_3=2\) against \(1\): a non-generic sample. There the lower bound comes from the lemma and only the upper bound \(g\le1\) from prop:one-dependency-series-exactness, whose position hypothesis, a last plane meeting both earlier planes' components, is satisfiable at \(m=3\). So the first part of the conjecture holds for all \(n\le11\) and all \(m\) (for \(m>\binom n2\) the index is two and there is nothing to prove). In 198 cases the example also vanishes from the index on, giving the second part there; the two others, \((3,3)\) and \((10,5)\), are again non-generic samples: at \((10,5)\) the ten forms are dependent, at \((3,3)\) the three two-vectors, and generic tuples vanish there by independence and by spanning, so the second part holds in all 200 cases. For \(n=11\) the index is \(7,6,5,5,5,4\) at \(m=6,\ldots,11\) and three from \(m=19\); for example \(h=1,11,48,102,99,21\) at \(m=7\).

An earlier run, two_form_series.m2 (output, stopped by its time limit after 69 cases at \(n=8,10,12\)), compared \(\mathbb F_8\) with \(\mathbb F_2\), two seeds each: all 35 examples over \(\mathbb F_8\) equal the series below the index, among them \(n=12\) with \(m=7,8,9,12,18\); of the 34 over \(\mathbb F_2\) only 15 do, the others exceeding it one or two degrees below the index. So random planes over \(\mathbb F_2\) are not generic at these sizes, as the position hypotheses of the two propositions already indicated.

Scope. One random example per case; the lemma makes the conclusion rigorous for generic planes over the algebraic closure, not for any particular system and not over \(\mathbb F_2\). Macaulay2's Hilbert functions are not cross-checked by a second system here; the case \(n=2M\), \(m=M+1\) agrees with prop:two-dependency-series-exactness (at \(n=10\): \(1,10,39,72,57,6\)).

What this means for the route

For width two the obstacle has changed form: generic exactness for all \(n\) is the existence of good examples. Three things stand between that and a lower bound on refutation degree. The field: formulas have rows over \(\mathbb F_2\), where random planes fall short; whether the shortfall persists as \(n\) grows, or a different family of planes over \(\mathbb F_2\) is generic enough, is not known. The passage from the graded ideal to the Boolean closure, queued. And size: at width two the index is a small fraction of \(n\) once rows are many; the same induction for products of \(k\) forms uses only that each of the \(k\) forms kills the product, so the lemma's first part generalises with \(n-k\) in place of \(n-2\) and degree shift \(k\); that is the case that matters and is queued.

Reviewer's suggestions, unverified

  • Explicit families to try for the upper bound: planes \(\langle x_i,\sum_ja_{ij}x_j\rangle\) with a Cauchy or Vandermonde matrix over \(\mathbb F_{2^r}\), or the lines of a spread, \(\mathbb F_{q^2}\)-lines in \(\mathbb F_q^{2k}\), where a torus or Singer cycle acts. The upper bound is a maximal-rank statement of Fröberg type, open in general for symmetric algebras. Record. Searched "generic Hilbert function lower bound Froberg inequality semicontinuity examples induction": the record has semiregularity conjectures for other systems (pin and parity-clause) and nothing on these quotients. Queued below as the explicit-examples check.
  • Literature to search before any claim of novelty: generic forms and generic quadrics in exterior algebras, and ideals generated by powers or products of generic linear forms. Record. Same search; none of these sources is recorded or was read. No novelty is claimed in this entry.

Specification decision. No change to the accepted specification. The result concerns generic rows over an extension field in the graded ring; it names no family, and the observation that random \(\mathbb F_2\) planes are not generic at small sizes is a warning for any candidate built from random parity rows, not yet a condition that could be imposed.

Verification gate. One fresh-context medium reviewer checked the lemma, read both scripts and compared the entry with the output files. It confirmed that the post-processing implements the lemma's rules exactly, both trivial upper bounds, the 200 cases and 199 proved, the indices and Hilbert functions quoted, and the counts 35 of 35 and 15 of 34. Corrections applied: 198 and not 197 examples vanish from the index, the case \((5,3)\) having been miscounted by me; the alternative "or the example vanishing there" is dropped as false where the smaller coefficient is negative, and the alignment of indices is kept as an unproved proviso with the reviewer's arithmetic check; examples with zero or repeated generators still bound \(g\); the openness step of the lemma is rewritten as semicontinuity of the image quotient with both inequalities for its minimum; \(n\ge2\), \(m\ge m_0\) added; the source of each bound at \((5,3)\); the overstated requirement for width \(k\). Unused: algebraic closure, an infinite field sufficing. Record: review.txt.

Follow-up. Developed: three and more dependencies are settled for generic planes on at most eleven variables by ex:small-generic-two-form-exactness with lem:generic-series-lower-bound; the general case is reduced to examples and queued below.

Sub-ideas

  • Width \(k\): state and prove the colon recursion and the lower-bound lemma for products of \(k\) linear forms (annihilator generated by the forms, quotient on \(n-k\) variables, series \((1+z)^{n-km}((1+z)^k-z^k)^m\)), and run the full-range check at \(k=3\) for small \(n\).
  • Explicit examples for all \(n\) at width two: find a structured family of planes (for instance from a field extension or a Vandermonde arrangement) whose quotient can be computed in closed form and attains the series below the index, which by the lemma proves the conjecture's first part.
  • Over \(\mathbb F_2\): measure how the shortfall of random planes behaves as \(n\) grows at fixed density, and whether it is confined to the top degrees below the index.

Process assessment. I set out to run the reviewer's three-dependency test and saw while sizing it that the recursion's inequality composes with semicontinuity; the run was then designed for the induction, over the whole range of \(m\), instead of a few cases. The first version of the post-processing reported failures at degree two that were gaps in the table, not in the mathematics, and was fixed by adding the two trivial bounds. The lemma is short and its one delicate point is the genericity of the image configuration.
