10 October 2026 — A minimal counterexample to the paired row conjecture has slices depending only on their own pairs, and every nonzero slice shares each \((w-1)\)-subset of its pairs with another nonzero slice

Working proofs of two lemmas about a minimal counterexample; the conjecture itself stays open. Second entry on the queue's head, through its remaining sub-idea. Queue development while draining. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort low).

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement: can conj:paired-row-symbols be proved by induction on the number of pairs, using the slice identities of the last entry?

New mathematics. lem:distance-degree-bound: a nonzero function of degree at most \(\delta-2\) on a cube of dimension at least \(\delta-1\) is not supported on a set of minimum distance at least \(\delta\); this is standard Reed–Muller duality, recorded for use. lem:paired-row-minimal-counterexample: let \(f\) be a counterexample to the conjecture on a row with the least number \(h\) of pairs. Then each slice \(f_J\) is a function of \(z_J\) alone; the sign patterns \(Y_J\) have minimum distance at least \(w\); for every set \(I\) of \(w-1\) pairs, every pair \(j\) and every point \(z^*\), the values of the slices over deviation sets containing \(I\cup\{j\}\), each taken at its unique pattern near \(z^*\), sum to zero; consequently every nonzero slice shares each \((w-1)\)-subset of its pairs with another nonzero slice. Separately, for every \(f\) and not only minimal ones, a single non-preferred slice is impossible with no assumption on \(Y_J\). The induction does not close: the sharing statement is not yet a contradiction. The lemma is vacuous if the conjecture holds.

Goal progress. Unchanged. The conjecture concerns the paired source at two levels and is not proved.

General statement. lem:paired-row-minimal-counterexample, for every paired central row with \(w\ge3\) in characteristic two and every counterexample of least \(h\); conj:paired-row-symbols remains the claim.

A distance bound

Lemma (distance degree bound). Let \(\delta\ge2\), \(N\ge\delta-1\), and let \(g\ne0\) be a function on \(\{0,1\}^N\) with values in a field, of degree at most \(\delta-2\) as a multilinear polynomial. Then its support contains two distinct points at Hamming distance at most \(\delta-1\).

Proof. Take \(x\) with \(g(x)\ne0\) and any set \(I\) of \(\delta-1\) coordinates. For \(N<\delta-1\) the statement is false, the indicator of a point having degree \(N\) (the reviewer's correction of my first version). In characteristic two the sum of \(g\) over the subcube \(x+\operatorname{span}(e_i:i\in I)\) is the coefficient extraction of a monomial of degree \(\delta-1\) from a polynomial of smaller degree after translation, hence zero; in general characteristic the signed sum \(\sum_y(-1)^{|y+x|}g(y)\) over the subcube vanishes for the same reason. So the subcube holds another point of the support, at distance at most \(\delta-1\) from \(x\). \(\square\)

The minimal counterexample

Setting and coordinates of the last entry: a paired central row on \(h\) pairs, odd prime modulus \(q\), \(w\ge3\) the least size of a set of pairs carrying a signed zero-sum, characteristic two; \(R=\{(z,t)\}\) with \(Q=\{t=0\}\) and, for \(J=\operatorname{supp}t\ne\emptyset\), \(z_J\in Y_J\). A counterexample is a function \(f\) supported on \(R\), of degree at most \(h+w-3\), with some slice \(f_J\ne0\), \(J\ne\emptyset\). Let \(\mathcal J\) be the set of such \(J\). For \(h<w\) no deviation set carries a zero-sum, \(R=Q\), and there is no counterexample; so a counterexample with least \(h\) exists if any does.

Lemma (paired row minimal counterexample). Let \(f\) be a counterexample on a row with the least number of pairs among all paired central rows with zero-sum size at least three. Then:

  1. For every \(J\in\mathcal J\), \(f_J\) does not depend on \(z_i\) for \(i\notin J\): \(f_J(z)=\alpha_J(z_J)\) with \(\alpha_J\) supported on \(Y_J\).
  2. Two distinct patterns in \(Y_J\) differ on a set carrying a signed zero-sum, hence in at least \(w\) coordinates.
  3. For every \(I\subseteq[h]\) with \(|I|=w-1\), every \(j\in[h]\) and every \(z^*\in\{0,1\}^h\), \[\sum_{J\in\mathcal J,\ J\supseteq I\cup\{j\}}\alpha_J\bigl(y_J(z^*,I)\bigr)=0,\] where \(y_J(z^*,I)\) is the unique point of \(Y_J\) agreeing with \(z^*_J\) outside \(I\), and the term is zero if there is none.
  4. Every \(J\in\mathcal J\) has \(|J|\ge w\), and for every \((w-1)\)-subset \(I\subseteq J\) there is another \(J'\in\mathcal J\), \(J'\ne J\), with \(J'\supseteq I\); likewise for every \(w\)-subset. In particular \(|\mathcal J|\ge2\).

Proof. (1) Fix \(i\notin J\), put \(H=[h]\setminus\{i\}\) and \(g(z_H,t_H)=\sum_{z_i}f(z,(t_H,0))\). Restricting to \(t_i=0\) does not raise the degree and, in characteristic two, summing over \(z_i\) extracts the coefficient of \(z_i\) and lowers the degree by one, so \(\deg g\le(h-1)+w-3\). The points of \(R\) with \(t_i=0\) are those of the row on the pairs \(H\), whose membership does not involve \(z_i\); so \(g\) is supported on that row, which is a paired central row on \(h-1\) pairs with zero-sum size \(w_H\ge w\). If \(w_H\) is infinite that row is its preferred cube and the slices of \(g\) over nonempty \(J\subseteq H\) vanish by support. Otherwise \(\deg g\le(h-1)+w_H-3\) and, by minimality of \(h\) over all rows, moduli and fields of characteristic two, \(g\) is not a counterexample: those slices vanish. That slice is \(\sum_{z_i}f_J\), the coefficient of \(z_i\) in \(f_J\). So \(f_J\) has no \(z_i\).

(2) If \(p\ne p'\) in \(Y_J\) differ exactly on \(D\ne\emptyset\) and \(\eta\) are the signs of \(p\), then \(\sum_J\eta_ja_j\equiv0\) and \(\sum_J\eta_ja_j-2\sum_D\eta_ja_j\equiv0\), so \(\sum_D\eta_ja_j\equiv0\) as \(q\) is odd, and \(|D|\ge w\).

(3) By identity 2 of the last entry with \(C=\{j\}\), \(G_j=\sum_{J\ni j}f_J\) has degree at most \(w-2\); the sum runs over \(J\in\mathcal J\). Sum \(G_j\) over the subcube \(z^*+\operatorname{span}(e_i:i\in I)\), of dimension \(w-1\): the result is zero. For one \(J\), by (1), \(\sum_z\alpha_J(z_J)\) over the subcube is \(2^{|I\setminus J|}\) times the sum of \(\alpha_J\) over \(z^*_J+\operatorname{span}(e_i:i\in I\cap J)\), which vanishes in characteristic two unless \(I\subseteq J\); and for \(I\subseteq J\) that subcube of \(\{0,1\}^J\) has dimension \(w-1\) and by (2) contains at most one point of \(Y_J\). This gives the identity.

(4) \(Y_J\ne\emptyset\) needs \(|J|\ge w\). Let \(J\in\mathcal J\), \(\sigma\) with \(\alpha_J(\sigma)\ne0\), \(I\subseteq J\) with \(|I|=w-1\), and \(j\in I\) (or \(j\in J\setminus I\) for the \(w\)-subset \(I\cup\{j\}\)); take \(z^*\) with \(z^*_J=\sigma\). Then \(y_J(z^*,I)=\sigma\) and the term of \(J\) in (3) is \(\alpha_J(\sigma)\ne0\), so another term is nonzero. \(\square\)

Remarks. The single-slice statement of the last entry holds for every \(f\) without its hypothesis on \(Y_{J_0}\): a single slice \(f_{J_0}\) has degree at most \(w-2\); fix \(z\) outside \(J_0\) at a point where it is nonzero; the restriction to the \(J_0\)-cube, of dimension \(|J_0|\ge w\), is nonzero of degree at most \(w-2\) and supported on \(Y_{J_0}\), of minimum distance at least \(w\), against the distance degree bound. The identities respect the known boundary: at degree \(h+w-2\) the subcubes have dimension \(w\) and may contain both points of a complementary pair, which is the recorded counterexample. Parts (1), (3) and (4) use minimality; (2) does not. Only oddness of \(q\) is used, not primality.

Why this is not yet a proof

Take \(J\in\mathcal J\) of least size and \(\sigma\) in the support of \(\alpha_J\). By (4) and its proof, for each \(w\)-subset \(I\cup\{j\}\) of \(J\) there is \(J'\ne J\) in \(\mathcal J\) containing it, with a pattern \(y'\in Y_{J'}\) agreeing with \(\sigma\) on \((J\cap J')\setminus I\) and with \(z^*\) elsewhere. Subtracting the two zero-sums gives a relation \(\sum_{J\setminus J'}\pm a-\sum_{J'\setminus J}\pm a+2\sum_E\pm a\equiv0\) with \(E\subseteq I\): a zero-sum with coefficients \(\pm1,\pm2\), which the hypothesis on \(w\) does not forbid. Summing (3) over the free coordinates of \(z^*\) loses everything to characteristic two. So the family \(\mathcal J\) must be rich, every \(w\)-set of a member lying in two members, but I have no contradiction. Heuristically, for weights with \(q\) much larger than \(2^h\) such families do not exist, zero-sum sets being too few. The recorded evidence does include rows with many: besides fifteen rows with \(h\le6\), the registry lists three rows \((h,q,w)=(10,211,4),(10,1009,5),(12,1009,4)\) in which non-preferred points outnumber the preferred cube up to 4.4 times, and the conjecture held there. My first draft said the evidence sampled only rows with few zero-sum sets; that was wrong, and the reviewer's count for the first of these rows, about 280 zero-sum patterns, shows it. Whether the sharing property of part (4) holds in those rows, so that they already test the regime the lemma leaves open, I have not checked.

Specification decision. No change to the accepted specification. The paired source remains excluded at three or more levels and only conditionally at two; these lemmas narrow what a failure of the condition would look like and prove nothing about the source.

Verification gate. One fresh-context medium reviewer, by hand. It found parts (1) to (4) correct as written, including the degree count in (1), the form of the smaller row, the case \(j\in I\) and the coefficients-two relation, and minimality well defined. Corrections applied: the distance lemma was false for \(N<\delta-1\) and now carries that hypothesis; characteristic two is named where summation lowers the degree; infinite \(w_H\) is handled by support; part (4) is stated for \((w-1)\)-subsets, which its proof gives; the unconditional single-slice statement gets its restriction argument; "do not exist" is labelled heuristic. Process audit. The reviewer found: my claim that the evidence sampled only rows with few zero-sum sets unsupported and probably false, with the doubt and the queued check resting on it (claim withdrawn against the registry, doubt removed, check replaced by reading the existing outputs first); the title imprecise (fixed); the distance bound standard and to be recorded as known (so recorded); the minimal-counterexample lemma acceptable if its status says it is vacuous should the conjecture hold (said); one of the two failed attempts not described (said). It supported "Continuing" and "unchanged". Record: review.txt.

Follow-up. Continuing. Second entry of the head's spell. The conjecture, its remaining sub-idea, is not decided. Next attempt: the check below, then a proof that the coefficients-two relation above cannot hold for all \((w-1)\)-subsets at once, using the reviewer's remark that the unused bound \(\deg(f_\emptyset+\alpha_{J_0})\le h+w-3-|J_0|\) for an inclusion-minimal \(J_0\) combines with (3) at varying \(z^*\).

Sub-ideas

  • Read the zero-sum sets of the three larger computed rows from their saved outputs and test whether every \((w-1)\)-subset of each lies in a second one: if so those rows already sample the regime that part (4) leaves open; if not, search rows with small modulus and \(w=3\) where it does, as the place a counterexample could live.

Process assessment. The induction came from asking which operation lowers the degree bound by exactly what the smaller row needs: summing over one \(z_i\) does, restriction does not. One attempt to finish, by choosing \(z^*\), is described above; another, through a monomial of top degree among all slices, stopped at cancellation between slices containing the same monomial and is not written out. Registry searches for the distance bound and for a minimal-counterexample statement found nothing. Two errors were caught in review: the distance lemma was false in a case I added without checking, and I asserted that the conjecture's evidence sampled only rows with few zero-sum sets without reading its registry record, which says otherwise; on that false premise I had written a doubt about the conjecture. Prevention. The rule to reread a claim's record before relying on it exists and covers characterizing its evidence; the reviewer's process audit checked the claim against the registry and caught it, which is the check working. No new check is added.

10 October 2026 — Goal-level review: six entries on upper-bound conjectures left the family statement where it was; the next cycles go to the lower-bound side and to the level count that decides what two levels are worth

Goal-level route review: one open statement, unchanged across fifty-seven research entries. No outside leads or bridges while the queue drains. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort low).

Question. Six research entries since the last review: three on a conjecture that random clause systems are refuted at their product index, one failed count for it, two on the paired row conjecture. Were they well spent, and what should the next six do?

Architecture test. The last review's decisive test was carried out in the index-span entry: as posed it failed at the graded index; at the cumulative index the statement held in all 24 measured systems (ex:index-span-degree-six). It became a conjecture with an exact kill formula and no proof. The required implication did not change.

New mathematics. No result. The reviewer's independent proposal named one class not yet examined, rows that are bundles of many narrow clauses on a large common scope, and a test: does the model's deficit scale with the scope or with the clause width? For same-sign bundles the recorded prop:same-sign-saddle-bound already answers: its bound \(1/2-0.17/(k\log_2N)\) has \(k\) the logarithm of the number of clauses and \(N\) the number of literals, and does not see how clauses are grouped into rows. So in the model such bundles have deficit of order \(n/\log^2n\) whatever their scope, and by the reviewer's criterion the class is cut off for the every-depth form, under that proposition's hypotheses: unsatisfiability by first moment, generic relations among the forms, and the extrapolated conjecture that the index is \(n\sup\Phi\). Not covered: bundles with mixed signs, where thm:saddle-deficit-bound still allows \(n\ln k/k\) in the scope; structured relations; systems unsatisfiable otherwise than by first moment.

Goal progress. Unchanged. Six entries produced two finite checks, five lemmas and one conjecture; none is about a family.

General statement. The line's claim is the family statement. The block's all-parameter results are lem:sequential-kill-formula, lem:support-flat-rank, lem:parallel-class-kill-bound, lem:distance-degree-bound and lem:paired-row-minimal-counterexample; conj:cumulative-index-span is a conjecture.

Across the goal

  • Near-half Boolean PC family. Open. No lower bound over \(\mathbb F_2\) beyond about a quarter of the dimension for any family; the one criterion that is not expansion, colon regularity, is unproved for random rows beyond trivial degrees and capped at two levels. Every class examined is cut off for the every-depth form, by ceilings or in the model.
  • Complete Frege transfer. Working proof within its recorded limits, conditional on Pang's Theorem 4.3 as the simulation entry states. The level overhead \(c_F\) of the simulation is still not computed, so it is not known which Frege depth a two-level family would serve, or whether any.

Obstacle

As before: no lower-bound method. What this block adds is a clearer view of how the cycles were spent. Following the correction of 10 October, that an upper bound with a deficit term is a specification clause, I gave six entries to two upper-bound conjectures. Both concern classes that earlier reviews had already set aside for the every-depth form: random clause systems, in the model, and the paired source, by an actual ceiling at three or more levels. Proving either would turn a model verdict or a conditional exclusion into a theorem; it would not change what must be found. The correction was right about closing items; I over-applied it to choosing them.

Architecture review

Necessary target. Unchanged: literal CNFs of polynomial length with auxiliary affine equations, of free dimension \(n\), with no PC refutation over \(\mathbb F_2\) at \(\lfloor n/2-s\rfloor\), \(s+w\le n^{1-\epsilon}\); at \(\ell=d+c_F\) levels, \((s+w)(\log n)^{\ell-2}=o(n)\). Sufficient, not shown necessary.

Extra requirements. The every-depth form asks for a deficit that no examined class has even in the model. The two-level form asks only \(s+w=o(n)\), which clause rows of slowly growing width meet in the model and which cor:two-level-regularity-reduction reduces to colon regularity of one random family. What the two-level form is worth depends on \(c_F\), which the record does not contain.

Independent alternative. Before seeing this route the review's medium reviewer received the goal and the available results (stage-one-brief.txt) and answered (independent-review.txt): no materially different architecture it could vouch for. It judged the last six cycles not defensible for this goal, both conjectures being exclusions of classes already abandoned, and would have spent them on the lower-bound side: colon regularity for random rows of width two at degree three, then at growing degree. It named one unexamined class, bundle rows, with the test answered above, and said that if the deficit scales with clause width every class it can name is the open problem restated. As a different endpoint it offered only the two-level form through colon regularity, with the caveat that its worth is unverified, and recommended declaring it the working endpoint with the every-depth goal recorded as lacking a mechanism. It added that the evidence for regularity is at indices three to five, \(n\le28\), one degree beyond the trivial. Compared with this route: it agrees with the review of 10 October that capped the criterion at two levels, and disagrees with that review's decision to stop work on it.

Rank normalization. Does not apply: no dimension count is compared in this review. For the regularity question the relevant count is the one of thm:colon-regular-closure, in the graded quotient, and the kill formula of this block is stated in the same Boolean quotient as the static span.

Decision. Change the allocation, not the goal. The every-depth statement stays the open statement and is not parked; no mechanism for it is known and none is claimed. The next cycles go to the lower-bound side. The object studied in this block, functionals killing the static span, is the same there, but the question is harder, as the reviewer points out: at the ceiling the aim is no killer besides the solutions, and a first moment suffices; regularity asks for a codimension exactly \(2^h\)-many killers for the right \(h>0\), so the expected number must be right up to a factor \(1+o(1)\), not in the exponent; the one count made, at \(k=2\) and degree three, failed even in the exponent; and thm:colon-regular-closure asks for regularity in the graded algebra, to which a Boolean codimension must first be related. So the lower-bound side is taken up with those four difficulties stated, not as an application of ready tools. The same cycle settles what two levels are worth. The two upper-bound conjectures stay queued and receive no further cycles until an item on the lower-bound side has had its spell.

Decisive test. Two parts in one cycle. First, from the recorded transfer and simulation, identify the sequent system that \(\ell=2\) levels of the transfer speak about and whether it contains a proof system for which superpolynomial bounds are open; resolution over parities is the candidate, and that its bounds are open is from memory and to be checked. My first form of this test, computing \(c_F\), was ill-posed: the reviewer showed that \(c_F\) is an upper bound for one simulation of an arbitrary Frege system, not a least value, that this simulation gives \(\ell\ge3\) for every depth, and that \(\ell\ge3\) there does not make the two-level form worthless. Second, state what colon regularity at degree three for random rows of width two requires of the count of killing functionals, with the sharp constant, and attempt it. Outcomes: if two levels cover a system with open bounds, the two-level form becomes the working endpoint with regularity its missing implication, at widths tending to infinity, where all evidence is still at widths two and three; if they cover only systems with known bounds, the two-level form is dropped and that is recorded. A question this review leaves to the cycle after: the model points uniformly at a deficit of about \(n/\log^2n\) for polynomial covers, and a general ceiling of that order would change the goal and not only exclude a class; whether one cycle should test it is the reviewer's question, and unlike the class-specific conjectures it is on the path.

For it: nothing. The reviewer states that the every-depth goal does not look reachable by this line as it stands; I have no evidence to set against that, and no proof of it either.

10 October 2026 — Level-one lines of the transfer's system are those of resolution over parities, with a larger system at level two; regularity of width-two rows at degree three is a tail bound for the bias of a random cubic functional

Working proof of one criterion; the regularity statement itself is not proved. The review's decisive test, both parts. Queue development of a chosen check while draining. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort low).

Chosen. The queued check on the refutation degree of random products of two affine forms bears on the family statement in its two-level form, where a lower bound for such rows of growing width is the missing implication; it comes first because the review of 10 October made it the decisive test, which the finisher requires in this cycle.

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement: which proof system do two levels of the recorded transfer cover, and are bounds for it open; and what exactly must be shown for random rows of width two to be colon regular through degree three?

Architecture test. The review named this test. First part: at level one the lines of the transfer's system are sets of formulas built from variables by negation and parity, that is disjunctions of affine forms, with cut and weakening: the lines and rules of resolution over parities; level two contains more. A literature search reports that superpolynomial bounds for unrestricted resolution over parities are open; the main notebook holds a working theorem for it on the pigeonhole principle by another route. If the search summary is right and the simulation of that system at level one is polynomial, which I did not check, the two-level form is worth pursuing: it would give bounds for a system containing resolution over parities. Second part: regularity at degree three is reduced to a precise tail bound, which I did not prove. By the review's stated outcome the two-level form becomes the working endpoint, with regularity at growing width and linear degree as its missing implication; this entry reaches degree three at width two only as a criterion.

New mathematics. prop:cubic-regularity-moment-criterion: for \(m\) random products of two linear forms in \(A=\mathbb F_2[x]/(x_i^2)\), colon regularity through degree three is the independence of the \(m\) products in degree two and of their \((n-2)m\) multiples in degree three, and the probability that the multiples are dependent is at most \(2^{(n-2)m-N}\bigl(1+\sum_{\varphi\ne0}q(\varphi)^m\bigr)-1\), \(N=\binom n3\), where \(q(\varphi)\) is the probability that a random row is killed by the cubic functional \(\varphi\). So regularity for \(m\le(1/6-\epsilon)n^2\) follows, by this first-moment method, from two things together: the functionals with \(q(\varphi)\ge2^{-t}\) number at most \(2^{N-(n-2-t)m}\) times a factor summable to \(o(1)\) over the levels \(t\le n-3\), and \(q\) is within a factor \(1+o(1/m)\) of \(2^{-(n-2)}\) for all but a negligible weighted share of the rest, a concentration statement; together a tail bound for the kill probability of a uniformly random functional. I checked the smallest dependencies only.

Goal progress. Unchanged. The two-level form is identified as worth having; nothing toward it is proved beyond a criterion at degree three.

General statement. prop:cubic-regularity-moment-criterion, for all \(n\) and \(m\); the regularity statement it would give is conj:parity-clause-regular-index at \(k=2\), degree three.

What two levels cover

In the system of thm:bounded-depth-degree-transfer (entry), formulas are built from variables by negation, unbounded disjunction and unbounded parity; a line is a set of formulas read as a disjunction; negation and parity do not raise the level, a disjunction has level one more than the disjunctions properly inside it, and a line has level one more than the disjunctions in its members. A line of level one has members without disjunctions, each a parity of variables possibly negated, an affine form: the line is a clause of affine equations. With the parity axioms, weakening and cut on such forms, refutations of level one are refutations in resolution over parities, up to the cost of deriving that system's semantic weakening syntactically, which I did not check. A line of level two may also contain disjunctions of affine forms, their negations, which are conjunctions of affine equations, and parities and negations of such formulas: the system at level two contains the lines that are disjunctions of affine subspaces and more. By cor:bounded-depth-size-bound, a family with no refutation at \(\lfloor n/2-s\rfloor\) and \(s+w=o(n)\) has no polynomial-size refutation at one or two levels, conditionally on the imported rank theorem as recorded there. The corollary is for CNFs of width \(w\) with auxiliary affine equations in free dimension \(n\); rows on dense parities enter through that encoding.

Status of bounds, from a search of 10 October and not from sources read: superpolynomial bounds for unrestricted, dag-like resolution over parities are reported open (a 2025 paper of Efremenko and Itsykson is quoted to that effect); the known bounds are for tree-like, regular and bounded-depth fragments, the last up to depth about \(N^{2-\epsilon}\). In this repository the main notebook's thm:ordinary-unary-PHP-Res-parity-superpolynomial is a working theorem for the unrestricted system on the pigeonhole principle, not independently reviewed. So a two-level family would give a second proof for resolution over parities and a first bound for the level-two system. It would not give the goal: the simulation entry gives \(\ell=d+c_F\) levels for depth \(d\), and by the reading of the review's reviewer that is three or more for every depth.

Regularity at degree three

\(A=\mathbb F_2[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/(x_i^2)\), graded; rows \(\omega_r=\ell_{r1}\ell_{r2}\), \(r\le m\), with \(\ell_{r1},\ell_{r2}\) uniform linear forms conditioned to be linearly independent, the rows independent of one another; \(U_r\) their span; \(N=\dim A_3=\binom n3\). These are the top forms of clause rows of width two, the setting of thm:colon-regular-closure with \(k=2\), \(D=3\).

Proposition (cubic regularity moment criterion). (a) The system is colon regular through degree three exactly when the \(\omega_r\) are linearly independent in \(A_2\) and the vectors \(\lambda\omega_r\), \(r\le m\), \(\lambda\) in a basis of \(A_1/U_r\), are linearly independent in \(A_3\). (b) Let \(\kappa\) be the dimension of the space of dependencies among the latter vectors and \(\kappa'\) that of the functionals \(\varphi\in A_3^*\) vanishing on all of them. Then \(\kappa-\kappa'=(n-2)m-N\) for every choice of rows with independent pairs, and \(\mathbb E\,2^{\kappa'}=\sum_{\varphi}q(\varphi)^m\), \(q(\varphi)=\Pr_{\ell_1,\ell_2}[\varphi(\lambda\ell_1\ell_2)=0\ \forall\lambda\in A_1]\). Hence \[\Pr[\kappa>0]\le\mathbb E\,2^{\kappa}-1=2^{(n-2)m-N}\Bigl(1+\sum_{\varphi\ne0}q(\varphi)^m\Bigr)-1.\] (c) With \(T_\varphi(a,b,c)=\varphi(abc)\), a symmetric trilinear form on \(A_1\) with \(T(a,a,\cdot)=0\), \(q(\varphi)=\Pr_{\ell_1,\ell_2}[T_\varphi(\ell_1,\ell_2,\cdot)=0]\), over independent pairs. Without the conditioning the corresponding probability is the bias of \(T_\varphi\), \(\mathbb E_{a}2^{-\operatorname{rank}T_\varphi(a,\cdot,\cdot)}\), which equals \(q(1-p)+p\) with \(p\) about \(3\cdot2^{-n}\) the probability of a dependent pair; \(p\) is of the order of the generic \(q\), so the identification of \(q\) with the bias is usable only for \(t\) well below \(n\) (the reviewer's correction; unconditioned, every functional would have probability at least about \(\tfrac74\,2^{-(n-2)}\) and the bound would be vacuous).

Proof. (a) In the closure theorem the condition for row \(i\) and \(e\le D-k=1\) is \((I_{i-1}:\omega_i)_e=(I_{i-1}+(U_i))_e\). \(I_{i-1}\) is generated in degree two, so for \(e=0\) the right side is zero and the condition says \(\omega_i\notin\operatorname{span}(\omega_r:r<i)\); for \(e=1\) the right side is \(U_i\), which lies in the colon because \(\ell\,\ell=0\) in \(A\), and the condition says that \(\lambda\omega_i\in(I_{i-1})_3=\operatorname{span}(x_j\omega_r:r<i)\) only for \(\lambda\in U_i\). Over all \(i\) these are the two independence statements, of which the second implies the first, a dependency among the \(\omega_r\) giving one in degree three on multiplication by a form outside the relevant \(U_r\): a dependency \(\sum_r\lambda_r\omega_r=0\) with some \(\lambda_r\notin U_r\) gives, for its largest such \(r\), a violation, and conversely. (b) The matrix with rows \(\lambda\omega_r\) and \(N\) columns has \((n-2)m\) rows, the \(\lambda\) running over a basis of \(A_1/U_r\) of dimension \(n-2\); \(\kappa\) and \(\kappa'\) are the dimensions of its left and right kernels, so both equal the number of rows, respectively columns, minus the rank. A functional \(\varphi\) lies in the right kernel exactly when it kills every row's multiples; the rows are independent and identically distributed, so the expected number of such \(\varphi\) is \(\sum_\varphi q(\varphi)^m\), and this number is \(2^{\kappa'}\). (c) is the definition. \(\square\)

The criterion is the mirror of the first moment of the last block. There the system was overdetermined and the aim was \(\kappa'=0\), needing \(\sum_{\varphi\ne0}q^m\to0\). Here \((n-2)m<N\), \(\kappa'\ge N-(n-2)m\) always, and this first-moment method obtains \(\kappa=0\) only if \(\sum_\varphi q(\varphi)^m=(1+o(1))2^{N-(n-2)m}\): the sum must equal its trivial lower bound up to a factor tending to one. A uniformly random row in place of a product has probability \(2^{-(n-2)}\) for every \(\varphi\ne0\) whose contraction has full rank, which gives equality; for products the same holds only if the functionals whose bias exceeds the generic one are negligible at every level.

What that requires. Write \(q(\varphi)=2^{-t}\). The functionals at level \(t\) contribute \(N_t2^{-tm}\), to be compared with \(2^{N-(n-2)m}\): the requirement is \(\sum_{t<n-2}N_t2^{(n-2-t)m}=o(2^N)\) together with \(q\) within a factor \(1+o(1/m)\) of \(2^{-(n-2)}\) for all but a negligible weighted share of the rest. In words, a uniformly random cubic functional has bias \(2^{-t}\) with probability \(o(2^{-(n-2-t)m})\). Three ranges, none proved here. For small \(t\) the functionals are structured and a count is needed; the theorems bounding partition rank by analytic rank that the last review's reviewer named would give a bound of the shape \(N_t\le2^{O(t\log t)n^2}\) if they hold over \(\mathbb F_2\) with such constants (my guess at the shape, with no source read), enough for \(t\) up to a small multiple of \(n/\log n\) when \(m=cn^2\), \(c<1/6\); this is unverified. For \(t\) within a constant of \(n-2\) the requirement is a concentration statement for the bias of a random tensor. Between them it is a tail bound I do not know. The one case computed: dependencies involving two rows need two equal decomposable cubics, of probability about \(2^{-3n}\) for each pair, against \(2^{2n}\) choices of the two multipliers, an expected number of order \(m^22^{-n}\).

Prior work in the record. A registry search for the criterion ("row dependencies killing functionals rank nullity moment identity Macaulay matrix regularity degree three") returned the last block's kill bounds and, from the main notebook, thm:generic-top-directness: for Zariski-generic elements of an irreducible set stable under the general linear group, over an algebraically closed field, the multiples are direct up to a count within an additive term of the dimension bound. Products of two linear forms are such a set, so over the algebraic closure generic rows are regular at degree three nearly up to \(N/(n-2)\). That is the generic analogue of what is wanted; it does not give random rows over \(\mathbb F_2\), and the closure theorem needs coefficients in \(\mathbb F_2\). I read its registry summary only. The first moment of the last block is in the support-flat entry.

Distance from what the two-level form needs. That form needs regularity through degree \(n/2-o(n)\) for rows of width tending to infinity. This criterion is at degree three and width two, and even there the statement is a tail bound not in hand. The step from fixed to linear degree is of the kind of the open conjectures on semi-regular sequences, of which the Semaev–Tenti introduction (ePrint 2019/903, page 3) says that the conjecture that random systems over \(\mathbb F_2\) are semi-regular with probability tending to one was disproved in that form, while most systems are still believed to behave like semi-regular ones. I record the two-level form as the working endpoint because the review's test says so, and record equally that no part of its missing implication is proved.

10 October 2026 — The kill probability of a cubic functional is its number of isotropic planes; its mean is exactly generic and its relative variance is of order \(2^{-n}\), while the tail needed for regularity stays open

Working proof of exact first and second moments; regularity at degree three is not proved. Second entry on the chosen check, on the lower-bound side of the two-level form. Queue development while draining. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort low).

Chosen. The queued check on random products of two forms bears on the family statement in its two-level form, the working endpoint since the review of 10 October; this is the second moment named as its next attempt, and the item is not the queue's head.

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement: in prop:cubic-regularity-moment-criterion, how is the kill probability \(q(\varphi)\) distributed over cubic functionals: its mean, its variance, and the structured functionals for which it is large?

New mathematics. prop:isotropic-plane-count. In \(A=\mathbb F_2[x]/(x_i^2)\), the exterior algebra in characteristic two, a functional on \(A_3\) is an alternating trilinear form \(T\) on \(V=\mathbb F_2^n\), a row is a plane \(U\), and the row is killed exactly when \(U\) is isotropic, \(T(a,b,\cdot)=0\) for \(a,b\in U\). With \(Z(T)\) the number of pairs \((a,b)\in V^2\) with \(T(a,b,\cdot)=0\), \(q(T)=(Z(T)-3\cdot2^n+2)/((2^n-1)(2^n-2))\). Over uniformly random \(T\): \(\mathbb E\,q=2^{-(n-2)}\) exactly, and \(\operatorname{Var}q=(\mathbb Eq)^2\,(p_1+p_0(2^{n-2}-1))\) with \(p_1,p_0\) the probabilities that two random planes meet in a line or coincide, about \(10.5\cdot2^{-n}(\mathbb Eq)^2\); the reviewer confirmed mean and second moment by enumerating all forms and planes for \(n=3,4,5\). The \(m\)-th moment is \(\mathbb E\,2^{-\dim\sum_rU_r\wedge V}\) over \(m\) random planes. Two structured families are estimated, forms with a kernel and direct sums of two; on unproved typical values in lower dimension they are negligible for \(m=cn^2\), \(c<1/6\). The tail bound that regularity needs is not obtained.

Goal progress. Unchanged. The criterion is consistent at the second moment, which says nothing at \(m\) of order \(n^2\); no regularity statement is proved.

General statement. prop:isotropic-plane-count, for all \(n\ge3\); the statement it serves is regularity of random rows of width two at degree three, conj:parity-clause-regular-index in its smallest case.

Planes and forms

In characteristic two the algebra \(A=\mathbb F_2[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/(x_i^2)\) is the exterior algebra of \(V^*\), commutativity and anticommutativity agreeing. \(A_3^*\) is the space of alternating trilinear forms on the dual, which I write on \(V=\mathbb F_2^n\): \(T\) symmetric trilinear with \(T(a,a,\cdot)=0\), of dimension \(N=\binom n3\). A row \(\omega=\ell_1\ell_2\) with independent forms is the plane \(U=\langle\ell_1,\ell_2\rangle\), uniformly distributed over planes when the pair is uniform among independent pairs; its multiples in degree three are \(U\wedge V=\{a\wedge b\wedge x\}\), \(a,b\) a basis of \(U\), a space of dimension \(n-2\) consisting of decomposable elements. A functional kills the row exactly when \(T(a,b,x)=0\) for all \(x\): call \(U\) isotropic for \(T\).

Proposition (isotropic plane count). Let \(Z(T)=\#\{(a,b)\in V^2:T(a,b,\cdot)=0\}\) and \(G=(2^n-1)(2^n-2)/6\) the number of planes.

  1. \(q(T)=\dfrac{Z(T)-3\cdot2^n+2}{(2^n-1)(2^n-2)}\); and \(Z(T)=\sum_a2^{d(a)}\), \(d(a)\) the dimension of the radical of the bilinear form \(T(a,\cdot,\cdot)\), which contains \(a\).
  2. For \(T\) uniform, \(\mathbb E\,q(T)=2^{-(n-2)}\).
  3. For planes \(U_1,\ldots,U_m\), \(\Pr_T[\text{all isotropic}]=2^{-\dim\sum_rU_r\wedge V}\); so \(\mathbb E_T\,q^m=\mathbb E_{U_1,\ldots,U_m}2^{-\dim\sum_rU_r\wedge V}\).
  4. \(U_1\wedge V\cap U_2\wedge V\) has dimension \(n-2\), \(1\) or \(0\) according as \(U_1=U_2\), \(\dim(U_1\cap U_2)=1\), or \(U_1\cap U_2=0\). Hence \[\mathbb E\,q^2=2^{-2(n-2)}\bigl(1+p_1+p_0(2^{n-2}-1)\bigr),\qquad p_1=\frac{3(2^{n-1}-2)}{G},\quad p_0=\frac1G,\] and \(\operatorname{Var}q/(\mathbb Eq)^2=p_1+p_0(2^{n-2}-1)=(10.5\cdot2^{n}-42)/((2^n-1)(2^n-2))\), which is \((10.5+o(1))2^{-n}\).

Proof. (1) An isotropic plane has six ordered bases, each a pair counted by \(Z\). The other pairs counted by \(Z\) are the linearly dependent ones, all of which satisfy \(T(a,b,\cdot)=0\) because \(T(a,a,\cdot)=0\): \((0,0)\), the \(2(2^n-1)\) pairs with \(a\ne0\), \(b\in\{0,a\}\), and the \(2^n-1\) pairs with \(a=0\ne b\); \(3\cdot2^n-2\) in all. So \(Z=6\cdot\#\{\text{isotropic planes}\}+3\cdot2^n-2\) and \(q=\#\{\text{isotropic}\}/G\). For fixed \(a\) the \(b\) with \(T(a,b,\cdot)=0\) form the radical of \(T(a,\cdot,\cdot)\). (2), (3) The conditions \(T(\tau)=0\) for \(\tau\) in a subspace \(S\subseteq\Lambda^3V\) are \(\dim S\) independent uniform conditions on a uniform \(T\in(\Lambda^3V)^*\), so the probability is \(2^{-\dim S}\); for one plane \(\dim U\wedge V=n-2\). (4) A nonzero element of \(U\wedge V\) is \(a\wedge b\wedge x\) with \(x\notin U\), the decomposable trivector of the three-space \(U+\langle x\rangle\), which determines that three-space. A common nonzero element of \(U_1\wedge V\) and \(U_2\wedge V\) therefore comes from a three-space containing \(U_1+U_2\): none if \(\dim(U_1+U_2)=4\), exactly one if it is three, and for \(U_1=U_2\) the whole space. The planes meeting \(U_1\) in exactly a line: three lines, each in \((2^n-2)/2\) planes, one of which is \(U_1\). Then \(\mathbb Eq^2=\sum\Pr[\text{case}]\,2^{-2(n-2)+\dim\cap}\). \(\square\)

So the kill probability is the bias of the form, \(Z(T)/2^{2n}\), with its trivial part removed, and over random forms it is concentrated: by Chebyshev \(q\le2\,\mathbb Eq\) outside a set of forms of measure about \(10.5\cdot2^{-n}\). This is the near-generic range at the level of the second moment. It is far from what the criterion needs, which by part (3) is the whole \(m\)-th moment, \(m\) of order \(n^2\): the criterion's quantity \(\mathbb E\,2^{\kappa}\) equals \(2^{(n-2)m}\,\mathbb E_Tq^m\) by the last entry, and \(\mathbb E_Tq^m=\mathbb E\,2^{-\dim\sum U_r\wedge V}\) shows again what the criterion's quantity counts: \(\mathbb E\,2^\kappa\) is the expected number of tuples \(p_r\in U_r\wedge V\), zero allowed, with \(\sum_rp_r=0\), each nonzero \(p_r\) the trivector of a three-space through \(U_r\), and \(\mathbb E_Tq^m\) is that number times \(2^{-(n-2)m}\).

Two structured families

Estimates, not registered, each resting on a typical value of \(q\) in lower dimension, that is, on the same unproved tail. Forms with a kernel \(K\) of dimension \(j\ge1\), \(T\) pulled back from \(V/K\): a plane meeting \(K\) is isotropic, of probability about \(3\cdot2^{j-n}\), and otherwise the plane's image in \(V/K\) must be isotropic, about \(4\cdot2^{j-n}\) for a typical form there; so \(q\approx7\cdot2^{j-n}\) for \(j\) not close to \(n\), larger than generic by \(\tfrac74\,2^j\). Such forms number at most \(2^{j(n-j)+\binom{n-j}3}\), a loss of \(\binom n3-\binom{n-j}3-j(n-j)\) in the exponent, which is \(jn^2/2+O(jn)\) for bounded \(j\). At \(j=1\) their weight in \(\sum_Tq^m\) relative to the generic total is about \(2^{n^2(1.81c-1/2)}\) at \(m=cn^2\), negligible for \(c<0.27\); at \(j=tn\) the condition is \(c<(3-3t+t^2)/6\), which decreases to \(1/6\) as \(j\) approaches \(n\), so \(1/6\) is the binding value over all \(j\) (the reviewer's computation). Direct sums of two, \(T=T_1\oplus T_2\) on \(V=V_1\oplus V_2\): \(Z\) is multiplicative, \(Z(T)=Z(T_1)Z(T_2)\), about \(49\cdot2^n\) for typical summands, so \(q\) exceeds the generic value by about \((49-3)/4=11.5\); for summands of equal size the share of such forms is about \(2^{-n^3/8}\) against a gain \(11.5^m=2^{3.5cn^2}\), negligible. More summands and unequal sizes are not treated.

What a proof needs, in the form the reviewer corrected. Not only a count of forms with large \(Z\): the criterion needs \(\mathbb E_T(q/\mathbb Eq)^m=1+o(1)\). For the dyadic levels, forms with \(Z\) in \([2^j,2^{j+1})\cdot7\cdot2^n\) must number at most \(2^{N-(j+1+0.81)cn^2-\omega(1)}\), summably in \(j\). And below the first level, \(\Pr[q\ge(1+\delta)\mathbb Eq]\) must be much smaller than \((1+\delta)^{-m}\) for all \(\delta\) down to about \(1/m\); Chebyshev gives \(10.5\cdot2^{-n}/\delta^2\) there, against a weight \(2^{cn^2}\), so the second moment does not touch this range. I have neither bound. The reviewer suggests working on the other side of part (3): a union bound over the pattern in which the planes of a zero-sum tuple share three-spaces.

Specification decision. No change to the accepted specification. The result is about a criterion for regularity at degree three; it constrains no candidate.

It found no error in the proposition and confirmed the mean, the second moment and the variance ratio by exhaustive enumeration of all alternating 3-forms and planes for \(n=3,4,5\) (its own run, not archived here; an \(n=6\) attempt timed out). Corrections applied, all outside the proposition: the kernel estimate's range of \(j\) and the binding value \(1/6\); the factor for direct sums, \((7^k-3)/4\); the form of the needed bound, which was short by a dyadic factor and missed the range just above the mean; the wording of what the moment counts. Process audit. The reviewer found: the summary calling both families negligible without the qualifier the body has (added); "passes its second-moment test" overstating what a second moment shows at \(m\) of order \(n^2\) (reworded); the threshold 0.27 sourced only for \(j=1\) (said). It found the decisions justified and the record search stated. Record: review.txt.

Follow-up. Continuing. Second entry of the spell. The mean and variance are exact; the tail is open and is a statement about how many alternating 3-forms over \(\mathbb F_2\) have bias above \(2^j\) times the generic one. Next attempt: the reviewer's suggestion, a union bound for \(\mathbb E\,2^\kappa\) over the incidence pattern of a zero-sum tuple of decomposable trivectors, which planes share three-spaces and which three-spaces share planes; with the recorded analogue in the main notebook, lem:catalecticant-count and lem:low-rank-strata, read in full for comparison.

Passing to planes and alternating forms made the last entry's criterion transparent; I should have written that entry in this language, the algebra being an exterior algebra in characteristic two, which I noticed only now. A registry search for isotropic planes and biases of random 3-forms found nothing. Prevention. 10 October 2026 — Dependencies among the rows' multiples are circuits of three-spaces; the plain union bound over their spans fails, and it would succeed for small circuits if a circuit of \(k\) three-spaces spanned at most \(\alpha k+\beta\) dimensions with \(\alpha<2\)

Working proof of one lemma and one conditional proposition; regularity at degree three is not proved. Third entry on the chosen check, on the lower-bound side of the two-level form. Queue development while draining. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort low).

Chosen. The queued check on random products of two forms bears on the family statement in its two-level form, the working endpoint; this is the union bound over dependency patterns named as its next attempt, and the item is not the queue's head.

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement: can the expected number of dependencies among the degree-three multiples of \(m\le(1/6-\epsilon)n^2\) random planes be bounded by a union bound over the pattern of the dependency, and if not, which pattern defeats it?

New mathematics. lem:trivector-circuit-overlap: a dependency is a set of rows with three-spaces \(P_r\supset U_r\) whose trivectors sum to zero; in a minimal one, a circuit, for every proper nonempty part \(S'\) the spans \(W_{S'}\) and \(W_{S'^c}\) meet in dimension at least three, so each \(P_r\) lies in the span of the others and \(\dim W\le\dim W_{S'}+\dim W_{S'^c}-3\); circuits of two are equal three-spaces and circuits of three are pencils through a common plane in a four-space, with exact expected numbers. prop:small-circuit-union-bound, conditional: if every circuit of \(k\) three-spaces spans at most \(\alpha k+\beta\) dimensions with \(\alpha<2\), then for \(m\le n^C\) the expected number of circuits of size between a constant \(k_1\) and \(\epsilon n\) tends to zero; with \(\alpha=\beta=1\), \(k_1=3\), and size two is covered by an exact count. The plain bound \(3k-3\), which the lemma gives, is not enough: the union bound over spans then diverges from size four on. I conjecture \(k+1\); it holds for \(k\le3\) by the lemma, and the reviewer reports from an exhaustive search of its own that the largest span is five at \(k=4\) and six at \(k=5\). Circuits of size beyond \(\epsilon n\) are not treated at all.

Goal progress. Unchanged. Regularity at degree three is not proved; the open part is now two named statements, a span bound for circuits and a count for large circuits.

General statement. lem:trivector-circuit-overlap for all \(n\) and all circuits; prop:small-circuit-union-bound for all \(\alpha<2\), \(\beta\), \(C\), conditional on its span hypothesis.

Dependencies as circuits

Notation of the last entry: \(V=\mathbb F_2^n\), rows are uniform random planes \(U_r\), \(r\le m\), independent; the multiples of row \(r\) are \(U_r\wedge V\), whose nonzero elements are the trivectors \([P]\) of the three-spaces \(P\supset U_r\), \(2^{n-2}-1\) of them. A dependency is a nonempty set \(S\) of rows with a choice of \(P_r\supset U_r\), \(r\in S\), such that \(\sum_{r\in S}[P_r]=0\) in \(\Lambda^3V\); \(\mathbb E\,2^\kappa-1\) is the expected number of dependencies. A circuit is a dependency no proper nonempty subset of which, with the same three-spaces, is one; every dependency contains a circuit, so the rows are regular through degree three exactly when there is no circuit. For a set \(S'\) write \(W_{S'}=\sum_{r\in S'}P_r\) and \(W=W_S\).

Lemma (trivector circuit overlap). Let \((P_r)_{r\in S}\) be a circuit, \(|S|=k\). (a) For every proper nonempty \(S'\subset S\), \(\tau=\sum_{r\in S'}[P_r]\) is nonzero and lies in \(\Lambda^3(W_{S'}\cap W_{S\setminus S'})\); so \(\dim(W_{S'}\cap W_{S\setminus S'})\ge3\) and \(\dim W\le\dim W_{S'}+\dim W_{S\setminus S'}-3\). In particular each \(P_r\subseteq W_{S\setminus\{r\}}\) and \(\dim W\le3k-3\). (b) \(k\ge2\); for \(k=2\), \(P_1=P_2\); for \(k=3\), the three-spaces are the three containing a common plane inside a four-space. (c) For independent uniform planes the expected number of circuits of size two is \(\binom m2(p_1+p_0(2^{n-2}-1))\), about \(5.25\,m^22^{-n}\), and of size three exactly \(\binom m3(2^{n-2}-1)^3\,7(2^{n-2}-2)/G_3^2\), about \(129\,m^32^{-2n}\), with \(G_3=(2^n-1)(2^n-2)(2^n-4)/168\) the number of three-spaces.

Proof. (a) \(\tau\ne0\) by minimality, and \(\tau=\sum_{r\notin S'}[P_r]\) as the total is zero, so \(\tau\in\Lambda^3W_{S'}\cap\Lambda^3W_{S\setminus S'}\). For subspaces \(A,B\), \(\Lambda^3A\cap\Lambda^3B=\Lambda^3(A\cap B)\): take a basis of \(A\cap B\) extended to bases of \(A\) and of \(B\), together a basis of \(A+B\); an element of both is supported on basis trivectors using vectors of \(A\) only and of \(B\) only, hence of \(A\cap B\). A nonzero element of \(\Lambda^3X\) needs \(\dim X\ge3\). The dimension formula follows, and for \(S'=\{r\}\), \([P_r]\in\Lambda^3X\) forces \(P_r\subseteq X\). (b) A single trivector is nonzero. For two, \([P_1]=[P_2]\) means \(P_1=P_2\). For three, \([P_3]=[P_1]+[P_2]\) with \(P_1\ne P_2\). If \(\dim(P_1\cap P_2)=2\), with \(P_1=\langle a,b,c\rangle\), \(P_2=\langle a,b,d\rangle\), the sum is \(a\wedge b\wedge(c+d)\), the third three-space through \(\langle a,b\rangle\) in \(\langle a,b,c,d\rangle\). If \(\dim(P_1\cap P_2)=1\), the sum is \(a\wedge(b\wedge c+d\wedge e)\) with \(a,\ldots,e\) independent; contracting with functionals dual to this basis produces \(b\wedge c+d\wedge e\), of rank four, so the sum is not the trivector of a three-space, whose contractions have rank at most two. If \(P_1\cap P_2=0\), the sum is \(e_1\wedge e_2\wedge e_3+e_4\wedge e_5\wedge e_6\) on independent vectors; contracting with a functional equal to one on \(e_1\) and \(e_4\) and zero on the others gives \(e_2\wedge e_3+e_5\wedge e_6\), again of rank four. (c) Two rows form a circuit when some three-space contains both planes: the planes meet in a line, with one such three-space, or coincide, with \(2^{n-2}-1\); this is the count of the last entry. For three rows, the expected number of triples of three-spaces through the planes with zero sum is \((2^{n-2}-1)^3\) times the probability that three independent uniform three-spaces sum to zero, which is the probability \(7(2^{n-2}-2)/G_3\) that the second meets the first in a plane, seven planes each in \(2^{n-2}-1\) three-spaces of which one is the first, times \(1/G_3\) for the third. \(\square\)

The union bound and what it needs

A circuit of size \(k\) with span \(W\) of dimension \(w\) has all \(P_r\subseteq W\). For a fixed \(W\), the expected number of choices \(P_r\supset U_r\) with \(P_r\subseteq W\) for one row is the number of three-spaces in \(W\) over \(G_3\) times \(2^{n-2}-1\), at most \(c_0\,2^{n-2-3(n-w)}\) for an absolute constant \(c_0\). So the expected number of circuits of size \(k\) with span of dimension at most \(w\) is at most \[\binom mk\,2^{w(n-w)+1}\bigl(c_02^{3w-2n-2}\bigr)^k,\] with \(2^{w(n-w)+2}\) in place of \(2^{w(n-w)+1}\), the number of \(w\)-spaces being at most \(2^{w(n-w)+2}\). With only \(w\le3k-3\) from the lemma the exponent is \((k-3)n+O(k^2+k\log m)\): the bound diverges from \(k=4\) on. The pattern responsible is \(k-1\) three-spaces in general position and one more inside their span, which is cheap to have and, for \(k\ge3\), is not a circuit, a sum of trivectors of independent three-spaces having full support by contractions as in part (b), an argument I have not written out for general \(k\); the union bound cannot tell. It needs a better span bound.

Proposition (small circuit union bound, conditional). Suppose that for some \(1\le\alpha<2\) and \(\beta\), every circuit of \(k\) three-spaces over \(\mathbb F_2\) spans at most \(\alpha k+\beta\) dimensions. Put \(k_1=\max\{1,\lfloor2\beta/(2-\alpha)\rfloor+1\}\). Then for every \(C\) there is \(\epsilon>0\) such that for \(m\le n^C\) the expected number of circuits of size between \(k_1\) and \(\epsilon n\) among \(m\) independent uniform planes tends to zero.

Proof. For \(k\le\epsilon n\) with \(\epsilon\) small, \(w=\lfloor\alpha k+\beta\rfloor\le n\). By the display the logarithm of the expected number at size \(k\) is at most \[k\log_2(em)+(\alpha k+\beta)n+2+k(3\alpha k+3\beta-2n-2+\log_2c_0)=-\bigl((2-\alpha)k-\beta\bigr)n+3\alpha k^2+kL+2,\] with \(L=\log_2(em)+3\beta-2+\log_2c_0=O(\log n)\). Take \(\epsilon\) with \(3\alpha\epsilon\le(2-\alpha)/4\) and \(n\) so large that \(L\le(2-\alpha)n/4\). Then \(3\alpha k^2+kL\le(2-\alpha)kn/2\) and the exponent is at most \(-\bigl((2-\alpha)k/2-\beta\bigr)n+2\), which for \(k\ge k_1\) is at most \(-\eta n+2\) with \(\eta=(2-\alpha)k_1/2-\beta>0\). Summing over \(k\le\epsilon n\) gives at most \(\epsilon n\,2^{-\eta n+2}\to0\). \(\square\)

The hypothesis. I conjecture that a circuit of \(k\) three-spaces spans at most \(k+1\) dimensions, by analogy with circuits of \(k\) vectors spanning \(k-1\). It holds for \(k=2\) (span three) and \(k=3\) (span four) by the lemma. For \(k=4\) and \(5\) the reviewer ran an exhaustive search in \(\mathbb F_2^6\), \(\mathbb F_2^7\), \(\mathbb F_2^8\) with the first two three-spaces fixed by their intersection type and reports largest spans five and six, with a hand reduction, which I have not verified, that these dimensions settle both sizes; the run is the reviewer's and is not archived here, so I record it as a report and queue its reproduction. It also notes that gluing two circuits along a shared three-space preserves the excess \(w-k-1\), so a counterexample would be a circuit not obtained by gluing. The bound is for \(\mathbb F_2\). With \(\alpha=\beta=1\) the proposition covers sizes from three to \(\epsilon n\), and size two is the exact count of part (c).

What would remain. Circuits larger than \(\epsilon n\). For those the span may be all of \(V\) and the union bound over spans says nothing; heuristically the count is the generic one, \(2^{(n-2)k-N}\) per choice of rows, and summing it needs the tail bound of the last entry in some form. So even with the span conjecture this is half a proof.

10 October 2026 — A circuit of three-spaces with a decomposable partial sum splits into two smaller circuits with subadditive excess, so a least counterexample to the span bound has no two members meeting in a plane; every circuit of four is such a splitting and spans at most five

Working proofs of a lemma and of the span bound at size four; the span bound in general, and regularity at degree three, are not proved. Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement: does a circuit of \(k\) three-spaces over \(\mathbb F_2\) span at most \(k+1\) dimensions, the hypothesis of prop:small-circuit-union-bound?

New mathematics. lem:circuit-gluing-excess: if a circuit splits into two parts of size at least two whose partial sum is the trivector of a three-space \(Q\), then each part with \(Q\) is a smaller circuit and the excess \(w-k-1\) of the whole is at most the sum of the two excesses. So in a counterexample of least size no partial sum over a part of size between \(2\) and \(k-2\) is decomposable; in particular no two of its three-spaces meet in a plane. prop:four-circuit-span: every circuit of four three-spaces has two members meeting in a plane, splits into two pencils, and spans four or five dimensions, by a case analysis using the support of a sum of two trivectors. The bound for \(k\ge5\) is open; for \(k=5\) there is the reviewer's unarchived search.

Goal progress. Unchanged. The span conjecture is proved through size four and reduced to circuits without plane intersections; regularity at degree three is not proved.

General statement. lem:circuit-gluing-excess, for all circuits of three-spaces over \(\mathbb F_2\); the claim under test is the span hypothesis of prop:small-circuit-union-bound with \(\alpha=\beta=1\).

Two facts about sums of two trivectors

For a trivector \(\tau\) let \(\operatorname{supp}\tau\) be the smallest subspace \(Y\) with \(\tau\in\Lambda^3Y\); it is the span of the vectors obtained from \(\tau\) by contracting with two functionals, and \(\tau=[P]\) for a three-space exactly when the support has dimension three. Let \(P_1\ne P_2\) be three-spaces and \(\tau=[P_1]+[P_2]\).

  • If \(\dim(P_1\cap P_2)=2\), \(\tau=[P']\) for the third three-space through \(P_1\cap P_2\) in \(P_1+P_2\) (the last entry).
  • If \(P_1\cap P_2=\langle a\rangle\), \(\tau=a\wedge\omega\) with \(\omega=b\wedge c+d\wedge e\) of rank four, \(a,b,c,d,e\) independent; \(\operatorname{supp}\tau=P_1+P_2\), of dimension five, since contractions give \(a\) and each of \(b,c,d,e\) modulo \(a\); and the vectors \(v\) with \(v\wedge\tau=0\) are \(0\) and \(a\): for \(v\notin\langle a\rangle\) inside the support, \(v\wedge\omega\ne0\) modulo \(a\), a bivector of rank four on a four-space being annihilated by no nonzero vector, and for \(v\) outside the support \(v\wedge\tau\ne0\).
  • If \(P_1\cap P_2=0\), \(\operatorname{supp}\tau=P_1\oplus P_2\), of dimension six, by contractions dual to a basis adapted to the sum; and the vectors \(v\) of the support for which \(v\wedge\tau\) is the four-vector of a four-space are exactly the nonzero vectors of \(P_1\cup P_2\): for \(v=v_1+v_2\) with both components nonzero, \(v\wedge\tau=v_2\wedge[P_1]+v_1\wedge[P_2]\) is a sum of the four-vectors of \(P_1+\langle v_2\rangle\) and \(P_2+\langle v_1\rangle\), which meet in the plane \(\langle v_1,v_2\rangle\); it equals \(v_1\wedge v_2\wedge(x\wedge y+z\wedge u)\) with a bivector of rank four on a complement, so its support has dimension six.

Gluing

Notation of the last entry: a circuit \((P_r)_{r\in S}\), \(|S|=k\), spans \(W\) of dimension \(w\); its excess is \(e=w-k-1\). The span conjecture is \(e\le0\).

That gluing two circuits along a shared three-space preserves the excess was noted by the reviewer of the last entry. The lemma proves the splitting direction; that every gluing is a circuit is not proved here.

Lemma (circuit gluing excess). Let \(S=S'\sqcup S''\) with \(|S'|,|S''|\ge2\) and suppose \(\tau=\sum_{r\in S'}[P_r]\) equals \([Q]\) for a three-space \(Q\). Then \(Q\) is none of the \(P_r\); \(C'=(P_r)_{r\in S'}\cup\{Q\}\) and \(C''=(P_r)_{r\in S''}\cup\{Q\}\) are circuits, of sizes \(|S'|+1\) and \(|S''|+1\), both smaller than \(k\); and \(e(C)\le e(C')+e(C'')\). Consequently, if the span conjecture fails, a circuit of least size with positive excess has no part \(S'\) with \(2\le|S'|\le k-2\) and decomposable partial sum, and no two of its three-spaces meet in a plane.

Proof. If \(Q=P_r\) with \(r\in S'\), then \(S'\setminus\{r\}\) is a nonempty proper subset of \(S\) with zero sum; if \(r\in S''\), then \(S'\cup\{r\}\) has zero sum and is proper as \(|S''|\ge2\); both contradict minimality. \(C'\) has zero sum. A proper nonempty subset of \(C'\) with zero sum either avoids \(Q\), and is a proper nonempty subset of \(S\) with zero sum, or contains \(Q\) with a proper subset \(S_0\subsetneq S'\), and then \(\sum_{S'\setminus S_0}[P_r]=0\) with \(S'\setminus S_0\) nonempty; so \(C'\) is a circuit, and likewise \(C''\), using \(\sum_{S''}[P_r]=[Q]\). Their sizes are less than \(k\) because the other part has at least two members. By the overlap lemma \(Q\subseteq W_{S'}\cap W_{S''}\), so the spans of \(C'\) and \(C''\) are \(W_{S'}\) and \(W_{S''}\), and \(w\le\dim W_{S'}+\dim W_{S''}-3\). Hence \(e(C)=w-k-1\le(\dim W_{S'}-|S'|-2)+(\dim W_{S''}-|S''|-2)=e(C')+e(C'')\). For the consequence, take a circuit of least size with \(e>0\); a part as described would give two smaller circuits, with \(e\le0\) by leastness, and \(e(C)\le0\). Two three-spaces meeting in a plane form a part of size two with decomposable sum, and \(k\ge4\) since circuits of size two and three have excess zero. \(\square\)

Circuits of four

Proposition (four circuit span). Every circuit of four three-spaces over \(\mathbb F_2\) has two members meeting in a plane, hence splits by the lemma into two circuits of size three, and spans four or five dimensions.

Proof. Write \([P_1]+[P_2]=[P_3]+[P_4]=\tau\); the four are distinct and \(\tau\ne0\). If some pair, say \(P_1,P_2\), meets in a plane, \(\tau=[Q]\) and by the lemma the circuit splits into two circuits of size three, each spanning four dimensions and sharing \(Q\): \(w\le4+4-3=5\), and \(w\ge4\) as \(P_1\ne P_2\). Suppose now that every pair meets in dimension at most one; this cannot happen. If \(P_1\cap P_2=0\), the support of \(\tau\) has dimension six, so \(P_3,P_4\), which do not meet in a plane, are disjoint with \(P_3\oplus P_4=P_1\oplus P_2\), by the facts applied to both representations; and by the last statement of the third fact \(P_1\cup P_2=P_3\cup P_4\) as sets of vectors, which forces \(\{P_3,P_4\}=\{P_1,P_2\}\): the seven nonzero vectors of \(P_3\) cannot be covered by two proper subspaces of it, of at most three nonzero vectors each. This contradicts distinctness. If \(P_1\cap P_2=\langle a\rangle\), the support of \(\tau\) has dimension five, so \(P_3\cap P_4\) is a line, and by the annihilator statement of the second fact applied to both representations that line is \(\langle a\rangle\). Modulo \(a\), \(\tau\) becomes \([L]+[M]\) for the planes \(L=P_1/a\), \(M=P_2/a\) of the four-space \(L\oplus M\), and equally \([P_3/a]+[P_4/a]\). \(P_3/a\) meets \(L\) and \(M\) trivially, as \(P_3\) meets \(P_1\) and \(P_2\) in dimension at most one, so it is the graph of an isomorphism \(L\to M\), and its bivector is \([L]+[M]\) plus terms in \(L\wedge M\); likewise \(P_4/a\). Their sum has no component in \(\Lambda^2L\oplus\Lambda^2M\), in characteristic two, and cannot equal \([L]+[M]\). (This case was shown empty by the reviewer; my draft had wrongly counted it as the source of span five.) \(\square\)

Both values occur. Span four: in \(\mathbb F_2^4\) three-spaces are the kernels of nonzero functionals and \(\Lambda^3\) is the dual space, so the kernels of \(f_1,f_2,f_3\) independent and of \(f_1+f_2+f_3\) form a circuit. Span five: \(\langle a,b,c\rangle\), \(\langle a,b+d,c\rangle\), \(\langle a,d,e\rangle\), \(\langle a,d,c+e\rangle\), the first two and the last two each summing to \(a\wedge c\wedge d\) (the reviewer's example). With the lemma, a counterexample to the span conjecture has size at least five and pairwise intersections of dimension at most one.

State of the degree-three question

For random rows of width two at \(m\le(1/6-\epsilon)n^2\): circuits of size two and three have expected numbers of order \(m^22^{-n}\) and \(m^32^{-2n}\); circuits of size four span at most five dimensions, and by the displayed union bound of the last entry at \(w=5\), \(k=4\), whose exponent is \(4\log_2m-3n+O(1)\), their expected number is \(o(1)\); sizes from five to \(\epsilon n\) are excluded if the span conjecture holds, which is proved to size four; sizes beyond \(\epsilon n\) need a count that is not in hand. No part of this reaches the width or the degree that the two-level form needs.

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement: is there a mechanism giving every polynomial cover of \(\mathbb F_2^n\) by affine subspaces a refutation of degree below \(n/2\) by a margin like the model's \(n/\log^2n\), independent of the class of the cover?

New mathematics. prop:row-algebra-ceiling. For a cover by subspaces of codimension at most \(w\) with indicators \(R_r\), let \(I\subseteq\{0,1\}^M\) be the set of incidence patterns of points and \(t^*\) the least degree of a polynomial over \(\mathbb F_2\) in \(M\) variables that vanishes at \(0\) and equals \(1\) on \(I\). Then the cover is refuted in degree \(w\,t^*\). Two bounds on \(t^*\): at most the largest number of rows through a point, which is contained in the recorded lem:violated-rows-ceiling; and at most \(2^{\tau+1}-1\), \(\tau\) the largest 2-adic valuation of the number of rows through a point, which extends the recorded statement that odd covers are refuted in degree \(w\). Dually, \(t^*>t\) exactly when an odd set of points meets every intersection of at most \(t\) rows evenly. No ceiling near half for general covers follows: for random dense covers the two explicit bounds exceed \(n\) by a heuristic count, and \(t^*\) itself is not evaluated.

Goal progress. Unchanged. A necessary condition on candidates is added, weaker than what is needed to change the goal.

General statement. prop:row-algebra-ceiling, for every cover of \(\mathbb F_2^n\) by affine subspaces, every \(M\) and \(w\).

Polynomials in the rows

A cover: affine subspaces \(V_1,\ldots,V_M\) of \(\mathbb F_2^n\) of codimension \(w_r\le w\) with union everything; \(R_r\) the indicator of \(V_r\), a product of \(w_r\) affine forms; the system is \(R_r=0\) for all \(r\) with the Boolean axioms, \(C_D\) its closure. For a point \(x\) let \(\rho(x)\in\{0,1\}^M\) be its incidence pattern, \(\rho_r(x)=R_r(x)\), \(c(x)\) its weight, the number of rows through \(x\), and \(I=\{\rho(x)\}\); \(0\notin I\) because the subspaces cover.

Proposition (row algebra ceiling). Let \(p\in\mathbb F_2[z_1,\ldots,z_M]\) have degree \(t\), after reduction by \(z_i^2=z_i\), with \(p(0)=0\) and \(p(y)=1\) for all \(y\in I\). Then \(1\in C_{tw}\). With \(t^*(I)\) the least such \(t\): the system has a PC refutation of degree at most \(w\,t^*(I)\). Moreover:

  1. \(t^*\le c_{\max}=\max_xc(x)\).
  2. \(t^*\le2^{\tau+1}-1\), where \(\tau=\max_xv_2(c(x))\) and \(v_2\) is the 2-adic valuation.
  3. \(t^*>t\) if and only if there is a set \(X\) of points of odd size such that for every nonempty set \(A\) of at most \(t\) rows, \(\bigcap_{r\in A}V_r\) contains an even number of points of \(X\).

Proof. Each monomial \(z_A\) of \(p\), \(A\ne\emptyset\), \(|A|\le t\), gives \(\prod_{r\in A}R_r\), a multiple of the axiom \(R_{r_0}\), \(r_0\in A\), by a product of at most \((t-1)w\) affine forms, so it is derived within degree \(tw\) by multiplying one variable at a time and reducing by the Boolean axioms; \(p(R_1,\ldots,R_M)\) is a sum of these and is the function \(x\mapsto p(\rho(x))=1\). A polynomial of degree at most \(tw\) lying in \(C_{tw}\) and equal to the constant \(1\) as a function has multilinear form \(1\), so \(1\in C_{tw}\). (1) Take \(p=\sum_{1\le|A|\le c_{\max}}z_A\): on a pattern of weight \(u\) with \(1\le u\le c_{\max}\) its value is \(\sum_{j=1}^u\binom uj=2^u-1\), odd. (2) Let \(e_j\) be the elementary symmetric polynomial of degree \(j\) in \(z\). On a pattern of weight \(u\), \(e_{2^j}=\binom u{2^j}\), which modulo two is the \(j\)-th binary digit of \(u\) by Lucas's theorem. Take \(p=1+\prod_{j=0}^{\tau}(1+e_{2^j})\), reduced by \(z_i^2=z_i\), of degree at most \(\sum_{j\le\tau}2^j=2^{\tau+1}-1\), with \(p(0)=0\); on a pattern of weight \(u\ge1\) it is \(1\) unless the digits \(0,\ldots,\tau\) of \(u\) all vanish, which would mean \(v_2(u)>\tau\). (3) \(t^*>t\) says that every polynomial of degree at most \(t\) vanishing on \(I\) vanishes at \(0\) (apply this to \(1+p\)), that is, evaluation at \(0\) on polynomials of degree at most \(t\) is a combination of evaluations at points of \(I\): a subset \(J\subseteq I\) with \(\sum_{y\in J}m(y)=m(0)\) for every monomial \(m=z_A\), \(|A|\le t\). For \(A=\emptyset\) this says \(|J|\) is odd; for \(A\ne\emptyset\), that an even number of \(y\in J\) contain \(A\). Choosing one point \(x\) with \(\rho(x)=y\) for each \(y\in J\) gives \(X\); conversely a set \(X\) as stated gives \(J\) as the patterns occurring an odd number of times in \(X\). \(\square\)

Relation to the record. Part (1) is weaker than lem:violated-rows-ceiling, which has the rank of the forms of the rows through a point in place of \(w\,c(x)\), by the same product expansion; that lemma applies because a subspace row is a relation on \(w_r\) independent forms. The same refinement holds here: the degree of the product over \(A\) is at most the rank of the forms of the rows in \(A\), and monomials \(z_A\) with \(\bigcap_{r\in A}V_r=\emptyset\) give zero and may be ignored, so a weighted form of \(t^*\) can be much smaller (the reviewer's remark, not developed here). Part (2) at \(\tau=0\) is part (c) of lem:cover-sum-gap, odd covers. The proposition is the restriction of the static span to products of rows, and part (3) is the corresponding restriction of prop:local-design-criterion: a functional \(\sum_{x\in X}\mathrm{ev}_x\) with value one at \(1\) killing all products of at most \(t\) rows. So nothing here is stronger than the static span; the content is the two explicit bounds and the condition in (3). A registry search for multiplicity, incidence patterns and valuations of covers found only the two lemmas named.

What it requires of a candidate, and what it does not give

A cover with no refutation at degree \(D\) must have \(t^*>D/w\): some point in more than \(D/w\) rows, in fact a point whose number of rows is divisible by a power of two exceeding \(D/(2w)\), and an odd set of points meeting evenly every intersection of at most \(D/w\) rows. For \(D\) near \(n/2\) and \(w=O(\log n)\) this asks for multiplicities of order \(n/\log n\). A general cover has mean multiplicity at least one and no more is forced. Covers by \(M\) subspaces of one codimension \(w\) with \(M\) at the first-moment count \(n\ln2/(-\ln(1-2^{-w}))\) have mean multiplicity \(M2^{-w}\ge(1-2^{-w})n\ln2\), so for them the condition on multiplicity holds on average; and for random such covers, heuristically, the realized multiplicities fill an interval of length of order \(n\), so some point has valuation about \(\log_2n\) and the bounds \(w\,c_{\max}\) and \(w(2^{\tau+1}-1)\) exceed \(n\). The condition in (3) is the informative one and I have not evaluated it for any class.

On the review's question. The model assigns the classes it was applied to a deficit of order \(n/\log^2n\) or more (prop:same-sign-saddle-bound, thm:saddle-deficit-bound). The ceilings in the record that hold for all covers are static certificates: lem:violated-rows-ceiling and this proposition are built from products of rows and governed by how much meets at a point, which for dense covers is of order \(n\), so those two are void there; prop:transversal-rank-ceiling uses fibre indicators times combinations of rows and is governed by a transversal rank, with recorded instances at \(n/2+2\), and is not void but gives no deficit either. The model's deficit has another source, a count of dimensions of the static span, which becomes a ceiling only if the span is as large as counted, the content of conj:cumulative-index-span for random rows. I found no derivation mechanism that would give a deficit for an arbitrary polynomial cover, and no cover for which a deficit is excluded. The question is not answered, in either direction.
