Chosen. The ceiling check bears on the family statement through the question whether any cover can be hard above half; it continues the spell begun in the last entry, taken before the head under the user's permission to select the order (9 October 2026), because the last review put this question on the path.

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement: does a known lower bound for CNFs of logarithmic width refute conj:covering-half-ceiling, degree at most \(\lceil n/2\rceil+w\) over \(\mathbb F_2\), and do the formulas of the strongest known width bounds supply candidates?

New mathematics. Two lemmas. lem:parity-width-degree-bound: a refutation in resolution over parities of width \(W\) gives a PC refutation over \(\mathbb F_2\) of degree at most \(W+1\). lem:gadget-lift-degree-bound: if a CNF \(\psi\) of width \(m\) on \(n\) variables has PC degree \(d\) over \(\mathbb F_2\), its lift by gadgets of degree at most \(\gamma\) on blocks of \(\ell\) variables has degree at most \(\max\{m\ell,(d+1)\gamma\}\); so the ratio of degree to the number of variables does not exceed \(\max\{m,d+1\}/n\), and for parity gadgets the degree is at most \(\max\{m\ell,d+1\}\). Read, not verified: Efremenko and Itsykson (ECCC TR25-188, Corollary 8.4) state, for each fixed \(\epsilon\), CNFs of width \(O(\log n\cdot\mathrm{poly}(1/\epsilon))\) and size \(n^{\mathrm{poly}(1/\epsilon)}\) on \(N=O(n\log n/\epsilon)\) variables, \(n\) the base parameter, whose every refutation in resolution over parities has width at least \((1-\epsilon)N\). Outcome: no bound I found refutes the half ceiling; if that statement is right, those formulas have no parity-resolution refutation of width \(cN+o(N)\), \(c<1-\epsilon\), so the first lemma cannot be the route to a ceiling for them; and lifted formulas are candidates only if their bases already are.

Goal progress. Unchanged. No family is obtained and the ceiling stays undecided.

General statement. lem:parity-width-degree-bound and lem:gadget-lift-degree-bound, for all CNFs, widths and gadgets; the statement under test is conj:covering-half-ceiling.

Width in resolution over parities bounds degree from above

Resolution over parities, as defined in the source: lines are linear clauses \(C=\bigvee_i(f_i=a_i)\) over \(\mathbb F_2\); the resolution rule derives \(C\vee D\) from \(C\vee(f=a)\) and \(D\vee(f=a+1)\); weakening derives any \(D\) semantically implied by \(C\); the width of \(C\) is the rank of the system \(\neg C\), and of a refutation the largest width of a line. For a linear clause \(C\) let \(A_C\) be the affine subspace of solutions of \(\neg C\), the assignments falsifying \(C\), and \(P_C\) its indicator, a product of \(\operatorname{codim}A_C\) affine forms, or \(0\) if \(A_C=\emptyset\). For a clause of a CNF, \(P_C\) is its clause polynomial.

Lemma (parity width degree bound). If a CNF has a refutation in resolution over parities of width \(W\), then its clause polynomials with the Boolean axioms have a PC refutation over \(\mathbb F_2\) of degree at most \(W+1\).

Proof. Derive \(P_C\) for every line, in multilinear form, within degree \(W+1\). First, if \(A'\subseteq A\) are affine subspaces, the indicator of \(A'\) is that of \(A\) times \(\operatorname{codim}A'-\operatorname{codim}A\) affine forms; multiplying by one form at a time and reducing by the Boolean axioms, every intermediate polynomial is the indicator of an intermediate subspace, so the derivation stays within degree \(\operatorname{codim}A'\). Weakening: \(C\models D\) means \(A_D\subseteq A_C\), and \(\operatorname{codim}A_D\le W\). Resolution: put \(E=C\vee D\), so \(A_E=A_C\cap A_D\), of codimension at most \(W\) or empty. The subspace \(A_E\cap\{f=a+1\}\) lies in \(A_{C\vee(f=a)}=A_C\cap\{f=a+1\}\), and \(A_E\cap\{f=a\}\) in \(A_{D\vee(f=a+1)}\); their indicators \(P_E\cdot(f+a)\) and \(P_E\cdot(f+a+1)\) are derived from the two premises within degree \(W+1\), and their sum is \(P_E\). The empty clause has \(A=\mathbb F_2^N\) and \(P=1\). \(\square\)

So the direction is one way: degree is at most width plus one, and a width lower bound for resolution over parities gives no degree lower bound. This is the comparison the two-level entry described in terms of lines; here it is stated for width and degree.

Lifts keep the ratio of the base

Let \(\psi\) be a CNF of width \(m\) on \(y_1,\ldots,y_n\) and \(g_i:\{0,1\}^\ell\to\{0,1\}\) gadgets on disjoint blocks \(X_i\) of \(\ell\) variables, of degree at most \(\gamma\le\ell\) as multilinear polynomials over \(\mathbb F_2\). The lift replaces \(y_i\) by \(g_i(X_i)\) and writes each lifted clause as a CNF on the variables of its at most \(m\) blocks; \(N=n\ell\).

Lemma (gadget lift degree bound). If \(\psi\) has a PC refutation of degree \(d\) over \(\mathbb F_2\), the lift has one of degree at most \(\max\{m\ell,(d+1)\gamma\}\). Hence its degree divided by \(N\) is at most \(\max\{m,d+1\}/n\); for parity gadgets, \(\gamma=1\), the degree is at most \(\max\{m\ell,d+1\}\le\max\{m\ell,n+1\}\).

Proof. For a clause \(C\) of \(\psi\), \(P_C(g)\) is a function of at most \(m\ell\) variables vanishing wherever the CNF of the lifted clause holds. On a cube of \(t\) variables every such function is derived from the clauses of that CNF in degree \(t\): each falsifying point falsifies a clause, whose polynomial times the remaining literals is the indicator of the point. So every \(P_C(g)\) is derived in degree \(m\ell\). Now substitute \(y_i\mapsto g_i\) in the refutation of \(\psi\), kept multilinear in \(y\); a line \(p\) of degree at most \(d\) becomes \(p(g)\), of degree at most \(d\gamma\), and sums of lines become sums. For a step from \(p\) to the multilinear form of \(y_jp\), of degree at most \(d\): write \(p=p_0+y_jp_1\) with \(p_0,p_1\) free of \(y_j\); both have degree at most \(d-1\), because the new line \(y_j(p_0+p_1)\) has degree at most \(d\). The image of the new line is \(g_j\,p(g)\) reduced multilinearly in the \(x\) variables, which realizes \(g_j^2=g_j\). It is obtained from \(p(g)\) as the sum over the monomials \(x_T\) of \(g_j\), \(|T|\le\gamma\), of \(x_T\,p(g)\), each reached one variable at a time through polynomials \(x_{T'}p(g)=x_{T'}p_0(g)+x_{T'}g_j\,p_1(g)\), \(T'\subseteq T\), of degree at most \(\max\{(d-1)\gamma+\gamma,\ 2\gamma+(d-1)\gamma\}=(d+1)\gamma\). \(\square\)

The lemma needs the lifted clauses written as CNFs on the block variables alone; it does not cover encodings with extension variables. The field plays no role in it. For parity gadgets the lift's degree is also at least \(d\): setting all but one variable of each block to zero restricts the lift to a formula equivalent to \(\psi\) clause by clause (the reviewer's remark; a restriction does not raise degree).

Applied to the literature, as far as I read it. (a) The formulas of the source's Corollary 2.10 are \(\psi\circ\oplus_k\) with \(\psi\) an \(m\)-CNF of resolution width \((1-\delta)n\), which the source takes as its Lemma 2.9 from its reference [9], a paper of Bonacina and Talebanfard that I could not retrieve; the corollary states size bounds \(2^{(1-o_\ell(1))N}\) for resolution refutations free of certain long paths, not a width bound for the lift. These formulas have \(\mathbb F_2\) degree at most \(\max\{mk,N/k+1\}\), a fraction about \(1/k\) of \(N\) for large \(N\), below one half once \(k\ge3\); \(k\) is fixed with the width. (b) The formulas of Corollary 8.4 lift the same \(\psi\), an \(m_1\)-CNF, by a collection of gadgets on \(\ell=O(\log n/\epsilon)\) bits with a surjectivity property, which exists by the source's Theorem 5.8; by that corollary their parity-resolution width is at least \((1-\epsilon)N\), and by the lemma their degree is at most \(\ell\max\{m_1,d_\psi+1\}\), a fraction \((d_\psi+1)/n\) of \(N\) at most for large \(n\). Whether \(d_\psi/n\) exceeds one half for these \(\psi\), of constant width, is the family statement itself for one class with deficit zero; I know no lower bound of that strength and have not read the definition of \(\psi\).

What this says about the ceiling

  • No refutation. A width lower bound for resolution over parities does not contradict a degree ceiling at half, by the direction of the first lemma; and example (a) shows formulas with size bounds of the strongest known form for restricted resolution whose \(\mathbb F_2\) degree is a small fraction of \(N\).
  • One route excluded for one class. If Corollary 8.4 is right, its formulas have no parity-resolution refutation of width below \((1-\epsilon)N\), so a ceiling for them cannot come through the first lemma. Nothing more is shown: a derivation that charges no degree for affine consequences, as the adaptive conditioning of the induction attempt does, is not bounded below by that width, and I draw no conclusion about that attempt.
  • No candidate from lifting alone. By the second lemma a lift's ratio is at most \(\max\{m,d+1\}/n\): the base must itself have degree above \(n/2\), up to the width term.
  • Not done: the weighted form of the row-algebra bound on a dense cover, named as a next step. Every product of rows is a multiple of a row within the degree, so the bound is a restriction of the static span, as stated with prop:row-algebra-ceiling; the static span was measured on dense random covers in the index-span runs. I dropped the step for that reason; the reviewer did not verify the reason.

Specification decision. No clause added. Two screening remarks are recorded for candidates: width in resolution over parities near the number of variables is not evidence of degree near half, and a candidate obtained by a gadget lift on block variables alone needs a base with \(\max\{m,d+1\}>n/2\) in ratio; the accepted specification already demands the barrier of the formula itself, so nothing changes in it.

10 October 2026 — Goal-level review: the block proved lemmas at degree three and two comparison lemmas and left the family statement where it was; the missing thing is a lower-bound method over the binary field, and the next cycles test whether a ceiling of order \(n/\mathrm{polylog}\,n\) below half holds for all polynomial covers

Goal-level route review: one open statement, unchanged across sixty-three research entries. No outside leads or bridges while the queue drains. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort low).

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement: what did the six entries since the last review change, was the allocation right, and what is the next test on the highest-risk item?

Architecture test. The last review's decisive test had two parts and both were run in the entry after it: two levels of the transfer contain resolution over parities, whose unrestricted size bounds are open, so the two-level form became the working endpoint; and regularity at degree three for rows of width two was reduced to a moment condition and not proved.

New mathematics. None in this review. The block's results are listed below with their anchors.

Goal progress. Unchanged. No family, no lower bound beyond a quarter of the free dimension, no ceiling.

General statement. The line's claim is the open statement near-half-pc-family: polynomial-length CNFs with auxiliary affine equations, of free dimension \(n\), with no PC refutation over \(\mathbb F_2\) at \(\lfloor n/2-s\rfloor\), \(s+w\le n^{1-\epsilon}\). The main goal needs exactly this with the proved transfer; for a single depth, \((s+w)(\log n)^{\ell-2}=o(n)\).

Across the goal

  • Entries covered: two-level worth and the moment criterion; isotropic plane count; circuits of three-spaces; splitting and size four; row algebra ceiling; parity width comparison.
  • What they obtained. The two-level form is worth having. At degree three and width two: a criterion, exact first and second moments of the kill probability, the description of dependencies as circuits, their classification to size four, and a conditional union bound; regularity there is not proved, the span bound from size five and all large circuits being open. A class-independent certificate from polynomials in the rows, weaker than the static span. Width in resolution over parities bounds degree from above only, and a gadget lift is at best as good as its base. One preprint read, unverified.
  • What they did not obtain. Anything at a degree growing with \(n\); any lower bound over \(\mathbb F_2\) beyond those recorded; any ceiling below half for all covers.

Obstacle

The line is stuck on one thing: there is no method for lower bounds on PC degree over \(\mathbb F_2\) that reaches half of the free dimension. In the independent reviewer's opinion no new family will supply one. The methods on record: expansion, whose certified degree stayed below about \(n/4\) in the random models examined, with no proved cap; the binomial criterion, for systems whose degree is at most \(\min\{n/3,n/4+w\}+o(n)\), multiplicative systems that are not flows being open in short encodings; and colon regularity, a sufficient criterion whose reach is the product index, conjecturally about \((1/2-\ln k/k)n\) for clauses of width \(k\), and which is not proved for random rows even at degree three and width two. On the other side, no ceiling below \(n/2\) is proved for all polynomial covers, so the endpoint is not known to be inconsistent either. The block worked on the smallest case of the third method and on the second question, and settled neither.

Architecture review

Necessary target. Unchanged: the family of the general statement above; sufficient by the proved transfer, not shown necessary. The two-level form, \(s+w=o(n)\), is a weaker target that the transfer turns into a bound for a system containing resolution over parities.

Extra requirements. The route through colon regularity asks for more than the target: regularity is exact agreement of a quotient with a product series at every degree up to \(D\), where the target asks only that one polynomial, the constant, stay outside the closure. The count attempted for it must be right up to a factor \(1+o(1)\). A weaker demand, that no functional of a restricted kind kills the span, has not been formulated. The ceiling question asks for a deficit of order \(n/\mathrm{polylog}\,n\) for all polynomial covers; that would cut the every-depth form. A ceiling only for covers by rows of logarithmic codimension would not: such rows may cover all but a polynomially small measure, with rows of codimension up to \(n^{1-\epsilon}\) finishing the cover, and a reduction from the general case to the narrow one is not on record.

Independent alternative. Before seeing this route the review's medium reviewer received the goal and the available results (stage-one-brief.txt) and answered (independent-review.txt): no materially different architecture. It tried one, binary-encoded pigeonhole with the pigeon argument, and killed it: querying the top bit of every pigeon and keeping the majority side gives resolution width \(O(n)\) on \(n\log n\) variables, hence degree \(o(N)\) by the width lemma; I checked that count and agree: at level \(j\) one holds \(j+1\) bits of about \(n/2^j+1\) pigeons, at most \(n+2\) in all. It concluded that a new architecture needs a new lower-bound method over \(\mathbb F_2\), not a new family. It would spend the next cycles deciding whether the endpoint is consistent: prove or refute a ceiling \(n/2-n/\mathrm{polylog}\,n\) for all polynomial covers, starting by turning the reason behind thm:saddle-deficit-bound into an actual refutation for dependent covers, padded ones first; and it named what would change its mind, a dependent cover whose exact degree exceeds the cumulative product index of independent rows with the same profile by more than a constant. Of this block it judged the level-one identification, the two comparison lemmas and the reading defensible; the degree-three work, the criterion and the three entries after it, not defensible for this goal, serving only the two-level form at its first nontrivial degree; the row algebra ceiling of low value; and the half ceiling \(n/2+w\) mis-aimed, its threshold being the wrong one. It said the goal is not reachable by anything on record as it stands. My comparison with this route: the reviewer recommends the ceiling side, where the last review turned to the lower-bound side and left the ceiling for the cycle after; it rejects how the block was spent.

Rank normalization. Applies to the ceiling question. The static span of \(M\) rows is compared with \(B_{\le D}\) in the same Boolean quotient, and by the dimension count it can be all of it near half only when the covering sum is at least \(1+c\,sw/n\), for \(s\) at least about \(\sqrt n\). The count is neither a lower bound nor a ceiling: not a lower bound, because the constant can lie in a proper span, an exact partition having covering sum one and degree \(w\); not a ceiling, because the dimension inequality does not imply that the span is full. For regularity the count is in the graded quotient, as the last review noted.

Decision. I accept the reviewer's assessment of the allocation in part. The degree-three work was the second part of the last review's decisive test, "state and attempt"; the entry after the review attempted it and did not complete it, and the entry on the moments computed what the criterion needs, which is arguable either way. The two entries on circuits classified small dependencies with no prospect of reaching growing degree and were not justified. The second error is the one the reviewer asked about: the last review posed the ceiling of order \(n/\log^2n\) for the cycle after its test. The first ceiling entry asked that question and found no mechanism; the second went back to the threshold \(n/2+w\), which is the wrong one. So what follows is a return to the posed question, not a new aim: the next cycles go to a class-independent ceiling of order \(n/\mathrm{polylog}\,n\) below half, under the ceiling check, which is not the queue's head and is taken with a Chosen paragraph as the queue rules allow. The goal is not changed and not parked. The two-level endpoint stays the working endpoint; it does not give the goal, and the ceiling test does not touch it, a deficit of that order being \(o(n)\); work on it resumes only with an argument that says something at degree growing with \(n\). The lifted formulas of the preprint get a cycle only if their base is not a flow system, which needs the source requested from the user.

Decisive test. Next cycle, two parts. First, the reviewer's comparison, with the series \((1+z)^n\bigl(1-(z/(1+z))^w\bigr)^M\) for \(M\) independent rows of codimension \(w\), its graded index the first non-positive coefficient and its cumulative index the first non-positive partial sum, computed by a committed tool. One size cannot decide "more than a constant": for the orbit cover at \(n=18\) (342 rows, codimension four, degree exactly six) the reviewer's hand count gives graded index six and cumulative index seven, unverified by me. So the comparison is posed on the sequence of recorded covers with known exact degree (\(n=10\), \(18\), and the measured random covers), and it counts as answered in the negative if none exceeds its cumulative index. Second, the attempt: for a polynomial cover, derive from the isoperimetric inequality behind thm:saddle-deficit-bound, which suggests a deficit of order \(n\ln w/w\) under its hypothesis of covering sum at least \(n/2\), or from prop:same-sign-saddle-bound, which suggests \(n/w^2\), an actual certificate, first for padded covers and for same-sign rows with arbitrary relations, and state the step where dependence among rows or wide rows defeat it. Outcomes: a proof for all polynomial covers ends the every-depth route through this transfer and leaves the low-depth forms; a proof under the theorem's covering-sum hypothesis, or for narrow rows only, or for a class with a named hypothesis, becomes a specification clause and leaves the complementary covers as the search; a failure at a stated step is recorded with the cover that causes it; a dependent cover above its cumulative index makes structured relations the search.

Falsification attempt on this line

The claim: some polynomial-size family is hard within \(n^{1-\epsilon}\) of half over \(\mathbb F_2\). Against it after this block: binary pigeonhole, the one further class the reviewer could name, falls far below half by a width argument; lifted formulas inherit at best the ratio of their bases; the reviewer's general remark that polynomially many rows force logarithmic codimension on most of the measure, where the recorded methods have certified nothing beyond a quarter or are bounded by the product index. For it: no ceiling below half is proved for all covers, and two attempts at a class-independent mechanism, the conditioning inductions and the row algebra, found none. Neither side has a proof.

Reading. In no case is the degree above the cumulative index; in eight it equals it (both orbit covers; \(7{:}2{:}13\), \(8{:}2{:}15\), \(9{:}2{:}17\), \(10{:}2{:}14\), \(10{:}2{:}15\), \(7{:}3{:}21\)). Covers with few rows fall far below an index that the series does not even reach: for them the model permits hardness and they are easy for another reason, few rows through any point. The reviewer's hand count of a cumulative index seven at \(n=18\) was off by one; the tool gives six, and the test checks the coefficients by hand. The reviewer ran all 93 distinct combinations of \(n\), \(w\), size and degree in the saved series: none above the cumulative index, ten equal, the graded index exceeded only at \(10{:}2{:}15\); the table shows the extremes. Scope: a finite check at small sizes; at \(n=7\) to \(9\) every restart of that search has degree \(w+1\), which may reflect its reach; the orbit cover at \(n=18\) has independent multiples below its index and so barely tests dependence; "more than a constant" cannot be decided at these sizes, only that nothing on record points that way.

The certificate attempt

Setting: a cover of \(\mathbb F_2^n\) by affine subspaces \(V_1,\ldots,V_M\) of codimension at most \(w\), indicators \(R_r\), static span \(S_D=\sum_rR_rB_{\le D-w_r}\subseteq C_D\).

Proposition (row product error set). For every \(t\ge1\) there are sets of rows \(T_1,\ldots,T_t\) such that \(q=\prod_{i\le t}\bigl(1+\sum_{r\in T_i}R_r\bigr)\) is the indicator of a set \(E\) with \(|E|\le2^{n-t}\). For arbitrary sets of rows \(T_i\), \(q\) is the indicator of a set \(E\) and \(1+1_E\in S_{tw}\). Consequently, for \(D\ge tw\), \(1\in C_D\) if and only if \(1_E\in C_D\).

Proof. Each factor takes values in \(\{0,1\}\), so \(q\) is an indicator. Choose the \(T_i\) independently and uniformly among all sets of rows. A point \(x\) lies in at least one row, so \(\sum_{r\in T_i}R_r(x)\) is a uniform bit and \(\Pr[q(x)=1]=2^{-t}\); the expected size of \(E\) is \(2^{n-t}\) and some choice does not exceed it. Expanding, \(1+q\) is a sum of products of between one and \(t\) rows; a product of rows is zero or the indicator of their intersection, a multiple of one of them by at most \((t-1)w\) affine forms, hence in \(S_{tw}\) after multilinear reduction. The last statement follows from \(S_{tw}\subseteq C_D\). \(\square\)

For \(t=1\) and \(T_1\) all rows this is part (b) of lem:cover-sum-gap, with \(E\) the evenly covered set. It is the approximation of a disjunction by a low-degree polynomial in its terms, in the manner of Razborov and Smolensky, applied to the rows; a registry search for that found no statement for covers.

Where the attempt stops.

  • From approximation to refutation. At degree \(tw\) the cover is refuted outside \(E\). To finish, \(1_E\) must be derived. It has degree at most \(tw\) and support at most \(2^{n-t}\), and each of its points lies in a row; writing \(1_E=\sum_rR_rg_r\) by assigning points to rows gives \(g_r\) of degree up to \(n-w\) in the worst case, and iterating the proposition on \(E\) is the same construction with larger \(t\), whose guarantee empties \(E\) only at \(t>n\). So this argument gives no deficit; I do not show that no polynomial in the rows does, and prop:row-algebra-ceiling records the exact condition for one.
  • From the model to a certificate. The deficit of thm:saddle-deficit-bound and prop:same-sign-saddle-bound is a property of the series of rows whose multiples are independent up to forced relations. The crude count \(M\binom{n-w}{\le D-w}\) is an upper bound for the dimension of the span, so dependence can only lower the span below it; I have no such statement for the alternating series. A refutation does not need a large span, only the constant in the closure, as an exact partition shows; but the model's reason for a refutation at the index is that the span is everything there, and for dependent covers that passage from the count to the span is not justified. It does not always fail: the orbit cover at \(n=10\) has five non-forced relations and its degree equals the index. This restates, for the attempt, the Rank normalization paragraph of the review.
  • Padded covers are not an easier first case. By lem:barely-covering-padding the degree of a padded cover is at least that of the cover inside the subspace, so a ceiling for padded covers in dimension \(n\) gives one for all covers in dimension \(n-w\), with the width larger by \(w\) and the half shifted by \(w/2\).
  • What the table adds. The dependent covers on record are at or below the index; those far below have few rows through a point, where lem:violated-rows-ceiling applies, its hypotheses for affine rows being those of the row algebra entry. A cover above the index would need non-forced relations and, by that lemma, a point through which the rows have joint rank at least the degree. I have neither such a cover nor an argument that none exists.
  • A statement of the reviewer, which I have not verified: in \(\mathbb F_2^3\) the thirteen two-point rows meeting \(\{000,100,010\}\) evenly form a cover with \(1\notin S_2\) while the cumulative index is two, so statically a dependent cover can exceed the index; whether its PC degree does is untested, since the closure may exceed the span. The construction, all subcubes of codimension \(w\) on which a fixed odd function has low restricted degree, is the natural source of static barriers and is queued.

The equivalent static question, recorded as the kernel test: \(1\notin S_D\) exactly when some function \(f\) on \(\mathbb F_2^n\) of odd weight restricts to every \(V_r\) with degree at most \(n-D-1\). A static barrier near half is such an \(f\) with restrictions of degree about \(n/2+s\) on every row of a polynomial cover; it is necessary for the family statement, and registry searches for odd mass, kernel test, static barrier and local design returned no example near half and no exclusion. That is the smallest statement on which the ceiling question and the family question meet.

Both are necessary conditions already implied by the accepted demand that the formula itself be hard; neither is adopted as a clause, because no candidate is known against which to check non-vacuity.

10 October 2026 — Static barriers from symmetric functions stop at \(2w-3\), products average the ratio \((D+1)/w\), and the three-variable example is refuted at its index

Working proofs of a proposition and a lemma; one small example decided by hand; no static barrier near half and no exclusion of one. Fourth entry of the spell on the ceiling check, its boundary; the item rotates. Queue development while draining. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort low).

Chosen. The ceiling check bears on the family statement through the static question on which the ceiling and the family meet; this is the attempt named in the last entry and the last of the item's spell; it is not the queue's head and is taken under the user's permission to select the order (9 October 2026).

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement: can an explicit odd-weight function give a static barrier far above the row width, toward \(n/2\), and does the reviewer's three-variable cover exceed its index in PC degree?

New mathematics. prop:symmetric-barrier-bound: for a symmetric function and rows that are subcubes fixing \(w\) coordinates, a static barrier at \(D\) exists exactly when some \(u\) with \(D\le u\le2w-2\) has \(\binom u{w-1}\) odd; so \(D\le2w-3\) for \(w\ge2\), with equality exactly when \(w-1\) is a power of two. lem:static-barrier-product: barriers multiply, \(D+1\) and widths adding and row counts multiplying. ex:saturated-cover-degree-fall: the three-variable example of the last entry has a static barrier at degree two and is nevertheless refuted in degree two, its index. The barriers of this entry and their products have \((D+1)/w<2\); I know no explicit witness beyond that, and two registry searches (static barrier; local design, odd mass) surfaced none, which does not show there is none.

Goal progress. Unchanged. Bearing. At the goal's parameters, \(D\ge n/2-s\) with \(s+w\le n^{1-\epsilon}\), the proposition excludes symmetric witnesses with subcube rows outright, since \(2w-3\) is far below \(n/2\), and the lemma shows products cannot raise \((D+1)/w\) above the largest factor's; neither says whether a non-symmetric witness exists, which is the question that matters.

General statement. prop:symmetric-barrier-bound, for all \(n\ge2w-1\), \(w\ge1\) and \(D\); lem:static-barrier-product for all pairs of barriers.

Static barriers

As in the last entry: for a cover of \(\mathbb F_2^n\) by affine subspaces \(V_r\) of codimension at most \(w\), \(1\notin S_D\) exactly when some \(f:\mathbb F_2^n\to\mathbb F_2\) of odd weight has \(\deg(f|_{V_r})\le e=n-D-1\) for every \(r\). Call \((f,\{V_r\})\) a static barrier at \(D\) of width \(w\). Given \(f\), the rows may be any family of subspaces on which \(f\) has restricted degree at most \(e\), so a barrier exists for \(f\) exactly when those subspaces cover.

Lemma (static barrier product). If \((f_1,\mathcal V_1)\) is a static barrier at \(D_1\) of width \(w_1\) in dimension \(n_1\) with \(M_1\) rows, and \((f_2,\mathcal V_2)\) likewise, then \(f(x,y)=f_1(x)f_2(y)\) with the rows \(V\times V'\) is a static barrier at \(D_1+D_2+1\) of width \(w_1+w_2\) in dimension \(n_1+n_2\) with \(M_1M_2\) rows.

Proof. The weight of \(f\) is the product of the weights, odd. The products of rows cover. On \(V\times V'\), \(f\) is the product of the restrictions, of degree at most \(e_1+e_2\), and \(n_1+n_2-(e_1+e_2)-1=(n_1-e_1-1)+(n_2-e_2-1)+1\). \(\square\)

So \((D+1)/w\) of a product is the mean of its factors' ratios weighted by their widths. The number of rows of a product of \(t\) factors is the product of theirs: with factors of bounded dimension it is exponential in the total dimension, and it is polynomial only when the factors are few and themselves polynomial, that is, when a factor already is the object sought.

Symmetric functions

Let \(f(x)=g(|x|)\) with \(g:\{0,\ldots,n\}\to\mathbb F_2\), and let the rows be subcubes fixing at most \(w\) coordinates, \(2w-1\le n\). A subcube fixing fewer is a union of subcubes fixing exactly \(w\), and restriction does not raise degree, so it is enough to treat rows fixing exactly \(w\). The weight of \(f\) is \(\sum_k\binom nkg(k)\).

Proposition (symmetric barrier bound). A static barrier at \(D\) with a symmetric \(f\) and such rows exists if and only if there is \(u\) with \(D\le u\le2w-2\) and \(\binom u{w-1}\) odd. Hence the largest such \(D\) is at least \(w-1\), at most \(2w-3\) for \(w\ge2\), and equal to \(2w-3\) exactly when \(w-1\) is a power of two. When it exists, \(2\binom{2w-1}w\) rows suffice.

Proof. (i) A subcube fixing \(T\), \(|T|=w\), with \(j\) ones restricts \(f\) to \(y\mapsto g(j+|y|)\) on \(m=n-w\) variables. A symmetric function \(h(|y|)\) equals \(\sum_{i\le m}(\Delta^ih)(0)\,e_i(y)\) over \(\mathbb F_2\), by Newton's expansion \(h(k)=\sum_i\Delta^ih(0)\binom ki\) and \(e_i(y)\equiv\binom{|y|}i\); the \(e_i\) are multilinear of degree \(i\), so its degree is at most \(e\) exactly when \(h\) agrees on \(\{0,\ldots,m\}\) with some \(\sum_{i\le e}a_i\binom ki\). Call the window \([j,j+n-w]\) good for \(g\) when this holds for \(k\mapsto g(j+k)\). (ii) The all-zero point lies only in subcubes with \(j=0\) and the all-one point only in those with \(j=w\); so a barrier needs both extreme windows good. Conversely, if both are good, fix a set \(B\) of \(2w-1\) coordinates: every point has \(w\) zeros or \(w\) ones on \(B\), so the subcubes \(\{x_T=0\}\) and \(\{x_T=1\}\), \(T\subseteq B\), \(|T|=w\), cover. (iii) Suppose both windows are good. Let \(P_0(k)=\sum_{i\le e}a_i\binom ki\) agree with \(g\) on \([0,n-w]\), and write \(g=P_0+h\) on \([w,n]\); then \(h(w+i)=\sum_{m\le e}b_m\binom im\) for \(0\le i\le n-w\), and \(h\) vanishes for \(0\le i\le n-2w\), which forces \(b_m=0\) for \(m\le n-2w\). Coefficients \(b_m\) with \(m>n-w\) do not matter, \(\binom im\) vanishing on the window; they correspond to \(u<w-1\), where \(\binom u{w-1}=0\), and this covers the case \(e\ge n-w\). Since \(w\le n-w+1\), \(g=P_0+h\cdot[k\ge w]\) on all of \([0,n]\). The function \(P_0(|x|)\) has degree at most \(e<n\) and even weight. Modulo two, \[\sum_{i}\binom n{w+i}\binom im=\sum_i\binom n{n-w-i}\binom{-m-1}{i-m}=\binom{n-m-1}{n-w-m}=\binom{n-m-1}{w-1},\] by \(\binom im\equiv\binom{-m-1}{i-m}\) and Vandermonde's identity. So the weight of \(f\) is \(\sum_{m=n-2w+1}^{e}b_m\binom{n-m-1}{w-1}\) modulo two, and with \(u=n-m-1\) running over \([D,2w-2]\) it is odd for some choice of the free bits \(b_m\) exactly when some \(\binom u{w-1}\) is odd. Conversely such a choice with \(P_0=0\) defines \(g\) with both windows good and odd weight. (iv) \(u=w-1\) always works; \(\binom{2w-2}{w-1}\) is even for \(w\ge2\); and with \(a=w-1\), \(\binom{2a-1}{a}=\tfrac12\binom{2a}a\), whose 2-adic valuation is, by Kummer, the number of binary digits of \(a\) minus one, so it is odd exactly when \(a\) is a power of two. \(\square\)

Check, not a proof: an enumeration over all \(g\) for \(4\le n\le11\), \(w\le n/2\) (so never \(n=2w-1\)) and \(D\le n-w\), allowing every subset of windows that covers all weights, agrees with the criterion in every case; the reviewer checked \(n=2w-1\) and \(2w\), \(w\le5\), every \(D\), and the binomial identity for \(n\le25\); the script was run from the scratch directory and is archived unchanged (script, output).

What the bound teaches. Two rows on which a symmetric function has low degree overlap in a long window, and low degree on an interval of weights propagates: the two local polynomials agree once the overlap has \(e+1\) points. The barrier survives only while the overlap is shorter, which is \(D\le2w-2\); the last step to \(2w-3\) is a parity. My interpretation, not a statement proved: the reason is rigidity under a large symmetry group together with rows that are few up to that symmetry; it does not apply to functions without such symmetry, and for rows that are general affine subspaces a symmetric function restricts to a non-symmetric one, a case not treated.

The three-variable example

The reviewer's cover: in \(\mathbb F_2^3\), with \(E=\{000,100,010\}\), the thirteen two-point rows contained in \(E\) or in its complement. Here \(f=1_E\) is constant on every row, so \(e=0\) and there is a static barrier at \(D=2\): \(S_2\) is the span of the rows, the functions even on \(E\) and even on its complement, of dimension six. But \(S_2\) contains the indicator of the plane \(x_1=0\), which meets \(E\) in two points and its complement in two; it has degree one, and its product with \(x_2\) is the indicator of \(\{010,011\}\), of degree two and odd on \(E\). So \(C_2\) properly contains \(S_2\), hence is all of \(B_{\le2}\), of dimension seven, and \(1\in C_2\). The degree is not below two, the rows having degree two, so that \(C_1=0\): the PC degree is two, equal to the cumulative index. The static barrier is destroyed by one degree fall. In this example the weakness of a static barrier of the saturated kind is visible: low-degree elements of the span are indicators of larger subspaces, and their multiples are new rows.

Specification decision. No clause added. For screening: for \(1\notin C_D\), which is more than a static barrier, the witness must survive degree falls, that is, restrict with degree at most \(n-D-1\) also to every subspace whose indicator the closure derives below degree \(D\); and it cannot be a symmetric function with subcube rows unless \(D\le2w-3\). Both are properties of witnesses, not of formulas, and are recorded here without change to the accepted specification.

New mathematics. lem:avoided-subspace-hilbert-defect: a point set disjoint from an affine subspace of codimension \(w\) has, for every \(D\ge w\), at least \(\binom{n-w}{\le D-w}\) independent polynomials of degree at most \(D\) vanishing on it, with equality for the complement of the subspace; so the quotient by the closure of a system with a row of codimension \(w\le D\) has dimension at most \(\binom n{\le D}-\binom{n-w}{\le D-w}\) through degree \(D\). Nothing else.

At the goal's parameters, \(D=n/2-s\) with \(s\) far above \(\sqrt n\), the code \(\mathrm{RM}(D,n)\) has rate tending to zero and the theorem as stated does not cover it; the lemma bounds a quotient's dimension and gives neither a barrier nor a ceiling there. The cycle was spent to decide a queued item on the current question, and it did not decide it.

General statement. lem:avoided-subspace-hilbert-defect, for all \(n\), \(w\le D\) and all point sets.

What the theorem says and needs

Kudekar, Kumar, Mondelli, Pfister, Şaşoğlu and Urbanke, arXiv:1601.04689; I read the abstract, not the paper. As stated there: a sequence of linear codes of increasing length and converging rate whose permutation groups are doubly transitive achieves capacity on the erasure channel under MAP decoding; Reed–Muller codes are the main case; the proof combines the sharp threshold of symmetric monotone Boolean functions with the area theorem for EXIT functions. My reading in this notebook's language, which goes beyond the abstract in three places the reviewer marked: for \(D\) with \(\binom n{\le D}=R\,2^n\), a uniformly random set of points of density above \(R\) carries, with high probability, no nonzero polynomial of degree at most \(D\) vanishing on it, which is the block form of the criterion and may not be what is proved; the dual statement below \(R\) is the theorem applied to the dual codes; and a rate converging inside \((0,1)\) means \(D=n/2\pm O(\sqrt n)\).

Against the goal. The goal's degree \(n/2-s\), with \(s\) up to \(n^{1-\epsilon}\), has rate tending to zero. That regime is outside the theorem as the abstract states it; the reviewer names Abbe, Shpilka and Wigderson for rates tending to zero, which I have not read and whose range I do not know. This is the first hypothesis that fails, and I had not confronted it in my draft.

Three formulations

Original translation (the review's): read the quotient by the closure as functions on a small set \(Z\) of pseudo-solutions, thin because a set of \(N\) points has at most \(N\) standard monomials. The capacity theorem is not needed for that count and does not apply to \(Z\): the set is determined by the rows, not random. What remains is the relative question, a relaxation whose closure is its full vanishing ideal with one further hard constraint, queued on its own as the fourth sub-idea of the same review.

Lemma (avoided subspace Hilbert defect). Let \(Z\subseteq\mathbb F_2^n\) be disjoint from an affine subspace \(V\) of codimension \(w\), with indicator \(R\). For \(D\ge w\) the polynomials \(Rg\), \(g\) of degree at most \(D-w\) on \(V\), vanish on \(Z\) and span a space of dimension \(\binom{n-w}{\le D-w}\) inside \(I(Z)_{\le D}\); so \(h_Z(D)\le\binom n{\le D}-\binom{n-w}{\le D-w}\). For \(Z=\mathbb F_2^n\setminus V\) this is an equality.

Proof. In affine coordinates with \(V=\{y_1=\cdots=y_w=1\}\), \(R=y_1\cdots y_w\) and \(Rg\) for a multilinear \(g\) in the remaining coordinates has degree \(w+\deg g\); distinct \(g\) give distinct functions on \(V\), and \(Rg\) vanishes off \(V\). A polynomial vanishing off \(V\) is \(R\) times its restriction to \(V\), of degree \(w\) plus that of the restriction, which gives the equality. \(\square\)

The lemma says that such a \(Z\) always carries polynomials of degree \(w\); it does not say that \(Z\) fails to impose independent conditions, which a small set avoiding \(V\) may well do, a single point for instance. So it excludes only the statement "no polynomial of degree at most \(D\) vanishes on \(Z\)", the side of the theorem above capacity, and is not an obstruction to the bridge's own side, small sets.

Dual formulation (the last two entries): a static barrier is an odd-weight function whose restriction to every row \(V\) is a codeword of \(\mathrm{RM}(n-D-1,V)\); as a point set, an erasure pattern on \(V\) that is not correctable for that code, and a parity check of its dual \(\mathrm{RM}(D-w,V)\). A random pattern on \(V\) is a codeword with probability \(2^{\dim\mathrm{RM}(n-D-1,V)-2^{n-w}}\), so the witness is structured on every row, and by the minimum distance it has at least \(2^{D-w+1}\) points on each row it meets, the recorded support bound. The capacity theorem, about random patterns, does not speak to this; I found no use of it here and do not claim there is none.

Method (symmetry and sharp thresholds): being refuted at degree \(D\) is monotone under adding rows and invariant under the symmetries of a family of all rows of one kind. From memory, with the form supplied by the reviewer and unverified by me: the threshold window of Friedgut and Kalai has width of order \(p\log(1/p)/\log N\) at density \(p\) on a ground set of \(N\) elements, which is informative at constant density; polynomial covers have \(p=\mathrm{poly}(n)/N\). I did not work out what it gives there. An analogue of the area theorem for rows, through the chain rule for the rank of the span, was not attempted.

Specification decision. No change. Recorded: a clause may not ask that no polynomial of degree at most \(D\) vanish on a relaxation's solutions, by the lemma; it may ask that the closure equal the vanishing ideal, which is a queued question.

Unused: double transitivity was never confronted. Suggestions: low-degree testing as the theory of the barrier's shape; the references for sparse thresholds and for rates tending to zero. Record. Both queued as sub-ideas. Process audit. The reviewer found: the title resting on a statement from memory (retitled); the closure made on an abstract, the one-step objection (not made); the Chosen paragraph without the permission it relies on (cited); no record search for the lemma (a search for vanishing ideals of sets avoiding a subspace returned nothing related; the lemma is one line and is registered only because an entry must cite a claim); a statement about the thin endpoint without a link (removed with the closure). Next attempt, the reviewer's: a static barrier is a function of full degree that passes exact tests of degree at most \(e\) on a covering family of flats of codimension \(w\); low-degree testing is the theory of that shape, and its theorems say when passing tests on flats forces closeness to low degree.

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement: what does the theory of local tests for low degree say about a static barrier, a function of full degree whose restriction to every row of a cover has low degree?

New mathematics. lem:static-degree-local-gap. For a cover of \(\mathbb F_2^n\) by affine subspaces let \(d_{\mathrm{st}}\) be the least \(D\) with \(1\in S_D\), and for a nonzero function \(f\) let \(\operatorname{locdeg}f\) be the largest degree of its restrictions to the rows. Then \(\deg f\le\operatorname{locdeg}f+d_{\mathrm{st}}\) for every \(f\), with equality for some \(f\): \(d_{\mathrm{st}}=\max_f(\deg f-\operatorname{locdeg}f)\). So a static lower bound \(d_{\mathrm{st}}>D\) is witnessed by any function whose degree exceeds its local degree by more than \(D\); the recorded criterion is the case of full degree, and the two are equally easy, a witness of any degree becoming one of full degree on multiplication by a monomial. In the testing literature, as far as I can state it from memory, I found no statement about an exact condition on a sparse covering family.

Goal progress. Unchanged; an equivalent form of a necessary condition. Bearing. At the goal's parameters a family must have \(d_{\mathrm{st}}>n/2-s\), so by the theorem it must admit a function whose global degree exceeds its degree on every row by more than \(n/2-s\); that is necessary, not sufficient, since the closure may exceed the span and the PC degree is at most \(d_{\mathrm{st}}\); the lemma supplies no such function.

General statement. lem:static-degree-local-gap, for every cover of \(\mathbb F_2^n\) by affine subspaces.

The gap lemma

Setting: affine subspaces \(V_1,\ldots,V_M\) covering \(\mathbb F_2^n\), \(V_r\) of codimension \(w_r\) with indicator \(R_r\); \(S_D=\sum_rR_rB_{\le D-w_r}\), the static span; \(d_{\mathrm{st}}\) the least \(D\) with \(1\in S_D\), which exists because the rows cover (\(D=n\) works). Degrees are of multilinear representatives; the degree of a function on \(V_r\) is taken in affine coordinates of \(V_r\) and does not depend on their choice. For \(f\ne0\), \(\operatorname{locdeg}f=\max_r\deg(f|_{V_r})\), over the rows on which \(f\) is not identically zero; there is one, since the rows cover.

Lemma (static degree local gap). (a) If \(1\in S_{D'}\), then every \(f\) satisfies \(\deg f\le\operatorname{locdeg}f+D'\). (b) There is \(f\) with \(\deg f=n\) and \(\operatorname{locdeg}f\le n-d_{\mathrm{st}}\). Hence \(d_{\mathrm{st}}=\max_{f\ne0}(\deg f-\operatorname{locdeg}f)\).

Proof. (a) Write \(1=\sum_rR_rg_r\) with \(\deg g_r\le D'-w_r\). Then \(f=\sum_rR_rg_rf\), and \(R_rg_rf=R_r\cdot(g_rp_r)\) where \(p_r\) is a polynomial of degree at most \(e=\operatorname{locdeg}f\) agreeing with \(f\) on \(V_r\): in affine coordinates \(y_1,\ldots,y_n\) with \(V_r=\{y_1=\cdots=y_{w_r}=1\}\), take \(p_r\) in \(y_{w_r+1},\ldots,y_n\). The product \(R_rg_rp_r\) has degree at most \(w_r+(D'-w_r)+e=D'+e\), and multilinear reduction does not raise degree. (b) By the dual criterion recorded with the deficit ceiling test, \(1\notin S_D\) for \(D=d_{\mathrm{st}}-1\) gives a function of odd weight, that is of degree \(n\), whose restriction to every row has degree at most \(n-D-1=n-d_{\mathrm{st}}\); if \(d_{\mathrm{st}}=0\), a row being the whole space, any function of degree \(n\) serves. The formula follows: (a) with \(D'=d_{\mathrm{st}}\) bounds every gap by \(d_{\mathrm{st}}\), and (b) attains it. \(\square\)

Remarks. The identity \(1=\sum_rR_rg_r\) is a partition of unity subordinate to the cover, of degree \(D'\); part (a) is gluing with it. \(d_{\mathrm{st}}\) is the Nullstellensatz degree of the system \(R_r=0\) with the Boolean axioms, and the criterion behind (b) is the standard duality with designs. For a partition into rows of codimension exactly \(w\), \(d_{\mathrm{st}}=w\) and the gap is attained by a function with unrelated low-degree pieces. The formula is for the static span. The PC closure can be larger, as the three-variable example shows, and I have no analogous formula for it; the refutation degree is at most \(d_{\mathrm{st}}\), in that example two against three. (My draft had this inequality reversed; the reviewer caught it.)

The witness is not freer. If \(\deg f=k\) with a top monomial \(x_S\), then \(f\cdot x_{[n]\setminus S}\) has degree \(n\) and local degree at most \(\operatorname{locdeg}f+n-k\): the gap is kept and the degree is full (the reviewer's remark; my draft had left open whether a witness of lower degree is easier to find). So part (a) adds a quantitative form, every function's degree is within \(d_{\mathrm{st}}\) of its local degree, and no new kind of witness.

One case the lemma settles. prop:symmetric-barrier-bound bounds symmetric witnesses. For the cover it constructs, the subcubes fixing \(w\) of a block of \(2w-1\) coordinates to all zeros or all ones, the rows involve only those coordinates, so \(d_{\mathrm{st}}\le2w-1\) for every witness, symmetric or not: on that cover non-symmetric functions gain at most one over the symmetric bound \(2w-2\) for the gap. The symmetric proposition says more only for symmetric functions of all \(n\) variables with arbitrary subcube rows.

Testing

The elementary fact behind low-degree tests over \(\mathbb F_2\), for \(e+1\le n\): \(\deg f\le e\) exactly when \(f\) sums to zero on every flat of dimension \(e+1\). A static barrier at \(D\), \(e=n-D-1\), is a function of degree \(n\) summing to zero on every \((e+1)\)-flat inside a row. From memory and unverified: the theorems on the optimal test (Bhattacharyya, Kopparty, Schoenebeck, Sudan and Zuckerman) bound from below the fraction of all \((e+1)\)-flats on which a function sums to one in terms of its distance from degree \(e\), and derandomized tests restrict the flats to those spanned by a small-bias set while keeping such a bound. Both quantify over a distribution on flats and conclude closeness. Here the passed flats are those inside the rows, a fraction at most about \(M2^{-w(e+2)}\) of all, chosen by the cover, and the conclusion wanted is exact. The exact results I know of, again from memory, are local characterizations of affine-invariant codes by a single orbit of constraints (Kaufman and Sudan) and lifted codes (Guo, Kopparty and Sudan); both need an affine-invariant family of flats, which a polynomial cover is not. I found no statement of that theory that applies; the gap lemma is what the exact, sparse case reduces to, and it is the partition-of-unity identity, not a testing theorem.

Specification decision. No clause added. Recorded for screening candidates: a family that is hard at \(D\) admits a function with \(\deg f-\operatorname{locdeg}f>D\) on its rows, with any degrees; a candidate for which every function has degree within \(n/2-s\) of its local degree is excluded. This is a necessary condition implied by hardness and equivalent to the static one already recorded, so the accepted specification is unchanged.

Verification gate. One fresh-context medium reviewer, with a brute-force check of the formula over all nonzero functions on fourteen covers (the thirteen-row example, the whole space, a partition at \(n=3\), six random covers at \(n=3\) and five at \(n=4\)): equality in all. It rederived the dual criterion and found the statement and proof correct. Corrections applied: the refutation degree is at most, not at least, \(d_{\mathrm{st}}\); the witness is not freer, by multiplication with a monomial, so the result is a lemma and a corollary of the recorded criterion and is registered as such; the case \(d_{\mathrm{st}}=0\) is added; the partition remark needs equal codimensions; the title's claim about testing is softened to what an unread survey supports; the exact local-characterization results are named and excluded, from memory. Suggestions: lower-degree symmetric functions through the monomial trick; the duality with the closure. Record. The first is answered in the text for the constructed cover; the second is the queued sub-idea. Process audit. The reviewer found: a title stronger than an unread survey supports (softened); "freer witness" overstated (withdrawn); no registry search stated (searches for local and global degree, gap, partition of unity and lifted codes returned nothing related; the criterion it follows from is prop:local-design-criterion); "theorem" generous (now a lemma); the first sub-idea should have asked for \(d_{\mathrm{st}}\) itself (answered and removed). It found Continuing and "unchanged" fair. Record: review.txt.

Next attempt: the same duality for the closure in place of the span, a function annihilating \(C_D\), which must have low degree on every derived row; and the reading of the capacity statements queued in the last entry.

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement: what replaces "low degree on every row" when the static span is replaced by the PC closure, and do the capacity theorem's statements reach the goal's degree?

New mathematics. lem:closure-dual-criterion: \(1\notin C_D\) exactly when some function \(f\) of odd weight satisfies \(\deg(fp)\le\deg p+n-D-1\) for every \(p\in C_D\); the closure is the least space containing the multiples of the rows and, with each of its elements \(p\) of degree below \(D\), the multiples \(p\,B_{\le D-\deg p}\). Consequently \(f\) has degree at most \(n-D-1\) on every affine subspace whose indicator lies in \(C_D\) with codimension at most \(D\), in particular on the falsifying subspace of every linear clause derivable from the rows in resolution over parities of width at most \(D-1\). This is the pseudo-expectation duality restated, a rediscovery in this notebook's language of the criterion recorded as prop:local-design-criterion; a registry search for closure dual and pseudo-expectation found no other registered form, which does not show there is none. Read: Theorems 20, 25 and 27 of the capacity paper hold for rates converging to a value strictly between zero and one.

Goal progress. Unchanged. Bearing. At the goal's parameters the lemma says what a witness of hardness at \(n/2-s\) must satisfy beyond the static condition, low degree \(n/2+s-1\) on every subspace whose indicator lies in \(C_D\), \(D=n/2-s\); it constructs none. The capacity theorems locate the threshold for degrees \(n/2+O(\sqrt n)\); for \(n/2-s\) with \(s\) of larger order they give, by passing to the subcode, recovery from random erasures of every constant density below one, and nothing at the scale of that code's own rate.

General statement. lem:closure-dual-criterion, for every system of rows over \(\mathbb F_2\) and every \(D\).

The closure and its dual

Setting as in the last entry: rows \(V_r\) of codimension \(w_r\) with indicators \(R_r\), not necessarily covering; \(B_{\le D}\) the multilinear polynomials of degree at most \(D\); \(C_D\) the PC closure at degree \(D\), the least subspace of \(B_{\le D}\) containing the \(R_r\) with \(w_r\le D\) and, with every \(p\) of degree at most \(D-1\), each \(x_ip\) reduced multilinearly. A function \(f\) defines the functional \(\varphi_f(g)=\sum_xf(x)g(x)\) on \(B_{\le D}\); every functional arises so, and \(\varphi_f=0\) exactly when \(\deg f\le n-D-1\). Put \(e=n-D-1\).

Lemma (closure dual criterion). (a) \(C_D\) is the least subspace \(T\subseteq B_{\le D}\) with \(R_r\in T\) for \(w_r\le D\) and \(p\,B_{\le D-\deg p}\subseteq T\) for every \(p\in T\). (b) For a function \(f\) and \(p\in B_{\le D}\): \(\varphi_f\) vanishes on \(p\,B_{\le D-\deg p}\) if and only if \(\deg(fp)\le e+\deg p\). (c) \(1\notin C_D\) if and only if there is \(f\) of odd weight with \(\deg(fp)\le e+\deg p\) for all \(p\in C_D\). (d) For such \(f\) and every affine subspace \(U\) of codimension \(c\le D\) with \(1_U\in C_D\): \(\deg(f|_U)\le e\). The condition \(c\le D\) is implied by \(1_U\in C_D\). This holds for every row with \(w_r\le D\), for every subspace of codimension at most \(D\) contained in such a row, and for the subspace \(A_L\) of assignments falsifying a linear clause \(L\) that has a derivation from the rows in resolution over parities in which every line has width at most \(D-1\).

Proof. (a) \(C_D\) has the two properties: for \(p\in C_D\) and a monomial \(m\) with \(\deg m\le D-\deg p\), multiply by the variables of \(m\) one at a time; each partial product lies in \(C_D\) and, before the last step, has degree at most \(D-1\). Conversely a space \(T\) with the two properties contains the rows and is closed under the rule, since \(x_ip\in p\,B_{\le D-\deg p}\) when \(\deg p\le D-1\). (b) \(\varphi_f(pg)=\varphi_{fp}(g)\), and a function is orthogonal to all polynomials of degree at most \(k\) exactly when its degree is at most \(n-k-1\); with \(k=D-\deg p\) that is \(e+\deg p\). (c) \(1\notin C_D\) exactly when some functional vanishes on \(C_D\) and not at \(1\), that is \(\varphi_f\) with \(f\) of odd weight; by (a) and (b) vanishing on \(C_D\) is the stated condition. (d) \(1_U\) has degree \(c\), and \(f\cdot1_U\) has degree \(c+\deg(f|_U)\) in coordinates adapted to \(U\); so (c) gives \(\deg(f|_U)\le e\). Rows are in \(C_D\); a subspace of a row of codimension \(c\le D\) has its indicator among the row's multiples. For clauses of resolution over parities, the proof of lem:parity-width-degree-bound derives the indicator of \(A_L\) for every line within degree one more than the largest width of a line, so within \(D\) for width at most \(D-1\). \(\square\)

Check on the three-variable example: \(D=2\), \(e=0\); \(f=1_E\) is constant on the thirteen rows but the closure contains the indicator of \(\{010,011\}\), on which \(f\) is not constant; so this \(f\) is no witness against the closure; that no function is one follows from \(1\in C_2\) by part (c).

What it adds to the static picture. Between the static span and the closure sits a combinatorial condition: the witness must be of degree at most \(e\) on every subspace reachable from the rows by narrow parity resolution. A function of odd weight with that property for all lines of width up to \(D-1\) certifies in particular that resolution over parities needs width at least \(D\), the empty clause's subspace being the whole space, where the function has degree \(n>e\); the converse direction, from a width lower bound to a witness, is not available, since degree can be far below width (parity width comparison). The formulas of the Efremenko and Itsykson preprint are reported to have such width near \(N\), a statement read and not verified; whether they carry a witness against the closure is the degree question itself.

Where half is used

From the reading of Alekhnovich and Razborov's proof recorded in the private direction entry, not fetched again. Recorded there: the operator reduces a term \(t\) modulo the rows of a set \(\mathrm{Sup}(t)\) inferred from \(t\), inferred sets being capped at \(r/2\) rows in Definition 3.15; Lemma 3.16 bounds \(|\mathrm{Sup}(t)|\le r/2\) for \(\deg t\le cr/2\), the boundary of the inferred rows lying among the variables of \(t\); Lemma 3.17 says that for \(I\supseteq\mathrm{Sup}(t)\) with \(|I|\le r/2\) the reduction modulo \(I\) equals that modulo \(\mathrm{Sup}(t)\). My inference, not in the record and not checked against the source: the cap \(r/2\) is there so that two such sets together still have at most \(r\) rows, where expansion applies, which is how reductions of \(t\) and of \(x_jt\) are compared; if so, half is spent on closing supports under union, and the bound is \(c\) times \(r/2\).

Two occurrences

Lemma (two occurrence clause degree). Let \(F\) be an unsatisfiable CNF, clauses being sets of literals of size at most \(s\), in which every variable occurs in at most two clauses. Then \(F\) has a refutation by unit resolution, and its clause polynomials with the Boolean axioms have a PC refutation of degree at most \(s\) over every field.

Proof. Take a minimal unsatisfiable subset \(F'\). It has no tautological clause. No variable is pure in \(F'\), occurring once or twice with one sign: the clauses containing it could be removed, a satisfying assignment of the rest being extended by that variable, against minimality. So every variable of \(F'\) occurs in exactly two clauses, with opposite signs. Form the multigraph \(G\) with the clauses as vertices and one edge per variable joining its two clauses; there are no loops, a variable occurring twice in one clause with opposite signs making it tautological. An assignment chooses for each edge the endpoint it satisfies, and every such choice comes from an assignment; so \(F'\) is satisfiable exactly when the edges can be assigned to endpoints covering all vertices, which holds for a connected component exactly when it contains a cycle. Hence some component is a tree, that component alone is unsatisfiable, and by minimality \(F'\) is a tree. A tree with one vertex is the empty clause. Otherwise a leaf is a clause with one literal; resolving it with its neighbour removes the leaf and deletes one literal from the neighbour, leaving a tree formula on fewer clauses; by induction the empty clause is reached by unit resolution with all clauses of width at most \(s\). In PC, with \(u\) the polynomial of the unit clause, of degree one, and \(P=\bar uQ\) the neighbour's, \(\bar u\) the opposite literal's polynomial and \(u+\bar u=1\): \(Q=P+uQ\), and \(uQ\) is the multiple of the unit clause by \(Q\), a product of literal polynomials, built one factor at a time within degree \(\deg P\le s\). The Boolean axioms are not needed, the polynomials being multilinear throughout. \(\square\)

The method's ceiling by number of occurrences

Corollary (occurrence expansion ceiling). Let \(A\) be an \((r,s,c)\)-boundary expander with \(m\) rows and \(v\) columns, \(1\le r\le m\), in which every column has at least \(d\ge2\) ones. Then \(rc\le(1-\tfrac1d)^{d-1}v+s\), so the bound \(rc/2\) of Theorem 3.13 is at most \(\tfrac12(1-\tfrac1d)^{d-1}v+s/2\): \(v/4\) at \(d=2\), \(2v/9\) at \(d=3\), decreasing to \(v/(2e)\).

Proof. In the proof of prop:two-occurrence-expansion-ceiling a column with \(d'\) ones lies in the boundary of a uniformly random set of \(r\) rows with probability at most \(d'(1-\beta)\beta^{d'-1}+d'/m\), \(\beta=(m-r)/(m-1)\). The maximum over \(\beta\in[0,1]\) of the first term is \((1-1/d')^{d'-1}\), which decreases in \(d'\); so for \(d'\ge d\) it is at most \((1-1/d)^{d-1}\). Summing over columns, with \(\sum d'/m\le s\), the expected boundary is at most \((1-1/d)^{d-1}v+s\), and expansion gives the claim. \(\square\)

For pure clause systems with at most two occurrences the lemma makes the degree at most the width, so the theorem's bound there is below \(s\). When every variable has at least three occurrences the method stops at \(2v/9+s/2\). For mixed systems neither statement helps: a fraction \(\epsilon\) of three-occurrence variables lowers the averaging bound only to about \((1/2-\epsilon/8)v/2\), which tends to \(v/4\), and the lemma does not make the two-occurrence variables removable, since resolving on one merges two clauses into a wider one. New mathematics. prop:clause-occurrence-ceiling: an unsatisfiable CNF of width \(s\) in which at most \(h\) variables occur in three or more clauses has a PC refutation of degree at most \(h+s\) over every field. General statement. prop:clause-occurrence-ceiling, for all CNFs, widths, fields and \(h\).

The ceiling

Proposition (clause occurrence ceiling). Let \(F\) be an unsatisfiable CNF with clauses of size at most \(s\), and \(H\) a set of \(h\) variables such that every variable outside \(H\) occurs in at most two clauses. Then the clause polynomials of \(F\) with the Boolean axioms have a PC refutation of degree at most \(h+s\) over every field.

Proof. For an assignment \(\alpha\) to \(H\) let \(\chi_\alpha\) be its indicator, of degree \(h\), and \(F|_\alpha\) the restriction: clauses satisfied by \(\alpha\) are dropped and falsified literals deleted. \(F|_\alpha\) is unsatisfiable, of width at most \(s\), and each of its variables occurs in at most two clauses, so by lem:two-occurrence-clause-degree it has a refutation of degree at most \(s\). For a clause \(C\) not satisfied by \(\alpha\), \(\chi_\alpha P_{C|_\alpha}\) equals \(P_C\) times the literals of \(\chi_\alpha\) on the variables of \(H\) outside \(C\), exactly: the literal polynomials of \(C\) on \(H\), falsified by \(\alpha\), are already factors of \(\chi_\alpha\). So it is a multiple of \(P_C\) built within degree \(h+s\), without the Boolean axioms. Multiplying the refutation of \(F|_\alpha\) by \(\chi_\alpha\) line by line derives \(\chi_\alpha\) within degree \(h+s\), and \(\sum_\alpha\chi_\alpha=1\). \(\square\)

Relation to the record. thm:occurrence-degree-ceiling conditions on the same variables and bounds the two-occurrence remainder by the frontier ceiling for blocks of arity \(w\), a fraction \(c_w=\tfrac12-\tfrac1{4w-2}\) of the remaining variables, \(0.4\) at \(w=3\); for single clauses the remainder costs only the width. The recorded theorem does not give \(h+O(s)\) for clauses, and the proposition says nothing for blocks that are relations, where the recorded cap \(c_wv+o(v)\) for systems with every variable in two blocks stands; whether such systems can come near that cap is the open part of the sub-idea queued in the last entry.

What boundary arguments can certify for clauses

Let \(F\) be an unsatisfiable CNF in which every variable occurs in at least two clauses, as in a minimal unsatisfiable one, with \(h\) variables in three or more, and suppose its clause-variable matrix is an \((r,s,c)\)-boundary expander, \(1\le r\le m\). By the proof of cor:occurrence-expansion-ceiling, a column with two ones contributes at most \(1/2\) and one with more at most \(4/9\) to the expected boundary of a random set of \(r\) rows, so \(rc\le v/2-h/18+s\). An argument certifying degree at most \(\lambda rc\) with \(\lambda\le1\) is bounded, with the proposition, by \(\min\{v/2-h/18,\,h\}+s\le\tfrac9{19}v+s\), the two terms meeting at \(h=\tfrac9{19}v\): about \(0.474\,v\). With variables occurring once the bound fails. For a factor above one nothing is excluded: at \(h=v\), \(rc\) may be as large as \(4v/9\) as far as the averaging goes. The theorem on record certifies half of the boundary; if its hypotheses hold, which I did not recheck against the source, \(rc/2<h+s\) with the averaging bound gives \(rc/2\le\tfrac9{37}v+O(s)\), slightly below a quarter, a remark I do not register.

So for single-clause rows, the unweighted boundary of sets of \(r\) clauses with a factor at most one does not reach \(n/2-o(n)\). Weighted boundaries, sets of other shapes and factors above one are not covered. The reviewer's remark on what could replace it: any valid measure is at most \(h+s\) and vanishes on two-occurrence residues, so it would charge variables in three or more clauses of a clause set, not variables seen once.

Three occurrences: what was not obtained

For a 3-CNF with every variable in exactly three clauses the primal graph has \(v\) vertices and at most \(3v\) edges. From memory and unverified: resolution width is at most the pathwidth of the primal graph plus one, and pathwidth is at most about \(m/5.77\) for a graph with \(m\) edges, which gives \(0.52\,v\), no better than the trivial bound for the purpose. I found no upper bound below \(v/2\) for these systems and no family whose degree is known to exceed \(2v/9\); the reviewer of the last entry suggested the cubic incidence graph, whose pathwidth I did not convert into a degree bound.

Specification decision. I do not amend the accepted text: its blocks are relations, for which the recorded bound stands, and the witness of non-vacuity it carries is for that bound. Non-vacuity of the sharper condition is not verified: I expect unsatisfiable random \(k\)-CNFs to meet it, but have not checked the occurrence profile of their minimal cores.

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement: is there a measure on sets of clauses, other than the variables seen once, that passes the two filters now on record and is not capped below half by averaging?

New mathematics. lem:pure-boundary-sampling. Call a variable pure in a set \(I\) of clauses when it occurs in \(I\) and all its occurrences there have one sign. (a) In a minimal set of clauses implying a non-tautological clause \(C\), every variable pure in the set occurs in \(C\), with the same sign. (b) If each clause is put in \(I\) independently with probability \(\rho\), a variable with \(a\) positive and \(b\) negative occurrences is pure in \(I\) with probability \(q^a+q^b-2q^{a+b}\), \(q=1-\rho\). (c) That is at most \(1/2\) for \(a=b\), exceeds \(1/2\) for some \(\rho\) whenever \(a\ne b\), has maximum about \(0.528\) for \(\{a,b\}=\{1,2\}\), and approaches one for \(a=1\) as \(b\to\infty\) with \(\rho\to0\) and \(b\rho\to\infty\); for fixed \(\rho\) the value stays below \(1-\rho\). So averaging caps this boundary at \(v/2\) for sign-balanced systems and does not cap it for unbalanced ones. I did not establish that expansion in this boundary gives a degree bound, and for the unbalanced systems I can name, encodings with one variable per value, I argue heuristically that the gain disappears.

Goal progress. Unchanged. Bearing. At the goal's parameters this gives nothing: a measure is named, it is neither validated as a lower bound nor capped, and the unbalanced systems on which it is large are encodings whose degree is small relative to their variables. The cycle was spent because the last entry named this attempt as the test of whether the item has a next step.

General statement. lem:pure-boundary-sampling, for all CNFs, all \(a,b\ge1\) and \(\rho\in(0,1)\).

The measure and the lemma

For a CNF \(F\) and a set \(I\) of its clauses let \(\partial^{\pm}I\) be the set of variables pure in \(I\). It contains the variables seen once, the boundary of the expansion method.

Lemma (pure boundary sampling). (a) If \(I\) is a minimal set of clauses of \(F\) with \(I\models C\) for a non-tautological clause \(C\), then every variable of \(\partial^{\pm}I\) occurs in \(C\) with the sign it has in \(I\). (b) For a CNF without tautological clauses, under independent inclusion with probability \(\rho\), \(\Pr[x\in\partial^{\pm}I]=q^a+q^b-2q^{a+b}\) for a variable with \(a\) positive and \(b\) negative occurrences, \(q=1-\rho\). (c) With \(g_{a,b}(q)=q^a+q^b-2q^{a+b}\): \(g_{a,a}\le1/2\); for \(a<b\), \(\max_qg_{a,b}>1/2\); \(\max_qg_{1,2}=g_{1,2}(q_0)\approx0.528\) at \(q_0=(1+\sqrt7)/6\); and \(g_{1,b}(q)\to q\) as \(b\to\infty\) for fixed \(q<1\).

Proof. (a) Let \(x\) be pure in \(I\), say positive, and suppose \(x\) does not occur positively in \(C\). Let \(I'\) be the clauses of \(I\) without \(x\). An assignment falsifying \(C\) and satisfying \(I'\) can be changed to make \(x\) true without satisfying \(C\), which has no positive occurrence of \(x\), or affecting \(I'\), and then satisfies all of \(I\), contradicting \(I\models C\); so \(I'\models C\), against minimality, \(I'\) being a proper subset. (b) Without tautological clauses the \(a+b\) occurrences lie in distinct clauses. The variable is pure positive when no negative occurrence is chosen and some positive one is, probability \(q^b(1-q^a)\); likewise \(q^a(1-q^b)\); the events are disjoint. (c) \(g_{a,a}=2u(1-u)\) with \(u=q^a\). For \(a<b\), at \(q^a=1/2\) the value is \(1/2\) and \(g_{a,b}'=aq^{a-1}(1-2q^b)>0\) there, so larger values occur (the reviewer's computation). \(g_{1,2}'(q)=1+2q-6q^2\) vanishes at \(q_0\), where the value is about \(0.528\). For fixed \(q<1\), \(q^b\to0\). \(\square\)

Part (a) is the standard width argument with the boundary enlarged, likely folklore; it concerns resolution, and to bound width one would use sets of intermediate size as usual, which I do not state as a result here. Whether the pseudo-reduction of the expansion method works with this boundary I did not establish. From memory and unverified: the generalized method of Mikša and Nordström works with partitions of clauses and variables and a designated set of clauses to be respected; whether its boundary contains this notion I do not know, and the reviewer's recollection is that it is a unique-neighbour boundary over fixed partitions. The record holds only their Theorem 5.1 for the plain boundary (imp:cnf-boundary-degree).

The two filters, and the unbalanced case

Two occurrences. A variable occurring twice with opposite signs is pure in \(I\) exactly when exactly one of its clauses is in \(I\): the measure equals the plain boundary there, and the tree formulas of lem:two-occurrence-clause-degree have small expansion in it for the same reason as before, their leaves. No conflict.

Conditioning. prop:clause-occurrence-ceiling bounds the degree by \(h+s\). A certificate from this measure would be at most the number of variables, and I found no system in which half of the smallest pure boundary exceeds \(h+s\). No conflict, and no evidence either: the filter does not bite. The test named in the last entry, \(\mu(F)\le|H|+\max_\alpha\mu(F|_\alpha)\) for every \(H\), was not run, so "passes" would overstate it.

Averaging. For sign-balanced variables the expected pure boundary of a random set is at most \(v/2\) by (c), so if a theorem with the method's factor one half held for this boundary, which is not established, the cap would again be a quarter; this is conditional on that and on the passage from independent inclusion to sets of at most \(r\) clauses, which I did not write out. For unbalanced variables averaging gives no cap.

The unbalanced systems I can name are encodings. If every clause is monotone and every variable has one positive occurrence and many negative ones, the positive clauses partition the variables into blocks and the system is a constraint problem with one block per unknown, in the encoding with one variable per value and no exclusivity axioms. A set \(I\) containing the positive clause of a block makes its variables impure as soon as their negative clauses are present, and, by analogy with the pigeonhole arguments and not by an argument made here, a set that must respect the positive clauses counts blocks and not variables: the certificate would be at most half the number of blocks, a fraction \(1/(2k)\) of the variables for blocks of size \(k\). With blocks of size two, the two-rail encoding of a CNF \(G\) on \(p\) variables, substituting \(x'=1-x\) returns \(G\), the positive clause becoming a multiple of the Boolean axiom, so the degree is at least that of \(G\) on twice the variables, and nothing is gained in the ratio unless the encoding doubles the degree, which I did not examine.

Specification decision. No change, and nothing new necessary or excluded: the measure is not shown to bound degree, so no condition on candidates follows from it.

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement: what boundary does the generalized method of Mikša and Nordström use, and can its certificate exceed a quarter of the variables?

New mathematics. prop:generalized-method-ceiling: for a minimally unsatisfiable CNF on \(v\) variables, written as \(U\wedge E\) with a family \(\mathcal V\) of variable sets of overlap \(d\), if the resulting graph is an \((s,\delta,\xi,E)\)-expander in the sense of that method, then the method's bound \((\delta s-2\xi)/(2d)\) is at most \(v/4+\Delta/(2d)\), \(\Delta\) the largest number of sets of \(\mathcal V\) met by one member of \(U\). The proof is the averaging of the recorded ceiling, with one new step: in a minimal formula a variable set with a single neighbour is never in a boundary. The method's boundary is by unique neighbours among the sets of \(\mathcal V\), with satisfaction required to respect \(E\); it is not the sign-aware boundary of the last entry.
