General statement. prop:generalized-method-ceiling, for all minimally unsatisfiable CNFs and all admissible \((U,\mathcal V,E)\), conditional on the method's statement as given below.

The statement, as read

Source: Mikša and Nordström, A generalized method for proving polynomial calculus degree lower bounds, arXiv:1505.01358. I did not see the text; a fetch tool rendered the first two thirds of its HTML version and answered questions about it, and what follows is that rendering, which I could not check word for word; it agrees with what an earlier entry of another notebook recorded from the same paper (prop:dense-blocks-outside-mn-framework), found after the review. A CNF is written \(\mathcal F=U\wedge E\), with \(U\) a family of subformulas, the left vertices; \(\mathcal V\) is a family of sets of variables, the right vertices, which may overlap, each variable lying in at most \(d\) of them; \(F\in U\) and \(V\in\mathcal V\) are neighbours when they share a variable. A partial assignment respects \(E\) if every clause of \(E\) it touches is satisfied by it. \(V\) is a respectful neighbour of \(F\) if some assignment to \(V\) satisfies \(F\) and respects \(E\). The respectful boundary of \(U'\subseteq U\) consists of the \(V\) that are respectful neighbours of some member of \(U'\) and neighbours of no other member of \(U'\). The graph is an \((s,\delta,\xi,E)\)-expander if every \(U'\) with \(|U'|\le s\) has boundary at least \(\delta|U'|-\xi\), \(\xi\) a slack which I take to be nonnegative. Theorem 3.8 there: if moreover \(U'\wedge E\) is satisfiable for every such \(U'\), every PC refutation of \(\mathcal F\) has degree greater than \((\delta s-2\xi)/(2d)\).

The ceiling

Proposition (generalized method ceiling). Let \(\mathcal F=U\wedge E\) be a CNF on \(v\) variables that is minimally unsatisfiable, no clause being removable, with \(m=|U|\) members, each a nonempty set of clauses, and \(\mathcal V\) a family of nonempty variable sets with every variable in at most \(d\) of them. Let \(\Delta\) be the largest number of neighbours of a member of \(U\). If the graph is an \((s,\delta,\xi,E)\)-expander with \(\xi\ge0\) and \(1\le s\le m\), which the method's satisfiability hypothesis forces, the whole of \(U\) with \(E\) being unsatisfiable, then \[\frac{\delta s-2\xi}{2d}\le\frac v4+\frac{\Delta}{2d}.\]

Proof. First, a set \(V\) with exactly one neighbour \(F\) is not a respectful neighbour of it. Otherwise some assignment to \(V\) satisfies \(F\) and every clause of \(E\) containing a variable of \(V\); no other member of \(U\) contains such a variable; so it satisfies every clause of \(\mathcal F\) that contains a variable of \(V\). The remaining clauses are then unsatisfiable by themselves, since an assignment satisfying them could be changed on \(V\) to this one and would satisfy \(\mathcal F\); and they omit the clauses of \(F\), each of which contains a variable of \(V\), the assignment to \(V\) satisfying it; this contradicts minimality. So every \(V\) that can lie in a boundary has at least two neighbours. Second, let \(U'\) be a uniformly random set of exactly \(s\) members. A set \(V\) with \(j\ge2\) neighbours lies in the boundary only if exactly one of them is in \(U'\), which by the computation in the proof of prop:two-occurrence-expansion-ceiling has probability at most \(\tfrac12+j/m\); for \(m=1\) no set has two neighbours. Summing, the expected boundary is at most \(|\mathcal V|/2+\Delta\), the number of edges being at most \(m\Delta\). Some \(U'\) of size \(s\) has boundary at most that, so \(\delta s-\xi\le|\mathcal V|/2+\Delta\), and \(\xi\ge0\) gives \(\delta s-2\xi\le|\mathcal V|/2+\Delta\). Finally \(|\mathcal V|\le dv\), each variable lying in at most \(d\) nonempty sets. \(\square\)

The additive term. \(\Delta\le dw\) with \(w\) the largest number of variables in a member of \(U\), so the bound is at most \(v/4+w/2\), parallel to the term \(s/2\) of the recorded ceiling (the reviewer's remark). It is not negligible in general: a member meeting most sets makes the statement empty. Unused in the proof: \(\delta>0\), and any requirement that the sets cover the variables.

Not covered: formulas that are not minimal, where sets with one neighbour may be boundary; then the member they satisfy is redundant. This is a real loss: the method's own applications, pigeonhole formulas restricted to graphs, are in general not minimal, so the proposition does not speak to them. Formulas with auxiliary affine equations, where the free dimension is below \(v\). And the method's hypotheses themselves, which I take from the rendering.

None of this constructs or excludes an operator for rows on forms, which is the item's question and is untouched.

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement: does a condition on how many variables occur in three or more blocks survive when degree is measured against the free dimension of a system with auxiliary affine equations?

New mathematics. lem:copy-normal-form: for a CNF \(G\) of width \(s\) on \(n\) variables, replace every occurrence of a variable by its own copy and let \(\Lambda\) be the equalities between copies of one variable. The system \((F,\Lambda)\) has every variable in exactly one clause, free dimension \(n\), and PC degree \(d\) with \(\deg G\le d\le\max\{\deg G,s\}\), over every field. This shows only that the count of variables in three or more clauses, with affine rows left out of the count, is not necessary in the free dimension. The specification counts affine rows as rows; counted so, a representative copy lies in as many rows as the variable had occurrences, and the branching count of the copy system is that of \(G\). Whether the condition with affine rows counted, compared with the free dimension, is necessary is neither derived nor refuted.

General statement. lem:copy-normal-form, for every CNF, width and field.

The lemma

Conventions of the free dimension entry, which is over \(\mathbb F_2\): a system is a CNF \(F\) with a set \(\Lambda\) of affine equations; its refutations use the clause polynomials, the Boolean axioms and \(\Lambda\); its free dimension is the number of variables minus the rank of \(\Lambda\). The lemma below holds over every field with equalities as the affine equations; that extension is its own.

Lemma (copy normal form). Let \(G\) be an unsatisfiable CNF on \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), every variable occurring, with clauses of size at most \(s\). For each pair of a clause \(C\) and a variable \(x_i\) of \(C\) take a new variable \(x_{i,C}\), \(v\) of them in all; let \(F\) consist of the clauses \(C'\) obtained from the clauses \(C\) by replacing each \(x_i\) by \(x_{i,C}\), and \(\Lambda\) of the equations \(x_{i,C}=x_{i,C_i}\), \(C_i\) a fixed clause containing \(x_i\). Then: every variable of \(F\) occurs in exactly one clause; \(\Lambda\) has rank \(v-n\), so the free dimension is \(n\); and the least degree \(d\) of a PC refutation of \((F,\Lambda)\) satisfies \(\deg G\le d\le\max\{\deg G,s\}\).

Proof. The equations are independent, one for each pair other than the fixed one. Lower bound: the substitution \(x_{i,C}\mapsto x_i\) is a ring homomorphism compatible with the Boolean axioms, sends \(\Lambda\) to zero and the clause polynomials of \(F\) to those of \(G\), and does not raise degree; it maps a refutation of \((F,\Lambda)\) step by step to one of \(G\). Upper bound: for a clause \(C'\) and one of its copies \(y=x_{i,C}\) with representative \(z=x_{i,C_i}\), the clause polynomial is \(P=\ell(y)Q\) with \(\ell\) the literal polynomial and \(Q\) the product of the others, and \(\ell(y)Q-\ell(z)Q=\pm(y-z)Q\) is a multiple of an equation of \(\Lambda\) of degree at most \(s\). Replacing the copies one at a time derives, within degree \(s\), the clause polynomial of \(C\) in the representatives, which form a copy of \(G\); its refutation is then run on them. Unsatisfiability is used only for \(d\) to be finite. \(\square\)

What it does and does not decide

With clauses as the only blocks, the copy system has no variable in two blocks, so it violates the accepted clause that every variable lies in at least two blocks, and the comparison with the specification is not like for like. With the affine rows counted as rows, as the specification's "rows may include affine equations" counts them, the representative \(x_{i,C_i}\) lies in its clause and in one equality for each other occurrence of \(x_i\): it is in three or more rows exactly when \(x_i\) occurred three or more times in \(G\). So the number of branching variables is unchanged, \(h=h_G\), while the number of variables grew from \(n\) to \(v\). Over \(\mathbb F_2\) I see no other way to write these equalities as rows that lowers the count, and I have not proved there is none.

So the lemma decides one reading of the check, the count that ignores affine rows, and leaves the reading that matters: is \(h\ge n/(2w)\), with affine rows counted and \(n\) the free dimension, necessary for degree near \(n/2\)? The recorded theorem bounds degree by \(h+c_w(v-h)\) in the number of variables \(v\), which says nothing when \(v\) is much larger than \(n\). Equalities are a degenerate kind of affine row; systems with genuine parity rows are the test.

Specification decision. No change: the branching-density clause stays required when there are no affine rows and withdrawn, provisionally as before, when there are. Nothing new is necessary or excluded.

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement: can a system of clauses and parity equations over \(\mathbb F_2\) in which every variable lies in at most two rows, affine rows counted, be hard, and what does the answer give for the number of branching variables?

New mathematics. prop:two-row-clause-parity-degree: an unsatisfiable system of clauses of size at most \(s\) and parity equations over \(\mathbb F_2\), every variable in at most two rows, has a PC refutation of degree at most \(\max\{s,1\}\). A minimal unsatisfiable such system, after merging connected groups of parity rows, is a tree, and a tree has a leaf that fixes a variable. cor:affine-branching-count: if at most \(h\) variables lie in three or more rows, the degree is at most \(h+\max\{s,1\}\). The count does not involve the number of variables or the free dimension, so it answers the check for blocks that are single clauses: with affine rows counted as rows, a system with no refutation at \(D\) has more than \(D-s\) branching variables.

Goal progress. Unchanged. Bearing. At the goal's parameters, over \(\mathbb F_2\), a candidate consisting of clauses of width \(w\) and auxiliary parity equations, with no refutation at \(D=\lfloor n/2-s'\rfloor\), has more than \(D-w\) variables each lying in three or more of its rows, in every presentation of its affine equations: about half of the free dimension. This is a necessary condition that applies to candidates with affine equations, which the conditions of the earlier entries did not. It gives no candidate and no lower bound.

General statement. prop:two-row-clause-parity-degree and cor:affine-branching-count, for all such systems, all \(s\) and \(h\), over \(\mathbb F_2\).

Systems with every variable in at most two rows

A system consists of clauses, sets of literals of size at most \(s\) without complementary pairs, and parity equations \(\sum_{x\in S}x=b\) over \(\mathbb F_2\); a row is a clause or a parity equation; refutations use the clause polynomials, the Boolean axioms and the parity equations as polynomials of degree one. Let \(\mathcal L\) be the span of the parity equations; its elements are derived in degree one.

Proposition (two row clause parity degree). Let \(N\) be an unsatisfiable system in which every variable lies in at most two rows. Then \(N\) has a PC refutation of degree at most \(\max\{s,1\}\).

Proof. Induction on the number of variables. Take a minimal unsatisfiable subsystem \(M\). If \(1\in\mathcal L(M)\) or \(M\) contains the empty clause, there is a refutation of degree at most one. Assume neither.

Structure of \(M\). (i) No variable lies in exactly one row \(R\) of \(M\): an assignment satisfying \(M\setminus\{R\}\), which exists by minimality, could be changed on that variable alone to satisfy \(R\), a clause through its literal and a parity equation through its sum. So every variable of \(M\) lies in exactly two rows. (ii) Call two parity rows linked if they share a variable, and let the groups be the classes of the generated equivalence. For a group \(g\), the variables lying in two rows of \(g\) are internal and those lying in one row of \(g\) are its boundary, each boundary variable lying also in a clause. The sum of the rows of \(g\) is the equation \(\sum_{\text{boundary}}x=\beta_g\) in \(\mathcal L\), the internal variables cancelling. For any values of the boundary variables satisfying it, the rows of \(g\) can be solved in the internal variables: the rows of \(g\) with the internal variables form the vertex-edge incidence system of a connected multigraph, whose only linear dependency among the rows is their sum. (iii) Let \(H\) be the multigraph whose vertices are the clauses and the groups, with one edge for every variable that is not internal, joining its two rows' vertices; groups are not adjacent. \(H\) is connected, a disconnected \(H\) splitting \(M\) into parts on disjoint variables one of which would be unsatisfiable. (iv) \(H\) has no cycle. Otherwise it has at least as many edges as vertices and, being connected, admits a choice of a distinct incident edge for every vertex. Set every variable that is neither chosen nor internal to \(0\); set the variable chosen by a clause to satisfy it; then set the variable chosen by a group to make its boundary equation hold, which changes no other group's equation, groups being non-adjacent, and no clause's chosen variable, the clause containing it being already satisfied by its own chosen literal; then solve the internal variables. Every clause and every parity row is satisfied, contradicting unsatisfiability. If a group has no boundary, it is all of \(M\) by connectedness and its equation \(0=\beta_g\) holds, \(1\notin\mathcal L\), so \(M\) is satisfiable, again a contradiction. So \(H\) is a tree, with at least two vertices since a single clause without edges is empty and a single group was just excluded.

The step. A tree with two or more vertices has a leaf. If the leaf is a clause, it has one variable \(y\) and is a unit clause, giving \(y=\epsilon\). If it is a group, its boundary equation is \(y=\beta_g\), an element of \(\mathcal L\). In both cases an equation \(y=\epsilon\) is derived in degree at most one. Restrict \(M\) by it: a clause containing \(y\) is dropped if its literal is satisfied and loses the literal otherwise; a parity row containing \(y\) has its constant shifted. Each restricted row is derived from a row of \(M\) and \(y-\epsilon\) within degree \(\max\{s,1\}\): for a clause polynomial \(P=\ell Q\) whose literal polynomial \(\ell\) equals one at \(y=\epsilon\), \(\ell=1\pm(y-\epsilon)\) and \(Q=P\mp(y-\epsilon)Q\), the last term a multiple of \(y-\epsilon\) by a product of at most \(s-1\) literal polynomials; for a parity row a combination of degree one. The restricted system is unsatisfiable, has one variable fewer, and every variable still lies in at most two rows. By induction it has a refutation of degree at most \(\max\{s,1\}\), and so has \(N\). \(\square\)

For systems without parity rows this is lem:two-occurrence-clause-degree. With parity rows only it is linear algebra. Equalities between copies are parity rows of size two, and the copy system of a CNF is not of this kind, its representatives lying in many rows.

The branching count with affine rows

Corollary (affine branching count). Let \(N\) be an unsatisfiable system of clauses of size at most \(s\) and parity equations over \(\mathbb F_2\), and \(H_0\) a set of \(h\) variables such that every other variable lies in at most two rows. Then \(N\) has a PC refutation of degree at most \(h+\max\{s,1\}\).

Proof. For an assignment \(\alpha\) to \(H_0\) the restriction \(N|_\alpha\) is an unsatisfiable system of the same kind in which every variable lies in at most two rows, so it has a refutation of degree at most \(\max\{s,1\}\). With \(\chi_\alpha\) the indicator of \(\alpha\), of degree \(h\): for a clause not satisfied by \(\alpha\), \(\chi_\alpha\) times the restricted clause polynomial is a multiple of the clause polynomial, as in prop:clause-occurrence-ceiling; for a parity row \(L\), \(\chi_\alpha L|_\alpha=\chi_\alpha L\) after reduction by the Boolean axioms, of degree \(h+1\). Multiplying the refutation of \(N|_\alpha\) by \(\chi_\alpha\) derives \(\chi_\alpha\) within degree \(h+\max\{s,1\}\), and the \(\chi_\alpha\) sum to one. \(\square\)

What it answers. The bound does not mention the number of variables, so it is a statement in any normalization: a system of clauses and parity rows with no refutation at \(D\) has more than \(D-\max\{s,1\}\) variables in three or more rows, whatever its free dimension, and this holds for every way of writing its affine part as rows, since an equivalent set of parity equations has the same span, derived in degree one, and so the same refutation degree whenever that degree is at least one. For the check as posed: the recorded condition is a density in the number of variables, \(\liminf h/v\ge1/(2w)\); what is derived here is \(h>D-s\), a density relative to the free dimension, \(h/n\ge1/2-o(1)\) at the goal's degree, for systems whose non-affine blocks are single clauses; it is stronger only in that sense and says nothing about \(h/v\). For blocks that are relations on bounded scopes the proposition is not proved, and two steps fail: in (i) a variable lying in one block can be projected out but the block cannot be discarded, and in (iv) one chosen variable does not satisfy a relation, so a cycle no longer gives a satisfying assignment (the reviewer's analysis; my draft had named a step that does not fail). In the canonical clause encoding of a relation forbidding two or more tuples the corollary is vacuous, the block's variables lying in several clauses.

Specification decision. For candidates whose non-affine blocks are single clauses, the branching condition is restored in the presence of affine rows, in the form: more than \(D-w\) variables lie in three or more rows, affine rows counted, a count relative to the free dimension and over \(\mathbb F_2\). I record it here as a proved necessary condition for that class and do not amend the accepted text, whose blocks are relations and for which the condition with affine rows remains withdrawn. Non-vacuity is not an issue for a necessary condition of this kind: any system with all variables in three or more rows meets it.

The lemma

Lemma (symmetric period degree). Let \(f(x)=\varphi(|x|)\) be a symmetric function on \(\{0,1\}^n\) with values in \(\mathbb F_2\), and \(i\ge0\). (a) If the multilinear degree of \(f\) is less than \(2^i\), then \(\varphi(a)=\varphi(b)\) whenever \(a\equiv b\pmod{2^i}\), \(0\le a,b\le n\). (b) If moreover \(\varphi(a)=\varphi(a+q)\) for all \(0\le a\le n-q\), with \(q\) odd, and \(2^i+q-2\le n\), then \(\varphi\) is constant. Hence a non-constant \(f\) with \(\varphi\) of odd period \(q\) has degree at least \(2^i\) for every \(i\) with \(2^i\le n-q+2\), and so degree greater than \((n-q+2)/2\) when \(n\ge q-1\).

Proof. (a) A symmetric multilinear polynomial of degree less than \(2^i\) is a combination of elementary symmetric polynomials \(e_k\), \(k<2^i\), and \(e_k(x)=\binom{|x|}{k}\bmod2\), which by Lucas' theorem depends only on the binary digits of \(|x|\) at the positions where \(k\) has a one, all below \(i\). (b) The word \(\varphi(0)\ldots\varphi(n)\) has length \(n+1\ge2^i+q-1=2^i+q-\gcd(2^i,q)\) and periods \(2^i\) and \(q\); by the theorem of Fine and Wilf it has period \(\gcd(2^i,q)=1\). For the last statement take the largest \(i\) with \(2^i\le n-q+2\); then \(2^{i+1}>n-q+2\). \(\square\)

The theorem of Fine and Wilf is quoted from memory in its standard form: a word of length at least \(p+q-\gcd(p,q)\) with periods \(p\) and \(q\) has period \(\gcd(p,q)\). The lemma is classical in content and no novelty is claimed; a registry search for symmetric functions, Lucas and weight modulo a power of two returned the ceiling lemma and prop:symmetric-barrier-bound, not this statement. The bound is weak: the reviewer's enumeration for \(q=3,5,7\) and \(n<40\) found no violation and, for \(q=3\), degree \(n-1\) or \(n\). By (a) a threshold function at \(t\) with \(2^i\le\min\{t,n-t+1\}\) has degree at least \(2^i\), since weights \(t-2^i\) and \(t\) differ.

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement: when a wide symmetric row is encoded at small width by a sequential counter, what is the refutation degree of the encoded system, and what does it cost in dimension?

New mathematics. lem:decomposition-degree-bound: an unsatisfiable system of polynomial rows with Boolean axioms, over any field, whose rows each lie inside a bag of a tree decomposition with bags of at most \(k\) variables, has a PC refutation of multilinear degree at most \(k\). cor:common-order-counters: \(m\) counting conditions modulo \(q_1,\ldots,q_m\) on subsets of \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), each encoded by a sequential counter along the same order of the variables, form with any further rows on single counters a system refuted in degree at most \(1+2\sum_j\lceil\log_2q_j\rceil\) whenever unsatisfiable, whatever \(n\). The degree bound does not depend on \(n\) while the free dimension is at least \(n\), so the ratio is at most \((1+2\sum_jb_j)/n\) for every \(m\): counters along a common order are never near half. A threshold is covered only as a count with modulus above \(n\), in degree \(1+2\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) per row pair.

Goal progress. Unchanged. Bearing. At the goal's parameters this gives nothing toward a family. It says a candidate, written with any presentation of its affine equations, has no tree decomposition with bags of at most \(D\) variables.

General statement. lem:decomposition-degree-bound, for all systems, fields and \(k\); cor:common-order-counters, for all \(n\), \(m\) and moduli.

The lemma

Degrees are taken in \(B=\mathbb F[x]/(x_i^2-x_i)\), as elsewhere in this notebook. A row is a polynomial \(p\) with the constraint \(p=0\); a clause is its clause polynomial. A tree decomposition of a system is a tree \(T\) with a bag \(B_t\) of variables at each node such that every row has all its variables in some bag and, for each variable, the nodes whose bags contain it form a subtree.

Lemma (decomposition degree bound). Let \(N\) be a system of rows over a field \(\mathbb F\) with no common zero in \(\{0,1\}^V\), and \((T,(B_t))\) a tree decomposition with \(|B_t|\le k\) for all \(t\). Then \(N\) has a PC refutation of degree at most \(k\).

Proof. Root \(T\) at \(r\) and assign each row to one node whose bag contains its variables. For a node \(t\) let \(N_t\) be the rows assigned to nodes of the subtree at \(t\) and \(V_t\) the variables in bags of that subtree. For a child \(c\) of \(t\) put \(S_c=B_c\cap B_t\). Call an assignment \(\alpha\) to \(B_t\) dead if no extension of it to \(V_t\) satisfies \(N_t\), and let \(\chi_\alpha\) be its indicator, a polynomial of degree \(|B_t|\). Claim: \(\chi_\alpha\) is derivable in degree at most \(k\) for every dead \(\alpha\). By the subtree property \(V_c\cap B_t=S_c\) and \(V_c\cap V_{c'}\subseteq B_t\) for different children \(c,c'\) of \(t\), and a row of \(N_c\) has its variables in \(V_c\); so extensions chosen separately below each child, all agreeing with \(\alpha\), glue to one assignment of \(V_t\); so \(\alpha\) is dead exactly when it violates a row assigned to \(t\), or for some child \(c\) every assignment \(\beta\) to \(B_c\) agreeing with \(\alpha\) on \(S_c\) is dead. In the first case, for the violated row \(p\), \(p(\alpha)\ne0\) and \(\chi_\alpha p=p(\alpha)\chi_\alpha\) in \(B\); the left side is obtained from \(p\) by multiplying by variables of \(B_t\) and reducing, all intermediate polynomials being in the variables of \(B_t\) and so of degree at most \(k\) in \(B\); a convention counting degree before reduction would give \(k+1\). In the second case, by induction on the height every such \(\chi_\beta\) is derived in degree at most \(k\); their sum over the assignments of \(B_c\setminus S_c\) is the indicator of \(\alpha|_{S_c}\), and \(\chi_\alpha\) is its multiple by the indicator of \(\alpha\) on \(B_t\setminus S_c\), of degree \(|B_t|\le k\). At the root every assignment to \(B_r\) is dead, \(N\) being unsatisfiable, and the indicators sum to one. \(\square\)

This is the PC form of the standard bound of resolution width by tree-width and I take it to be folklore; no novelty is claimed. A registry search for pathwidth, treewidth, bags, separators and tree decompositions returned no statement of it. It holds for affine rows as for any others, each affine equation needing a bag that contains its support.

Counters along a common order

Corollary (common order counters). Let \(A_1,\ldots,A_m\subseteq\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}\) and \(q_1,\ldots,q_m\ge2\). For each \(j\) take counter states \(s^j_0,\ldots,s^j_n\), each encoded in \(b_j=\lceil\log_2q_j\rceil\) Boolean variables, with rows stating \(s^j_0=0\), and \(s^j_i=s^j_{i-1}+x_i\bmod q_j\) if \(x_i\in A_j\), \(s^j_i=s^j_{i-1}\) otherwise, each such row a set of clauses on \(2b_j+1\) variables; and any rows each on the variables of \(s^1_i,\ldots,s^m_i\) for one \(i\), for instance \(s^j_n=a_j\). If \(n\ge1\) and the system is unsatisfiable it has a PC refutation of degree at most \(1+2\sum_jb_j\), over any field. The form of the rows is not used: any rows lying inside the bags below give the same bound.

Proof. The bags \(B_i=\{x_i\}\cup\{s^j_{i-1},s^j_i:j\le m\}\), \(i=1,\ldots,n\), on a path form a tree decomposition: each row lies in one bag, \(x_i\) is in one bag and the variables of \(s^j_i\) in two consecutive ones. Apply the lemma. \(\square\)

Dimension. The encoded system has \(n+(n+1)\sum_jb_j\) variables. Some of its rows are affine equations in the bits, the initial states, the transitions \(s^j_i=s^j_{i-1}\) for \(x_i\notin A_j\), and for \(q_j=2\) the whole counter, so the free dimension depends on which set \(\Lambda\) of them is named; for two counts modulo three on all variables the reviewer computes \(5n-4\) with \(\Lambda\) maximal, against my draft's "no affine equations". In every case, if \(\Lambda\) consists of affine consequences of the initial and transition rows and the transitions determine each state from the previous one, the \(2^n\) inputs give \(2^n\) points satisfying \(\Lambda\), so the free dimension is at least \(n\). Two contradictory counts modulo three, with transition clauses that force the next state, are refuted in degree at most nine. Unused code words do not affect the bound; states in one-hot encoding give bags of \(1+2\sum_jq_j\) (the reviewer's remark). I make no claim for counters arranged along a balanced tree.

What part (ii) of the test now says

For modular counts encoded by counters along one order: such systems are easy, the ratio of degree to free dimension being at most \((1+2\sum_jb_j)/n\). Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement: for \(m=\theta n^2\) random products of two linear forms in \(A=\mathbb F_2[x]/(x_i^2)\), \(\theta<1/6\), are the multiples in degree three independent with high probability? Can that tail be had from the moments of \(q\) that can be computed?

New mathematics. prop:plane-moment-bound: for \(1\le t\le n\), \(\mathbb E\,q^t\le2^{-t(n-2)}\bigl(1+Ct\,2^{(t-1)^2}\bigr)\) with an absolute constant \(C\), and hence \(\Pr[q\ge2^j\,\mathbb E q]\le C'j\,2^{-j^2/4-j/2}\) for \(1\le j\le n-2\). The proof: planes in direct sum have independent multiples; among \(t\) planes spanning dimension \(2t-d\) at least \(t-d\) are in direct sum; and the deficiency \(d\) has probability at most \(c\,2^{-d(n-2t+d)}\). The criterion needs the number of forms with \(q\ge2^j\mathbb Eq\) to be about \(2^{N-j\theta n^2}\) at most; the bound gives \(2^{N-j^2/4}\), with \(j\le n\). The attempt fails by the factor \(4\theta n^2/j\) in the exponent: at least of order \(n\), and of order \(n^2\) at bounded \(j\). The exponent \(j^2/4\) reflects the lossy step (b), not the true low moments, which the reviewer's sampling at \(n=5,6\) found far below the bound.

Goal progress. Unchanged. Bearing. At the goal's parameters this gives nothing: the statement attempted is itself only the first case of a conjecture whose deficit serves two levels at best, and the attempt did not prove it.

General statement. prop:plane-moment-bound, for all \(n\ge4\) and \(1\le t\le n\).

Setting

As in prop:isotropic-plane-count: \(V=\mathbb F_2^n\), a row is a plane \(U\subseteq V\), uniform; for a plane, \(U\wedge V\) denotes the subspace \(\Lambda^2U\wedge V\) of \(\Lambda^3V=A_3\), of dimension \(n-2\); \(T\) is a uniformly random alternating trilinear form, \(q(T)\) the fraction of planes it kills, and for independent uniform planes \(U_1,\ldots,U_t\), \[\mathbb E_T\,q(T)^t=\mathbb E\,2^{-\dim\sum_rU_r\wedge V},\qquad\mathbb E\,q=2^{-(n-2)}.\] Both are from that proposition. A uniform plane is the span of a uniform pair of vectors conditioned on independence.

The proposition

Proposition (plane moment bound). Let \(n\ge4\) and \(1\le t\le n\). (a) If \(U_1,\ldots,U_t\) are in direct sum, \(\dim\sum_rU_r\wedge V=t(n-2)\). (b) If \(\dim\sum_rU_r=2t-d\), some \(t-d\) of the planes are in direct sum, so \(\dim\sum_rU_r\wedge V\ge\max\{t-d,1\}(n-2)\). (c) For independent uniform planes, \(\Pr[\dim\sum_rU_r\le2t-d]\le c\,2^{-d(n-2t+d)}\) with an absolute constant \(c\). (d) \(\mathbb E\,q^t\le2^{-t(n-2)}\bigl(1+2ct\,2^{(t-1)^2}\bigr)\). (e) For \(1\le j\le n-2\), \(\Pr_T[q(T)\ge2^{j-(n-2)}]\le(1+2c(j+1))\,2^{-j^2/4-j/2}\).

Proof. (a) Choose bases \(a_r,b_r\) of the planes and extend their union to a basis of \(V\). \(U_r\wedge V\) is spanned by the monomials \(a_rb_rx\), \(x\) a basis vector other than \(a_r,b_r\), which are \(n-2\) distinct basis monomials of \(\Lambda^3V\). A monomial \(a_rb_rx\) equals \(a_sb_sy\) with \(s\ne r\) only if \(a_s,b_s\in\{a_r,b_r,x\}\), which is impossible since \(a_s,b_s\) are two basis vectors different from \(a_r,b_r\). So the \(t(n-2)\) monomials are distinct. (b) Go through the planes in order, keeping a plane when it meets the sum of those kept so far in zero. The kept planes are in direct sum. A discarded plane meets the sum of the kept ones before it, so it adds at most one to the dimension of the running sum of all planes. With \(k\) kept, \(2t-d\le2k+(t-k)\), so \(k\ge t-d\); and \(k\ge1\). Then apply (a) to the kept planes, the sum over all planes containing the sum over them. (c) Let first the \(2t\) vectors be independent and uniform in \(V\). If they span dimension at most \(2t-d\), the space of their linear dependencies in \(\mathbb F_2^{2t}\) contains a subspace of dimension \(d\). For a fixed such subspace, a basis of it gives \(d\) linear combinations of the vectors, jointly uniform in \(V^d\) since the coefficient vectors are independent; they all vanish with probability \(2^{-nd}\). The number of \(d\)-dimensional subspaces of \(\mathbb F_2^{2t}\) is at most \(c_0\,2^{d(2t-d)}\), \(c_0=\prod_{i\ge1}(1-2^{-i})^{-1}<3.5\). So the probability is at most \(c_0\,2^{-d(n-2t+d)}\). Conditioning each pair on independence, an event of probability at least \((1-3\cdot2^{-n})^t\ge e^{-6t2^{-n}}\ge e^{-3/2}\) for \(t\le n\), \(n\ge4\), multiplies the bound by at most \(e^{3/2}\); \(c=c_0e^{3/2}\). (d) By (b) and (c), splitting by the exact deficiency, \[\mathbb E\,2^{-\dim\sum_rU_r\wedge V}\le2^{-t(n-2)}+\sum_{d\ge1}c\,2^{-d(n-2t+d)}\,2^{-\max\{t-d,1\}(n-2)}.\] For \(1\le d\le t-1\) the term is \(2^{-t(n-2)}\,c\,2^{d(2t-2-d)}\), and \(d(2t-2-d)\le(t-1)^2\). For \(d\ge t\) it is \(2^{-t(n-2)}\,c\,2^{(t-1)(n-2)-d(n-2t+d)}\); the exponent decreases in \(d\) for \(d\ge t\), its derivative being \(-(n-2t+2d)<0\), and at \(d=t\) equals \(t^2-2t+2-n\le(t-1)^2\). The deficiency is at most \(2t-2\). So the sum is at most \(2^{-t(n-2)}\cdot2ct\,2^{(t-1)^2}\). (e) Markov's inequality for \(q^t\) with \(t=\lfloor j/2\rfloor+1\le n\): \((t-1)^2\le j^2/4\), \(jt\ge j(j+1)/2\), and \(1\le2^{(t-1)^2}\). \(\square\)

Why this is not the proof, and why no tail bound by Markov from moments of \(q\) can be

The criterion's sum is \(\sum_T q(T)^m=2^N\,\mathbb E\,q^m\), the \(m\)-th moment for \(m=\theta n^2\) planes, and \(2^{(n-2)m}\,\mathbb E\,q^m=\mathbb E\,2^{\kappa}\), \(\kappa\) the number of dependencies among the multiples. Since \(\mathbb E(q/\mathbb Eq)^t\ge1\), Markov's inequality from the moment of order \(t\) gives at best \(2^{-jt}\) at level \(j\), so the needed \(2^{-j\theta n^2}\) forces \(t\ge m\) (the reviewer's argument, which my draft lacked). So a tail of the needed strength obtained by Markov from moments is a bound on moments of order \(n^2\), and those are the regularity of that many rows: with the criterion's second clause, concentration of \(q\) within a factor \(1+o(1/m)\) of its mean for the bulk, which a dyadic tail does not address, "a tail bound strong enough for the criterion" and "\(\mathbb E\,2^\kappa=1+o(1)\) for \(m\) planes" are the same statement. Moments of order up to \(n\), which the proposition bounds, concern at most \(n\) rows, where the planes are nearly in direct sum and nothing of the difficulty appears. The earlier entries, the plane count and the criterion, phrased the open step as a tail bound; this cycle shows that phrasing gains nothing unless the tail comes from outside, from a structure theorem for forms of large bias.

What a structure theorem could cover, as arithmetic on hypothetical inputs and not a result. \(q(T)\ge2^{j}\,\mathbb Eq\) says roughly that the analytic rank of \(T\) is at most \(n-j\). If analytic rank at most \(r\) implied partition rank at most \(\gamma r\), and forms of partition rank at most \(\rho\) number at most about \(2^{\rho n^2/2}\), my own count of a linear form times a quadratic one per term, unsourced, the count at level \(j=\beta n\) would be \(2^{\gamma(1-\beta)n^3/2}\), to be compared with the needed \(2^{n^3/6-\beta\theta n^3}\): this holds only for \(\beta\ge(\gamma/2-1/6)/(\gamma/2-\theta)\), which for \(\gamma=1\) and small \(\theta\) is \(\beta\ge2/3\), and for \(\gamma\ge1\) and \(\theta\) near \(1/6\) is \(\beta\) near one. So theorems of that kind, with any constant, can cover only the top levels, forms within a constant factor of the largest bias, and never the range of small \(j\), where the count is decided by forms of full rank. This is a reason to expect little from the queued reading of those theorems; it does not replace the reading.

A calibration of the needed tail, corrected at review: forms with a kernel of dimension \(j'\) number about \(2^{N-j'n^2/2}\) for \(j'=o(n)\) and have \(q\ge(3/4)2^{j'}\,\mathbb Eq\) roughly, unconditionally; their exact size of \(q\) rests on an unproved typical value in lower dimension. The plane count entry estimated their contribution and found the constraint \(\theta<1/6\) binding over all \(j'\), with about \(0.27\) at \(j'=1\); my draft's "consistent for \(\theta<1/2\)" contradicted that and is withdrawn. I have not proved that these are the extremal forms.

Specification decision. No change: a failed proof attempt on one case of a conjecture adds no necessary condition and withdraws none.

Verification gate. One fresh-context medium reviewer, by hand, with numerical checks: the constant in (c) for \(4\le n<40\), and sampling at \(n=5\) and \(6\) for all \(t\le n\) with no violation of (a) or (b). It found (a) to (e) correct, the identities of the circularity paragraph and the reading of the criterion correct, and the hypothetical arithmetic right and labelled. Corrections applied, all in the prose: the size of the shortfall; the circularity claim restricted to Markov from moments and given its missing argument, with the criterion's concentration clause named; the calibration paragraph, which contradicted a recorded estimate; an unsupported claim in the follow-up; the source of one count. Unused: \(\theta<1/6\) in the proposition; \(n\ge4\) and \(t\le n\) only for the constant. Suggestions: the true dimension for planes in a \((t+1)\)-space; minimal dependent sets at \(u\) around \(n/\log n\). Record. Both are the next attempt. Process audit. The reviewer found no record search stated: before drafting I searched the registry for moment, kill probability, tail, planes and deficiency, and for analytic and partition rank, and found the two propositions this entry builds on and no moment bound. It found the title fair after the heading's restriction, the bearing and goal statements accurate, and no decision taken. Record: review.txt.

Follow-up. Continuing. First entry of a new spell on this check. Markov from moments is exhausted. My draft said that (a) to (c) dispose of dependencies involving at most \(n/2\) rows; that is unsupported: among \(m\) rows the union bound \(\binom mu2^{2u-n}\) for \(u\) rows not in direct sum is small only for \(u\) of order \(n/\log n\), and random vectors do have dependencies at that scale. Next attempt, as the reviewer suggested: count dependencies by their minimal dependent sets of planes, starting at \(u\) around \(n/\log n\), with the true dimension of \(\sum U_r\wedge V\) for planes in a space of dimension \(t+1\) in place of the lossy step (b).

Process assessment. The attempt was sized in advance only roughly, and the comparison of what a moment bound can give with what is needed could have been made before proving anything: it is three lines. I made it after the proof. The observation that the tail phrasing is the first moment again was available to the two earlier entries and to their reviewer and was not made. Prevention. The research rules already ask, before refining a mechanism, to check accumulated costs against the goal's budget; applied here that is the three-line comparison. I state it in the entry and add no rule.
